All sixteen stops

13.8 billion years ago

The Universe Switches On

Every atom in your body has a very, very long backstory.

Strong
You are there

Stand on the young Earth about 4.4 billion years ago and the ground is brand new. Tiny zircon crystals that will one day turn up in the Jack Hills of Western Australia are forming right now, and their chemistry hints that liquid water already pools at the surface. The Sun overhead is fainter than today's, perhaps 70 percent as bright, yet the planet is not frozen solid, a puzzle scientists still argue about. Rocks from space crash down far more often than they ever will again. The Moon, most likely born when a planet-sized body slammed into the growing Earth, hangs much closer than it does now; it has been drifting away ever since and still retreats about 3.8 centimetres a year. There is no life anyone can point to yet, no oxygen to breathe, and nobody to watch. But the ingredients are here: water, rock, energy, and carbon and oxygen cooked inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born.

The big debate

How exactly did the Moon form?

A single giant impact between the proto-Earth and a planet-sized body (often called Theia) threw debris into orbit that became the Moon.The Moon's small iron core, the Earth-Moon system's spin, and signs of an early lunar magma ocean all fit a violent, hot origin; a 2023 model suggests remnants of the impactor may still sit deep in Earth's mantle.
The simple 'Mars-sized Theia' recipe does not work as told, so the impact was different (faster, more energetic, or several smaller hits).Moon rocks are near-identical to Earth's in oxygen and titanium isotopes, which a distinct impactor should have left different; alternatives include a vaporised 'synestia' or multiple impacts.

The bold claim: A giant impact made the Moon.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

Some kind of giant impact explains more of the evidence than any rival idea, so the general claim is strong. What is still open is the recipe: the size, speed and number of impacts, and why Earth and Moon are isotopic twins.

Did you know?

Most of the hydrogen in the water in your body has nuclei that formed in the first minutes of the universe; the heavier atoms such as carbon and oxygen were forged later inside stars.

Two careful ways of measuring how fast the universe expands today disagree by roughly 8 percent (the 'Hubble tension'), and no one yet knows why.

4.2 billion to 66 million years ago

From Slime to Dinosaurs

For most of Earth's history the planet belonged to microbes, and they did a lot of the heavy lifting.

Strong
You are there

It is about 508 million years ago and you are drifting over a muddy sea floor at the foot of an underwater cliff, in rocks that will one day be lifted into the Canadian Rockies. The water is busy. Trilobites plough through the mud on jointed legs. Opabinia swims past with five stalked eyes and a long flexible nozzle tipped with a grasping claw. Hallucigenia, a spiny, worm-like creature so strange that scientists first drew it upside down and back to front, picks its way across a sponge. Anomalocaris, a predator with spiny grasping limbs in front of its mouth, cruises overhead. On land there is almost nothing to see: no forests, no flowers, nothing walking on the dry ground beyond crusts of microbes. Oxygen has been building up in the air for nearly two billion years, thanks to microbes that learned to split water using sunlight. Now animals with eyes, shells and appetites are trying out every way to build a body. Soon a flow of mud will bury this scene and preserve it in astonishing detail.

The big debate

What really killed the dinosaurs: the asteroid or the volcanoes?

The Chicxulub asteroid impact was the main trigger.A worldwide iridium-rich layer, shocked quartz, glass spherules and a buried crater about 180 km wide, all at the extinction level; climate models find the extinction pattern fits the impact better than volcanism alone.
Massive Deccan Traps eruptions in India played a major role.Precise dating shows huge lava pulses before and after the boundary, releasing greenhouse gases that could have stressed ecosystems and shaped the recovery.

The bold claim: The Chicxulub asteroid impact was the main cause of the dinosaurs' extinction.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

The timing, global debris layer and crater together make the impact the leading explanation. Volcanism probably added stress, and how much it contributed is still actively debated.

Did you know?

Ruthenium isotopes suggest the dinosaur-killing asteroid was a carbonaceous type that formed beyond Jupiter, not a comet.

Birds are living dinosaurs: every pigeon on a city square belongs to the same group as Tyrannosaurus rex.

7 million to 400,000 years ago

Getting Up on Two Feet

Before big brains, fire or spears, our ancestors made one bold move: they stood up.

Hot debate
You are there

About 3.66 million years ago, on the plains of what is now northern Tanzania, the volcano Sadiman has been puffing out fine ash. A light shower turns the grey powder into something like wet cement, and raindrops leave little craters in it. Every creature that crosses leaves a record. Hares hop through. Three-toed horses clip past. Guineafowl scratch about. Then come upright walkers, small by our standards, probably members of Australopithecus afarensis, the species of the famous Lucy skeleton. Their feet have an arch and a big toe in line with the others, much like yours, and their stride looks surprisingly human. Some prints are small; tracks found nearby in 2015 suggest one individual stood around 1.65 metres tall. Nobody carries a spear or wears clothes. They are simply going somewhere, across a landscape shared with grazing animals. The sun bakes the ash hard, more ash falls on top, and the walk is sealed away until Mary Leakey's team uncovers it in 1978.

The big debate

Was 7-million-year-old Sahelanthropus already walking upright?

Yes, it was a habitual (though not full-time) biped, near the root of the human line.A 2026 study reports a femoral tubercle, a ligament attachment known only in hominins, plus femur twisting and limb proportions that point to upright walking; a 2022 study reached a similar conclusion.
No, or not demonstrably; it may be an ape outside our lineage.Other researchers who studied the same thigh bone in 2020 found it more consistent with a quadrupedal ape, and the fossils are fragmentary and were found without a clear association to one individual.

The bold claim: Sahelanthropus tchadensis walked upright on two legs.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The newest analyses strengthen the case for some upright walking, but the evidence rests on a few broken bones and experts reading the same anatomy disagree. Expect this one to stay argued until more skeleton turns up.

Did you know?

Lucy was named after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds', which was playing at the camp on the night of the discovery.

Notched logs from Kalambo Falls, Zambia, show someone built a wooden structure at least 476,000 years ago, long before Homo sapiens existed.

1 million to 40,000 years ago

Meet the Cousins

For most of our story we were not alone: the world was full of other kinds of humans.

Hot debate
You are there

In a limestone cave above the Anui River in Siberia's Altai Mountains, roughly 90,000 years ago, a girl of at least 13 is living her short life. No one will ever know her name; scientists will call her Denisova 11, or Denny. Her mother is a Neanderthal whose ancestors were more closely related to Neanderthals living far to the west, in Europe. Her father is a Denisovan, a member of a population so poorly known that most of what we know about it comes from DNA pulled out of bone crumbs and teeth. Her father himself carries a little Neanderthal ancestry from further back. The cave has been used on and off by both groups for a very long time. Of Denny herself, only a sliver of long bone about 2 centimetres long survives, sorted as an unremarkable scrap among thousands until a protein screen flagged it as human. Her genome is the first direct genetic evidence of a child whose parents came from two different kinds of humans.

The big debate

Did small-brained Homo naledi bury its dead?

Yes: bodies were deliberately placed in dug pits in the Rising Star cave system, possibly with an object and engravings nearby.Excavators report oval features cut into the cave floor, articulated skeletons, a stone near one hand, and cross-hatched marks on nearby walls, published in revised form in eLife in 2025.
Not shown: natural processes could explain the remains, and the engravings are undated.eLife reviewers and a 2024 critique argue the papers do not demonstrate a dug pit, cannot rule out bodies sinking or sediment slumping, and do not link the marks to naledi.

The bold claim: Homo naledi, with a brain about a third the size of ours, deliberately buried its dead.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The Rising Star remains are extraordinary and something unusual clearly happened there. But peer reviewers judged the burial evidence incomplete, and until the pit and the marks are independently tested the claim stays in dispute.

Did you know?

The Harbin skull was reportedly found in 1933 by a worker building a bridge, who hid it in an abandoned well; his family only revealed it around 2018.

A gene variant that helps many Tibetans cope with high altitude (EPAS1) appears to have come from Denisovans.

~315,000 to 45,000 years ago

Enter Homo sapiens

Our species starts out in Africa, then spreads everywhere, flirting with the cousins along the way.

Hot debate
You are there

On Muna, a small island off southeast Sulawesi, someone steps into the cave now called Liang Metanduno at least 67,800 years ago. They press a hand flat against the limestone wall and blow a spray of red pigment around it, probably by mouth. Then they do something clever: they adjust the outline so the fingertips look narrow and pointed, almost like claws. When the hand lifts away, a ghostly red silhouette remains. What did it mean? A signature, a ritual, a joke between friends? Nobody can say. Over tens of thousands of years, thin mineral crusts grow over the paint, and in the 2020s scientists date those crusts with uranium-series methods, which gives a minimum age for the art beneath. The artist was probably one of our own species, perhaps among the people whose relatives went on to reach Australia, though the researchers admit they cannot fully rule out another kind of human. Either way, it is one of the oldest known marks of imagination still on a cave wall.

The big debate

Did Homo sapiens come from one cradle, or from all over Africa?

A single birthplace, usually placed in East Africa, from which modern humans spread.Early fossils such as Omo Kibish and Herto are East African, and older genetic models often assumed one ancestral population.
A pan-African story: several linked populations across the continent mixed over hundreds of thousands of years.The oldest sapiens-like fossils are in Morocco, early fossils are scattered widely, and 2023 genetic modelling fits best with a weakly structured stem of populations exchanging genes.

The bold claim: Homo sapiens evolved in a single cradle in East Africa.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The weight of evidence has shifted toward a continent-wide, networked origin, but the fossil record is patchy and models differ. Most specialists now treat the single-cradle picture as too simple.

Did you know?

A hand stencil in Maltravieso Cave, Spain, dated to at least 66,700 years ago, has been attributed to Neanderthals, although that date is itself debated.

Everyone living outside Africa today seems to carry Neanderthal DNA mostly from one shared, long-running episode of mixing.

~26,500 to 14,700 years ago

Life in the Big Freeze

Sea levels dropped, land bridges opened, and people walked into places no human had ever seen.

Strong
You are there

It is about 22,000 years ago in what is now New Mexico. Ice sheets bury most of Canada, but here in the Tularosa Basin a shallow lake spreads across the valley floor, fringed by soft, damp mud. A group of people splash along the edge. Many of the footprints they leave are small: teenagers and children, some tracks crossing and recrossing as if they were playing or running errands. The same basin's mud also holds tracks of mammoths and giant ground sloths, animals that still roam North America. Seeds of a water plant called ditchgrass sink into the shallows, and pollen from conifers drifts down from the hills. Thousands of years later, those seeds, that pollen, grains of quartz and ancient lake mud will each be dated by independent teams and methods, and they keep landing between roughly 21,000 and 23,000 years ago. If those dates hold, these kids were walking in the Americas thousands of years before most textbooks said anyone had arrived.

The numbers

Last Glacial Maximum
~26,500–19,000 years ago
The interval when ice sheets were at their largest.
Clark et al. 2009, Science
Sea level at the peak
~125–135 m lower
So much water was locked in ice that continental shelves became dry land.
Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS
Beringia
up to ~1,000 km wide
A broad land connection between Siberia and Alaska, not a narrow 'bridge'.
Hoffecker et al. 2014, Science
NEWWhite Sands footprints
~21,000–23,000 years old
Dated with seeds, pollen, quartz grains and lake mud; the 2025 study added evidence from the old lake itself.
Bennett et al. 2021, Science; Pigati et al. 2023, Science; Holliday et al. 2025, Science Advances
Cooper's Ferry, Idaho
~16,000 years ago
Stone tools and bones at a river site point to people south of the ice before an inland ice-free corridor opened.
Davis et al. 2019, Science
Monte Verde, Chile
~14,500 years ago
A camp near the far end of South America, with preserved plant remains and structures.
Dillehay et al. 2015, PLOS ONE
Doggerland
now under the North Sea
A lowland of rivers and marshes joined Britain to mainland Europe during the Ice Age.
Gaffney et al. 2009, Europe's Lost World

The big debate

Were people really in North America 23,000 years ago?

Yes: the White Sands tracks show humans south of the ice sheets during the Last Glacial Maximum.Four kinds of material, dated by different labs and methods (radiocarbon on seeds and pollen, luminescence on quartz, and lake-sediment chronology), give consistent ages of about 21,000–23,000 years.
Maybe not: something may be skewing the dates, and there is little else from that time.Critics argued the aquatic seeds could absorb old carbon, and point out that no stone tools, hearths or bones have been found with the tracks, while most early American sites are younger than 16,000 years.

The bold claim: Humans walked at White Sands, New Mexico, 21,000–23,000 years ago.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

Independent dating methods now agree, which answers the main criticism of the 2021 study. What remains uncertain is how these people got there and why so few other sites of that age have been found.

Did you know?

The ice sheets were so heavy they pushed the land down; parts of Canada and Scandinavia are still rising back up today.

At the height of the Ice Age you could have walked from England to the Netherlands without getting your feet wet.

14,700 to 8,000 years ago

The Great Melt

The ice cracked, the seas rose, and the climate lurched like a car with a learner driver.

No receipts yet
You are there

Somewhere on the coast of what is now South Australia, generation after generation, the sea is coming closer. As the world's great ice sheets melt, ocean levels climb: on average about a metre a century, and faster during meltwater pulses. Grandparents point to places where they once walked dry-footed that are now under water. Hunting grounds turn into shallows, then open sea. Hills become islands. People adjust: they move camps, rename places, and above all they tell each other what happened. Thousands of years later, Aboriginal stories recorded by outsiders in the 19th and 20th centuries describe a time when the coastline lay far out, when islands were joined to the mainland, and when the sea rose and drowned the land. Geographer Patrick Nunn and linguist Nicholas Reid argue that some of these stories may preserve real memories of shorelines that vanished more than 7,000 years ago. If they are right, these are among the oldest surviving accounts passed down by word of mouth anywhere on Earth.

The numbers

Bølling warming
~9 °C in decades
Around 14,700 years ago Greenland warmed abruptly by about 9 ± 3 °C.
Severinghaus & Brook 1999, Science
Meltwater Pulse 1A
~14–18 m in under 350 years
Sea level jumped between about 14,650 and 14,310 years ago.
Deschamps et al. 2012, Nature
Younger Dryas onset
~12,900 years ago
Greenland ice places the start of this cold snap at 12,896 ± 138 years before 2000 CE; it lasted about 1,200 years.
Rasmussen et al. 2006, Journal of Geophysical Research
Holocene begins
11,700 years before 2000 CE
The end of the Younger Dryas formally marks the start of our current epoch.
Walker et al. 2009, Journal of Quaternary Science
Climate flips fast
1–3 years
Some Greenland ice-core indicators switched state within a few years at the start and end of the Younger Dryas.
Steffensen et al. 2008, Science
Storegga tsunami
~8,150 years ago
A huge undersea landslide off Norway sent a tsunami across the North Sea as Doggerland was drowning.
Weninger et al. 2008, Documenta Praehistorica
Australian flood stories
21 coastal locations
Stories from around Australia describe coastlines that drowned as the sea rose after the Ice Age.
Nunn & Reid 2016, Australian Geographer

The big debate

Did a comet or asteroid trigger the Younger Dryas?

Yes: a cosmic airburst or impact around 12,800 years ago set off the cold snap, fires and megafaunal and Clovis collapse.Proponents report layers rich in microspherules, nanodiamonds, platinum and melt glass at many sites; a platinum spike does appear in Greenland ice near the onset.
No: the markers are not unique, not synchronous and not reproducible, and ocean circulation explains the cooling.A 2023 review found the proposed markers are common in ordinary sediments and poorly dated; in 2026 a PLOS ONE paper on shocked quartz was retracted over age-model and sampling problems, following the 2025 retraction of the same group's Tall el-Hammam airburst paper.

The bold claim: A comet airburst caused the Younger Dryas and wiped out the Clovis culture and the megafauna.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

After nearly two decades, the impact markers have not held up to independent testing and no crater has been found, while freshwater-driven changes in Atlantic circulation are a well-supported cause of the cooling. A small group of researchers continues to defend the idea, so it remains debated in public, but it lacks broad support among specialists.

Did you know?

The Greenland platinum spike near the Younger Dryas onset is real, but what caused it is still debated.

The start of the Holocene, the epoch you live in, is defined by a specific layer in a Greenland ice core.

~11,600 to 10,000 years ago

Monuments Before Farms

People carved giant stone pillars before they had fully become farmers, which flipped an old textbook story on its head.

Hot debate
You are there

On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain in what is now southeastern Türkiye, around 11,000 years ago, people are cutting a pillar out of the bedrock. They have no metal tools and no domesticated animals to haul loads, only stone, rope, wood and muscle. When a T-shaped pillar is finished, carvers bring it to life with foxes, boars, snakes, cranes and vultures. On some pillars, arms and hands wrap around the sides above a belt and a fox-pelt loincloth, as if the stone were a stylised person. Nearby, grinding slabs turn wild cereals into mash or dough. Bones of wild gazelle and aurochs pile up, perhaps from large gatherings. Out in the quarry, an unfinished pillar about 7 metres long still lies in the rock, abandoned, possibly after it cracked. Nobody here is a farmer in the full sense yet. That is exactly why archaeologists are still arguing about what this place was for.

The numbers

Göbekli Tepe begins
~9500 BCE
Radiocarbon dates put the large pillar enclosures in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, about 11,500 years ago.
Dietrich et al. 2012, Antiquity
Biggest pillars
up to ~5.5 m tall
Central pillars in the largest enclosures may weigh around 10 tonnes.
Dietrich et al. 2012, Antiquity
Cereal processing
grinding stones in abundance
Plant remains and tools show wild cereals were processed on site, suggesting people also lived or stayed there.
Dietrich et al. 2019, PLOS ONE
Karahan Tepe
~11,000 years old
A related site with a rock-cut room of pillars and a carved human head emerging from the wall.
Karul 2021, Türk Arkeoloji ve Etnografya Dergisi
Tower of Jericho
~8.5 m tall, 22 steps
A stone tower built around 8300–8000 BCE; one study argues it lines up with the midsummer sunset.

debated
Researchers have argued that 'temple' versus 'house' may be a modern distinction that did not apply then.

The big debate

Was Göbekli Tepe a temple where nobody lived?

Yes: a ritual centre in the hills where scattered hunter-gatherer groups gathered to build, feast and worship.Monumental carved enclosures, abundant feasting remains, and (in early excavations) no obvious houses led the original excavator to call it a sanctuary.
No: it was also a settlement, where ritual and daily life overlapped.Later work found rainwater cisterns, domestic-style buildings, large numbers of grinding tools and cereal processing; some scholars argue the sharp temple-versus-home split is a modern idea.

The bold claim: Göbekli Tepe was the world's first temple, a purely ritual site where no one lived.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

That monuments were built by people before fully domesticated crops is solid. Whether anyone lived there is the live question, and recent excavations point toward a mixed settlement rather than a remote temple.

Did you know?

The Tower of Jericho is more than 5,500 years older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.

A popular claim that Pillar 43 (the 'Vulture Stone') records a comet strike 12,900 years ago is not accepted by the site's excavators and remains unsupported.

~12,000 to 8,000 years ago

Farming Changes Everything

Humans tamed wheat, rice, maize, goats and cattle, and in return, farming tamed us.

Hot debate
You are there

It is around 7000 BCE on the Konya Plain in central Anatolia, and there are no streets. Çatalhöyük is a honeycomb of mud-brick houses packed wall to wall, and you get home by walking across the rooftops and climbing down a ladder through a hole that also lets the smoke from the oven out. Inside, the walls are plastered white and sometimes painted; horns of wild cattle are set into benches and walls. Some of the dead lie beneath the platforms where the living sleep. Families grow wheat, barley, peas and lentils, herd sheep and goats, and still hunt wild animals. Ancient DNA from more than a hundred people buried here hints at a surprise: relatives buried beneath the same houses were often linked through their mothers' lines, and females tended to receive more grave goods. Life is crowded and busy, and in some ways harder than foraging; skeletons show rising tooth decay and head injuries. Still, people keep living here for well over a thousand years.

The numbers

Independent farming inventions
at least 11 regions
Plants and animals were domesticated separately in places including the Fertile Crescent, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica and the Andes.
Larson et al. 2014, PNAS
Domesticated wheat and barley
by ~10,500 years ago
Domestication in the Fertile Crescent was a slow process spread over centuries to millennia.
Zeder 2011, Current Anthropology
Maize from teosinte
~8,700 years ago

Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS
Oldest bread
~14,400 years ago

Arranz-Otaegui et al. 2018, PNAS

Liu et al. 2018, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports
NEWÇatalhöyük

more cavities, more injuries

Larsen et al. 2019, PNAS

The big debate

Did people start farming grain for bread or for beer?

Beer first: brewing for feasts gave people a reason to tend and harvest cereals.Residues at Raqefet Cave suggest brewing around 13,000 years ago, and large stone vessels and feasting debris at sites such as Göbekli Tepe fit a social role for fermented drinks.
Food first: cereals were valued as staple food, and bread-making came very early.Flatbread at Shubayqa 1 is older than the Raqefet residues, and the brewing interpretation of stone mortars has been questioned; porridge and bread are simpler explanations.

The bold claim: Humans started farming cereals mainly in order to brew beer.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

Both bread and possibly beer predate farming, which is fascinating. But there is no way yet to show that beer, rather than food security, drove cultivation, and many researchers think several motives worked together.

Did you know?

Genetic studies trace domesticated einkorn wheat to wild populations on Karacadağ, a mountain not far from Göbekli Tepe.

In many regions early farmers ended up shorter, on average, than the foragers who came before them.

~5,500 to 3,900 years ago

Cities and the First Writing

Writing was not invented for poetry. It was invented because somebody needed to count the barley.

No receipts yet
You are there

Uruk, southern Mesopotamia, around 3200 BCE. The city is enormous for its time, with perhaps tens of thousands of people, temple precincts decorated with mosaics of coloured clay cones, and canals branching off from the Euphrates. In a storeroom, an administrator wets a lump of clay, flattens it into a tablet and presses a reed stylus into it: a sign for barley, round and crescent-shaped marks for quantities, a sign group that might be a person's name or a job title. This is not literature. Most of the earliest tablets are bookkeeping: rations, livestock, workers, beer. One often-quoted tablet tallies barley over 37 months and carries a sign group read as Kushim, which might be the earliest recorded name of a person, or might simply be an office. Nobody here thinks they are inventing history. They are trying not to lose track of the grain. Within a few centuries, scribes will be writing hymns, laws and stories.

The numbers

Earliest cuneiform tablets
~3300–3100 BCE
About 85 percent of the proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are administrative records; most of the rest are word lists.
Englund 1998, Texts from the Late Uruk Period
Earliest Egyptian writing
~3250 BCE
Small bone and ivory labels from tomb U-j at Abydos carry some of the first hieroglyphic signs.
Dreyer 1998, Umm el-Qaab I
Writing invented
at least 3 times
Independently in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably also in Egypt.
Woods (ed.) 2010, Visible Language
Indus inscriptions
~5,000 known
Mostly on seals, averaging about five signs each, which makes decipherment very hard.
Rao et al. 2009, Science
Indus sign inventory
~400–700 signs
Scholars disagree on the number of distinct signs, one reason the script remains unread.
Parpola 1994, Deciphering the Indus Script
NEWLinear Elamite
claimed decipherment 2022
A team proposed readings for this Iranian script of about 2300–1880 BCE; many specialists find it promising but are still testing it.
Desset et al. 2022, Zeitschrift für Assyriologie
Last cuneiform
~75 CE
The latest datable cuneiform tablet is an astronomical almanac from Uruk, roughly 3,000 years after the first.
Hunger & de Jong 2014, Zeitschrift für Assyriologie

The big debate

Does the Indus script record a language, and has anyone read it?

It is writing: the signs encode a spoken language (often proposed as Dravidian or another South Asian family).Sign order is structured, and a 2009 statistical study found the script's conditional entropy resembles that of linguistic systems.
It may not encode language at all; perhaps it was a system of emblems or labels.A 2004 paper pointed to the very short inscriptions and many one-off signs, and critics argued the entropy test cannot separate writing from other symbol systems.

The bold claim: Someone has deciphered the Indus script.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Dozens of decipherments have been announced, but none has produced readings that others can check against new inscriptions. Without a bilingual text or much longer inscriptions, the script remains unread, and in 2025 the Tamil Nadu government offered a US$1 million prize for a verifiable decipherment.

Did you know?

Cuneiform was in use for about 3,000 years, longer than the Latin alphabet has been used for English.

Many early clay tablets survived because the buildings they were in burned, which baked the clay hard.

~4,700 to 4,000 years ago

The Age of Pyramids

Giant tombs, giant stones hauled across Britain, and a drought that may or may not have toppled kings.

Hot debate
You are there

Around 2560 BCE, an inspector named Merer is keeping a logbook on papyrus. He leads a team of roughly 40 men, and they work the Nile by boat. Their job: collect blocks of fine white limestone at the quarries of Tura, across the river, and ferry them to Giza, where King Khufu's pyramid is rising. The diary notes, day by day, where the crew sleeps and when they sail, and it mentions a basin called the Lake of Khufu near the building site, reachable by boat when the water is high. Merer's crew are not the whip-driven masses of old films; they are organised, supplied and recorded, part of a state machine able to move millions of tonnes of stone. About 4,500 years later, in 2013, fragments of Merer's diary turn up at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast, a harbour where his team later worked. They are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found, and they give us the building of the Great Pyramid in the words of someone who was there.

The numbers

Great Pyramid
146.6 m (original height)
Built for Khufu around 2560 BCE; it stayed the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Lehner 1997, The Complete Pyramids
Merer's diary
found 2013
The oldest known inscribed papyri, recording limestone transport for the Great Pyramid.
Tallet & Lehner 2021, The Red Sea Scrolls

~64 km long
Satellite radar and cores reveal a buried Nile branch running beside 31 pyramids, likely used to move materials.
Ghoneim et al. 2024, Communications Earth & Environment
NEWFirst whole Egyptian genome
2855–2570 BCE
An Old Kingdom man from Nuwayrat had about 78 percent North African Neolithic and 22 percent eastern Fertile Crescent ancestry.
Morez Jacobs et al. 2025, Nature
Stonehenge's big stones
~2500 BCE
The great sarsen circle and trilithons were raised in this phase.
Darvill et al. 2012, Antiquity

700+ km
The six-tonne Altar Stone came from northeast Scotland's Orcadian Basin, not Wales.
Clarke et al. 2024, Nature

~4,200 years ago
A climate shift so widely recorded it defines the start of the Meghalayan Age.
Walker et al. 2019, Journal of Quaternary Science

The big debate

Did a megadrought 4,200 years ago bring down great states?

Yes: abrupt aridification helped topple the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom and stressed the Indus cities.At Tell Leilan in Syria, occupation ends as dust and dry-climate indicators rise, and many records around 2200 BCE show drying.
Too simple: the 'event' differs from place to place, and politics mattered at least as much.Climate records vary in timing and even direction across regions, and Egypt's Old Kingdom was already fragmenting through long reigns, provincial power and succession troubles.

The bold claim: A global megadrought 4,200 years ago toppled the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

A real climate shift around 4,200 years ago is well documented. Its link to specific collapses depends on how well local climate and political timelines line up, and those remain uncertain.

Did you know?

Woolly mammoths were still living on Wrangel Island in the Arctic when the Great Pyramid was built.

Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

~3,700 to 3,100 years ago

The First Global Economy Crashes

Copper from Cyprus, tin from far inland, amber from the Baltic: then the whole network fell apart.

Hot debate
You are there

It is about 1300 BCE off the rocky cape of Uluburun in southwestern Türkiye, and a merchant ship is in trouble. She is roughly 15 metres long, built of cedar, and she is carrying the Bronze Age in her hold: about ten tonnes of copper in 354 flat 'oxhide' ingots, roughly a tonne of tin to turn it into bronze, some 175 ingots of blue and turquoise glass, logs of African blackwood, hippo and elephant ivory, amber probably from the Baltic, jars of terebinth resin, and a gold scarab bearing the name of Egypt's Queen Nefertiti. The cargo comes from lands stretching from Egypt and Canaan to Cyprus, Mycenaean Greece and beyond. The ship goes down in about 45 metres of water. In 1982 a young sponge diver describes seeing 'metal biscuits with ears' on the sea floor, and archaeologists spend eleven summers bringing her story back up.

The numbers

Uluburun cargo
~10 t copper, ~1 t tin
The right 10:1 ratio to make about 11 tonnes of bronze; the wreck dates to around 1300 BCE.
Pulak 1998, International Journal of Nautical Archaeology
Thera eruption date
~1600 BCE or ~1560 BCE
Radiocarbon from a buried olive branch favours the late 17th century BCE; tree-ring radiocarbon and a 2023 olive shrub favour the mid-16th century.
Manning et al. 2006, Science; Pearson et al. 2018, Science Advances; Ehrlich et al. 2023, Scientific Reports
NEWHittite megadrought
~1198–1196 BCE
Tree rings from Anatolia show three consecutive severe dry years just as the Hittite state fell apart.
Manning et al. 2023, Nature
The '1177 BCE' marker
Year 8 of Ramesses III
Temple inscriptions at Medinet Habu describe a land and sea battle against the 'Sea Peoples'.
Cline 2014, 1177 B.C.
Collapse was multi-causal
drought, quakes, raids, revolt
Most specialists now see a systems failure in which several stresses hit an interconnected network.
Knapp & Manning 2016, American Journal of Archaeology
Tin's long road
possibly Central Asia
Isotope studies suggest some Late Bronze Age Mediterranean tin came from as far as Central Asia.
Berger et al. 2019, PLOS ONE

The big debate

Did the Sea Peoples destroy the Bronze Age world?

Yes: waves of seaborne raiders and migrants sacked cities from Anatolia to the Levant.Egyptian inscriptions depict and name them, and letters from Ugarit describe enemy ships burning its towns shortly before the city was destroyed.
They were a symptom as much as a cause of a wider breakdown.Tree rings show severe drought, some destruction layers fit earthquakes, trade routes broke, and some groups among the 'Sea Peoples' may themselves have been displaced people.

The bold claim: Invading Sea Peoples destroyed the Late Bronze Age civilisations.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The Sea Peoples were real and did fight Egypt, but no single cause fits all the evidence. Most historians favour a cascade of drought, famine, conflict and trade failure in which raiders played a part.

Did you know?

A sponge diver's description of 'metal biscuits with ears' is what led archaeologists to the Uluburun wreck: they were copper oxhide ingots.

Bronze is mostly copper with about 10 percent tin, and tin sources were so rare that bronze-making depended on long-distance trade.

800 to 200 BCE

The Age of Big Questions

Across Eurasia, people started asking what a good life is, and they also invented pocket change.

Hot debate
You are there

Sardis, capital of Lydia in western Anatolia, a little before 600 BCE. Grains of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, wash down the Pactolus stream, and Lydian craftsmen have learned to turn them into something new: small lumps of standard weight, struck with a punch and stamped with a lion's head. A trader no longer has to weigh metal at every deal. He can count. Within a few generations Lydian refiners are separating pure gold from pure silver, and the idea of the coin spreads through the Greek world, while China and India develop metal money of their own. In these same centuries, from Greek cities and Persian lands to the Ganges plain, the hills of Judah and the rival states of China, teachers and writers are asking restless questions about justice, suffering, duty and how to live. Did coins, cities and busy markets help make room for these new ideas? Historians are still arguing.

The numbers

'Axial Age'
800–200 BCE
Philosopher Karl Jaspers coined the term in 1949 for a burst of new thought across Eurasia.
Jaspers 1949, Vom Ursprung und Ziel der Geschichte
First coins
~630–600 BCE
Stamped electrum pieces from Lydia and Ionia; Sardis later had a gold-refining workshop.
Ramage & Craddock 2000, King Croesus' Gold
Confucius
traditionally 551–479 BCE
His sayings were compiled by students into the Analects after his death.
Bellah & Joas (eds) 2012, The Axial Age and Its Consequences
The Buddha's dates
debated by a century or more
Estimates range from about 563–483 BCE to about 480–400 BCE; a timber shrine at Lumbini may date to the 6th century BCE.
Coningham et al. 2013, Antiquity
Zarathustra's dates
highly uncertain
Scholarly estimates for the founder of the Zoroastrian tradition span roughly 1500 to 500 BCE.
Stausberg & Vevaina (eds) 2015, Wiley Blackwell Companion to Zoroastrianism
Affluence threshold
~20,000 kcal per person per day
One study links the rise of ascetic, moralising traditions to societies crossing this level of energy capture.
Baumard et al. 2015, Current Biology
Not so synchronised
centuries of spread
A study of global historical data found the key changes were spread over a much longer period than 800–200 BCE.
Mullins et al. 2018, American Sociological Review

The big debate

Was there really a single 'Axial Age'?

Yes: a real, shared turning point in which reflective, universal ethical ideas appeared in several civilisations at once.Greek philosophy, the Hebrew prophets, the Upanishads, early Buddhism and Jainism, and Confucian and Daoist thought all took shape in overlapping centuries.
No: it is a tidy label on a messier, longer process.Comparative historical data show 'axial' features appearing earlier in some places (such as Egypt and Mesopotamia) and later in others, and dates for key figures are uncertain.

The bold claim: There was a single, synchronised Axial Age revolution across Eurasia.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

Something important clearly happened to ideas in many societies in the first millennium BCE. Whether it was one connected event with a common cause, or several parallel developments, is still an open question.

Did you know?

The saying 'rich as Croesus' comes from the Lydian king who ruled Sardis in the mid-6th century BCE.

The Greek coin called an obol takes its name from obelos, a metal roasting spit once used as a kind of money.

~550 BCE to 220 CE

Empires and Long Roads

Persia, Rome, the Mauryas and the Han built roads so good that ideas, silk and germs could travel them too.

No receipts yet
You are there

In 126 BCE a battered traveller rides back into the Han capital, Chang'an. His name is Zhang Qian, and about thirteen years earlier he set out with roughly a hundred companions on a mission for Emperor Wu: find the Yuezhi people in the far west and recruit them against the Xiongnu. It went badly. The Xiongnu captured him and held him for about ten years; he married there and had a son. He escaped, reached the Yuezhi, failed to persuade them, was captured again, and escaped again. Of the original party, only he and one companion make it home. But Zhang Qian brings back something more valuable than an alliance: reports of Ferghana and its magnificent horses, of Bactria's markets where he saw cloth and bamboo from southwest China that had come by way of India, and of Parthia and lands beyond. The court listens. Within decades Han envoys and caravans are heading west, and the web of routes later nicknamed the Silk Road is humming.

The numbers

~5.5 million km²
At its height around 500 BCE, one of the largest empires of the ancient world.

Persian Royal Road
~2,700 km, 111 stations
Herodotus says a traveller on foot needed about 90 days from Sardis to Susa; relay riders were far faster.
Herodotus, Histories 5.52–53

57.7 million people in 2 CE
One of the earliest surviving large-scale census counts in the world.
Bielenstein 1947, Bulletin of the Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities

~260 BCE

−2.5 to −3 IQ points

hot-mixed lime

Coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen; ancient travellers never used it.
Hansen 2012, The Silk Road: A New History

The big debate

Did lead poisoning bring down the Roman Empire?

Yes: lead in pipes, pots and sweetened wine poisoned Rome's elite and weakened the empire.A 1983 paper argued Roman aristocrats consumed large amounts of lead, and Roman-era lead pollution is clearly visible in Greenland ice.
No: lead exposure was real but far from enough to explain the fall.Rome's tap water carried raised lead but not catastrophic levels, the 2025 ice-core study estimates an average loss of about 2.5–3 IQ points rather than collapse, and the western empire fell centuries after lead pollution peaked.

The bold claim: Lead poisoning caused the fall of the Roman Empire.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Lead pollution was a real public-health burden in the Roman world. But its timing does not match the fall, its estimated effects are modest, and historians explain the western collapse through political, military, fiscal and epidemic pressures.

Did you know?

The motto carved on New York's old main post office, 'Neither snow nor rain...', comes from Herodotus describing Persian relay riders.

Pliny the Elder complained that India, China and Arabia drained 100 million sesterces a year from the Roman Empire for luxuries.

~300 to 950 CE

Faiths, Plagues and a Dim Sun

New faiths spread across continents while volcanoes, plague and drought tested every empire.

Hot debate
You are there

Constantinople, 536 CE. The historian Procopius notices something eerie and writes it down: for the whole year, he says, the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon. Far to the west, Irish annals will record a 'failure of bread'. Ice cores show why: a large volcanic eruption that year filled the northern sky with sulphate haze, and another followed around 540. Tree rings across the Northern Hemisphere record some of the coldest summers of the last two thousand years. Then, in 541, a new terror arrives by ship at Pelusium in Egypt: plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It reaches Constantinople the next year. Procopius, still writing, claims that at the peak ten thousand people a day are dying in the city. Historians argue over that number and over how deadly the pandemic was across the whole Mediterranean. They agree it was a frightening time to be alive, and that the people living through it had no idea the two disasters were linked to faraway volcanoes and fleas.

The numbers

536 CE eruption
eruptions in 536 and ~540
Ice cores reveal two eruptions that caused one of the sharpest Northern Hemisphere coolings of the last two millennia.

Late Antique Little Ice Age
~536–660 CE

Büntgen et al. 2016, Nature Geoscience

Yersinia pestis
DNA from 6th-century burials in Germany, and in 2025 from a mass grave at Jerash, Jordan, confirms the first plague pandemic.
Wagner et al. 2014, Lancet Infectious Diseases; Adapa et al. 2025, Genes
Christians in the Roman Empire
~10% by 300 CE
A rough estimate; within a century Christianity had become the empire's official faith.

Islam emerged in western Arabia around Muhammad (c. 570–632); within about a century the caliphate reached from Iberia to the Indus.
Donner 2010, Muhammad and the Believers

The big debate

How deadly was the first plague pandemic?

Catastrophic: it killed a quarter to a half of the Mediterranean population and helped end antiquity.Contemporary writers such as Procopius and John of Ephesus describe mass death, and ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis in 6th-century graves.
Serious but possibly overstated: its long-term demographic and economic impact is hard to find.A 2019 review of papyri, coins, laws, inscriptions and pollen found little sign of a sharp, lasting collapse in many regions.

The bold claim: The Justinianic Plague killed up to half of the Mediterranean population.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The pathogen is confirmed and the outbreak was real and terrifying where it struck. The death toll remains uncertain, because ancient numbers are rhetorical and material evidence is uneven.

Did you know?

The Chinese monk Faxian walked to India around 399–412 CE to collect Buddhist texts and wrote a travel account that still survives.

The Islamic calendar begins in 622 CE, the year of the migration (hijra) from Mecca to Medina.

~900 to 1500 CE

The World Joins Up

Norse ships, Polynesian canoes, camel caravans and Chinese paper money: the planet was getting connected.

No receipts yet
You are there

The northern tip of Newfoundland, the year 1021. Norse voyagers from Greenland have built turf halls around timber frames near a shallow bay, and today someone is cutting wood with an iron blade, leaving clean, flat cuts that no stone tool would make. They have no idea the wood carries a hidden timestamp. In 993 a burst of cosmic radiation, most likely from a storm on the Sun, left a spike of radiocarbon in every tree growing that year. A thousand years later, scientists count the rings outward from that spike to the bark edge on three pieces of wood from three different trees, and each one was felled in 1021. The Norse do not stay long; the sagas describe voyages to a land called Vinland and tense meetings with the people already living there. But for a moment, as far as we know, human journeys have looped all the way around the planet: travellers who came west across the Atlantic meet the descendants of people who came east into the Americas from Asia.

Cahokia
Monks Mound ~30 m high
The largest earthwork north of Mexico; the city peaked around 1050–1200 and declined as floods and drought hit.
White et al. 2019, PNAS

The big debate

Did Rapa Nui's people destroy their island and crash their own population?

Yes: deforestation led to ecological 'suicide' and a population collapse before Europeans arrived in 1722.The island's palm forest did disappear after settlement, and this story became famous through popular books about societal collapse.
No: the population stayed small and resilient until European contact brought disease and slave raids.Ancient genomes show no severe population bottleneck in the 1600s, and a 2024 survey of rock gardens suggests the island never supported the huge population the collapse story needs.

The bold claim: Rapa Nui's population collapsed in the 1600s because islanders destroyed their own environment.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Deforestation happened, but the genetic and farming evidence no longer supports a pre-contact population crash. The catastrophic decline came later, with 19th-century epidemics and slave raids.

Did you know?

The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows Mansa Musa seated on a throne holding a gold nugget, a sign of how famous Mali's wealth was in Europe.

The sweet potato, an American crop, was growing in Polynesia before any European reached the Pacific.

Fresh from the field

  • 2024Ancient Rapa Nui genomes reject a 1600s population collapse and show contact with Native Americans around 1250–1430.Moreno-Mayar et al. 2024, Nature
  • 2024An island-wide survey of rock gardens points to a modest, sustainable Rapa Nui population.Davis et al. 2024, Science Advances

Legends

Legends on trial

Floods, lost cities, miracles and relics. Each legend meets the evidence and leaves with a stamp, from Busted to Rock solid. Only the testable part is rated.

All the legends

Flood

Everyone Remembers the Flood. The Rocks Do Not.

Primeval age (setting); texts c. 1700 BCE onward. Told by: Mesopotamian, Hebrew Bible, Greek, Hindu.

Busted

A single flood covered the whole Earth within the span of human history.

The story

The account. Atrahasis; Epic of Gilgamesh Tablet XI; Genesis 6-9; Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1; Deucalion in Apollodorus. Written: Atrahasis c. 1700 BCE; Genesis flood strands probably 1st millennium BCE; Shatapatha Brahmana c. 800-500 BCE

A divine decision to wipe the world clean, one favoured man warned in advance, a boat stocked with living things, and a landing on a mountain. The Babylonian Utnapishtim sends out birds; Noah does the same; the Hindu Manu is towed to safety by a fish that grows enormous; the Greek Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulate the Earth by throwing stones over their shoulders. The shared skeleton is striking, and the Mesopotamian versions are the oldest written ones.

The flood then swept away all these creatures, and Manu alone remained here.

Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.6, trans. Julius Eggeling (1882)

The evidence

  1. Greenland ice cores preserve unbroken annual layers counted back some 60,000 years; a planet-wide sea over the ice sheet would have left a break that is not there.Svensson et al. 2008 Climate of the Past
  2. Flood deposits in Mesopotamian cities (Ur, Kish, Shuruppak) exist but date to different centuries and do not line up, which fits repeated local river floods, not one deluge.Woolley 1929; Mallowan 1964 Iraq
  3. The Black Sea did flood from the Mediterranean in the early Holocene, around 7,500 years ago, which was proposed as a memory source.Ryan et al. 1997 Marine Geology
  4. Other cores suggest the Black Sea rise was gentler, with the lake only about 18 m below today, which weakens the catastrophe version.Gorur et al. 2001 Marine Geology
  5. The Babylonian flood tablets predate Genesis and share plot details (birds released, sacrifice after landing), showing literary transmission across cultures.George 2003 The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic

The suspects

Memory of big regional floods

Southern Iraq is a flat floodplain where Tigris and Euphrates floods could erase the known world of a city.

Black Sea inundation

A real early Holocene sea rise flooded shelf lands, though how fast is disputed.

Postglacial sea-level rise generally

Seas rose about 120 m after the last ice age, drowning coasts that people lived on.

A literal global flood

No continuous geological, ice or tree-ring record shows it.

The verdictBusted
BustedRock solid

A worldwide flood in human times is contradicted by ice, rock and tree rings; big local floods are the likely seed.

Plot twist

When George Smith of the British Museum first read the Babylonian flood tablet in 1872, a colleague later recalled that he was so excited he began taking off his clothes.

Sources (5)

  3. Gorur N. et al. 2001. Is the abrupt drowning of the Black Sea shelf at 7150 yr BP a myth? Marine Geology 176: 65-73 doi:10.1016/S0025-3227(01)00148-7
  4. George A.R. 2003. The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic. Oxford University Press
  5. Mallowan M.E.L. 1964. Noah's Flood reconsidered. Iraq 26: 62-82

Lost city

Atlantis: The Island That Sank Into a Footnote

c. 9600 BCE (setting); told c. 360 BCE. Told by: Greek.

Busted

A large island civilisation in the Atlantic sank around 9600 BCE.

The story

The account. Plato, Timaeus 24e-25d and Critias. Written: c. 360 BCE

Plato has Critias relay a story said to come from Egyptian priests via the Athenian lawgiver Solon: 9,000 years earlier, a mighty island empire beyond the Pillars of Heracles attacked the Mediterranean world, was repelled by a heroic ancient Athens, and then vanished beneath the sea in a single day and night of earthquakes and floods. Plato uses the tale to illustrate his ideal state. No earlier writer mentions Atlantis.

the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea.

Plato, Timaeus 25d, trans. Benjamin Jowett (1892)

The evidence

  1. Plato is the only source; no Egyptian text or earlier Greek author mentions Atlantis, and the story is embedded in a philosophical dialogue.Plato, Timaeus and Critias
  2. The Atlantic floor beyond Gibraltar is young oceanic crust spreading from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; there is no foundered continent-sized block.standard plate-tectonic mapping
  3. Around 9600 BCE people everywhere lived as foragers or very early cultivators; no metal-using naval empires existed anywhere.global archaeological record
  4. The real Bronze Age eruption of Thera (Santorini) is now dated to the 16th century BCE, about a millennium before Plato, and devastated Aegean coasts.Pearson et al. 2018 Science Advances; Pearson et al. 2023 Scientific Reports

The suspects

Philosophical fiction

Plato built a moral fable, a common view since antiquity.

Echo of the Thera eruption and Minoan Crete

A real island catastrophe could have supplied colour, though dates and location do not match.

Helike, 373 BCE

A Greek city swallowed by earthquake and sea in Plato's own lifetime may have inspired the ending.

Real Atlantic continent

Contradicted by seafloor geology.

The verdictBusted
BustedRock solid

A sunken Atlantic empire is ruled out by the seafloor itself; Atlantis is best read as Plato's brilliant thought experiment.

Plot twist

In 373 BCE, while Plato was alive, the Greek city of Helike was destroyed by an earthquake and drowned by the sea overnight; later travellers said its ruins could still be seen underwater.

Sources (4)
  1. Pearson C.L. et al. 2018. Annual radiocarbon record indicates 16th century BCE date for the Thera eruption. Science Advances 4: eaar8241 doi:10.1126/sciadv.aar8241
  2. Pearson C. et al. 2023. Olive shrub buried on Therasia supports a mid-16th century BCE date for the Thera eruption. Scientific Reports 13 doi:10.1038/s41598-023-33696-w
  3. Friedrich W.L. et al. 2006. Santorini eruption radiocarbon dated to 1627-1600 B.C. Science 312: 548 doi:10.1126/science.1125087
  4. Plato, Timaeus and Critias, trans. B. Jowett 1892

Lost city

Troy: The Myth That Had an Address

c. 1250-1180 BCE (setting). Told by: Greek, Hittite.

Strong

A real, powerful Late Bronze Age city stood at Hisarlik (Hittite Wilusa) and was destroyed around the era Greeks placed the Trojan War.

The story

The account. Homer, Iliad and Odyssey; later Epic Cycle. Written: Homeric epics probably fixed c. 750-650 BCE, from older oral tradition

A coalition of Achaean Greeks besieges the rich walled city of Troy for ten years after the Trojan prince Paris carries off Helen. Achilles sulks, Hector falls, and the city is finally taken by the trick of the wooden horse. For centuries many scholars treated it as pure poetry until excavators began digging at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey in the 1870s.

The evidence

  1. Hisarlik has at least ten superimposed cities; Troy VI and VIIa were large Late Bronze Age fortified settlements, and VIIa ended in fire around 1180 BCE.Blegen excavations; Jablonka and Rose 2004 AJA
  2. Hittite archives name a western Anatolian kingdom Wilusa (Greek Wilios, Ilios) and a treaty with its king Alaksandu around 1280 BCE.Hittite treaty texts; Latacz 2004
  3. Hittite letters also record disputes with Ahhiyawa, widely read as Achaeans, including one concerning Wilusa.Tawagalawa letter
  4. Magnetometry and excavation under Korfmann (1988-2005) found a lower town and ditch, making Troy a substantial city rather than just a citadel.Jablonka and Rose 2004 AJA
  5. Critics argue the lower town was smaller and less urban than claimed, so the scale is debated.Kolb 2004 AJA

The suspects

Real city, remembered war

A Bronze Age conflict over Wilusa could lie behind the epic.

Real city, composite war

Several raids and destructions merged into one poetic war.

Wooden horse as literal event

No evidence; possibly a poetic image for a siege engine or earthquake.

The verdictStrong
BustedRock solid

Troy was real and it did burn; the ten-year war, Helen and the horse remain poetry unless new evidence turns up.

Plot twist

A Hittite treaty names a king of Wilusa called Alaksandu, strikingly close to Alexandros, the other name Homer gives Paris of Troy.

Sources (3)
  1. Jablonka P., Rose C.B. 2004. Late Bronze Age Troy: a response to Frank Kolb. American Journal of Archaeology 108(4): 615-630 doi:10.3764/aja.108.4.615
  2. Kolb F. 2004. Troy VI: a trading center and commercial city? American Journal of Archaeology 108(4): 577-613
  3. Latacz J. 2004. Troy and Homer: Towards a Solution of an Old Mystery. Oxford University Press

Miracle

The Exodus and the Night the Sea Stepped Back

c. 13th century BCE (usual setting). Told by: Hebrew Bible, Egyptian.

No receipts yet

A mass departure of Israelites from Egypt, including a sea crossing, happened as described in the 13th century BCE.

The story

The account. Exodus 1-15; Numbers 33. Written: Composed and edited over centuries, broadly c. 8th-5th century BCE, from older traditions

Enslaved Israelites in Egypt are freed after ten plagues, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn. Some 600,000 men plus families leave, are trapped at the Yam Suph, and cross on dry ground when a strong east wind blows all night; the pursuing chariots are drowned when the waters return. The story became the founding memory of Israel and a universal symbol of liberation.

the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night

Exodus 14:21, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. No Egyptian record mentions Israelite slaves, the plagues, or the loss of an army; Egypt's records for the period are rich but silent.Egyptological record
  2. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) already names Israel as a people in Canaan, fixing a latest date for its presence there.Merneptah Stele, Cairo Museum
  3. Sinai surveys and excavations, including at Kadesh Barnea, have not found traces of a huge 13th-century BCE population in the desert.Finkelstein and Silberman 2001
  4. Ocean modelling shows a steady 28 m/s (about 63 mph) wind for 12 hours could expose a 3-4 km land bridge for about 4 hours at an ancient lagoon near Tanis in the Nile Delta.Drews and Han 2010 PLoS ONE
  5. Earlier modelling of the Gulf of Suez found wind setdown there is also physically possible under strong winds.Nof and Paldor 1992 BAMS
  6. Semitic groups did live in the Delta, and the Hyksos were expelled around 1550 BCE, a possible distant echo.Bietak excavations at Avaris

The suspects

Small-group memory

A modest band escaping Egypt, later magnified; Egyptian names among Levites (Moses, Phinehas) hint at an Egyptian link.

Hyksos expulsion echo

A real mass departure of Semitic rulers from Egypt c. 1550 BCE, reworked centuries later.

Wind setdown at a reedy lagoon

Physics allows a temporary crossing, but modelling shows possibility, not occurrence.

Plagues from Thera or Nile ecology

Ash, algal blooms or disease chains have been proposed; none is independently tied to Egypt at the right time.

The verdictNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The physics of a wind-parted crossing works on a computer, but archaeology has not found the Exodus on the ground; divine action itself is beyond what a trowel can test.

Plot twist

The Hebrew Yam Suph most likely means Sea of Reeds, and reeds grow in fresh or brackish marshes, which is one reason modellers look at Delta lagoons rather than the deep Red Sea.

Sources (4)
  1. Drews C., Han W. 2010. Dynamics of wind setdown at Suez and the Eastern Nile Delta. PLoS ONE 5(8): e12481 doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0012481
  2. Nof D., Paldor N. 1992. Are there oceanographic explanations for the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea? Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 73: 305-314 doi:10.1175/1520-0477(1992)073<0305:ATOEFT>2.0.CO;2
  3. Finkelstein I., Silberman N.A. 2001. The Bible Unearthed. Free Press
  4. Hoffmeier J.K. 1997. Israel in Egypt: The Evidence for the Authenticity of the Exodus Tradition. Oxford University Press

Miracle

Jericho: Walls That Fell at the Wrong Time

c. 1400-1200 BCE (setting). Told by: Hebrew Bible.

No receipts yet

Jericho's walls collapsed and the city was destroyed in the Late Bronze Age, when an Israelite conquest would fit.

The story

The account. Joshua 6. Written: Book of Joshua compiled c. 7th-6th century BCE from older material

After crossing the Jordan, the Israelites march around Jericho once a day for six days, carrying the Ark, with priests blowing rams' horns. On the seventh day they circle seven times, shout, and the walls fall flat, letting them storm the city. Only Rahab, who had hidden the Israelite spies, is spared with her family, and Joshua curses anyone who would rebuild the city. The episode became one of the Bible's most famous images of faith in action.

the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city

Joshua 6:20, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. John Garstang in the 1930s dated collapsed walls to about 1400 BCE, which seemed to confirm the story.Garstang excavations 1930-36
  2. Kathleen Kenyon's 1950s excavation redated the destruction of the fortified city to the end of the Middle Bronze Age and found little Late Bronze occupation.Kenyon 1957 Digging Up Jericho
  3. Radiocarbon dates on short-lived cereal grains place the final Middle Bronze destruction in the late 17th or 16th century BCE.Bruins and van der Plicht 1995 Radiocarbon
  4. A minority view (Bryant Wood) argues from pottery and scarabs for a destruction around 1400 BCE; most specialists do not accept it.Wood 1990 Biblical Archaeology Review

The suspects

Earlier ruin, later story

Israelites settling nearby explained an ancient ruined mound through a conquest tale.

Earthquake collapse

The Jordan Rift is seismically active and could topple walls, but the dated destruction is too early.

Destruction c. 1400 BCE

Requires rejecting the radiocarbon results.

The verdictNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Jericho's walls really did fall, but the best dates put that collapse centuries before any Israelite arrival.

Plot twist

Jericho's Neolithic stone tower, about 8.5 m tall, is roughly 11,000 years old, making it one of the oldest known monumental buildings on Earth; it may have been aligned to the midsummer sunset.

Sources (3)
  1. Bruins H.J., van der Plicht J. 1995. Tell es-Sultan (Jericho): radiocarbon results of short-lived cereal and multiyear charcoal samples from the end of the Middle Bronze Age. Radiocarbon 37(2): 213-220 doi:10.1017/S0033822200030666
  2. Kenyon K.M. 1957. Digging Up Jericho. Ernest Benn
  3. Barkai R., Liran R. 2008. Midsummer sunset at Neolithic Jericho. Time and Mind 1(3): 273-283 doi:10.2752/175169708X329345

Miracle

Sodom and the Comet Paper That Came Back Down

Middle Bronze Age (proposed), c. 1650 BCE. Told by: Hebrew Bible.

No receipts yet

A Tunguska-sized cosmic airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam in the Jordan Valley around 1650 BCE, possibly inspiring the Sodom story.

The story

The account. Genesis 18-19. Written: Genesis narratives probably fixed c. 7th-5th century BCE from older traditions

Two angels visit Lot in Sodom, one of the cities of the plain near the Dead Sea. After the townsmen threaten the guests, Lot's family is led out at dawn and fire and brimstone rain from heaven, overthrowing the cities and the whole plain. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The story became a byword for sudden, total destruction.

Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven

Genesis 19:24, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. A 2021 paper reported melted pottery, shocked quartz and other markers at Tall el-Hammam and proposed an airburst destruction.Bunch et al. 2021 Scientific Reports (retracted)
  2. A reanalysis found no mineralogic or geochemical evidence of impact and flagged errors in data interpretation.Jaret and Harris 2022 Scientific Reports
  3. Scientific Reports retracted the paper on 24 April 2025, saying the airburst claim was not sufficiently supported and that Tunguska comparisons overestimated that event's blast.Retraction Note 2025 Scientific Reports
  4. Eleven authors disagreed with the retraction, and the team republished an expanded version in 2025 in the journal Airbursts and Cratering Impacts.Retraction Note 2025; Bunch et al. 2025 ACI
  5. Whether Tall el-Hammam is Sodom at all is disputed; other scholars favour sites at the southern Dead Sea or see the tale as aetiology for a salty, barren landscape.biblical geography debates

The suspects

Ordinary Bronze Age destruction or abandonment

War, fire or earthquake can explain burned layers without a cosmic cause.

Cosmic airburst

Still defended by its authors, but its flagship paper was retracted.

Landscape aetiology

A story explaining the Dead Sea's salt pillars and sterile shores.

The verdictNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The airburst idea lost its main peer-reviewed support when the paper was retracted in 2025; Sodom's fate remains a text without a confirmed crater or site.

Plot twist

On Mount Sodom, a ridge of solid rock salt beside the Dead Sea, erosion carves pillars that locals have nicknamed Lot's Wife; the landscape itself seems to tell the story.

Sources (4)
  1. Bunch T.E. et al. 2021. A Tunguska sized airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam a Middle Bronze Age city in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea. Scientific Reports 11: 18632 (retracted 2025) doi:10.1038/s41598-021-97778-3
  2. Retraction Note to Bunch et al. 2025. Scientific Reports doi:10.1038/s41598-025-99265-5
  3. Jaret S.J., Harris R.S. 2022. No mineralogic or geochemical evidence of impact at Tall el-Hammam. Scientific Reports 12 doi:10.1038/s41598-022-08216-x
  4. Bunch T.E. et al. 2025. A Tunguska sized airburst destroyed Tall el-Hammam (expanded). Airbursts and Cratering Impacts doi:10.14293/ACI.2025.0003

Wonder

The Tower of Babel Had a Building Permit

Primeval age (setting); real tower rebuilt 7th-6th century BCE. Told by: Hebrew Bible, Mesopotamian.

Strong

The Babel story reflects Babylon's real stepped temple-tower, Etemenanki.

The story

The account. Genesis 11:1-9. Written: Probably 1st millennium BCE, final form possibly influenced by the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE)

All humanity speaks one language and settles in the land of Shinar, where people decide to build a city and a tower reaching to heaven to make a name for themselves. God confuses their language so they can no longer understand one another, and they scatter across the Earth. The city is called Babel, with a pun on the Hebrew word for confuse.

let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven

Genesis 11:4, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. Etemenanki, the ziggurat of Marduk in Babylon, had a square base about 91 m on each side; its foundations survive.Koldewey excavations; George 2005
  2. A cuneiform tablet (the Esagila tablet) gives its dimensions, and Herodotus described a tower of eight stages in the 5th century BCE.Esagila tablet; Herodotus 1.181
  3. The Tower of Babel stele (Schoyen MS 2063, 604-562 BCE) shows Nebuchadnezzar II beside a stepped tower and records its rebuilding with labour from many lands.George 2011, Schoyen Collection
  4. Judean exiles lived in Babylon while the tower was being completed, giving a plausible route for the image into Genesis.historical chronology
  5. Comparative linguistics shows language families diverged gradually over many millennia, not in one moment.historical linguistics

The suspects

Etemenanki as model

The name Babel is Babylon and the tower matches Mesopotamian ziggurats.

Older ziggurat, e.g. Eridu

Some scholars suggest an earlier, abandoned ziggurat inspired it.

Story of language origins as history

Contradicted by linguistics.

The verdictStrong
BustedRock solid

The tower behind Babel very probably stood in Babylon; the single-day scattering of languages is theology, not linguistics.

Plot twist

Alexander the Great ordered Etemenanki pulled down so it could be rebuilt grander; he died in Babylon before rebuilding began, and the tower was never raised again.

Sources (3)
  1. George A.R. 2005/2006. The Tower of Babel: archaeology, history and cuneiform texts. Archiv fur Orientforschung 51: 75-95
  2. George A.R. 2011. A stele of Nebuchadnezzar II. In Cuneiform Royal Inscriptions and Related Texts in the Schoyen Collection. CDL Press
  3. Herodotus, Histories 1.181

Miracle

Joshua's Long Day: An Eclipse in Disguise?

Late 13th century BCE (proposed 30 October 1207 BCE). Told by: Hebrew Bible, Egyptian.

Hot debate

Joshua 10 records the annular solar eclipse visible from Canaan on 30 October 1207 BCE.

The story

The account. Joshua 10:12-14, citing the Book of Jashar. Written: Book of Joshua compiled c. 7th-6th century BCE; the poetic lines may be older

During a battle at Gibeon, Joshua commands the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon, and the text says they stopped until the Israelites had defeated their enemies. The narrator adds that there was no day like it before or after. The lines are quoted from a lost poetic source, the Book of Jashar.

And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies.

Joshua 10:13, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. An annular eclipse visible from Canaan did occur on 30 October 1207 BCE; this is a solid astronomical calculation.Humphreys and Waddington 2017 Astronomy and Geophysics
  2. The authors argue the Hebrew verb dom can mean 'be dark' or 'cease shining' rather than 'stand still', turning the text into an eclipse report.Humphreys and Waddington 2017
  3. The Merneptah Stele shows Israel in Canaan by about 1208 BCE, so the date is historically possible.Merneptah Stele
  4. Critics argue the verse is poetry, that the reading of dom is strained, and that other eclipses (e.g. 1399 BCE) have been proposed with equal confidence.Osborn 2018 Astronomy and Geophysics; van der Sluijs, Culture and Cosmos

The suspects

Annular eclipse of 1207 BCE

A real eclipse fits date and place if the translation is accepted.

Poetic hyperbole

A victory song describing a day that felt endless.

Omen language

Sun and moon positions read as signs, common in Near Eastern texts.

Literal halt of Earth's rotation

No physical or independent record supports it.

The verdictHot debate
BustedRock solid

The eclipse is real and datable; whether Joshua's poet was describing it is a live, unresolved argument.

Plot twist

If the eclipse reading is right, it would be the oldest datable eclipse record known and would pin Ramesses II's accession to 1276 BCE and Merneptah's to 1210 BCE.

Sources (3)
  1. Humphreys C., Waddington G. 2017. Solar eclipse of 1207 BC helps to date pharaohs. Astronomy and Geophysics 58(5): 5.39-5.42 doi:10.1093/astrogeo/atx178
  2. Osborn W. 2018. Bible and the first recorded eclipse. Astronomy and Geophysics 59(4): 4.10 doi:10.1093/astrogeo/aty185
  3. van der Sluijs M.A. Joshua's celestial miracle was not an eclipse. Culture and Cosmos 23(1)

Miracle

The Star of Bethlehem: Comet, Conjunction or Code?

c. 7-4 BCE (setting). Told by: Christian, Chinese.

Hot debate

A real astronomical event between about 7 and 4 BCE lies behind Matthew's star.

The story

The account. Gospel of Matthew 2:1-12. Written: c. 80-90 CE

Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews is, saying they saw his star at its rising. Herod consults scholars, who point to Bethlehem. The star goes before the Magi and stops over the place where the child is. Only Matthew tells this story, and it has inspired astronomers from Kepler onward to search the sky of the time.

the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was.

Matthew 2:9, King James Version (1611)

The evidence

  1. Jupiter and Saturn had a triple conjunction in Pisces in 7 BCE, first proposed by Johannes Kepler.Kepler 1614; modern ephemerides
  2. Chinese Han-dynasty records note a 'sparkling star' or comet in spring 5 BCE, visible for over 70 days.Humphreys 1991 QJRAS
  3. A 2025 orbital study showed a comet on a close pass in 5 BCE could appear to hang stationary over a location for a time, matching the 'stood over' detail.Matney 2025 Journal of the British Astronomical Association
  4. Herod the Great died around 4 BCE (some argue 1 BCE), bounding the window.Josephus, Antiquities
  5. Many scholars read the star as literary, echoing Numbers 24:17 ('a Star out of Jacob'), so an astronomical search may be chasing theology.New Testament scholarship

The suspects

Comet of 5 BCE

Independently recorded by Chinese astronomers at the right time.

Jupiter-Saturn conjunction, 7 BCE

Astrologically meaningful and precisely datable.

Jupiter occultation in Aries, 6 BCE

An astrological 'king' sign argued by Michael Molnar.

Literary symbol

A scriptural motif, not an observation.

The verdictHot debate
BustedRock solid

The sky of 7-4 BCE offers several real candidates; whether Matthew was describing any of them divides astronomers and biblical scholars alike.

Plot twist

The strongest independent witness to a 'star' in that window is not Roman or Jewish at all but a Chinese court astronomer's log.

Sources (3)

  2. Matney M. 2025. The star that stopped: the Star of Bethlehem and the comet of 5 BCE. Journal of the British Astronomical Association 135(6): 387-406 doi:10.64150/193njt
  3. Molnar M.R. 1999. The Star of Bethlehem: The Legacy of the Magi. Rutgers University Press

Flood

Yu the Great, the Dam That Burst, and the First Dynasty

c. 2000-1900 BCE (proposed). Told by: Chinese.

Hot debate

An outburst flood on the Yellow River around 1920 BCE lies behind Yu's flood and marks the beginning of the Xia dynasty.

The story

The account. Shujing (Book of Documents), Canon of Yao and Tribute of Yu; Shiji of Sima Qian. Written: Shujing chapters c. 1st millennium BCE; Shiji c. 94 BCE

A catastrophic flood overwhelms the land. Yu's father Gun fails by building dykes; Yu succeeds over thirteen years by dredging channels and guiding the waters to the sea, famously passing his own door three times without entering. His merit earns him the throne, and his son founds the Xia, traditionally China's first dynasty, later overthrown by the Shang. Chinese historians long treated the Xia as fact.

In their vast extent they embrace the hills and overtop the great heights, threatening the heavens with their floods

Shujing, Canon of Yao, trans. James Legge (1865)

The evidence

  1. Sediments at Jishi Gorge indicate a landslide dam and a huge outburst flood, dated to about 1920 BCE, with peak discharge estimated at roughly 480,000 cubic metres per second.Wu et al. 2016 Science
  2. Critics argued the lake had drained far earlier, that the dating and discharge are uncertain, and that the Lajia disaster was not caused by this flood.Han 2017 Science; Huang et al. 2017 Science
  3. Further work suggests the Lajia disaster happened over a century after the proposed flood and involved earthquakes and mudflows.Dong et al. 2017 Science China Earth Sciences
  4. Erlitou, the leading Xia candidate, is dated to about 1750-1530 BCE, and no Xia-period writing names a Xia state, so any link rests on later texts.Liu and Xu 2007 Antiquity
  5. A Western Zhou bronze vessel (the Bin Gong or Sui Gong xu, c. 9th century BCE) already describes Yu dredging rivers, showing the legend is at least that old.Sui Gong xu inscription

The suspects

Jishi outburst as seed

A real megaflood at about the right time.

Long memory of many floods

Yellow River floods recur; Yu may gather generations of flood-taming.

Xia as later construct

Zhou-era writers may have created a predecessor dynasty for political legitimacy.

The verdictHot debate
BustedRock solid

A real megaflood struck the upper Yellow River, but tying it to Yu and a datable Xia founding divides the specialists.

Plot twist

The same Lajia site that drew attention to the flood also preserved a bowl of 4,000-year-old millet noodles, among the oldest known.

  2. Han J. 2017. Comment on 'Outburst flood at 1920 BCE supports historicity of China's Great Flood and the Xia dynasty'. Science 355: 1382 doi:10.1126/science.aal1369
  3. Huang C.C. et al. 2017. Comment on 'Outburst flood at 1920 BCE...'. Science 355: 1382 doi:10.1126/science.aak9657
