How many of us were there?

For 10,000 years humanity grew slower than a sleepy snail: about 0.04% per year on average. Today that same growth takes a few weeks. Before about 1 CE every figure is a model estimate, often uncertain by a factor of two or more. The line follows McEvedy and Jones (1978), with two gaps filled by interpolation; the shaded band spans the other published estimates (HYDE 3.2, Biraben).

Nine clocks for dating the past

Every date on this site rests on one of these clocks. Each has a range where it works and a margin where it wobbles.

Radiocarbon (C-14)
Measures: Remaining carbon-14 in once-living material (wood, bone, seeds, charcoal, cloth).
Range: About 300 to 50,000 years. Precision: Typically +/- 20-50 years after calibration for Holocene samples; wider near 50,000 years and on calibration plateaus.
Famous date: Dead Sea Scrolls, Qumran: parchment dates agree with handwriting styles (about 3rd c. BCE to 1st c. CE).
Like you are twelve: Living things soak up a tiny bit of radioactive carbon; when they die it leaks away by half every 5,730 years, so what is left works like a sand timer.
Dendrochronology (tree rings)
Measures: Patterns of wide and narrow annual growth rings matched against master chronologies.
Range: Up to about 12,000+ years (European oak and pine master chronologies). Precision: Exact calendar year, sometimes the season of felling.
Famous date: L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland: wood cut by Norse visitors in 1021 CE, pinned by the 993 CE cosmic-ray spike in the rings.
Like you are twelve: Trees grow one ring a year, fat in good years and skinny in bad ones, so the pattern is a barcode you can match like a fingerprint.
Ice-core layer counting
Measures: Annual layers of snow (dust, chemistry, isotopes) in polar ice; deeper ice dated with flow models.
Range: Counted layers to about 60,000 years (Greenland); modelled ages to about 800,000 years (Antarctica). Precision: About 1-2% counting error in the Holocene; e.g. end of the Younger Dryas at 11,703 +/- 99 years b2k.
Famous date: NGRIP, Greenland: the official start of the Holocene epoch, 11,700 years before 2000 CE.
Like you are twelve: Each winter and summer leave a slightly different stripe of snow, so scientists count ice stripes like pages in a very cold diary.
Potassium-argon and argon-argon
Measures: Argon-40 built up from decay of potassium-40 in volcanic minerals.
Range: From a few thousand years to billions of years. Precision: Often better than 0.1% for old rocks; the K-Pg boundary is 66.04 +/- 0.03 million years.
Famous date: Pompeii: argon-argon on the 79 CE pumice gave 1,925 +/- 94 years before 1997, matching Pliny's eyewitness date.
Like you are twelve: Volcanic rock starts with zero argon gas trapped inside; potassium slowly turns into argon, so measuring the gas tells you when the lava cooled.
Uranium-thorium (U-series)
Measures: Thorium-230 grown from uranium in carbonate crusts (cave calcite, corals, bone).
Range: About 1,000 to 500,000 years. Precision: Often about 1%; for cave art it gives a minimum age because the crust formed on top of the paint.
Famous date: Muna Island, Sulawesi: a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old, the oldest known rock art.
Like you are twelve: Water drips carry uranium but no thorium; once a crust forms, uranium slowly turns into thorium, like a timer that starts when the crust hardens.
Luminescence (OSL and TL)
Measures: Radiation dose stored in quartz or feldspar grains since they were last heated (TL) or exposed to sunlight (OSL).
Range: About 100 to 300,000+ years (up to about 500,000 in good cases). Precision: Typically +/- 5-10%.
Famous date: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco: TL on burnt flints put early Homo sapiens at about 315,000 years.
Like you are twelve: Buried sand grains collect tiny energy from natural radioactivity like a battery charging; heat or light empties them, so the charge tells how long they sat in the dark.
Amino acid racemization
Measures: Slow flip of protein building blocks from 'left-handed' to 'right-handed' forms inside shells or eggshell.
Range: Thousands to a few million years (depends strongly on temperature). Precision: Mostly relative ages; about 10-20% when calibrated against other methods.
Famous date: Pakefield, Suffolk: snail shells helped date the earliest known humans in northern Europe to about 700,000 years ago.
Like you are twelve: Living things only use left-handed amino acids; after death they slowly flip to right-handed, like a mirror version creeping in.
Ancient DNA and molecular clocks
Measures: Genetic differences between genomes, and lengths of inherited DNA segments, converted to time using mutation and recombination rates.
Range: Directly sequenced DNA to about 1-2 million years (permafrost); clock estimates reach far deeper. Precision: Often +/- 10-30%, dependent on assumed mutation rates.
Famous date: Ust'-Ishim, Siberia: a 45,000-year-old genome with long Neanderthal segments placed the interbreeding at about 50,000-60,000 years ago.
Like you are twelve: DNA picks up small spelling mistakes at a roughly steady pace, so counting the differences between two genomes is like reading a clock hidden in our cells.
Historical chronology (king lists and astronomy)
Measures: Written sequences of rulers, anchored by eclipses and other sky events that astronomers can back-calculate.
Range: About the last 5,000 years, where written records exist. Precision: Exact year in the Assyrian eponym list from 910 BCE on; decades of debate for the 2nd millennium BCE.
Famous date: Assyria: a solar eclipse recorded in the year of Bur-Sagale is fixed to 15 June 763 BCE, pinning the whole eponym list.
Like you are twelve: Ancient scribes listed who ruled each year and noted when the Sun went dark; astronomers can calculate exactly when that eclipse happened.

How the legends did

Every case file ends on the Receipt Meter. Most famous stories land in the middle or lower half: not because the traditions are foolish, but because extraordinary physical claims need extraordinary physical traces, and those are rare.

Coherence is the measure, not final demonstration.
How We Know

The rules of the game

This site is built to be fun and to be right, in that order of visibility and the reverse order of importance. Here is how the verdicts are made, what they can and cannot say, and every source behind them.

Receipts or it did not happen

Every claim points to a source you can check. Links go to DOIs, the permanent address of a scientific paper.

Rate the testable part

Archaeology cannot test a miracle. It can test whether a city burned, a sea rose or a wall fell, so that is what gets rated.

Show the argument

Where experts disagree, both sides get their best case before the verdict.

Say when we are wrong

Retracted papers, revised dates and corrected verdicts are logged, not quietly edited.

No proof language

History is weighed, not proved. The Receipt Meter says how heavy the evidence is, never that a question is closed forever.

Fun is not a licence

Every scene is built from evidence. Where a story has to guess, it uses the word probably.

The Receipt Meter, in full

Seven readings. "Mixed record" is used only for whole texts, where some parts are confirmed and others are not.

Rock solidRock solid
BustedRock solid

Independently confirmed.

StrongStrong
BustedRock solid

Good evidence, minor doubts.

PlausiblePlausible
BustedRock solid

A real kernel is likely; the details are unconfirmed.

Mixed recordMixed record
BustedRock solid

Some parts hold up, others do not.

Hot debateHot debate
BustedRock solid

Serious scholars are split.

No receipts yetNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Nothing solid supports it so far.

BustedBusted
BustedRock solid

The evidence contradicts it.

Recently overturned

Knowledge moves. These changes, all from 2025 and 2026, are already reflected on the site.

The oldest known cave art moved back to at least 67,800 years, with a hand stencil on Muna Island, Sulawesi (Nature, January 2026).

PLOS ONE retracted a 2025 paper claiming shocked quartz at the start of the Younger Dryas, citing problems with its age model and sampling (February 2026).

Scientific Reports retracted the 2021 paper that blamed a cosmic airburst for destroying Tall el-Hammam, a candidate for Sodom (April 2025).

Remote Sensing retracted a 2022 satellite-radar paper claiming hidden structures inside the Great Pyramid (August 2026).

How to read an ancient text

Composed is not copied

A text can be written centuries before its oldest surviving copy, or long after the events it describes. The Library lists both dates for every book.

Every writer had a reason

King lists flatter kings, chronicles defend dynasties, scriptures teach. That is not lying; it is purpose, and it shapes what gets recorded.

Translation is interpretation

Quotes on this site name their translator. Where a key word is disputed, the case file says so.

Silence is weak evidence

Absence of a trace can mean it never happened, or that nobody has dug in the right place yet. Verdicts of No receipts yet leave that door open.

People

Meet the ancients

Real people, known from their bones, footprints, letters and complaints. No invented dialogue.

Filter by era

All the people

Laetoli, Tanzania

The Laetoli footprint makers

A few upright walkers crossed a field of wet volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago, and their stride is still there.

3.66M yrs ago
The first walkers whose actual steps we can followabout 3.66 million years ago

In 1976, at Laetoli in northern Tanzania, a playful fight with dried elephant dung sent the researcher Andrew Hill diving to the ground, where he noticed animal tracks pressed into hardened ash. The search that followed, led by Mary Leakey, uncovered in 1978 what she had hoped for: a trail of about 70 hominin footprints stretching some 24 metres at Site G. They were made about 3.66 million years ago, after ash from a nearby eruption was dampened by light rain and then set almost like cement. At least two walkers left the trail, and a third probably stepped into the prints of one of them. Heel strikes, raised arches and big toes in line with the other toes show upright striding. The story keeps growing. In 2015 a new trail at Site S revealed an individual nicknamed S1 who may have stood about 165 cm, much taller than Lucy, hinting at large size differences within the species. In 2019 a team re-excavated odd tracks at Site A, first uncovered in 1976 and once blamed on a bear. They concluded a hominin made them, walking with a cross-over step, which suggests more than one kind of biped shared this landscape.

What we actually haveHominin trackways in the Footprint Tuff at Laetoli Sites G, S and A, plus casts, photographs and 3D scans.
How we knowRadiometric dating of the volcanic tuffs; footprint shape compared with humans, other primates and bears; stature estimated from footprint length.

The Site G trail was reburied in 1979 and re-protected in the 1990s after tree roots began damaging the prints.

Sources (3)

  3. McNutt, E. J. et al. (2021). Footprint evidence of early hominin locomotor diversity at Laetoli, Tanzania. Nature 600, 468-471. doi:10.1038/s41586-021-04187-7

Hadar, Ethiopia

Lucy (AL 288-1), also called Dinkinesh

She is the most famous skeleton on Earth, and much of what people think they know about her is wrong.

3.2M yrs ago
Celebrity fossil who never asked to be the 'missing link'about 3.2 million years ago

On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson and Tom Gray spotted a piece of arm bone in a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia. Over the following weeks the team recovered several hundred bone fragments from one individual, about 40 percent of a skeleton. That night the camp played the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' over and over, and the name stuck. In Ethiopia she is Dinkinesh, 'you are marvelous'. She stood about 1.1 metres tall, weighed perhaps 29 kg, and walked upright, while keeping long, strong arms useful for climbing. Now, what she was not. She was not the 'missing link': human evolution is a branching bush, not a chain. She was not the oldest hominin; older ones, such as Ardipithecus, are known. She was probably not alone: other hominin species likely shared the region at around the same time. And her death is an open case. A 2016 CT study argued that her unhealed fractures fit a fall from a tall tree; critics answer that many breaks could have formed long after death, as the bones fossilized and eroded. In 2025 she left Ethiopia for her first European exhibition, in Prague.

What we actually haveSeveral hundred fragments of a single skeleton (about 40 percent complete), held at the National Museum of Ethiopia, Addis Ababa.
How we knowRadiometric dating of volcanic layers bracketing the find; comparative anatomy of pelvis, knee and ankle for upright walking; high-resolution CT scanning (2008) of the bones for injury analysis.

During her US tour, Lucy was CT scanned at the University of Texas in 2008, producing about 35,000 digital slices.

Sources (2)
  1. Johanson, D. C. & Taieb, M. (1976). Plio-Pleistocene hominid discoveries in Hadar, Ethiopia. Nature 260, 293-297. doi:10.1038/260293a0
  2. Kappelman, J. et al. (2016). Perimortem fractures in Lucy suggest mortality from fall out of tall tree. Nature 537, 503-507. doi:10.1038/nature19332

Nariokotome, Kenya

The Nariokotome boy (KNM-WT 15000, 'Turkana Boy')

The icon of early human long-distance walking was a child, probably with a toothache.

1.5M yrs ago
Homo erectus kid with a sore back and a bad toothabout 1.5 million years ago

In August 1984 Kamoya Kimeu, the celebrated fossil finder of the National Museums of Kenya, spotted a small piece of skull on a slope near the Nariokotome River, west of Lake Turkana. Excavations led by Richard Leakey and Alan Walker grew it into the most complete early human skeleton then known: about 1.5 million years old and assigned to Homo erectus (some call it Homo ergaster). He was young. His teeth were still coming in, and studies of tooth growth lines suggest he was probably around 8 years old, although estimates have ranged from about 7 to 12, because his species likely grew up faster than we do. He was already tall for his age, long-legged and narrow-hipped, a body plan suited to walking in heat. Early estimates had him becoming a 180 cm giant; later work suggests a more modest adult height. His lower jaw shows signs of infection, and a 2013 re-study argued that his spine reflects a herniated disc rather than a growth disorder, as had once been proposed. So one of the best-known fossils of our lineage is probably best imagined as a lanky, sore-backed kid with a bad tooth.

What we actually haveA nearly complete skeleton, including skull, jaw, spine, ribs, pelvis and limb bones.
How we knowDental development and tooth microstructure for age; skeletal proportions for body size; comparative anatomy and pathology studies of the spine and jaw.

A fossil primate, Kamoyapithecus, is named in honour of Kamoya Kimeu, the man who found the boy.

Sources (2)
  1. Graves, R. R. et al. (2010). Just how strapping was KNM-WT 15000? Journal of Human Evolution 59, 542-554. doi:10.1016/j.jhevol.2010.06.007
  2. Schiess, R. & Haeusler, M. (2013). No skeletal dysplasia in the Nariokotome boy KNM-WT 15000 (Homo erectus): a reassessment of congenital pathologies of the vertebral column. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 150, 365-374. doi:10.1002/ajpa.22211

Denisova Cave, Russia

Denny (Denisova 11)

A bone splinter the size of a thumbnail revealed a girl whose parents came from two different human groups.

90,000 yrs ago
Daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan fatherabout 90,000 years ago

Denisova Cave in Siberia has produced thousands of bone scraps too broken to identify by eye. Researchers screened them with ZooMS, a method that fingerprints the collagen protein in bone, and in 2016 reported that one splinter, among roughly 2,000 fragments, came from a hominin rather than a mammoth or a bear. It was only about 2.5 cm long. Its genome, published in 2018, told one of the most surprising family stories in science. This individual, a girl at least 13 years old, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father: not distant mixed ancestry, but first-generation parents from two different groups. Her father's own genome carried traces of an earlier Neanderthal ancestor, so meetings like this had happened before. Her mother was genetically closer to Neanderthals who lived later in Croatia than to an earlier Neanderthal from the same Siberian cave, which hints that Neanderthal populations moved across Eurasia. Denny lived roughly 90,000 years ago. We have no face, no grave and no tools linked to her; just a sliver of long bone that changed estimates of how often these groups met and had children.

What we actually haveA single fragment of long bone (specimen DC1227), about 2.5 cm long.
How we knowZooMS collagen fingerprinting to spot the fragment; ancient DNA sequencing, including patterns of heterozygosity showing one Neanderthal and one Denisovan parent; bone cortex thickness for minimum age.

Only a handful of Denisovan fossils have ever been identified, so a large part of what we know about the group comes from DNA rather than bones.

Sources (2)
  1. Brown, S. et al. (2016). Identification of a new hominin bone from Denisova Cave, Siberia using collagen fingerprinting and mitochondrial DNA analysis. Scientific Reports 6, 23559. doi:10.1038/srep23559
  2. Slon, V. et al. (2018). The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Nature 561, 113-116. doi:10.1038/s41586-018-0455-x

Shanidar Cave, Iraq

Shanidar Z

Her skull had been flattened to about 2 cm thick; scientists put her face back together piece by piece.

75,000 yrs ago
Neanderthal woman rebuilt from 200 fragmentsabout 75,000 years ago

In 2018, working at Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan for the first time in about half a century, a team led by Cambridge researchers found the upper body of a Neanderthal. Her skull had been crushed in the ground to roughly 2 cm thick. Conservator Lucia Lopez-Polin strengthened the fragile pieces on site, and in the lab more than 200 fragments were reassembled, a high-stakes 3D jigsaw. Proteins in her tooth enamel point to a female; heavy wear, with front teeth ground down to the roots, suggests she died in her mid-40s, about 75,000 years ago. She stood roughly 150 cm tall and had some of the smallest adult arm bones in the Neanderthal record. She lay on her side with her left hand under her head, with a rock behind the head, within a cluster of burials beside a tall vertical rock. She lies close to Shanidar 4, the famous 'flower burial' reported in the 1960s. A 2023 study argues that the pollen there was most likely carried in by burrowing bees rather than left by mourners. The flowers may be gone, but the pattern of repeated burial at one spot still suggests these Neanderthals returned to, and remembered, their dead.

What we actually haveA crushed skull and upper skeleton excavated in 2018, reconstructed from more than 200 fragments.
How we knowEnamel peptide analysis for sex; dental wear for age; stratigraphy and luminescence dating of the cave deposits; palynology and bee-burrow analysis for the pollen question.

Her face was modelled by the palaeoartists Adrie and Alfons Kennis for the 2024 documentary Secrets of the Neanderthals.

Sources (2)
  1. Pomeroy, E. et al. (2020). New Neanderthal remains associated with the 'flower burial' at Shanidar Cave. Antiquity 94, 11-26. doi:10.15184/aqy.2019.207
  2. Hunt, C. O. et al. (2023). Shanidar et ses fleurs? Reflections on the palynology of the Neanderthal 'Flower Burial' hypothesis. Journal of Archaeological Science 159, 105822. doi:10.1016/j.jas.2023.105822

Lake Mungo, Australia

Mungo Lady (Lake Mungo 1)

Forty thousand years ago, on the shore of a lake that no longer exists, people cremated a young woman with care.

40,000 yrs ago
Woman at the centre of one of the oldest known cremationsabout 40,000 years ago

In July 1968 the geologist Jim Bowler was mapping ancient shorelines in the dry Willandra Lakes of New South Wales when he noticed burnt bone weathering out of a sand dune at Lake Mungo. The remains were of a young woman. Her body had been burned, the bones broken, and then burned again before being placed in a small pit: one of the oldest known cremations anywhere. In 1974, nearby, Bowler found a man buried on his back with his hands clasped, his body sprinkled with red ochre. Dating arguments ran for decades, with estimates from under 30,000 to over 60,000 years. A 2003 multi-method study placed both burials at about 40,000 years old, which makes these among the oldest funeral rituals known for modern humans. Her story also belongs to the present. Mungo Lady was returned to her Traditional Owners, the Paakantyi, Mutthi Mutthi and Ngiyampaa peoples, in 1992; Mungo Man was returned in 2015 and brought home to Lake Mungo in 2017. For these communities she is an ancestor, not a specimen, and her return reshaped how Australian science works with Aboriginal people and their dead.

What we actually haveBurnt and fragmented skeletal remains from a small pit in the Mungo lunette, plus the nearby ochre burial of Mungo Man.
How we knowOptically stimulated luminescence and other dating of the dune layers; osteology of burnt bone; burial context.

Lake Mungo has been dry for thousands of years; the burials sit in a crescent dune, the 'Walls of China', that formed along its old shore.

Sources (1)
  1. Bowler, J. M. et al. (2003). New ages for human occupation and climatic change at Lake Mungo, Australia. Nature 421, 837-840. doi:10.1038/nature01383

Rouffignac, France

The children of the Ice Age caves

Some of the marks in France's painted caves were made by toddlers, probably held up by an adult to reach the ceiling.

17,000–13,000 yrs ago
Toddlers who drew on ceilings and teenagers who fetched clayabout 17,000 to 13,000 years ago

In Rouffignac Cave in the Dordogne, probably around 13,000 years ago, people dragged soft fingers through the clay of a chamber ceiling, leaving looping lines called flutings. Kevin Sharpe and Leslie Van Gelder measured the width of three-finger marks and compared them with flutings made by modern volunteers. They concluded that some ceiling marks were made by children about 2 to 5 years old. Given the height of the ceiling, the smallest artists were probably lifted by adults. Picture an Ice Age grown-up holding a toddler up so the child could add their own lines. Footprints tell related stories. In 2013 three expert San trackers from Namibia, invited by the Tracking in Caves project, read Ice Age prints in caves of the French Pyrenees. At Tuc d'Audoubert they identified a man of about 38 and a boy of about 14 walking on their heels near a clay pit, probably gathering clay for the famous modelled bison about 15 metres away. At Niaux they read one set of prints as those of a girl of about 12, although those prints are not securely dated. Children were not just tagging along; they were probably taking part.

What we actually haveFinger flutings in Chamber A1 of Rouffignac; human footprints preserved in cave clay at Tuc d'Audoubert and Niaux.
How we knowMetric comparison of finger-mark widths with experimental flutings; expert Indigenous tracking combined with archaeological recording of footprints.

The San trackers read age, sex and even load-carrying from prints, using skills learned tracking animals in the Kalahari.

Sources (2)
  1. Sharpe, K. & Van Gelder, L. (2006). Evidence for cave marking by Palaeolithic children. Antiquity 80, 937-947. doi:10.1017/S0003598X00094527
  2. Pastoors, A. et al. (2015). Tracking in caves: experience based reading of Pleistocene human footprints in French caves. Cambridge Archaeological Journal 25, 551-564. doi:10.1017/S0959774315000050

Hoyo Negro, Mexico

Naia (Hoyo Negro 5/48)

A teenage girl fell into a pitch-black pit at the end of the Ice Age; divers found her lying among saber-toothed cats.

13,000–12,000 yrs ago
Teenager who helped link the first Americans to living Native peoplesabout 13,000 to 12,000 years ago

Around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, on the Yucatan Peninsula, a teenage girl walked through a dry cave system in the dark, probably searching for water. She fell into a deep pit now called Hoyo Negro, 'black hole'. Later, as the Ice Age ended and sea levels rose, the caves flooded. In 2007 cave divers exploring the drowned passages found her skeleton on the pit floor alongside the bones of saber-toothed cats, giant ground sloths and other animals that had made the same fatal mistake. Researchers named her Naia, after water nymphs. She was about 15 or 16. Her mitochondrial DNA belongs to a lineage (D1) found among living Native Americans, while her skull has the long, narrow shape typical of early Paleoamericans. Together these support the idea that the first Americans and today's Indigenous peoples share ancestry despite differences in appearance. Later analyses, presented at a 2017 conference, suggest she was small and slender, went through repeated periods of hunger, and may have given birth before she died. Hers was likely a hard and mobile life, cut short by a single misstep in the dark.

What we actually haveA nearly complete skeleton recovered from an underwater pit, with associated Ice Age animal bones.
How we knowRadiocarbon and uranium-thorium dating of tooth enamel and cave mineral deposits; mitochondrial DNA; skeletal and dental analysis.

Her remains lay underwater for thousands of years; mineral crusts on the bones helped scientists date her.

Sources (1)
  1. Chatters, J. C. et al. (2014). Late Pleistocene human skeleton and mtDNA link Paleoamericans and modern Native Americans. Science 344, 750-754. doi:10.1126/science.1252619

Tisenjoch, Italy

Otzi the Iceman

Hikers thought they had found a recent climber; he had been lying in the ice for 5,300 years, with an arrowhead in his shoulder.

5,300 yrs ago
Copper Age traveller, murder victim and the most studied body on Earthabout 5,300 years ago (c. 3350 to 3100 BCE)

On 19 September 1991, hikers Erika and Helmut Simon saw a brown body emerging from melting ice high in the Otztal Alps and assumed he was an unlucky modern climber. He had died about 5,300 years ago. Surveyors later placed the spot 92.56 metres inside Italy, which is why he now rests in a museum in Bolzano. For a decade he seemed to have died of exposure; then, in 2001, X-rays revealed a stone arrowhead in his left shoulder. He also had a head injury. His stomach, analysed in 2018, held a last meal eaten between half an hour and two hours before death: very fatty ibex meat, red deer, einkorn wheat and traces of bracken. The copper of his axe came from southern Tuscany. His 61 tattoos, a 2024 experimental study argues, were most likely hand-poked rather than cut. And a 2023 genome re-analysis changed his look: he probably had dark skin, dark eyes and male-pattern baldness, and more than 90 percent of his ancestry came from early farmers with roots in Anatolia. The pale, shaggy Iceman of older museum reconstructions reflected modern assumptions more than his DNA.

What we actually haveA naturally mummified body with clothing, a copper axe, a bow, arrows, a dagger and other gear.
How we knowRadiocarbon dating; X-ray and CT imaging; stomach-content analysis (proteomics, lipids, DNA, microscopy); lead-isotope sourcing of the axe; whole-genome sequencing.

After a long legal dispute, the couple who found him were awarded a finder's fee of 150,000 euros in 2008.

Sources (3)
  1. Maixner, F. et al. (2018). The Iceman's last meal consisted of fat, wild meat, and cereals. Current Biology 28, 2348-2355. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2018.05.067
  2. Artioli, G. et al. (2017). Long-distance connections in the Copper Age: new evidence from the Alpine Iceman's copper axe. PLOS ONE 12, e0179263. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0179263
  3. Wang, K. et al. (2023). High-coverage genome of the Tyrolean Iceman reveals unusually high Anatolian farmer ancestry. Cell Genomics 3, 100377. doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2023.100377

Uruk, southern Iraq

Kushim

The first individual whose name we may be able to read left no poem, no battle and no face; just a receipt.

3200–3000 BCE
Possibly the first named person in history, and possibly an accountantabout 3200 to 3000 BCE

Around 3200 to 3000 BCE, in the city of Uruk in what is now southern Iraq, administrators pressed signs into small clay tablets. The earliest writing, called proto-cuneiform, was not yet used for letters or poems; it was bookkeeping. One tablet, now in the Schoyen Collection, records a large total of barley over 37 months and ends with two signs read KU and SHIM. The same combination appears on about 18 tablets. Yuval Noah Harari's bestseller Sapiens made the reading famous, rendering it as 29,086 measures of barley, signed Kushim. Specialists are more cautious. The signs could be a personal name, but they could also be a job title or the name of an office, because the earliest script rarely made the difference clear. The texts linked to Kushim deal with barley and grain products, probably connected with the malting and brewing work of a large institution. If Kushim was a person, then the first name we can read belongs not to a king but to someone checking that the numbers added up. That is a rather reassuring start for written history.

What we actually haveProto-cuneiform clay tablets from Uruk (for example MS 1717 in the Schoyen Collection) bearing the sign sequence KU.SHIM.
How we knowDecipherment of proto-cuneiform numerical systems and administrative formats, comparing sign use across hundreds of archaic tablets.

A rival for the 'oldest known name', Gal-Sal, appears on a tablet from around 3100 BCE together with two enslaved people, En-pap X and Sukkalgir.

Sources (2)
  1. Nissen, H. J., Damerow, P. & Englund, R. K. (1993). Archaic Bookkeeping: Early Writing and Techniques of Economic Administration in the Ancient Near East. University of Chicago Press.
  2. Harari, Y. N. (2014). Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. Harvill Secker.

Tura quarries and Giza, Egypt

Merer, inspector of boatmen

The oldest inscribed papyri ever found are not royal decrees; they are the work diary of a mid-level boss hauling stone for the Great Pyramid.

2560 BCE
Middle manager whose logbook tracks work on the Great Pyramidabout 2560 BCE (reign of Khufu, year 27)

In 2013, at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on Egypt's Red Sea coast, a team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard found papyrus rolls left at the entrance of storage galleries cut into the rock. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known, from late in the reign of King Khufu, around 2560 BCE. Among them is the logbook of an inspector named Merer, who led a crew of about 40 boatmen. His entries are laid out day by day in neat columns, recording a steady rhythm: loading limestone at the Tura quarries across the Nile, sailing to Akhet-Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the ancient name for the Great Pyramid site at Giza, stopping overnight at places such as the She-Khufu basin, and heading back for more. The fine Tura limestone was probably destined for the pyramid's outer casing. Merer also mentions Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, as the official in charge of a harbour at Giza. No pharaoh speaks in these pages, and there are no secret machines; just a supervisor counting trips and days. It is the closest thing we have to a worker's view of the Great Pyramid in its final years of construction.

What we actually haveFragments of papyrus logbooks (the 'Diary of Merer') found at Wadi al-Jarf, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.
How we knowHieratic palaeography and translation; regnal-year dating in the texts; excavation of the Wadi al-Jarf harbour and storage galleries.

The papyri probably ended up at the Red Sea because Merer's crew was later sent to work at the harbour there.

Sources (2)
  1. Tallet, P. & Marouard, G. (2014). The harbor of Khufu on the Red Sea coast at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt. Near Eastern Archaeology 77, 4-14. doi:10.5615/neareastarch.77.1.0004
  2. Tallet, P. (2017). Les papyrus de la mer Rouge I: le journal de Merer. Institut francais d'archeologie orientale.

Royal Cemetery, southern Iraq

Puabi of Ur

Her headdress of gold leaves is one of the most dazzling objects of the ancient world; the people buried around her tell a darker story.

2600–2500 BCE
Queen or high lady buried in gold, and not aloneabout 2600 to 2500 BCE

In the late 1920s, Leonard Woolley's excavators at Ur opened a tomb numbered PG 800 and found a woman on a wooden bier, her upper body covered in beads of gold, silver, lapis lazuli and carnelian, with a spectacular headdress of gold leaves, ribbons and flowers. A lapis cylinder seal nearby named her Puabi, with the title nin, meaning 'queen' or 'lady'. Unusually, the seal names no husband, which likely signals that her rank stood on its own. She died around 2600 to 2500 BCE, probably at about 40 years old. She was not buried alone. Woolley recorded dozens of attendants in her burial complex, about 52 by one count, and imagined them calmly drinking poison. In 2011, CT scans of two skulls from other graves in the Royal Cemetery suggested a harsher end: blunt-force wounds, probably from a pointed, weighted weapon, plus signs of heating and traces of mercury sulphide, possibly used to slow decay while the bodies were laid out. Behind the glitter of the headdress sits a sobering question: what did royal display cost the people around it?

What we actually haveTomb PG 800 with Puabi's skeleton, jewellery, headdress and inscribed cylinder seals, now largely at the Penn Museum, Philadelphia.
How we knowExcavation records; reading of the cuneiform seal inscription; later CT scanning and forensic analysis of skulls from the Royal Cemetery.

Her name is Akkadian, not Sumerian, and may mean something like 'word of my father'.

Sources (2)
  1. Baadsgaard, A., Monge, J., Cox, S. & Zettler, R. L. (2011). Human sacrifice and intentional corpse preservation in the Royal Cemetery of Ur. Antiquity 85, 27-42.
  2. Woolley, C. L. (1934). Ur Excavations II: The Royal Cemetery. British Museum and University of Pennsylvania Museum.

Ur, southern Iraq

Enheduanna

The first author known by name in world literature may have been a princess-priestess writing about her own exile.

2300–2250 BCE
Princess, high priestess and the first named authorabout 2300 to 2250 BCE

Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad built the first great empire of Mesopotamia and installed his daughter as en-priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. She took, or was given, the name Enheduanna. In the 1920s Leonard Woolley's team at Ur found a calcite disk showing her at a ritual in a flounced robe, with an inscription naming her as Sargon's daughter. Her fame rests on poetry. Several Sumerian hymns, copied by scribes centuries later, name her as their author, which would make her the first named author in world literature. In the poem known as 'The Exaltation of Inana' she speaks in the first person: pushed out of her office during a revolt, she describes her exile with raw emotion and pleads with the goddess Inana to restore her. It is vivid, personal and startlingly angry. Scholars debate how much she composed herself, because the surviving copies are around 500 years younger than she is, and the attribution may partly reflect later tradition. Either way, Mesopotamian scribes chose to remember a woman as the voice behind some of their greatest hymns.

I, En-hedu-ana the en priestess, entered my holy jipar in your service.

The Exaltation of Inana (Inana B), ETCSL translation, University of Oxford
What we actually haveAn inscribed calcite (alabaster) disk from Ur (Penn Museum) naming her; Old Babylonian clay-tablet copies of hymns attributed to her; seals of her servants.
How we knowExcavation at Ur; reading of Sumerian and Akkadian inscriptions; philology of the hymn manuscripts and their colophons.

The disk showing her had been smashed in antiquity; it was pieced back together after excavation.

Sources (2)
  1. Helle, S. (2020). The birth of the author: co-creating authorship in Enheduana's Exaltation. Orbis Litterarum 75, 55-72. doi:10.1111/oli.12250
  2. Black, J. et al. (1998 to 2006). The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, text 4.07.2. University of Oxford.

Babylon, central Iraq

Hammurabi of Babylon

His famous law code was carried off as war loot, lost for three thousand years, and dug up in a different country.

1792–1750 BCE
King who carved his idea of justice into stonereigned about 1792 to 1750 BCE

Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE and turned a mid-sized city-state into the leading power of Mesopotamia. Late in his reign he set up a tall black stone stele, over 2 metres high, topped by a carving of the king standing before a god usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and guardian of justice. Below it: a prologue, about 282 laws, and an epilogue inviting anyone wronged to come and have the inscription read to them. The laws are not an even-handed modern code. Penalties depend on social status: destroying the eye of a free man could cost an eye, while injuring a commoner or an enslaved person meant a payment. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed the owner could be put to death. Many scholars now read the collection less as a rulebook judges followed and more as a royal showcase of wise judgments. The stele had its own adventures: an Elamite king carried it to Susa as war booty in the 12th century BCE, and French excavators found it there in 1901 and 1902. Today it stands in the Louvre, still making its case to visitors.

to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak

Prologue to the Laws of Hammurabi, trans. L. W. King (1910)
What we actually haveThe basalt stele in the Louvre, fragments of other copies, and later clay-tablet copies of the laws, plus Hammurabi's surviving letters.
How we knowDecipherment of Akkadian cuneiform; comparison with legal documents, contracts and royal letters of the period.

Several columns of text on the stele were probably erased by the Elamite captors, perhaps to make room for an inscription that was never carved.

Sources (2)
  1. Roth, M. T. (1997). Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (2nd ed.). Scholars Press.
  2. King, L. W. (1910). The Code of Hammurabi (translation). Public domain.

Ur, southern Iraq

Ea-nasir and Nanni

The oldest known customer complaint was found in the house of the merchant it was aimed at.

1750 BCE
Copper merchant with a bad reputation, and his furious customerabout 1750 BCE

Around 1750 BCE, a man named Nanni in the city of Ur was fed up. He had dealt with Ea-nasir, a merchant who brought copper up the Gulf through Dilmun (modern Bahrain), and received ingots he considered below the agreed quality. Worse, he said his servant had been treated rudely and his money had not come back. So he had a clay tablet written, and it survives: a small letter about 11.6 cm tall, now in the British Museum. He complains that messengers he sent to collect his money came back empty-handed, several times, even through dangerous territory, and he demands to be treated with respect. The best twist: the tablet was found in Ea-nasir's own house at Ur during Leonard Woolley's excavations, alongside other letters grumbling about copper deliveries. Either Ea-nasir kept his complaints on file, or complaints were simply a large share of his business correspondence. Nearly 4,000 years later he has become an internet legend, a sort of patron saint of bad suppliers. The tablet is also a serious window onto long-distance metal trade, credit and business etiquette in the Old Babylonian world.

What do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?

Nanni to Ea-nasir, UET V 81, trans. A. Leo Oppenheim, Letters from Mesopotamia (1967)
What we actually haveClay tablet BM 131236 (UET V 81), written in Akkadian cuneiform, plus other letters from the same house at Ur.
How we knowExcavation context at Ur; decipherment and translation of Old Babylonian Akkadian letters.

Guinness World Records lists the tablet as the oldest written customer complaint.

Sources (2)
  1. Oppenheim, A. L. (1967). Letters from Mesopotamia. University of Chicago Press, pp. 82-83.
  2. Figulla, H. H. & Martin, W. J. (1953). Ur Excavations Texts V: Letters and Documents of the Old-Babylonian Period. British Museum.

Thebes, Egypt

Hatshepsut

She ruled Egypt as king for about twenty years; the smashing of her statues afterwards may not have been the revenge story we were told.

1479–1458 BCE
Queen who made herself kingreigned about 1479 to 1458 BCE

Hatshepsut was the daughter of one pharaoh, the wife of another, and regent for a third, the young Thutmose III. Then she did something unusual: she had herself crowned king. For about two decades she ruled with full royal titles and was often shown with a king's kilt and false beard. Her projects include the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri, whose reliefs celebrate an expedition to the distant land of Punt that returned with incense trees and exotic animals. After her death her images were broken and her name cut from monuments, long read as Thutmose III's revenge. A 2025 study of 1920s excavation archives suggests a cooler motive. Many statues were broken at weak points such as the neck, waist and knees in ways consistent with ritual 'deactivation', some faces were left intact, and the pieces were reused as building material. The erasure also came years into Thutmose's sole reign, which fits succession politics better than personal hatred. Even her body is debated: a mummy from tomb KV60 was identified as hers in 2007 on the basis of a tooth, but that match has not been confirmed by DNA and some scholars remain unconvinced.

What we actually haveHer mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri, obelisks at Karnak, hundreds of statue fragments, inscriptions, and a debated mummy (KV60-A).
How we knowHieroglyphic inscriptions; archaeology of statue deposits and archival excavation records; CT imaging and dental comparison for the mummy.

Isotope analysis of mummified baboons, animals Egyptians imported from Punt, points to a source region around modern Eritrea, Ethiopia and neighbouring lands.

Sources (2)
  1. Wong, J. Y. (2025). The afterlife of Hatshepsut's statuary. Antiquity 99, 746-761. doi:10.15184/aqy.2025.64
  2. Dominy, N. J. et al. (2020). Mummified baboons reveal the far reach of early Egyptian mariners. eLife 9, e60860. doi:10.7554/eLife.60860

Valley of the Kings, Egypt

Tutankhamun

Behind the golden mask was a young man who probably walked with a cane.

1323 BCE
Teenage king whose body tells a story of illnessdied about 1323 BCE

Howard Carter's 1922 discovery of a nearly intact royal tomb made Tutankhamun the world's most famous pharaoh, although he was a minor king who died young, around 1323 BCE. What does his body tell us? A 2010 study combining CT scans and DNA from royal mummies concluded that he died at about 19 and that his parents were probably brother and sister: the mummy from tomb KV55, most likely Akhenaten, and an unnamed woman known as the 'Younger Lady' from tomb KV35. The study reported a clubfoot, bone death in part of his left foot (Kohler disease II), a cleft palate, and DNA from the most dangerous malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. It proposed malaria combined with the bone disease as the most likely cause of death. His tomb held about 130 walking sticks and staves, some with signs of use, which fits a king who probably walked with pain. Treat the details with care: other researchers have questioned the ancient DNA methods and some diagnoses, and a broken leg remains debated as either injury or damage from embalming or excavation. The golden mask covered a young man who was probably often unwell.

What we actually haveHis mummy, CT data, DNA samples, and the contents of tomb KV62, including about 130 sticks and staves.
How we knowCT scanning, ancient DNA (Y-chromosome and autosomal markers) for kinship, pathogen DNA testing, and study of the tomb objects.

Two mummified foetuses buried in his tomb may have been his daughters, according to the same 2010 DNA study.

Sources (1)
  1. Hawass, Z. et al. (2010). Ancestry and pathology in King Tutankhamun's family. JAMA 303, 638-647. doi:10.1001/jama.2010.121

Deir el-Medina, Egypt

The Deir el-Medina tomb builders (and the scribe Amennakht)

When the grain rations were late, the pharaoh's tomb builders put down their tools and walked out.

1157 BCE
Royal tomb workers who staged the first recorded strikeabout 1157 BCE (year 29 of Ramesses III)

The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, and were paid in rations of grain. In year 29 of Ramesses III, around 1157 BCE, those rations were badly overdue. So the crew did something no earlier record shows: they stopped work and walked out. The scribe Amennakht kept notes, which survive on a papyrus now in Turin. The workers marched past the guard posts of the necropolis, sat down behind temples on the west bank, and refused to go back, insisting their grievance be reported to Pharaoh. Officials delivered rations; the crew returned; supplies slipped again; they struck again. The dispute stretched over several months. For the officials it was an embarrassment. For historians it is priceless: a record of ordinary workers in a powerful state organizing, negotiating and getting at least part of what they were owed. The village was unusually literate, and its rubbish heaps have yielded thousands of inscribed potsherds and limestone flakes, including a register of work absences whose excuses range from illness to brewing beer.

On this day the crew passed the five guard-posts of the tomb saying: 'We are hungry.'

Turin Strike Papyrus, trans. P. J. Frandsen, 'Editing Reality: The Turin Strike Papyrus' (1990)
What we actually haveThe Turin Strike Papyrus (Museo Egizio, Cat. 1880), plus thousands of ostraca from the village.
How we knowTranslation of hieratic administrative documents; excavation of the village and its rubbish deposits.

The villagers' written notes are so abundant that historians can follow individual families, feuds and even court cases across generations.

Sources (2)
  1. Edgerton, W. F. (1951). The strikes in Ramses III's twenty-ninth year. Journal of Near Eastern Studies 10, 137-145. doi:10.1086/371037
  2. Frandsen, P. J. (1990). Editing reality: the Turin Strike Papyrus. In S. Israelit-Groll (ed.), Studies in Egyptology presented to Miriam Lichtheim, Magnes Press.

Bjaeldskovdal bog, Denmark

Tollund Man

His face looked so fresh that the peat cutters who found him called the police.

405–380 BCE
Iron Age man with a peaceful face and a noose around his neckabout 405 to 380 BCE

On 8 May 1950, peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark uncovered a face so well preserved that they called the police, fearing a recent death. He had died around 405 to 380 BCE. The acidic, oxygen-poor bog had tanned his skin and preserved his head in extraordinary detail: closed eyes, short-cropped hair and a faint stubble. He wore a pointed skin cap and a belt, and around his neck was a plaited leather noose. He was about 40 and had been hanged, then laid in an old peat cutting in a curled, sleeping position. Many archaeologists interpret him as a sacrifice, although the reasons remain uncertain. A 2021 re-examination of his gut found that his last meal, eaten roughly 12 to 24 hours before death, was a porridge made mainly of barley, pale persicaria seeds and flax, with some fish. He also carried whipworm, roundworm and tapeworm. The researchers found nothing obviously festive or special about the meal. A ritual death, then, but perhaps preceded by an ordinary day's food, which makes him feel even closer to us.

What we actually haveA bog body whose head is exceptionally well preserved, with the noose, cap and belt; gut contents.
How we knowRadiocarbon dating; autopsy, X-ray and CT scanning; macrofossil, pollen, protein and parasite analysis of gut contents.

At Silkeborg Museum his head is original, but most of the body on display is a replica, because only parts of it were conserved in 1950.

Sources (1)
  1. Nielsen, N. H. et al. (2021). The last meal of Tollund Man: new analyses of his gut content. Antiquity 95, 1195-1212. doi:10.15184/aqy.2021.98

Mawangdui, China

Xin Zhui, Lady Dai (Marquise of Dai)

Her body was so well preserved that doctors could perform an autopsy 2,100 years after she died, and they found melon seeds in her stomach.

168 BCE
Han dynasty noblewoman with a modern-looking medical filedied about 168 BCE

In 1972, at Mawangdui near Changsha, archaeologists excavated Tomb 1, a deep Han dynasty grave sealed with thick layers of charcoal and white clay. Inside four nested coffins, in a mysterious liquid, lay Xin Zhui, wife of Li Cang, Marquis of Dai and chancellor of the Changsha kingdom. She had died around 168 BCE, at about 50, and her body was astonishingly preserved: soft skin, joints that could still bend, hair still in place. The autopsy reads like a modern medical file. She had hardened coronary arteries, gallstones, spinal problems that probably caused back pain, and schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection. In her digestive tract were more than a hundred melon seeds, suggesting she ate melon a few hours before a heart attack killed her, probably in summer. She was buried with over a thousand objects, including silk garments, lacquerware, food and a painted T-shaped silk banner that depicts a journey from the underworld to the heavens. Her body suggests the privileged life of a Han noblewoman also brought diseases we still link to rich diets and little exercise.

What we actually haveA remarkably preserved body, her tomb furnishings and a painted silk banner, now in the Hunan Museum, Changsha.
How we knowModern medical autopsy and pathology (1972); study of tomb inscriptions and seals naming her household; later preservation research.

One of the silk robes from the Mawangdui tombs is so fine that it weighs under 50 grams.

Sources (1)
  1. Wang, X.-S. et al. (2019). Mawangdui-type ancient human cadavers in China and strategies for their long-term preservation. Biopreservation and Biobanking 17, 404-410. doi:10.1089/bio.2019.0018

Pompeii, Italy

The graffiti writers of Pompeii

Pompeii's walls were its social media, and one ancient writer complained that there was too much of it.

up–79 CE
A whole town of scribblers, gossips and election campaignersup to 79 CE

When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE it froze a town whose walls were covered in writing. Archaeologists have recorded thousands of painted notices and scratched graffiti: election endorsements, gladiator fan messages, greetings to friends, love notes, insults, sums and occasional crude boasts. One line, found in the Basilica, the Theatre and the Amphitheatre, is a joke about the whole scene: the wall deserves praise for not collapsing under so much boring writing. Graffiti were not mainly vandalism; studies of houses show messages answering one another, like comment threads. And the walls still make news. In 2018 a charcoal note in a house under renovation at the time of the eruption recorded a date equal to 17 October. The year is not written, but it supports other evidence, such as autumn fruits and lit braziers, that the eruption came later than the traditional 24 August. In January 2026, a Sorbonne-led team using reflectance transformation imaging, which lights a surface from many angles, announced 79 previously unknown graffiti in the corridor leading to the theatres, including a declaration of love and a drawing of two gladiators.

Admiror, paries, te non cecidisse ruinis, qui tot scriptorum taedia sustineas. (I wonder, wall, that you have not fallen in ruins, bearing the tedious scribbles of so many writers.)

CIL IV 1904, Pompeii; literal translation of the Latin
What we actually haveThousands of painted and incised inscriptions catalogued in the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum volume IV, plus new finds.
How we knowEpigraphy (reading and dating Latin inscriptions); stratigraphy; reflectance transformation imaging of faint incisions.

The same weary couplet about the overloaded wall was scratched in at least three public buildings, so it was probably a popular joke.

Sources (2)
  1. Benefiel, R. R. (2010). Dialogues of ancient graffiti in the House of Maius Castricius in Pompeii. American Journal of Archaeology 114, 59-101. doi:10.3764/aja.114.1.59
  2. Doronzo, D. M. et al. (2022). The 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius: a lesson from the past and the need of a multidisciplinary approach for developments in volcanology. Earth-Science Reviews 231, 104072. doi:10.1016/j.earscirev.2022.104072

Vindolanda, UK

Claudia Severa

The earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman is the end of a birthday invitation.

97–105 CE
Officer's wife who sent a birthday invitation on the Roman frontierabout 97 to 105 CE

Around 100 CE, at the Roman fort of Vindolanda in northern Britain (Hadrian's Wall came a couple of decades later), Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the commander Flavius Cerialis, received a thin wooden leaf tablet written in ink. It came from her friend Claudia Severa, wife of Aelius Brocchus, who commanded a fort nearby. The message: please come to my birthday celebration on 11 September; it will make the day more enjoyable. Most of the letter was written by a scribe. At the end, a different hand adds a personal farewell. Scholars identify this as Claudia herself, which makes these lines among the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. The tablet was excavated in 1985, one of hundreds of documents preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free layers at Vindolanda, alongside requests for beer, lists that mention socks, and a report sneering at the 'Brittunculi', the 'wretched little Britons'. What survives here is not grand history but friendship on a cold frontier: two women arranging a party, and one of them adding her own words.

Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail.

Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, Tab. Vindol. 291, trans. A. K. Bowman and J. D. Thomas
What we actually haveVindolanda tablet 291, a wooden leaf tablet written in ink, now in the British Museum (1986,1001.64).
How we knowExcavation of waterlogged deposits; infrared imaging of faded ink; palaeography comparing the scribe's hand with the closing hand.

Another letter from Claudia to Lepidina (Tab. Vindol. 292) also survives, again with a closing in what appears to be her own hand.

Sources (2)
  1. Bowman, A. K. & Thomas, J. D. (1994). The Vindolanda Writing-Tablets (Tabulae Vindolandenses II). British Museum Press.
  2. Roman Inscriptions of Britain online, Tab. Vindol. 291.

Alexandria, Egypt

Hypatia of Alexandria

She was the most respected teacher in a great city of learning, until local politics turned lethal.

March 415 CE
Mathematician, astronomer and philosopherdied March 415 CE

Hypatia taught in Alexandria in the late 300s and early 400s CE, a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in a city famous for learning. Her father Theon was a mathematician who edited Euclid and wrote on Ptolemy; a heading in his commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest credits Hypatia with revising the text of one book. Later sources say she wrote commentaries on Diophantus's Arithmetica and Apollonius's Conics, though none survive clearly under her name. What survives best is her reputation. Her student Synesius, later a bishop, wrote her admiring letters, including one asking her to have a hydroscope, an instrument for weighing liquids, made for him. The church historian Socrates Scholasticus, writing a generation later, praised her learning and her public standing among the city's officials. In March 415, amid a bitter feud between the city's prefect Orestes and its bishop Cyril, a mob seized her in the street, dragged her into a church and killed her. Modern films and slogans have turned her into many symbols. The ancient sources show something more human: a brilliant teacher caught in local power struggles.

made such attainments in literature and science, as to far surpass all the philosophers of her own time.

Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History 7.15, trans. A. C. Zenos (1890)
What we actually haveNo body and none of her own writings securely survive; the evidence is textual: Synesius's letters to her, Socrates Scholasticus, Damascius and the Suda, and her father's commentaries.
How we knowCritical reading and comparison of ancient Greek sources written by her student, by a near-contemporary historian, and by later compilers.

Seven letters from Synesius addressed to her survive, but not a single reply from Hypatia.

Sources (2)
  1. Dzielska, M. (1995). Hypatia of Alexandria. Harvard University Press.
  2. Watts, E. J. (2017). Hypatia: The Life and Legend of an Ancient Philosopher. Oxford University Press.

Palenque, Mexico

K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque

The inscriptions said he died at 80; his skeleton seemed to say 40; the argument took half a century to settle.

603–683 CE
Maya king who ruled for 68 years603 to 683 CE

K'inich Janaab Pakal was born in 603 CE and crowned king of the Maya city of Palenque in 615, at the age of 12, after a turbulent period in which his mother, Sak K'uk', held power. He ruled for 68 years, long enough to rebuild a battered kingdom into one of the most elegant cities of the Classic Maya world. His funerary monument, the Temple of the Inscriptions, carries one of the longest Maya hieroglyphic texts. In 1948 the archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier noticed a floor slab with holes for lifting it and found a rubble-filled staircase leading down into the pyramid. Clearing it took years. In 1952 he reached a crypt with a huge carved sarcophagus lid and a skeleton wearing a jade mosaic mask. Then came a puzzle: the inscriptions said Pakal died at 80, but the teeth suggested someone of 40 to 50. Decades of debate followed. A bioarchaeological team led by Vera Tiesler, working from 1999 to 2003, concluded the bones fit an elderly man; his soft, refined royal diet had probably spared his teeth. The texts, it seems, were right.

What we actually haveHis skeleton, sarcophagus, jade mask and tomb in the Temple of the Inscriptions, plus hieroglyphic texts recording his life dates.
How we knowDecipherment of Maya hieroglyphs and calendar dates; skeletal ageing methods; bioarchaeological analysis of the tomb.

His jade death mask was stolen from Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology in 1985 and recovered in 1989.

Sources (1)
  1. Tiesler, V. & Cucina, A. (eds.) (2006). Janaab' Pakal of Palenque: Reconstructing the Life and Death of a Maya Ruler. University of Arizona Press. doi:10.2307/j.ctv1qwwk7s

Birka, Sweden

The Birka warrior of grave Bj 581

For a century she was the textbook Viking warrior, assumed to be a man; then her DNA was read.

mid-900s CE
Viking-age woman buried with a full warrior's kitmid-900s CE

In the 1870s Hjalmar Stolpe excavated a chamber grave at Birka, a Viking-age trading town on an island in Lake Malaren, Sweden. Grave Bj 581, from the mid-900s, held one person buried with a sword, an axe, two spears, armour-piercing arrows, two shields, two horses and a gaming set with pieces and dice. For more than a century it served as the model of a high-status Viking warrior, assumed to be male. In 2016 the osteologist Anna Kjellstrom re-examined the skeleton and found female traits; in 2017 a genomic study found two X chromosomes and no Y. Isotopes suggest she was not born at Birka, and she was over 30 when she died. The reaction was huge, and so was the criticism. Had the bones been mixed up since the 19th century? Were the weapons gifts for someone who never fought? In 2019 the team replied, rechecking the excavation records and arguing the skeleton belongs to the grave. They left open whether she was a fighting warrior, a symbolic one or something else. The debate now centres less on her sex and more on how archaeologists read gender into grave goods for a century.

What we actually haveChamber grave Bj 581 with its skeleton, weapons, horses and gaming set, documented in Stolpe's records and stored in Stockholm.
How we knowOsteology; ancient DNA (sex chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA); strontium isotopes for mobility; re-examination of 19th-century excavation plans.

The gaming set placed on her lap has led some researchers to suggest she may have been a tactician or commander, though that remains speculative.

Sources (2)
  1. Hedenstierna-Jonson, C. et al. (2017). A female Viking warrior confirmed by genomics. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 164, 853-860. doi:10.1002/ajpa.23308
  2. Price, N. et al. (2019). Viking warrior women? Reassessing Birka chamber grave Bj.581. Antiquity 93, 181-198. doi:10.15184/aqy.2018.258

Mali Empire, West Africa

Mansa Musa of Mali

He arrived in Cairo with so much gold that, according to one chronicler, the price of gold fell.

1312–1337 CE
Emperor whose gold made headlines in Cairo and Europeruled about 1312 to 1337 CE; journey to Cairo in 1324

In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca and stopped in Cairo. He came with a huge caravan and, by every account, astonishing quantities of gold. The Damascus-born official al-Umari, writing about a dozen years later using interviews with Cairo officials who had met him, reports that Musa showered gold on courtiers and office holders, and that his people spent so freely that the value of gold in Egypt fell. He also reports a court drama: told to kiss the ground before the Mamluk sultan, Musa at first refused. The visit made Mali famous far beyond Africa; the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a West African king holding a gold nugget. Modern claims that Musa was the richest person who ever lived are guesses, since no figure can be calculated. And the historian Warren Schultz, checking Cairo exchange-rate records, found the gold slump real but temporary, not the twelve-year crash al-Umari describes. Even so, the episode shows West African gold at the heart of the medieval world economy.

They exchanged gold until they depressed its value in Egypt and caused its price to fall.

al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, trans. in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
What we actually haveArabic chronicles (al-Umari, Ibn Khaldun, al-Maqrizi and others), Cairo exchange-rate records, and the Catalan Atlas of 1375.
How we knowCritical comparison of medieval Arabic sources; economic history of Mamluk coinage and exchange rates; study of European maps.

Musa told his Cairo hosts that the ruler before him had sent a fleet out into the Atlantic to find its far edge, and had never returned.

Sources (2)
  1. Levtzion, N. & Hopkins, J. F. P. (eds.) (1981). Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History. Cambridge University Press.
  2. Schultz, W. C. (2006). Mansa Musa's gold in Mamluk Cairo: a reappraisal of a world civilizations anecdote. In J. Pfeiffer & S. A. Quinn (eds.), Post-Mongol Central Asia and the Middle East. Harrassowitz.
Coherence is the measure, not final demonstration.
Books

Words that survived

22 texts and finds from across the ancient world: who wrote them, where the oldest copy is today, and how their history holds up. The stamp rates history only, never a text's moral or religious worth.

All the books

Old Kingdom Egypt

Pyramid Texts

c. 2400-2300 BCE (carved); some spells likely older oral liturgy

Rock solid
Language and scriptOld Egyptian; hieroglyphs carved and painted on stone walls
Oldest copyWalls of the burial chamber and antechamber of the Pyramid of Unas, c. 2350 BCE (Unas's reign is dated anywhere from c. 2404-2374 to c. 2312-2282 BCE)
Where it is nowIn situ, Saqqara, Egypt
Size283 spells in Unas's pyramid alone; hundreds more across later Old Kingdom pyramids
Dating confidencehigh for the carvings, low for oral origins

What it says

A launch manual for a dead king. The spells help the pharaoh climb a ladder to the sky, ride a reed float across the heavens, join the boat of the sun god Ra and become one of the stars that never set. Others are practical charms against snakes and scorpions. The notorious Cannibal Hymn has the king swallowing gods to absorb their power. It reads less like a book than a ritual toolkit, carved in stone so it would keep working forever.

History check

The texts sit exactly where and when they appear to belong: inside securely identified royal pyramids at Saqqara (Unas, Teti, Pepi I, Merenre, Pepi II and several queens). Their content is religious, not a chronicle, but it matches temple and tomb evidence for Old Kingdom cults of Ra and Osiris. Absolute dates for Unas still vary by several decades between chronologies.

History checkRock solid
BustedRock solid

As a record of Old Kingdom royal belief and ritual.

Unas's burial chamber has a ceiling painted with golden stars. Until the 1880s, most scholars assumed pyramid interiors were blank; the carved spells were only discovered in 1880-81.

Sources (2)
  1. Allen, J. P. (2005). The Ancient Egyptian Pyramid Texts. Society of Biblical Literature.
  2. Lichtheim, M. (1973). Ancient Egyptian Literature, Vol. I. University of California Press.

Mesopotamia (Sumer and Babylonia)

Epic of Gilgamesh

Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE; Old Babylonian epic c. 1800 BCE; Standard version (attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni) c. 1200-1100 BCE

Mixed record
Language and scriptSumerian (early poems) and Akkadian (the epic); cuneiform on clay tablets
Oldest copyOld Babylonian epic tablets (e.g. the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets); the fullest version from Nineveh, c. 1800-1700 BCE; Nineveh copies 7th c. BCE
Where it is nowPenn Museum, Yale Babylonian Collection; British Museum (Nineveh tablets)
SizeAbout 3,000 lines on 12 tablets in the Standard Babylonian version, with gaps still being filled
Dating confidencemedium

What it says

Gilgamesh, a bullying king of Uruk, meets his match in Enkidu, a wild man the gods create to keep him busy. They become best friends, kill the forest guardian Humbaba, snub the goddess Ishtar and slay her Bull of Heaven. The gods punish them: Enkidu dies. Terrified of death, Gilgamesh travels to Utnapishtim, survivor of a great flood, seeking immortality. He finds a plant of youth, and a snake steals it. He goes home and admires his city's walls instead.

History check

A Gilgamesh of Uruk appears in the Sumerian King List (with an impossible 126-year reign), and one of his legendary rivals, Enmebaragesi of Kish, is attested in his own inscriptions, so a real king around 2700 BCE is plausible. No inscription of Gilgamesh himself has been found. Uruk's huge walls are real. The flood episode borrows from the older Atrahasis story; Mesopotamian flood layers are local and of different dates.

History checkMixed record
BustedRock solid

Real city and plausibly real king; the adventures are legend.

When George Smith of the British Museum read the flood tablet in 1872, he was reportedly so excited that he started taking off his clothes. A tablet bought by the Sulaymaniyah Museum and published in 2014 added new lines describing chattering monkeys in the Cedar Forest.

Sources (2)
  1. George, A. R. (2003). The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic. Oxford University Press.
  2. Al-Rawi, F. N. H., George, A. R. (2014). Back to the Cedar Forest: the beginning and end of Tablet V of the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh. Journal of Cuneiform Studies 66, 69-90.

Babylonia

Enuma Elish

Debated, c. 1800-1100 BCE; many favour the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I (c. 1125-1104 BCE)

Mixed record
Language and scriptAkkadian (Standard Babylonian); cuneiform on clay
Oldest copyTablet copies from Ashur, Kish and the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 1st millennium BCE (earliest c. 9th c. BCE)
Where it is nowBritish Museum and other collections
SizeAbout 1,100 lines on 7 tablets
Dating confidencelow-medium

What it says

Before sky and earth had names, sweet water (Apsu) and salt water (Tiamat) mingled. Their divine children are so noisy that Apsu plots to kill them; the clever god Ea strikes first. Furious, Tiamat raises an army of monsters. Young Marduk agrees to fight only if crowned king of the gods. He blasts her with winds, splits her body like a dried fish to make sky and earth, creates humans from a rebel god's blood to do the gods' chores, and builds Babylon.

History check

As an account of creation it is myth. As political history it fits well: it celebrates Marduk's rise to the top of the pantheon, which tracks Babylon's own rise. Later ritual texts indicate it was recited during the Akitu New Year festival. Its exact date of composition is still argued.

History checkMixed record
BustedRock solid

Mythic cosmology; reliable mirror of Babylonian politics and religion.

The title just means 'When on high', the poem's first two words. The last tablet is a victory list of Marduk's 50 names.

Sources (2)
  1. Lambert, W. G. (2013). Babylonian Creation Myths. Eisenbrauns.
  2. Dalley, S. (2000). Myths from Mesopotamia. Oxford World's Classics.

Middle Kingdom Egypt (set in the Old Kingdom)

The Instruction of Ptahhotep

Set in the reign of Djedkare Isesi (c. 2400 BCE); language suggests composition c. 2000-1800 BCE

Plausible
Language and scriptMiddle Egyptian; hieratic script on papyrus
Oldest copyPapyrus Prisse, c. 1800 BCE (12th Dynasty)
Where it is nowBibliothèque nationale de France, Paris
Size37 maxims plus a prologue and epilogue
Dating confidencelow for the attribution, medium for Middle Kingdom composition

What it says

An aging vizier asks the king to let him train his son, and opens with a grumpy list of what old age does to the body. Then comes the advice: stay humble, because 'good speech is more hidden than greenstone, yet it is found among the women at the grindstones'. Listen more than you talk. Do not gossip. Do not grab food at a superior's table. Be generous, love your wife, and do not let success make you arrogant. Some tips would suit a modern office.

History check

King Djedkare Isesi and viziers named Ptahhotep are attested, including tombs at Saqqara. But the grammar and style point to the Middle Kingdom, so the attribution is probably a literary device giving the text an ancient pedigree.

History checkPlausible
BustedRock solid

Real names and setting; authorship probably later than claimed.

Papyrus Prisse, acquired in Egypt in the 1840s by Émile Prisse d'Avennes, is often nicknamed 'the oldest book in the world'.

Sources (2)
  1. Lichtheim, M. (1973). Ancient Egyptian Literature, Vol. I. University of California Press.
  2. Parkinson, R. B. (1997). The Tale of Sinuhe and Other Ancient Egyptian Poems 1940-1640 BC. Oxford University Press.

Old Babylonian Mesopotamia

Code of Hammurabi

c. 1755-1750 BCE, late in Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792-1750 BCE, middle chronology)

Rock solid
Language and scriptAkkadian; cuneiform carved on a basalt stele
Oldest copyThe 2.25 m black stone stele, c. 1754 BCE
Where it is nowLouvre, Paris (found at Susa, Iran, in 1901-02)
SizePrologue, 282 laws (as numbered by modern scholars), epilogue
Dating confidencehigh relative date; absolute date depends on the chronology used

What it says

A king announces that the gods chose him 'to make justice appear in the land' and protect the weak from the strong. Then come the case rulings: theft, trade, wages, rent, marriage, divorce, adoption, surgeons' fees and building collapses. 'An eye for an eye' applies, but only between social equals; hurting a commoner or a slave costs silver instead. If a house falls and kills its owner, the builder dies. It is justice, Bronze Age style.

History check

Hammurabi is one of the best-attested kings of antiquity: his letters, year names, contracts and many tablet copies of the laws survive. Scholars debate whether courts actually applied the code; few trial records cite it, so it may have worked as royal showcase and model rulings.

History checkRock solid
BustedRock solid

The king, the text and its date are firmly attested; everyday legal use is debated.

The stele was itself war loot: an Elamite king, Shutruk-Nahhunte, carried it to Susa in the 12th century BCE, and several columns were chiselled off, perhaps for a boast he never carved.

Sources (2)
  1. Roth, M. T. (1997). Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor. 2nd ed. Scholars Press.
  2. Van De Mieroop, M. (2005). King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography. Blackwell.

Vedic Indo-Aryans, northwestern Indian subcontinent

Rigveda

c. 1500-1000 BCE (older hymns c. 1500-1200 BCE)

Plausible
Language and scriptVedic Sanskrit; transmitted orally, later written in scripts such as Sharada and Devanagari
Oldest copyManuscripts in the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute collection (UNESCO Memory of the World, 2007), Oldest dated: 1464 CE
Where it is nowBORI, Pune, India
Size10 books (mandalas), 1,028 hymns, about 10,600 verses
Dating confidencemedium; based on linguistics and external anchors

What it says

A collection of hymns sung at fire rituals. Agni, the fire, carries offerings to the gods. Indra, a thunder-wielding hero fuelled by the drink soma, slays the serpent Vritra and frees the rivers. Ushas, the dawn, is praised in some of its loveliest poems, and Varuna guards cosmic order. One late hymn wonders how creation began and ends with a shrug: perhaps even the highest overseer 'knows, or perhaps he does not know'.

History check

The hymns describe a mobile, cattle-herding society with horses and chariots, and their river names fit the Punjab region. A Hittite-Mitanni treaty of about 1380 BCE invokes Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas, an independent sign these gods were known by the 14th century BCE. Exact dates and the question of origins remain debated.

History checkPlausible
BustedRock solid

Reliable window on an early society; dating is approximate.

The text was preserved by memory for many centuries using cross-checking recitation patterns (pada, krama, jata, ghana) that make errors easy to spot. Vedic chanting is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

Sources (2)
  1. Jamison, S. W., Brereton, J. P. (2014). The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India. Oxford University Press.
  2. UNESCO Memory of the World Register: Rigveda manuscripts, BORI (2007).

New Kingdom to Ptolemaic Egypt

Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)

Emerges c. 1700-1550 BCE from earlier Coffin Texts; used until c. 50 BCE

Rock solid
Language and scriptEgyptian; hieroglyphic and hieratic on papyrus, coffins and shrouds
Oldest copyEarly spells on the coffin of Queen Mentuhotep (13th Dynasty); the famous Papyrus of Ani, c. 1700 BCE; Ani c. 1250 BCE
Where it is nowCoffin now lost (known from copies); Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum
SizeAbout 190 spells known; no single copy has them all. The Papyrus of Ani is over 20 m long
Dating confidencehigh

What it says

A personalized survival kit for the afterlife. Spells let the dead transform into a heron or a lotus, avoid walking upside down, and keep their heart in place. The big moment is spell 125: in the Hall of Two Truths the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat while the deceased recites a 'negative confession': I have not stolen, I have not lied. Fail, and the monster Ammit, part crocodile, part lion, part hippo, eats the heart.

History check

Thousands of copies come from dated tombs, so the text's use and development are very well documented. It records what elite Egyptians hoped for after death rather than events.

History checkRock solid
BustedRock solid

As evidence of Egyptian funerary belief and practice.

Some copies were prepared in advance with blank spaces where the buyer's name would be filled in later: a ready-made afterlife guide.

Sources (2)
  1. Taylor, J. H. (ed.) (2010). Journey Through the Afterlife: Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead. British Museum Press.
  2. Faulkner, R. O. (1985). The Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead. British Museum Press.

Ancient Israel and Judah; Jewish communities of the Persian and Hellenistic eras

Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), including the Torah

Written and edited over c. 9th/8th-2nd c. BCE; the Torah probably reached its present form c. 6th-5th c. BCE

Mixed record
Language and scriptBiblical Hebrew with some Aramaic; Paleo-Hebrew, later Aramaic square script
Oldest copyKetef Hinnom silver amulets (the Priestly Blessing, Numbers 6:24-26); oldest complete Hebrew Bible: Leningrad Codex, Amulets c. 600 BCE; Leningrad Codex 1008 CE
Where it is nowIsrael Museum, Jerusalem; National Library of Russia, St Petersburg
Size24 books in the Jewish count; the Torah alone is about 80,000 Hebrew words
Dating confidencelow-medium; actively debated

What it says

A library rather than a book: creation, a flood, the families of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Exodus from Egypt and laws given at Sinai, then settlement, judges, kings, prophets, exile to Babylon and return. Alongside the stories sit poetry (Psalms, Song of Songs), proverbs, the long argument of Job and the gloriously skeptical Ecclesiastes. It is history, law, poetry and argument woven together by many hands.

History check

Independent inscriptions confirm several figures and events: the Tel Dan stele mentions the 'House of David', the Mesha stele names Omri of Israel, Assyrian records name Jehu and Hezekiah, and Babylonian ration tablets list King Jehoiachin. The patriarchs, the Exodus and a sweeping conquest lack direct archaeological support, and the scale of the early monarchy is debated.

History checkMixed record
BustedRock solid

Later monarchy period often corroborated; earlier narratives largely untestable or unsupported.

The Ketef Hinnom amulets are tiny rolled silver scrolls, found in 1979, that are roughly 400 years older than the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Archaic Greece

Iliad and Odyssey

c. 750-650 BCE, from a much older oral tradition; fixed in writing between the 8th and 6th c. BCE

Plausible
Language and scriptHomeric Greek (an artificial poetic mix of dialects); Greek alphabet

What it says

The Iliad covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War: Achilles sulks after an insult, his friend Patroclus is killed, Achilles kills Hector in revenge, and old King Priam sneaks into the enemy camp to beg for his son's body. The Odyssey follows Odysseus's ten-year trip home past a Cyclops, the witch Circe, the Sirens and the land of the dead, ending with a bow contest and a hall full of doomed suitors.

History check

Troy is identified with Hisarlik in Turkey, a real city destroyed more than once around 1300-1180 BCE. Hittite texts mention Wilusa (likely Ilios), a king called Alaksandu and a western power called Ahhiyawa (likely Achaeans). The boar's-tusk helmet in the Iliad matches Mycenaean finds. The heroes, gods and a single ten-year war remain unattested.

History checkPlausible
BustedRock solid

A real Bronze Age setting with a possible kernel of conflict, heavily legendary.

There is no Trojan Horse in the Iliad. It appears only as a memory in the Odyssey (books 4 and 8), and the full tale is told much later by Virgil.
