What it says

At its heart are the Gathas, 17 hymns attributed to the prophet Zarathustra, who talks directly with the wise lord Ahura Mazda. The big theme is choice: every person sides with truth (asha) or with the lie (druj). Around the Gathas sit liturgies for the fire ritual, hymns to divine beings such as Mithra and Anahita, and the Vendidad, a rulebook on purity, dogs, and how to keep the dead from polluting earth, fire and water.

History check

The Gathas' language is very close to Rigvedic Sanskrit, which supports an early date. Achaemenid inscriptions of Darius I (c. 520 BCE) invoke Ahuramazda, so the god was central by then. Zarathustra himself has no external attestation, and his date is one of the most contested in the history of religion.

History checkHot debate
BustedRock solid

The tradition is ancient; the founder's date and life are uncertain.

The Avestan alphabet, with more than 50 letters, was invented centuries after the texts were composed, largely to record pronunciation precisely as priests chanted it.

China's oldest poetry anthology. The 'Airs of the States' are folk songs about love, flirting by the river, harvests, homesick soldiers and brides leaving home. The court odes and temple hymns praise Zhou ancestors such as King Wen and King Wu, who overthrew the Shang. It is sung history and everyday feeling in one.

History check

Kings and events named in the hymns match Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, including the Zhou conquest of the Shang (c. 1046 BCE). Bamboo manuscripts from the 4th century BCE show the poems circulated before the Qin book burning, with variant wording.

BustedRock solid

Names and institutions largely match bronze-age inscriptions.

Tradition says Confucius picked these 305 from about 3,000 poems; most scholars doubt it. He did tell his son that without studying the Odes, 'you will have nothing to say'.

Confucius (traditionally 551-479 BCE) is widely accepted as historical, and other early texts mention him and his disciples. But the Analects was assembled in layers over generations, so individual sayings are hard to pin on him directly.

A tiny book of big paradoxes. 'The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.' Water is soft yet wears down stone, so yielding beats forcing. The wise ruler practises wu wei, acting without straining, and governs a great state 'like cooking a small fish': do not poke it too much. It praises simplicity, humility and knowing when enough is enough, and it makes fun of cleverness and showy virtue.

Laozi's biography comes from Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE), who himself offered several candidates. The Guodian slips show that sections of the text existed by about 300 BCE, but not necessarily as one book by one author.

BustedRock solid

The Mawangdui silk copies put the 'Te' half first, so the oldest complete versions are really the Te Tao Ching.

Ashoka's inscriptions (3rd c. BCE) mention the Buddha, and the Lumbini pillar states that the Buddha was born there. The Buddha's own dates remain debated (c. 563-483 or c. 480-400 BCE). The oldest Buddhist manuscripts of all are Gandharan birch-bark scrolls in the Gandhari language, not Pali.

c. 400 BCE-400 CE, in layers

A family feud that becomes a world war. Just before the fighting, Krishna counsels the hesitant archer Arjuna: that dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita. The epic claims, with some justification, that what is here is found elsewhere, and what is not here is nowhere.

History check

The Kuru kingdom was real (Iron Age, c. 1200-500 BCE, associated with Painted Grey Ware culture), and excavations at Hastinapura found a settlement of that period. No archaeological trace of a great war has been found, and astronomical dates proposed for it (such as 3102 BCE) are disputed.

History checkHot debate
BustedRock solid

Real Iron Age polity; the war and heroes are unverified.

In the frame story the sage Vyasa dictates the epic to the elephant-headed god Ganesha, who agrees to write only if Vyasa never pauses, and breaks off a tusk to use as a pen.

The first big 'inquiry' (historia) in Greek: why did Greeks and Persians go to war? Along the way Herodotus detours into everything. Then the main event: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis, told with a sharp eye for pride and its fall.

Persian royal inscriptions and the Persepolis administrative tablets confirm many names and institutions; the Behistun inscription parallels his account of Darius's rise. BustedRock solid

Core events and many details corroborated; numbers and tall tales are not.

Explorer Michel Peissel proposed that the gold-digging 'ants' were Himalayan marmots, whose burrows on one high plateau throw up gold dust.

Most historians accept that Jesus existed and was executed under Pontius Pilate; Tacitus and Josephus mention him. A 1961 inscription from Caesarea names Pilate as prefect of Judea. Some details are problematic, such as the census of Quirinius (6 CE) versus Herod's death (4 BCE). Miracle claims lie outside what historical method can test.

Giza, Egypt

The Great Pyramid of Khufu

Six million tonnes of stone, one surviving boatman's diary, and a muon scanner still finding rooms nobody knew about.

Mystery

The quick read

c. 146.6 m (now c. 138.5 m)Original height
c. 230.3 m; the four sides differ by about 20 cmBase side

c. 6 million tonnesEstimated mass

The best evidence comes from the builders' own paperwork. Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt's oldest known harbour, include the logbook of an inspector named Merer, whose crew of about 40 men shipped white Tura limestone to Giza in Khufu's 27th year along canals into a harbour basin. A 2024 study mapped a buried Nile branch, the Ahramat, running past 31 pyramids, so boats could reach close to the building sites. Most core blocks were quarried on the plateau itself, a short haul from the pyramid. Sledges dragged over wetted sand, levers, ropes and ramps are well attested. The exact layout of the ramps used for the upper courses is still debated, and so is how the heaviest granite beams were lifted about 43 m to the King's Chamber.

The myth

The pyramid is too precise for Bronze Age tools, and satellite radar has revealed a hidden complex of shafts and chambers under Giza that points to a lost civilisation.

The reality

Quarries, tool marks, workers' settlements and cemeteries, bakeries and Merer's logbook document an organised Egyptian workforce. The radar paper on Khufu's pyramid was retracted by Remote Sensing in August 2026 over methodological flaws and statistical errors, and the larger underground claims of 2025 were never published for peer review. The genuine voids found by muon imaging (2017, 2023) are real but modest, and their purpose is still open.

Wow

Merer's papyri, among the oldest inscribed papyri known, were written while the pyramid was being finished, so we can read the work diary of a man who shipped its casing stones.

Mystery meterA few loose ends
The deep dive11 min read · 2,340 words · 2 animated drawings

01A diary from the building site

In 2013, in a cave gallery on the Red Sea coast at Wadi al-Jarf, a French and Egyptian team led by Pierre Tallet lifted out bundles of papyrus that had been sealed away for about 4,500 years. Some were accounts. The best preserved were a logbook kept by an inspector called Merer, who ran a crew of roughly 40 boatmen in the 27th year of King Khufu. Day after day, in tidy columns, Merer noted where the crew slept, where they loaded, and where they delivered.

What they carried was fine white limestone from the quarries at Tura, across the river from Giza. What they delivered it to was Akhet Khufu, 'Horizon of Khufu', the name of the king's pyramid. The entries mention a harbour basin and a stop called She-Khufu, and they name Khufu's half-brother Ankhhaf as the senior official in charge of the work. By Tallet's reading, the crew made two or three round trips about every ten days.

The oldest inscribed papyri we have are not hymns or laws. They are a boatman's timesheets from the Great Pyramid.

That is the right place to start, because the Great Pyramid is often presented as a riddle with no witnesses. It has witnesses. They were paid in bread and beer, and at least one of them kept a diary.

02A mountain, measured

When Flinders Petrie surveyed Giza between 1880 and 1882, he treated the pyramid like a laboratory instrument. His numbers, refined by J. H. Cole's survey of 1925, still frame everything: a square base about 230.3 m on a side, an original height of about 146.6 m, and faces rising at about 51.8°. The four sides differ in length by only about 20 cm, and they are aligned to the cardinal points to within a few arcminutes. Today the top 8 m or so are missing and the height is about 138.5 m.

The volume is about 2.6 million cubic metres. Divide by a typical block and you get the famous figure of about 2.3 million blocks, with a total mass near 6 million tonnes. Treat both as engineering estimates rather than counts: nobody has tallied the blocks, the core contains rubble and uneven fill, and the granite beams over the King's Chamber are far heavier than the average core block of a tonne or two.

How did they find north so precisely without a compass? Several methods would work. Egyptologist Kate Spence proposed in 2000 that surveyors waited for two circumpolar stars to line up vertically, then dropped a plumb line; because the stars drift slowly over centuries, her idea also offered a way to date the pyramids. Others have shown that simple sun-shadow methods, tracking the tip of a vertical rod through a day, can reach similar accuracy. Nobody knows which one Khufu's surveyors used, but none requires anything more exotic than patience, cord and a clear sky.

For about 3,800 years it was the tallest thing people had built, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England rose higher around 1311 CE. It was already an antique, more than 2,000 years old, when Greek writers put it on their list of wonders.

How do we know the height?

The capstone and the top courses are gone, so the original apex is reconstructed. Surveyors measure the surviving casing stones at the base to find the true slope, then extend the four faces upward until they meet. Because the angle is known from real casing blocks still in place on the north side, the uncertainty in the reconstructed height is small, well under a metre.

03Inside the mountain

The interior is surprisingly small: a few narrow passages and three main chambers inside six million tonnes of stone. The original entrance sits about 17 m up the north face. From it a passage runs down at about 26.5° through the masonry and into the bedrock, ending in a rough, unfinished chamber about 30 m below the base. Partway down, an ascending passage branches upward, once blocked by granite plugs, and opens into the Grand Gallery, a corbelled hall about 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high.

A level passage leads from the foot of the gallery to the so-called Queen's Chamber, sitting exactly on the pyramid's north to south midline. At the top of the gallery lies the King's Chamber, lined with Aswan granite and holding an empty lidless granite sarcophagus. Above it, five low compartments separated by huge granite beams, the 'relieving chambers', spread the weight of the masonry overhead. Workers' graffiti painted inside them include Khufu's name, one of the direct links between the monument and its king.

Four narrow shafts complicate the picture. The two from the King's Chamber run all the way out to the faces. The two from the Queen's Chamber stop some 60 m in, at small stone slabs with copper pins, first reached by Rudolf Gantenbrink's robot in 1993. Their purpose, whether for the king's spirit, for the stars, or for the builders, is still argued over.

04Merer's river road

Merer's logbook turns a mystery of logistics into a timetable. Casing stone was loaded at Tura, floated across the Nile and along a canal, and delivered to a harbour near the building site. Each round trip took about four days. Tallet estimates each boat carried about 30 blocks of 2 to 3 tonnes, on the order of 200 blocks a month for one crew. Granite for the King's Chamber came from Aswan, more than 900 km upstream by river, and would have travelled the same way.

In 2024 a team led by Eman Ghoneim added the missing landscape. Using radar satellite imagery, geophysical surveys and deep sediment cores, they traced a buried branch of the Nile, which they named the Ahramat ('pyramids') branch, about 64 km long and 200 to 700 m wide, running along the desert edge from Lisht to Giza. Thirty-one pyramids, built over about a thousand years, line its banks, and many causeways end at valley temples that would have stood near its water.

The pyramids were not built in the middle of nowhere. They were built on a waterfront that has since dried up and disappeared under fields and sand.

The Ahramat study does not settle every detail. Water levels changed from season to season and from century to century, and the exact course of the channel in Khufu's reign is still being refined. But together with Merer's harbour basin it fits a simple, practical picture: move heavy stone by water whenever you can, and drag it only for the last stretch.

05From quarry to course

Most of the pyramid did not travel far at all. The core blocks were cut from quarries on the Giza plateau itself, just south of the pyramid, where the cut faces and the channels left around half-freed blocks are still visible. Quarrymen used copper chisels, stone pounders and wooden levers to separate blocks along their natural beds.

Blocks were dragged on wooden sledges. A Middle Kingdom tomb painting of the official Djehutihotep shows a colossal statue on a sledge with a man pouring water onto the sand in front of it. In 2014 physicists at the University of Amsterdam tested why. Adding the right amount of water to desert sand makes it stiffer, so the sledge stops ploughing a ridge ahead of itself; in their experiments the pulling force needed could drop by about half. Too much water, and the benefit disappears.

Ramps are where the evidence thins. Remains of construction ramps survive at several Egyptian pyramids, and in 2018 a team working at the Hatnub alabaster quarry reported a steep ramp flanked by staircases and post holes, dated by inscriptions to Khufu's reign, which may have used a pulley-like system of posts and ropes. But for the Great Pyramid itself, whether the builders used one long straight ramp, ramps zigzagging up a face, a ramp wrapping around the pyramid, or some combination, is still debated. An internal spiral ramp, proposed by architect Jean-Pierre Houdin, has not been confirmed by any scan.

The hardest lifts were not the millions of ordinary blocks but a few dozen granite beams roofing the King's Chamber and the relieving chambers above it, carried from Aswan and raised more than 40 m. How exactly they were manoeuvred into place, perhaps by levering them up a few centimetres at a time on timber packing, perhaps by dragging them up a ramp while the pyramid was still low around them, is not recorded. The beams themselves carry the evidence of the struggle: several have cracked under the load, and some cracks in the chambers above appear to have been plastered over in antiquity, perhaps by the builders themselves.

The final skin was fine white Tura limestone, cut so that the outer face could be dressed smooth, probably from the top down as the ramps were removed. Almost all of it is gone. After earthquakes in the 14th century, Cairo's builders treated the pyramid as a convenient quarry, and only a few casing blocks remain in place at the base of the north face.

06The people who built it

About 400 m south of the Sphinx, beyond a massive stone boundary wall about 200 m long known as the Wall of the Crow, archaeologists led by Mark Lehner have excavated a planned settlement called Heit el-Ghurab since 1988. It has long galleries that may have housed rotating work gangs, bakeries with bread moulds, storerooms, and a large administrative building. Seal impressions date most of it to Khufu's successors Khafre and Menkaure, so it tells us how the Giza project was run in general, even if Khufu's own camp is less well preserved.

The menu was generous. Zooarchaeologist Richard Redding's estimate, based on the animal bones, is that the town consumed on the order of 11 cattle and 37 sheep or goats a day, supplied by herds raised on estates in the Delta. On the slope above, Zahi Hawass's team found from 1990 the tombs of workers and overseers, with titles such as 'overseer of the side of the pyramid'. Some skeletons show healed fractures and even an amputation, signs of medical care.

Of this oppression there passed ten years while the causeway was made by which they drew the stones ... For the making of the pyramid itself there passed a period of twenty years.

Herodotus, Histories 2.124, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890)

Herodotus visited Egypt about 2,000 years after Khufu and repeated the local story that the king drove 100,000 men in three-month shifts. The idea that slaves built the pyramids comes mostly from later retellings. The archaeology points instead to a mixed workforce: a permanent core of skilled builders, supported by larger rotating crews drafted from the provinces, fed and housed by the state. Most published estimates of the number on site at any one time range from about 10,000 to 25,000.

07Seeing through stone

Every minute, each square metre of the Earth's surface is crossed by about ten thousand muons, heavy cousins of the electron made when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere. Stone absorbs some of them. Place detectors inside or beside a pyramid and count the muons arriving from each direction: where more get through than expected, there is less stone in the way, which means a void.

The ScanPyramids project, launched in 2015 by Cairo University and the HIP Institute, used three independent detector technologies from Nagoya University, the Japanese laboratory KEK and the French agency CEA. In 2017 they reported in Nature a 'Big Void' above the Grand Gallery, at least 30 m long, with a cross-section similar to the gallery's. All three methods saw it. Its shape, slope and purpose are unknown; it could be one space or several.

A second, smaller anomaly lay just behind the great limestone chevrons above the original entrance. In 2023 a paper in Nature Communications characterised this North Face Corridor as about 9 m long with a cross-section of about 2 by 2 m, and a thin endoscope pushed through a joint in the masonry showed a real, empty, gabled corridor. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports combined radar, ultrasound and electrical imaging to confirm its size and position.

Fresh from the field

The North Face Corridor was photographed in February 2023 and independently confirmed by multi-method imaging in 2025. Most engineers suspect it helped relieve the load over the entrance, much as the chevrons do, but nobody has yet been inside it. The Big Void remains unvisited, and no drilling has been approved.

08Radar, a retraction and an underground city

Not every scan survives scrutiny. In 2022 Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga published a paper in the journal Remote Sensing claiming that a satellite radar technique had revealed undiscovered internal structures in the Great Pyramid. In 2025 the same researchers announced, at a press event rather than in a journal, far larger claims: vertical shafts and chambers reaching hundreds of metres beneath the neighbouring pyramid of Khafre. The story went viral as an 'underground city'.

Specialists in ground-penetrating radar objected from the start. Radar at the frequencies used by these satellites is absorbed and scattered by the first metres of rock; archaeological radar expert Lawrence Conyers put it bluntly, saying it is physically impossible for the signal to pass through the pyramid, reflect off internal structures and return to the satellite. No raw data or peer-reviewed paper supported the Khafre claims.

On 10 August 2026 Remote Sensing retracted the 2022 paper. The notice says an investigation by the editorial office and board 'confirmed serious methodological flaws and statistical errors that were deemed to undermine the scientific conclusions'. The authors disagreed with the decision. The retraction does not touch the muon results, which were produced by three independent teams using a method with a long record, from Luis Alvarez's scan of Khafre's pyramid in the 1960s to modern volcano imaging.

A good anomaly survives a second team, a second method and a peer review. The Big Void did. The underground city did not.

09What we still do not know

The broad story is well supported: a 4th Dynasty king, a state that could feed and organise many thousands of workers, local quarries, river transport, sledges, levers and ramps. What remains open is the fine print.

  • How the upper third was built: which ramp layout, or mix of ramps and lifting from the courses, carried blocks above about 100 m.
  • How the granite beams of the King's Chamber, some estimated at 25 to 80 tonnes, were raised about 43 m or more.
  • What the Big Void is: a second gallery, a construction space, a relieving structure, or several of these.
  • Why the Queen's Chamber shafts were sealed with small pinned slabs, and what lies a few metres beyond them.
  • How long it took. Herodotus's twenty years and the length of Khufu's reign make a range of about 20 to 27 years plausible, but there is no direct record of the start date.

The honest mystery rating is low, around 2 out of 5. The pyramid is astonishing, but its builders left their tools, their towns, their graves, their graffiti and their paperwork. Every new instrument has so far made the human story more detailed, not less likely.

The big debates

Did satellite radar reveal hidden structures inside and beneath the Giza pyramids?

Yes: the radar images show shafts, corridors and chambers far larger than the known interior.Biondi and Malanga 2022 (Remote Sensing) and their 2025 press announcement about Khafre's pyramid.
No: the method cannot see that deep, and the published analysis failed review.Radar at these frequencies is absorbed within the first metres of rock; the 2022 paper was retracted in August 2026 for methodological flaws and statistical errors; the 2025 claims were never peer reviewed.

The bold claim: Satellite radar has revealed a hidden complex of shafts and chambers inside and beneath the Giza pyramids.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The one peer-reviewed paper behind the claim has been retracted by its journal after an investigation, and the larger claims were never submitted to review or released as data. The physics is also against it: satellite radar does not penetrate hundreds of metres of limestone. The real voids detected inside the pyramid come from muon imaging, a different method confirmed by three teams.

How were the upper courses built?

External ramps: straight, zigzagging up a face, or wrapping around the pyramid.Ramp remains at other pyramids and quarries, including the Khufu-era Hatnub ramp with staircases and post holes; the practical need for access to every course.
An internal spiral ramp inside the pyramid, proposed by Jean-Pierre Houdin.A notch high on one edge and microgravity data interpreted by Houdin; no internal ramp has been seen in muon scans so far.

The bold claim: Khufu's builders raised the top of the pyramid using an internal spiral ramp.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

External ramps of various layouts are attested in Egyptian building, and some combination of them remains the leading explanation, although the exact layout at Khufu's pyramid is unknown. The internal ramp idea is ingenious and testable, but the muon surveys that found the Big Void and the North Face Corridor have not reported the spiral it predicts.

What is the Big Void?

A construction feature: a relieving space, a second gallery used during building, or a void left by the building method.Its position above the Grand Gallery and its similar size and slope; the pyramid already has relieving chambers and chevrons.
A hidden chamber, perhaps holding burial goods.The size of the void and the absence of any known access.

The bold claim: The Big Void is a sealed treasure chamber.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The muon data show only that there is a large volume with less stone, at least 30 m long. They cannot show contents, and the physicists who found it stress that it may be several spaces and may be inclined or horizontal. A structural purpose linked to the Grand Gallery is the most economical guess, but only a camera or future imaging can decide.

Göbekli Tepe

Stone giants with arms, belts and fox pelts, raised on a hilltop by people who had never seen a clay pot.

The builders quarried hard limestone on the plateau beside the site, cutting T-shaped slabs out of bedrock with flint and stone tools; an unfinished pillar still lies in one quarry. Pillars were moved a short way, set into sockets or low pedestals, and linked by rubble walls and stone benches into round to oval enclosures. The biggest, Enclosure D, has two central pillars about 5.5 m tall and eleven more set into its ring wall. Reliefs of arms, hands, belts and fox-pelt loincloths turn the pillars into stylised human figures, surrounded by foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions. More than 7,000 grinding-stone artefacts show that cereals were processed on site in bulk, probably to feed work parties. Rainwater cisterns and domestic buildings suggest people also lived here.

The myth

A lost advanced civilisation built Göbekli Tepe, buried it on purpose to hide it, and carved a star map of a comet catastrophe on the Vulture Stone.

The reality

Every find so far (flint tools, animal bones, grinding stones, houses, cisterns) fits a community of late hunter-gatherers on the threshold of farming. The excavators now think much of the fill slid in from higher slopes rather than being dumped in one ritual burial. The comet reading of Pillar 43 is a published hypothesis that the excavation team and most archaeologists reject, mainly because its date sits centuries before the oldest dates for Enclosure D. The real open questions are what the images meant and how the work was organised.

Wow

Its builders had no pottery, no metal and no farm animals, yet they raised 5.5 m stone figures some 7,000 years before the first Egyptian pyramid.

Mystery meterReal open questions
The deep dive11 min read · 2,396 words · 2 animated drawings

01A hill with a navel

Stand on the limestone ridge above the Harran plain on a spring morning and the wind carries the smell of wheat fields. Beneath a modern canopy, a ring of grey stone figures faces inwards towards two taller ones. They have no faces. They do have arms: long, bent arms carved in low relief down their sides, with hands whose fingers meet over the belly. Below the hands, a belt. Hanging from the belt, a fox pelt, tail down.

These figures were raised around 11,500 years ago. That is roughly 7,000 years before the first Egyptian pyramid and more than 6,000 years before the first stones went up at Stonehenge. The people who raised them had no pottery, no metal, no writing and, as far as the animal bones show, no domesticated livestock. They hunted gazelle and wild cattle, and they harvested wild or barely domesticated cereals.

The Turkish name, Göbekli Tepe, means roughly Potbelly Hill or Hill of the Navel. A 1963 survey by the Universities of Chicago and Istanbul noticed the mound and its broken limestone slabs, but took them for a medieval cemetery. In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt looked again, recognised the T-shaped slabs as Stone Age pillars, and began excavating in 1995 with the German Archaeological Institute (DAI) and the Şanlıurfa Museum. Thirty years later, only a small fraction of the 300 m mound has been dug.

Its builders had no pottery, no metal and no writing, yet they carved 5.5 m stone people with hands, belts and fox pelts.

02Rings of stone: Enclosures A to D

The famous part of the site is a cluster of big round to oval buildings that the excavators label with letters. Enclosures A, B, C and D sit in the main excavation area, and geophysical survey suggests more lie unexcavated in the mound. Each follows the same recipe: a wall of rubble stone, T-shaped pillars set into that wall at intervals with their narrow faces turned inwards, stone benches running between them, and a pair of larger pillars standing free in the middle.

Enclosure D is the best preserved and the most spectacular. Its interior is about 14 m across at its widest, according to the architectural analysis by Gil Haklay and Avi Gopher. Eleven pillars stand in the ring wall. The central pair, known as Pillars 18 and 31, reach about 5.5 m and are thought to weigh around 8 to 10 tonnes each. They stand in low pedestals cut out of the bedrock, roughly 20 to 30 cm high.

Haklay and Gopher noticed something else. If you mark the centre points of Enclosures B, C and D on a plan, they form an almost perfect equilateral triangle with sides of about 19.25 m, accurate to within about 1.5 per cent. They argue that the three buildings were planned together as one project, perhaps laid out with cords and pegs. Not everyone agrees that the pattern was intended, but the precision is striking, and it hints at design decisions made before the first pillar was raised.

Were the enclosures roofed? The question matters for everything from how they felt inside to whether anyone could watch the sky from within. The DAI team has argued that at least some of the buildings were probably roofed, pointing to the benches, the inward-facing pillars and later, smaller buildings with clear roof supports. Others see them as open-air. The honest answer is that the evidence for roofs is indirect.

03Stone people and a zoo of carvings

The T-shape is not decoration: it is a body. The horizontal top is a head seen from the side, and the shaft is a torso. On the two central pillars of Enclosure D, the carvers made this explicit. Arms run down the broad sides, bent at the elbow, and the hands meet on the front just above a belt. The belts carry symbols, and from each hangs a fox pelt, carved so clearly that the fur and tail are recognisable. Most researchers read the central pairs as supernatural beings or ancestors rather than portraits of individual people.

Around these stone figures swarms an entire bestiary. Foxes leap across the shafts. Wild boars, snakes, cranes, vultures, aurochs, wild asses and scorpions appear in low and high relief. Snakes often flow downwards. The choice is not random: dangerous, carrion-eating or night-active animals dominate, and the domestic, the gentle and the edible are rare. Wild cattle and gazelle, which were eaten here in large numbers, appear far less often than foxes.

Pillar 43 in Enclosure D, nicknamed the Vulture Stone, is the densest of all. On its upper front sits a large vulture with a circle beside one outstretched wing. Around it are smaller birds, a scorpion, a snake and, near the top, three rectangular objects with handles that visitors love to call handbags. At the bottom is a headless human figure with an erect phallus. Headless figures and carved human skulls at the site hint at a concern with the dead and with heads, a theme that returns at nearby sites.

04How to make a T-pillar

The raw material was right underfoot. The ridge is made of hard, flat-bedded limestone, and quarry traces on the plateau around the enclosures show where pillars were outlined, trenched and levered free. Schmidt described an unfinished pillar still lying in its bedrock bed, reported as around 7 m long. It shows the method: mark the outline, cut a channel around it with stone and flint tools, then split the slab off along a natural bedding plane.

Moving and raising a 10-tonne stone without metal or the wheel sounds heroic, but the distances were short, because the quarries lie on the same plateau. Ropes, wooden levers, rollers or sledges and a few dozen people would have been enough, though no ropes or sledges survive and the exact method is inferred rather than observed. The central pillars were then stood in their pedestals. Whether the reliefs were carved before or after raising is unclear; some details, like the hands wrapping around onto the front face, look easier to finish with the pillar upright.

Who fed the workers? Here the evidence is unusually concrete. A 2019 study led by Laura Dietrich analysed more than 7,000 grinding-stone artefacts from the site, including almost 3,400 handstones. Most were standardised tools worn in ways typical of grinding cereals. The authors argue that large quantities of porridge, bread-like food and possibly beer were produced for work feasts. An earlier study found large stone vessels with residues that might come from fermentation, though that reading is still debated.

How do we know?

The pillar method comes from three kinds of evidence: quarry scars and an unfinished pillar on the plateau, tool marks on the stones themselves, and comparison with experiments and with megalith building recorded by ethnographers. The feasting idea comes from the grinding tools, the animal bones (huge numbers of gazelle, plus aurochs and wild boar) and the lack of storage buildings. Each strand is indirect; together they make a coherent picture.

05Not alone: the Stone Hills

For two decades Göbekli Tepe looked unique. It is not. Across the Şanlıurfa region, surveys and excavations now recognise a family of about a dozen contemporary sites with T-shaped pillars, grouped since 2021 under the name Taş Tepeler, the Stone Hills. Nevalı Çori, excavated in the 1980s and 1990s before a reservoir drowned it, had T-pillars with arms. Karahan Tepe, about 46 km to the east, may be even more startling.

At Karahan Tepe, excavations led by Necmi Karul of Istanbul University since 2019 uncovered Structure AB, a room about 7 by 6 m cut partly into the bedrock. Ten of its eleven pillars were left standing out of the living rock as the room was carved around them, and they are shaped like phalluses. On the west wall, a human head with a beard and thick lips emerges from the rock, gazing towards the entrance steps. Next door, the larger Structure AD is about 23 m across.

In 2023 the team also reported a seated human statue about 2.3 m tall with a V-shaped collar motif, echoing the famous Urfa Man statue found in the city in 1993. The effect of these finds is to turn Göbekli Tepe from a lonely miracle into the best-known member of a regional culture, with shared images, shared building habits and, perhaps, shared ceremonies.

06How old, exactly? The trouble with fill

Dating Göbekli Tepe is harder than it sounds. Radiocarbon needs something that was once alive: bone, charcoal, seeds. The enclosures, however, are full of debris, and debris moves. Material in the fill can be older than the building (if it was scraped up from an earlier rubbish layer) or younger (if it sifted in later). The DAI team has found cases of inverse stratigraphy, where younger samples lie deeper than older ones.

The most direct dates come from organic material trapped in the wall plaster of the enclosures, since plaster was applied while the building was in use. One sample from Enclosure D gave 9984 ± 42 radiocarbon years, which calibrates to 9745–9314 cal BCE at 95 per cent probability. Charcoal from deep soundings in the same enclosure clusters between about 9660 and 9310 cal BCE. So Enclosure D was probably built and used in the mid to late 10th millennium BCE, and filled in later, in the 9th.

The exact figures will keep moving as more samples are dated, and it is worth holding the headline number loosely. What is not in doubt is the order of magnitude: these buildings belong to the earliest Neolithic, the period when people in this region were starting to cultivate cereals but had not yet become full-time farmers.

07Buried on purpose? Maybe not

Klaus Schmidt, who died in 2014, believed the enclosures had been deliberately backfilled when they went out of use, a ritual burial that sealed them for millennia. The idea was elegant and it spread widely, including into claims that the site was hidden on purpose.

After Schmidt's death, the team under Lee Clare re-examined the deposits. In a 2020 summary of the 2015–2019 work, Clare describes fill made of limestone rubble, flint and bone that seems to have slid into the buildings from higher knolls and slopes, mixing older and younger material. Moritz Kinzel and Clare argue that repeated slope slides damaged the enclosures during their use and that the builders repaired, reinforced and remodelled them. On this reading, the burial was gradual and partly accidental.

There is a twist. At Karahan Tepe, Karul describes fill that stayed inside the building, went in by stages, and was capped with large flat stones, one measuring about 2.65 by 1.65 m. That looks intentional. So deliberate burial may have been a real practice in the Stone Hills, even if Göbekli Tepe's own enclosures were largely filled by nature and time.

08A temple on a hill, or a village?

Schmidt called Göbekli Tepe a mountain sanctuary, a place where scattered hunter-gatherer bands met for ceremonies and feasts but where nobody lived. The phrase "the world's first temple" still appears on posters. The newer evidence is less tidy and more interesting.

Excavations since 2015 have found domestic buildings around the enclosures, first round to oval ones and, from about 8700 BCE, rectangular ones. They have found hearths, tool-making debris, the grinding stones mentioned above, and a system for catching rain. Channels cut into the rock plateau fed rock-cut cisterns; one large rock-cut pit, possibly a cistern, is about 8 m across and 2.8 m deep. On a dry limestone hill with no spring, water storage suggests people stayed for long periods, perhaps year round.

  • Domestic buildings: round to oval in the earliest phase, rectangular later (Clare 2020).
  • Rainwater harvesting: rock-cut channels and cisterns on the plateau.
  • Food processing: thousands of grinding tools, often on roofs and terraces (Dietrich L. et al. 2019).
  • Fresh from the field (August 2026): geophysical survey reported by Karul's team detected several large buildings near the enclosures whose layouts suggest dwellings.

None of this makes the enclosures ordinary. They still look like special buildings, used for gatherings and rituals. But the picture has shifted from a lonely temple visited by nomads to a settlement with monumental communal buildings at its heart. That shift matters for the big story of the Neolithic, because it means that settling down, building big and experimenting with farming happened together, feeding one another.

09The comet on the Vulture Stone

In 2017 the chemical engineer Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis proposed a bold reading of Pillar 43. Matching the animals to star patterns, they argued that the vulture, scorpion and other creatures form a sky map, and that the circle by the vulture's wing marks the Sun at a particular solstice. Their result: a date stamp of 10,950 BCE, give or take 250 years, which they linked to a proposed comet impact at the start of the Younger Dryas cold period. The headless man, they suggested, symbolises catastrophe and death.

The excavation team replied the same year in the same journal, and further critiques followed. The main problems are easy to state. First, the proposed date is roughly 700 to 1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon dates for Enclosure D, so the pillar would record an event that happened centuries before the building existed. Second, matching animals to constellations is very flexible: with more than 60 carved pillars to choose from, and freedom to decide which animal is which star group, patterns can be found almost anywhere. Third, the scene ignores parts of the pillar, such as the headless figure's phallus, that fit poorly with a message of death.

The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis itself remains contested among earth scientists, which is a separate debate. But the specific claim that Pillar 43 records a comet strike has not persuaded the archaeologists who work at the site or the wider field. Sweatman has kept developing the astronomical reading, most recently in a 2024 paper extending it to Karahan Tepe, so the debate is alive in print. Still, it remains an interpretation with a clear problem of dates, not an established finding.

The proposed comet date sits centuries before the oldest dates for the building that carries it.

10What we still don't know

Göbekli Tepe no longer needs to be a mystery to be astonishing. We know roughly when it was built, from what stone, with what tools, and what its builders ate. The unknowns are the deep ones. What did the stone figures represent: gods, ancestors, founding heroes? Why foxes, and why so many dangerous animals? How were work parties organised without chiefs that we can see in burials or houses? Were the enclosures roofed? And how many more lie under the mound and under the other Stone Hills?

Roughly nine tenths of the mound has not been excavated, and the Taş Tepeler project is only a few years old. The next surprises will probably come from the ordinary layers, the houses, hearths and rubbish, which tell us how people lived around their stone giants.

The big debates

Does Pillar 43 record a comet impact around 10,950 BCE?

Yes: the carvings are a star map with a date.Sweatman and Tsikritsis (2017) match the animals to constellations and read the scene as the sky at a solstice around 10,950 BCE, linked to a proposed Younger Dryas comet impact.
No: dates and method do not support it.The proposed date is 700–1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon dates for Enclosure D; animal-to-constellation matching is highly flexible; and the reading ignores parts of the pillar (Notroff et al. 2017).

The bold claim: Pillar 43 is a record of a comet strike at the start of the Younger Dryas.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The idea is specific and testable, which is to its credit, but it fails the most basic test: the carving would predate the building that carries it by centuries. Pattern matching between carved animals and star groups allows many possible fits, and no independent evidence at the site points to an impact. Unless older dates for Enclosure D emerge, the comet reading has no receipts.

Were the enclosures deliberately buried?

Yes: a ritual backfilling.Schmidt saw uniform rubble fill with bones and tools as intentional burial at the end of use. At Karahan Tepe, fill in stages capped by large slabs looks deliberate (Karul 2021).
Mostly no: slope slides and gradual infill.Clare (2020) and Kinzel and Clare (2020) describe mixed older and younger debris that slid in from higher ground, with repairs during use, and inverse stratigraphy in radiocarbon samples.

The bold claim: Göbekli Tepe's enclosures were intentionally buried in a single ritual act.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The current excavation team favours natural slope slides plus gradual filling for Göbekli Tepe itself, and the mixed dates support that. Yet intentional filling is well attested at Karahan Tepe and at other Neolithic sites, so some deliberate closing of buildings cannot be ruled out. The single-burial version looks weaker than it did in the 2000s.

Did people live at Göbekli Tepe, or only gather there?

A sanctuary only.Schmidt's original model: no houses, a ceremonial centre visited by hunter-gatherer groups for feasts and building work.
A settlement with monumental buildings.Domestic buildings, rock-cut cisterns, thousands of grinding tools and 2026 geophysical hints of large dwellings (Clare 2020; Dietrich L. et al. 2019).

The bold claim: People lived at Göbekli Tepe for long periods, not only visited it.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

Houses, water storage and bulk food processing are hard to explain for a site used only for brief gatherings. What remains unclear is how many people lived there, for how much of the year, and whether the enclosures and houses were in use at exactly the same time.

Salisbury Plain, England

Stonehenge

Stones from three corners of Britain, a sightline to the solstice sun, and a monument that its builders kept rebuilding for fifteen centuries.

Stonehenge grew in stages over about 1,500 years. A circular ditch and bank came first around 3000 BCE, with a ring of 56 pits, the Aubrey Holes. Around 2500 BCE the great sarsen circle and five trilithons were raised, and the smaller Welsh bluestones were set up and later rearranged several times. Geochemistry has matched most sarsens to West Woods, about 25 km north, and bluestones to outcrops in the Preseli Hills of Wales. In 2024 mineral dating showed the 6-tonne Altar Stone came from northeast Scotland. The stones were shaped with stone hammers, raised with levers, ropes and timber, and locked together with joints borrowed from carpentry.

The myth

The stones are too heavy and far-travelled for Neolithic farmers, so Merlin brought them by magic from Ireland, or glaciers dumped them conveniently nearby.

The reality

Quarries with stone wedges and hearths have been excavated in Preseli, and radiocarbon dates place quarrying around 3000 BCE. Mineral fingerprinting ties the sarsens, bluestones and Altar Stone to specific sources, and ice-sheet modelling rules out a glacial delivery of the Altar Stone. People moved them, using sledges, ropes and perhaps boats and cattle. The routes and the monument's full meaning remain uncertain.

Wow

The Altar Stone at the heart of Stonehenge travelled about 700 km from northeast Scotland, farther than any other known megalith in Neolithic Britain.

Mystery meterA few loose ends
The deep dive11 min read · 2,336 words · 2 animated drawings

01Sunrise on the longest day

Stand in the middle of Stonehenge before dawn on the summer solstice and look northeast, out through the gap in the great ring. The sun comes up close to the Heel Stone, a lone sarsen outside the circle, and its first light runs straight down the monument's axis to the centre. Turn around and you face the opposite direction, where the sun sets at midwinter. The whole design is threaded on that one line.

That alignment is one of the few things about Stonehenge nobody seriously disputes. Almost everything else, who built it, how, from what, and why, has been argued over for centuries. What has changed in the last decade is the quality of the receipts. Chemistry, mineral dating, isotopes in teeth and radiocarbon have turned a romantic ruin into one of the best-documented prehistoric monuments in the world, and the story they tell is more remarkable than the legends.

Since 1986 Stonehenge and the nearby circles of Avebury have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, part of a landscape packed with hundreds of burial mounds, earthworks and ritual monuments. Understanding the stones means reading that whole landscape, and some of the most important evidence of the last twenty years has come from outside the circle.

Stonehenge was not built once. It was built, rebuilt and rearranged for about fifteen centuries, like a cathedral that never stopped being renovated.

02Fifteen centuries of rebuilding

The standard framework, published by Timothy Darvill, Peter Marshall, Mike Parker Pearson and Geoff Wainwright in 2012, divides the site into five stages. Around 3000 BCE, people dug a circular ditch about 110 m across, piled the chalk into a bank inside it, and dug a ring of 56 pits now called the Aubrey Holes after the 17th-century antiquary John Aubrey. Cremated remains of many people were buried in and around them, making early Stonehenge one of the largest cemeteries of its time in Britain.

The Aubrey Holes may have held more than bones. When one of them, Aubrey Hole 7, was re-excavated in 2008, the chalk at its base was crushed as if by the weight of a standing stone. Many archaeologists now think the first bluestones stood in this outer ring around 3000 BCE, five centuries before they were moved into the centre. If so, the Welsh stones were there from the very beginning, and the monument started life as a stone circle and cemetery together.

Around 2500 BCE came the transformation that gives the site its silhouette: a circle of 30 sarsen uprights, each about 4.1 m high, capped by a continuous ring of lintels, with a horseshoe of five giant trilithons inside it, open towards the midsummer sunrise. The smaller bluestones were set up in arrangements that changed several times over the next five centuries. Around 2300 BCE the Avenue, a pair of banks and ditches, was laid out from the entrance towards the River Avon, about 2.8 km away. The last major work, rings of pits called the Y and Z Holes, dates to around 1600 BCE.

How do we know the dates?

Radiocarbon dating of antler picks left in the ditch and stoneholes, of cremated bone, and of animal bones gives the construction dates. The 2012 framework combined dozens of dates with the order in which features cut through one another. Individual stages still carry uncertainties of a century or more.

03The sarsens: a 25 km drag

The big stones are sarsen, a very hard silcrete that forms in blocks across southern England. For a long time the Marlborough Downs, about 25 to 30 km north, were assumed to be the source, but nobody could test it. The breakthrough came from an unlikely place. During restoration in 1958, a core was drilled through Stone 58, one of the trilithon uprights, and one of the workers kept it. In 2019, Robert Phillips returned it for study.

In 2020 a team led by geomorphologist David Nash published the results in Science Advances. Using portable X-ray fluorescence, they showed that 50 of the 52 surviving sarsens share a common chemistry. Analysis of the core matched it to sarsen at West Woods, about 25 km north of Stonehenge. Two stones differ and came from somewhere else, still unknown.

The core itself was a small revelation. Sarsen turns out to be almost pure quartz: sand grains cemented together by more quartz, which makes it one of the hardest and most durable building stones in Britain. That explains both why the stones have survived four and a half thousand years of weather and why shaping them was such hard work. Every flat face and curve was produced by pounding with hand-held mauls of the same material.

The sarsens were not simply found and dropped into place. They were dressed with hammerstones, sometimes to remarkably fine finishes, and shaped with subtle refinements: the uprights taper, and the lintels are curved in plan so that together they form a true circle. A sarsen upright of the outer circle weighs about 25 tonnes; the largest trilithon stones are heavier. Moving them 25 km over the rolling chalk probably meant sledges on timber rails, ropes and large, well-fed teams.

04The bluestones: from Wales, on purpose

The smaller stones, about 80 originally of which 43 survive, are a mixed family of volcanic and igneous rocks called bluestones, and they are not local at all. Since the 1920s geologists have traced them to the Preseli Hills in southwest Wales, about 230 km away. Since 2011 excavations by Parker Pearson and colleagues have found the actual quarries: Carn Goedog, source of the spotted dolerite, and Craig Rhos-y-felin, source of a distinctive rhyolite.

At both outcrops the rock forms natural pillars. The quarry workers left stone wedges driven into the joints, hearths, and artificial stone platforms at the foot of the outcrop where a freed pillar could be lowered onto a sledge. Radiocarbon dates from the quarries cluster around 3400 to 3000 BCE, around the time of Stonehenge's first stage. Typical pillars were about 4 m long and weighed around 2 tonnes.

Why go so far? One answer comes from the dead. Isotope analysis of cremated bone from the first stage, published in 2018, found that about 10 of 25 individuals had not lived locally in the last years of their lives, and their values are consistent with west Wales. Stonehenge seems to have been, from the beginning, a meeting place of distant communities, and the stones may have carried ancestral meaning from home.

Fresh from the field

In 2025 a team led by Jane Evans and Mike Parker Pearson analysed a cow's tooth buried at Stonehenge's south entrance around 3000 BCE. Lead and other isotopes show the animal spent part of its life on older Palaeozoic rocks like those of Wales, suggesting cattle, and perhaps cattle pulling sledges, came east with the bluestones.

05The Altar Stone: 700 km from Scotland

At the centre of the monument lies a fallen slab of greenish sandstone about 4.9 m long and weighing about 6 tonnes, partly buried under two collapsed sarsens. Since the 1920s it had been assumed to come from Wales, like the bluestones. In 2024, a team led by Anthony Clarke of Curtin University dated tiny zircon, apatite and rutile grains inside fragments of it. Their ages matched the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland, not Wales.

The distance is about 700 km in a straight line and at least 750 km by any realistic route, over mountains and rivers, or around the coast by sea. A follow-up study in 2024 ruled out Mainland Orkney itself, pointing to the Scottish mainland. In 2026, Clarke's team tested whether ice could have done the work. Their modelling suggests Ice Age glaciers might have carried it part of the way, perhaps as far as Dogger Bank in what is now the North Sea, but that no ice route reached southern England, so people still had to move it hundreds of kilometres, probably in stages combining overland hauling with river or coastal transport.

A six-tonne slab from the far north of Britain lies at the heart of a monument on the south coast plains. That is a statement about connections, not just muscle.

How would you move it? No Neolithic boat big enough has been found in Britain, but the absence of evidence is not surprising, since plank or hide boats rarely survive. By land, a sledge on timber rails over some 750 km of hills, bogs and rivers would have taken many months and a relay of communities along the way. Either route implies alliances stretching the length of the island, and a reason strong enough to make the effort worthwhile.

It also rewrites our picture of Neolithic Britain. Communities in Orkney, Wales and Wessex shared pottery styles, house designs and monument ideas around 3000 BCE; the Altar Stone shows they also shared enough trust and organisation to move a large sacred stone across the length of the island.

06Raising a trilithon

No Neolithic engineer left instructions, but excavated stoneholes preserve some of the method. Several have one sloping side, a ramp down which the base of a stone could slide, and a steep opposite face where it would come to rest. Once the stone had tipped into the hole, teams hauling on ropes, perhaps over a timber frame, pulled it upright, and the hole was packed with rammed chalk and broken stone.

Lintels posed the harder problem: lifting a stone of about 7 tonnes more than 4 m and setting it precisely. Two methods are usually proposed: an earth ramp, or a timber crib, a platform of crossed logs raised one layer at a time while the stone was levered up after it. The crib needs far less material and has been demonstrated experimentally, but there is no direct evidence for either.

What is certain is how the stones were locked together. Each lintel has two hollows, mortises, that fit over knobs, tenons, left projecting from the tops of the uprights. Neighbouring lintels in the outer circle join end to end with tongue-and-groove joints. These are carpenters' joints, translated into stone, a strong hint that the builders thought about their monument in terms of timber structures like the great wooden circles nearby.

The builders also cared how it looked from one particular direction. A laser scan of every stone surface, carried out for English Heritage in 2011 and 2012, showed that the stones facing someone walking up the Avenue from the northeast, towards the solstice view, were dressed most finely, while faces seen less often were left rougher. The monument was designed to be approached along its axis.

07Durrington Walls and the living

Stonehenge was not an isolated temple on an empty plain. About 3 km to the northeast lies Durrington Walls, a huge henge enclosure. Excavations between 2004 and 2007 found the remains of houses dating to around 2500 BCE, the time the sarsens went up, and enormous quantities of animal bone and pottery.

The pig bones are especially telling. Most pigs were killed at around nine months old, which, given spring births, puts the feasts in midwinter. Isotope studies published in 2019 show that pigs and cattle were brought to the feasts from across Britain, some probably from as far as Scotland. Parker Pearson has argued that Durrington, with its timber circles, was a place for the living and Stonehenge, in stone, a place for the ancestors, the two linked by the River Avon and their avenues. That interpretation is influential but not universally accepted.

Where the Avenue meets the River Avon, excavators in 2009 found the stoneholes of a small circle of about 25 stones, nicknamed Bluestonehenge. Its stones seem to have been removed around 2400 BCE, perhaps taken up the Avenue and added to Stonehenge itself. Monuments in this landscape were not fixed: they were dismantled, moved and combined, as if the stones themselves carried histories worth keeping.

The wider landscape keeps producing surprises. In 2020, geophysical survey revealed a ring of large pits, more than 20 of them, surrounding Durrington Walls on a circle about 2 km across, dug around 2500 BCE. Their purpose is unknown.

08Magic, glaciers and computers

In the 1130s the chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth told how the wizard Merlin brought a stone circle called the Giants' Dance from Ireland by his arts. Oddly, the legend of stones moved from the far west to Salisbury Plain has a grain of truth in it; only the magic and the Irish address are wrong.

The Druids arrived in the story much later. In the 17th and 18th centuries John Aubrey and William Stukeley linked Stonehenge to the Druid priests described by Julius Caesar, and the connection stuck. But the Druids belong to the Iron Age, roughly 2,000 years after the sarsens were raised. Modern Druid and pagan groups who gather at the stones for the solstice are part of the monument's long afterlife, not its origin, and English Heritage now opens the site to them on the longest and shortest days.

A more serious rival to human transport is ice. Some geologists have argued since the 1970s that glaciers carried the bluestones most of the way to Salisbury Plain. The evidence has turned against this: there are no scattered Welsh erratics across Wiltshire, the quarries at Carn Goedog and Craig Rhos-y-felin show human extraction, and the Altar Stone modelling rules out a glacial route from Scotland.

In 1965 the astronomer Gerald Hawkins proposed in Stonehenge Decoded that the monument was an astronomical computer, with the Aubrey Holes used to predict eclipses. Archaeologists, notably Richard Atkinson in a paper he titled 'Moonshine on Stonehenge', pointed out that the features Hawkins used belonged to different centuries and that many alignments occur by chance in any complex site. The solstice axis is real and deliberate; a Neolithic eclipse calculator is not supported.

09What is still unknown

  • The exact routes of the bluestones and the Altar Stone, and whether boats were used for part of either journey.
  • Whether the bluestones stood first in a circle in Wales. Excavations at Waun Mawn, published in 2021, were presented as a dismantled 'original Stonehenge', but that reading has been strongly challenged.
  • Whether the sarsen circle was ever complete. Parchmarks seen in the dry summer of 2013 suggest missing stones once stood, but not every hole has been dated.
  • Where the two non-West Woods sarsens came from.
  • What the monument meant: a temple of the sun, a monument to the ancestors, a place of healing, or several of these at different times.

The mystery rating is 2 out of 5. The how is increasingly well understood and the where is now known in startling detail. The why, as with most prehistoric monuments, may never be fully recoverable. But the builders' choices, a line to the solstice sun, stones hauled from three corners of Britain, joints copied from carpentry, tell us they were organised, ambitious and deeply connected to one another.

The big debates

Did glaciers or people bring the far-travelled stones?

Glaciers: ice sheets carried the bluestones, and perhaps the Altar Stone, much of the way.Britain was glaciated repeatedly; some geologists (e.g. Kellaway, Brian John) argue the Preseli quarries are natural features.
People: the stones were deliberately quarried and hauled.Excavated quarries with wedges, platforms and dated hearths; no trail of Welsh erratics across southern England; 2026 ice modelling finds no glacial route for the Altar Stone into southern England.

The bold claim: Ice, not people, delivered the Welsh bluestones and the Scottish Altar Stone to Salisbury Plain.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The glacial hypothesis was reasonable before the quarries were found. It now faces human-made quarry features dated to the right period, the absence of erratics where the ice would have dropped them, and modelling showing no glacier could carry the Altar Stone south from Scotland. Human transport is the far stronger explanation.

Was Stonehenge an astronomical computer?

Yes: many alignments, and the 56 Aubrey Holes could track eclipse cycles.Gerald Hawkins, Stonehenge Decoded (1965); Fred Hoyle's later eclipse model.
Only partly: the solstice axis is deliberate; the rest is over-reading.The features used date to different centuries; chance alignments are common in complex sites; the Aubrey Holes held cremations and possibly stones.

The bold claim: Stonehenge was a Neolithic computer for predicting eclipses.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset axis is solid and was built into every stage. But the eclipse-computer idea combines features that never existed together and relies on alignments that could arise by chance. Nothing in the excavated evidence requires or supports it.

Was there an 'original Stonehenge' in Wales?

Yes: the bluestones first stood in a circle at Waun Mawn in Preseli before being moved.Parker Pearson et al. 2021 reported empty stoneholes in an arc about 110 m across, the same diameter as Stonehenge's enclosure.
Not shown: Waun Mawn was a smaller, incomplete arrangement unrelated to Stonehenge.Later critiques question the dating, the reconstructed diameter and whether some holes are stoneholes at all.

The bold claim: The bluestones stood as a complete stone circle at Waun Mawn before being moved to Stonehenge.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The Waun Mawn excavations found real stoneholes in the right region, and the idea fits the Welsh links shown by cremations and the cow tooth. But the dating is loose, the circle is incomplete, and specialists disagree strongly about the reconstruction. It remains an interesting hypothesis.

Antikythera shipwreck, Greece

The Antikythera Mechanism

A shoebox of bronze gears that turned days into Moon phases, eclipses and Olympic years, two thousand years ago.

Mystery

The quick read

82Surviving fragments
30, hand-cut bronze with triangular teethSurviving gears
c. 13 cm across, 223 teethLargest gear (b1)
c. 34 × 18 × 9 cm (reconstruction)Case
Metonic (19 yr), Saros (18 yr), Callippic, Exeligmos, GamesBack dials
