c. 70–60 BCE, about 45 m deepShipwreck

A craftsman cut some 30 or more bronze gears by hand, with small triangular teeth about 1.6 mm apart, and mounted them in a wooden case with dials front and back. Turning a crank on the side drove the big main wheel, b1, once round for each year. Trains of gears with carefully chosen tooth counts turned that year into the motion of the Moon around the zodiac, the phase of the Moon, 19-year and 18-year calendar and eclipse cycles, and the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games. A pin-and-slot pair of gears reproduced the Moon's changing speed, following a theory of Hipparchos. X-ray computed tomography in 2005 revealed hidden tooth counts and thousands of letters of inscribed instructions.

The myth

Nothing like it existed for more than a thousand years, so it must be out-of-place technology, from time travellers, aliens or a vanished super-civilisation.

The reality

It fits a documented Greek tradition. Cicero describes geared bronze spheres attributed to Archimedes and Posidonius, and the Mechanism's inscriptions use Greek astronomical terms and Babylonian-derived cycles. What is extraordinary is its survival, since bronze was usually melted down. Open questions remain: who made it, where, exactly when, and how the lost planetary display worked.

Wow

Its gears modelled the Moon speeding up and slowing down along its orbit, using a pin sliding in a slot on a slowly rotating turntable, about two thousand years before modern clockwork.

Mystery meterA few loose ends
The deep dive10 min read · 2,237 words · 2 animated drawings

01A lump of bronze from the sea

In 1900 a boat of sponge divers from the island of Symi, blown off course by a storm, took shelter at Antikythera, a small island between the Peloponnese and Crete. One diver, Elias Stadiatis, went down about 45 m and came back, in the story told ever since, babbling about a heap of dead naked people on the seabed. They were bronze and marble statues. The captain, Dimitrios Kontos, reported the find, and in 1900 and 1901 the divers, supported by the Greek navy, raised statues, glass, pottery and coins in one of the first large underwater excavations in history.

Among the finds was a corroded lump of bronze and wood, not much bigger than a shoebox. It split into pieces as it dried. In May 1902, the archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gearwheel in one of them. A gearwheel, from a ship that coins and pottery date to around 70 to 60 BCE.

The ship itself was a large merchant vessel carrying luxury goods from the Greek east, probably towards Italy, where wealthy Romans collected Greek art. Its cargo included bronze and marble statues, fine glassware, jewellery and pottery. The Mechanism may have been part of that cargo, or a possession of someone on board. Either way, it was already old and perhaps already repaired when the ship went down, which helps explain why dating its making is so difficult.

A gearwheel, from a ship that sank more than two thousand years ago. It took a century to understand what it was for.

02Seventy years of squinting

The fragments were too fragile to take apart and too corroded to read easily. Early scholars, including the philologist Albert Rehm, guessed that it was an astronomical calculator, but the details were out of reach. The first person to make real progress was the historian of science Derek de Solla Price. From 1951 he studied the fragments, and in 1971 he worked with the Greek radiologist Charalampos Karakalos to make X-ray and gamma-ray images. His 1974 monograph, Gears from the Greeks, counted teeth, proposed a gear train and argued that the device was a calendar computer.

Price got many things right and some things wrong. In the 1990s and 2000s Michael Wright, then a curator at the Science Museum in London, working first with Allan Bromley, used linear tomography to see layers inside the fragments. Wright corrected parts of Price's scheme, identified the Moon-phase display and built a working model, completed in 2002, that included a speculative display of the planets. Each generation saw a little deeper into the corroded blocks.

032005: seeing inside the stone

The breakthrough came from new machines. In 2005 the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, a collaboration of British and Greek scientists and the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, brought two instruments to the museum. A high-energy X-ray computed tomography scanner built by the company X-Tek produced 3D slices through every fragment. A reflectance imaging dome developed at Hewlett-Packard photographed the surfaces under light from many angles, making faint letters on the corroded plates legible.

The results, published by Tony Freeth and colleagues in Nature in 2006, were spectacular. The team counted teeth on gears hidden deep inside the fragments, confirmed the purpose of the back dials, and doubled the amount of inscription that could be read. The text turned out to be a user's manual in Greek, naming the dials, the planets and the cycles. At least 30 gears survive, most in the largest fragment. The biggest, the four-spoked main wheel called b1, is about 13 cm across and carried 223 teeth, each a little triangle about 1.6 mm from the next, cut by hand.

04Turn the crank, move the Moon

Imagine holding the box. On its side is a crank. Turning it drives b1, and one full turn of b1 is one year: a pointer on the front moves the Sun once around the zodiac and a day-by-day calendar. From b1 a train of smaller gears speeds the motion up. The tooth counts tell the story: 64 teeth drive 38, then 48 drive 24, then 127 drive 32. Multiply it out and the result is 254 turns for every 19 turns of b1. That is the number of times the Moon goes around the zodiac in 19 years, a ratio the Babylonians knew well.

But the Moon does not travel at a steady speed. It moves faster when nearer to Earth and slower when farther away. The Greek astronomer Hipparchos, in the 2nd century BCE, modelled this with circles. The Mechanism models it with metal. Two gears, k1 and k2, sit face to face on slightly different axes. A pin on k1 slides in a slot in k2, so k2 runs a little ahead, then a little behind. Both ride on a large turntable, e3, which turns once in about 8.88 years, matching the slow swing of the Moon's orbit. The result, carried back to the front, is a Moon pointer that speeds up and slows down.

Cut by hand

No machine tools were involved. The gears were cut from thin bronze sheet, and the teeth were almost certainly marked out and filed by hand. Dividing a circle into exactly 223 equal teeth by eye is hard; CT scans show small irregularities in spacing and shape, the fingerprints of a human maker. The calendar holes, by contrast, were placed with astonishing care.

Finally, a small differential compares the motion of the Moon with that of the Sun and turns a little ball, half dark and half silvery, set in the Moon pointer. As the Moon moves away from the Sun, the ball turns to show a waxing crescent, a half, a full disc. It is a Moon-phase display on a hand-cranked machine from the Hellenistic world.

05The back of the box: calendars and eclipses

The back of the Mechanism carried two large spiral dials, one above the other. A pointer with a small follower tracked each spiral groove, stepping outwards turn by turn like the needle on a record.

  • Upper dial, Metonic: 235 lunar months in a five-turn spiral, equal to 19 years. It let the user keep a lunar calendar in step with the solar year. The month names on it are Corinthian, a clue to where the owner lived or the maker learned his trade.
  • Inside it, the Games dial: a four-sector dial naming the Panhellenic games, including Olympia, Isthmia, Nemea and Pythia, plus smaller festivals such as the Naa and the Halieia (Freeth et al. 2008).
  • Also inside the Metonic dial, a Callippic dial for the 76-year cycle, four Metonic cycles with one day removed.
  • Lower dial, Saros: 223 lunar months in a four-turn spiral, about 18 years and 11 days. Glyphs in 51 of the cells predict 38 lunar and 27 solar eclipses, some with the hour and, in later readings of the inscriptions, even the expected colour.
  • Inside it, the Exeligmos dial: three Saros cycles, 54 years and about a month, which brings eclipses back at nearly the same time of day.

The eclipse predictions are Babylonian in origin, based on long records of past eclipses, but written in Greek and cut into bronze. The Mechanism is a meeting of two traditions: Babylonian arithmetic cycles and Greek geometric models, packed into a portable box.

How would someone use it? Turn the crank until the front pointers show today's date. Then look at the back: the Metonic pointer shows which month of the 19-year cycle you are in, and the Games dial tells you which festival falls this year. Keep turning, and when the Saros pointer reaches a cell with a glyph, the inscription tells you to expect an eclipse that month, whether of Sun or Moon, and at about what hour. It was a calendar, an almanac and an eclipse forecaster in one.

06A cosmos on the front

The front dial is the most damaged part and the most debated. The inscriptions clearly mention the planets, and one fragment includes a list of synodic events for Venus and Mercury. But no planetary gears survive. In 2021 Freeth and colleagues at University College London published a full reconstruction, the Model of the Cosmos. They propose concentric rings on the front, displaying the Moon, the lunar nodes, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, with little index letters marking events such as stationary points and greatest elongations.

To drive the planets they needed accurate period relations that could be built from reasonably sized gears. The inscriptions contain the numbers 462 and 442, which the team identifies as periods for Venus and Saturn: 289 synodic cycles in 462 years for Venus and 427 in 442 years for Saturn, relations they argue could have been derived with ancient Greek methods. Their model has 69 gears in all, 34 of them in the lost planetary system in front of b1. It fits inside the case and accounts for surviving clues, such as features on the spokes of b1 and an unexplained gear in one fragment.

How do we know?

Much of the front is reconstruction, and the drawing marks it that way with dashed rings. The inscriptions tell us what was displayed; the surviving holes and bearings constrain where gears could sit; and the period relations must match ancient astronomy. Within those limits there could be more than one solution, so the 2021 model is a strong, carefully argued proposal rather than a recovered original.

07Fresh from the field: counting holes

Beneath the movable calendar ring on the front lies a ring of small holes, into which pins held the ring in place. Only part of it survives. How many holes were there? The calendar ring is marked with Egyptian month names and 365 days, so many assumed 365 holes. In 2020 a team led by Chris Budiselic measured the surviving holes on CT scans and argued statistically for about 354, the length of a lunar year.

In 2024 the Glasgow physicists Graham Woan and Joseph Bayley reanalysed the data with methods borrowed from gravitational-wave astronomy. Their best estimate is about 355, or 354 if holes near fractures are excluded; 360 is strongly disfavoured and 365 is implausible under their model. They also found the holes were placed with remarkable care: the radial scatter of their positions is only about 0.028 mm around a circle about 77 mm in radius. If the result holds, the Mechanism tracked a lunar calendar as well as the Egyptian solar one.

Other recent work adds healthy caution. A 2025 preprint by Esteban Szigety and Gustavo Arenas simulated the effect of the irregular, hand-cut triangular teeth and suggested that, as found, the gear train would have tended to jam or produce errors. That does not mean the device failed; it means the surviving, distorted fragments may not show the original precision, and that the maker was working at the edge of what hand tools allowed. A peer-reviewed response will be worth watching.

08Out of place? Not really

Because nothing comparable survives from antiquity, the Mechanism is a favourite of the ancient-mystery shelf. The argument goes like this: gearing of this complexity did not appear again for more than a thousand years, so it must come from outside history. Let us test that.

First, written sources describe such devices. Cicero, writing in the 1st century BCE, tells in On the Republic (1.21–22) how the general Marcellus brought home from captured Syracuse a bronze sphere made by Archimedes that showed the motions of the Sun, Moon and planets, and even eclipses. In On the Nature of the Gods (2.88) he mentions a similar sphere made by his teacher Posidonius on Rhodes. Second, the Mechanism is written in Greek, uses Greek astronomical terms, follows Hipparchos's lunar theory and uses Babylonian cycles known from cuneiform tablets. Third, its manufacture shows the marks of hand work: slightly irregular teeth, repairs and adjustments.

Why don't more survive? Because bronze was valuable and routinely melted down for reuse. The Mechanism escaped only because it sank. Its uniqueness is a fact about survival, not about origin.

The tradition did not vanish entirely either. A small geared sundial-calendar from the Byzantine world, about 1,500 years old and now in the Science Museum in London, shows that the idea of driving astronomical displays with gears survived in simpler forms. Medieval scholars in the Persian and Arabic-speaking world described geared calendars, and European astronomical clocks took the idea to new heights from the 14th century. The Antikythera Mechanism is the earliest and most complex known survivor of a long line, not an isolated miracle.

09Who made it, and when?

The Corinthian month names point to a place that used a Corinthian-style calendar, such as Corinth's colonies in northwest Greece or Syracuse in Sicily, the city of Archimedes. The Games dial includes the Naa, held at Dodona in Epirus, which supports a northwestern Greek connection for the user. Others have linked the astronomy to Rhodes, where Hipparchos worked and Posidonius later built his sphere. These ideas are not mutually exclusive: a device could be designed in one tradition and made or set for use in another.

The date is also debated. Letter forms and the ship's cargo suggest the 2nd or early 1st century BCE. In 2014 Christián Carman and James Evans argued from the eclipse predictor that its cycle begins in 205 BCE. A 2022 study by Aristeidis Voulgaris and colleagues proposed a starting date in 178 BCE. Neither date tells us when it was built, only the moment its calendar was set to start.

10What we still don't know

We know what most of it did. We do not know who made it, or for whom: a rich collector, a teacher, a temple? We do not know exactly how the planetary display worked, because those gears are lost. We do not know how accurate it was in use, or how many similar devices existed. And divers returning to the wreck since 2014 have found more objects, so small pieces of the story may still be lying on the seabed.

There is also the question of accuracy. The Mechanism's cycles are excellent over years, but its Babylonian-style models were not perfect, and any hand-made gear train accumulates small errors. A user would probably reset it from time to time against the sky or a calendar, much as we still adjust clocks. Future scans with even higher resolution may tell us more about wear on the teeth, which would show how much it was actually used.

What the Mechanism shows is simpler and more human: a Greek craftsman with files, saws and a head full of Babylonian and Greek astronomy built a pocket model of the sky, and it took twentieth- and twenty-first-century X-ray machines to read what he had written on it.

The big debates

Is the Mechanism out-of-place technology?

Yes: too advanced for its time.No comparable geared device survives from antiquity, and similar complexity reappears in European astronomical clocks only in the medieval period.
No: it belongs to a Greek tradition.Cicero describes geared spheres by Archimedes and Posidonius; the inscriptions are Greek; the gearing follows Hipparchos's lunar theory and Babylonian cycles; hand-work marks and errors are visible.

The bold claim: The Antikythera Mechanism could not have been made by ancient Greeks.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Every part of the device is explained by known Greek and Babylonian astronomy and by hand tools of the period. Written sources describe similar instruments, and bronze recycling explains why so few survive. Its rarity is a survival accident, not evidence of an outside origin.

Did the front show all five known planets?

Yes: a full cosmos.The inscriptions name the planets and list their synodic events; the 2021 model fits 34 planetary gears in front of b1 using ancient-style period relations (Freeth et al. 2021).
Unproven: the gears are lost.No planetary gear survives; alternative layouts are possible, and the 2021 relations are reconstructed rather than read directly from surviving teeth.

The bold claim: The Mechanism displayed the positions of Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The inscriptions make a planetary display very likely, and the 2021 model shows that it could fit. But without surviving planetary gears, the exact design remains a reconstruction.

Did the calendar ring count a 354-day lunar year?

Yes: about 354 holes.Two statistical analyses of hole positions on CT scans favour c. 354–355 holes; 360 is strongly disfavoured and 365 implausible (Budiselic et al. 2020; Woan & Bayley 2024).
Not certain.Only part of the ring survives, the fragments are distorted, and the visible calendar scale uses 365 Egyptian days.

The bold claim: The hidden ring of holes under the calendar ring had about 354 holes.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

Independent analyses using different statistical methods converge on about 354. The result depends on assumptions about how regularly the holes were spaced, but the precision of the surviving holes supports those assumptions.

Mediterranean and Mesopotamia

The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

A Greek tourist's bucket list of seven sights: one still stands, five left ruins, and one may never have existed where it was said to be.

The list itself was a Greek creation: a canon of theamata, 'things to be seen', not an official ranking, and its membership shifted before settling on the familiar seven. The wonders span 2,300 years and very different techniques: a mountain of cut limestone in Egypt, marble temples and tombs in western Anatolia, a gold and ivory statue at Olympia, a colossal bronze on Rhodes, and a stone tower with a fire at its summit at Alexandria. For the Hanging Gardens, Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley argues that the Greek accounts describe Sennacherib's palace garden at Nineveh, watered by canals and aqueducts, rather than a garden at Babylon.

The myth

The Colossus straddled the harbour of Rhodes, the Pharos had a mirror that burned enemy ships, and the Hanging Gardens were built by Nebuchadnezzar for a homesick queen.

The reality

Six wonders are well attested by ruins, excavated fragments, coins or reliable descriptions. The straddling Colossus comes from medieval and Renaissance imagination, and the burning mirror from later legend. The Gardens are the true puzzle: no Babylonian text mentions them, and whether they stood at Babylon, at Nineveh, or mainly in Greek literature is still debated.

Wow

Divers in Alexandria's Eastern Harbour have catalogued more than 3,300 architectural pieces since 1994, including granite blocks weighing 49 to 60 tonnes that probably fell from the Pharos.

Mystery meterReal open questions
The deep dive10 min read · 2,165 words · 2 animated drawings

01A bucket list, written in verse

Some time around or before 100 BCE, a poet from Sidon named Antipater wrote a short epigram that reads like a travel boast. He had seen the great sights of his world, he says, and then he saw one more that outshone them all. His poem is one of the earliest surviving lists of what we now call the Seven Wonders.

I have set eyes on the wall of lofty Babylon on which is a road for chariots, and the statue of Zeus by the Alpheus, and the hanging gardens, and the colossus of the Sun, and the huge labour of the high pyramids, and the vast tomb of Mausolus; but when I saw the house of Artemis that mounted to the clouds, those other marvels lost their brilliancy.

Antipater of Sidon, Greek Anthology 9.58, trans. W. R. Paton (1917)

Notice two things. First, Antipater's seven include the walls of Babylon, not the lighthouse of Alexandria; the list was not yet fixed. Second, he is not ranking engineering. He is describing theamata, 'things to be seen', the must-sees of a Greek-speaking traveller in the world opened up by Alexander's conquests.

Drawn together at one scale, the seven make an odd family. One is a geometric mountain. Two are temples or tombs, two are colossal statues, one is a tower and one is a garden nobody can find. Their ages span 2,300 years, so that the Great Pyramid was already an antiquity older than the Pharos is to us when Antipater wrote.

02Who chose the seven?

Nobody, exactly. Greek writers had compiled lists of marvels since at least the 3rd century BCE; the scholar-poet Callimachus is said to have written one, now lost. A short treatise On the Seven Wonders survives under the name of Philo of Byzantium, although scholars doubt it is by the famous engineer of that name and date it much later. Its list matches Antipater's, and the manuscript breaks off before the last entry.

Seven was a satisfying, sacred-feeling number, and the choices reflect a Greek view of the world: six of the seven stood in lands ruled by Greek-speaking kings after Alexander, and the seventh was in Egypt, which Greeks had long admired. The Pharos only displaced the walls of Babylon in later lists, and the canonical modern seven became standard in the Renaissance, when artists such as Maarten van Heemskerck engraved them as a set.

The Seven Wonders are less a verdict on ancient engineering than a snapshot of what Greek tourists thought worth the trip.

03The survivor: the Great Pyramid

The oldest wonder is the only one still standing. Built for Khufu around 2560 BCE, the Great Pyramid rose about 146.6 m on a base about 230 m square, the tallest human-made structure for roughly 3,800 years. We know unusually much about how it was built, from the quarries on the Giza plateau, the settlement of its workers, and even the logbook of a boatman named Merer who shipped its white casing stone. It has its own deep dive in this collection, so here it serves as the yardstick: every other wonder in the drawing above is measured against it.

04The garden nobody can find

The Hanging Gardens are the wonder that most resists evidence. The earliest known mention comes from Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek around 290 BCE, quoted centuries later by Josephus: Nebuchadnezzar II, he says, built a 'hanging paradise' for a wife from Media who missed her mountains. Later Greek and Roman writers describe terraces on vaulted galleries, deep soil for large trees, and machines lifting water from the river.

The park extended four plethra on each side, and since the approach to the garden sloped like a hillside and the several parts of the structure rose from one another tier on tier, the appearance of the whole resembled that of a theatre.

Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 2.10, trans. C. H. Oldfather (1933)

The trouble is Babylon itself. Nebuchadnezzar left many inscriptions about his building works, and none mentions a garden. Robert Koldewey, who excavated the city from 1899 to 1917, identified a vaulted building in the Southern Palace as the substructure of the Gardens. Tablets found there turned out to record oil rations for foreign captives, including Jehoiachin, king of Judah, which suggests storerooms rather than a garden.

In 1994, and at book length in 2013, Stephanie Dalley of Oxford proposed a bold solution. The Gardens were real, she argues, but they stood at Nineveh, more than 400 km to the north, in the palace of the Assyrian king Sennacherib around 700 BCE. Sennacherib boasted of a garden that was a wonder for all peoples, fed by a canal system that included a stone aqueduct at Jerwan about 280 m long, and he describes casting great bronze devices to raise water, which Dalley reads as early water screws. A relief from Nineveh shows a garden planted on terraces and arches, fed by an aqueduct. Later Greek writers, she suggests, confused Assyrian Nineveh with Babylon.

Critics answer that Greek sources consistently say Babylon, that no garden structure has been excavated at Nineveh either, and that parts of Babylon near the river remain unexplored. Some think the Gardens were mainly a literary creation. The honest position is uncertainty: a real Mesopotamian royal garden probably lies behind the legend, but where, and how much it resembled the descriptions, is open.

05Zeus at Olympia: a god too big for his house

Around 435 BCE the Athenian sculptor Pheidias made a seated Zeus for the god's temple at Olympia, the sanctuary of the Olympic Games. Its core was a wooden framework covered with ivory for the skin and gold for the robes. Modern estimates put it at about 12 m high, inside a temple only about 20 m tall. Ancient visitors found it overwhelming, and slightly too big.

The artist is thought to have missed the proper symmetry, for he showed Zeus seated but almost touching the roof with his head, thus making the impression that if Zeus arose and stood erect he would unroof the temple.

Strabo, Geography 8.3.30, trans. H. L. Jones (1927)

Keeping such a statue alive took maintenance. The traveller Pausanias, writing in the 2nd century CE, says the floor in front of it was paved with black stone and edged to hold a shallow pool of olive oil, which helped protect the ivory from the damp of the Olympian valley. He also records that the descendants of Pheidias held the hereditary job of cleaning the statue. A wonder, in other words, came with a staff.

The statue is gone, but its workshop was found. German excavators in the 1950s uncovered a building at Olympia with the same dimensions as the temple's inner chamber, containing tools, fragments of ivory and glass, and clay moulds used to shape the golden drapery. A small black-glazed jug from the site is inscribed on its base 'I belong to Pheidias'. Few ancient artists can be tied to a workshop so directly.

The end is less certain. The sanctuary declined after pagan festivals were banned in the late 4th century CE. One Byzantine tradition says the statue was taken to Constantinople and destroyed in a palace fire around 475 CE; another has it perishing with the temple at Olympia. Either way, nothing of it is known to survive.

06Artemis at Ephesus: the wonder that burned

Antipater's favourite was the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, on the coast of modern Turkey. The first great marble temple there was begun around 550 BCE with gifts from Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia. In 356 BCE a man named Herostratus set it on fire, by later accounts simply to make his name immortal. Ancient writers liked to add that it burned on the night Alexander the Great was born.

The Ephesians rebuilt it on the same plan and even larger. Pliny the Elder gives its size as 425 by 225 Roman feet, with 127 columns each 60 feet high, 36 of them carved with figures at the base. That makes a building about 125 m long and columns about 18 m tall. Damaged by Gothic raiders in the 260s CE and later quarried, it vanished into a marsh.

The English engineer John Turtle Wood searched for it for six years before finding its pavement in 1869, some 6 m below the surface. In 1904 and 1905 David Hogarth dug beneath the earliest levels and found a foundation deposit of small electrum coins, among the oldest coins in the world. Today a single column, reassembled from fragments, stands in a pond where storks nest.

07The tomb that named all tombs

Mausolus, a Persian-appointed ruler of Caria in southwest Anatolia, died in 353 BCE. His wife and sister Artemisia completed the tomb he had begun at his capital, Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum). Pliny says it was designed by the architects Satyros and Pytheos and decorated by four famous sculptors, Scopas, Bryaxis, Timotheus and Leochares, one on each side. It stood 140 Roman feet high by Pliny's account, about 41 m, and modern reconstructions range up to about 45 m: a tall podium, a ring of columns, a stepped pyramid roof and, on top, a four-horse chariot.

It was grand enough to give its name to every monumental tomb since. Earthquakes had damaged it by the Middle Ages, and between the 1490s and 1520s the Knights of St John reused its stones and burned its marble for lime while building their Castle of St Peter in Bodrum. In 1856 and 1857 Charles Newton excavated the site and shipped surviving sculptures to the British Museum, including two colossal figures long nicknamed Mausolus and Artemisia.

08The Colossus did not straddle anything

In 305 BCE the city of Rhodes survived a year-long siege by Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger. To give thanks to their sun god Helios, the Rhodians sold the siege machines he abandoned and commissioned the sculptor Chares of Lindos to make a colossal bronze statue. It took 12 years.

This statue, fifty-six years after it was erected, was thrown down by an earthquake; but even as it lies, it excites our wonder and admiration. Few men can clasp the thumb in their arms, and its fingers are larger than most statues.

Pliny the Elder, Natural History 34.41, trans. J. Bostock and H. T. Riley (1855)

Pliny gives its height as 70 cubits, about 33 m, a little shorter than the Statue of Liberty from heel to head. It fell in the earthquake of about 226 BCE, and according to Strabo an oracle warned the Rhodians not to raise it again. The pieces lay where they fell for roughly 800 years. A Byzantine chronicler says that in the 650s CE they were sold to a merchant who carried the bronze away on 900 camels.

How do you build a bronze giant? Pliny noticed that the broken limbs of the fallen statue gaped open and that large stones could be seen inside, which he took to be ballast used to steady it. The treatise attributed to Philo describes the figure being raised in place, course by course, with a mound of earth heaped around it as it grew, so that the workers were always on the ground. In 1956 the metalwork specialist Herbert Maryon argued that the skin was more probably made of hammered bronze plates fixed to an iron framework than of huge cast sections. The details are reconstruction, but a stone-weighted core inside an iron and bronze shell is the most widely accepted picture.

The famous image of the Colossus with one foot on each side of the harbour entrance comes from medieval travellers' tales and Renaissance engravings, not from ancient sources. It is also impossible as engineering: legs spread across a harbour mouth could not have carried a statue of that weight in bronze, and when it fell it would have blocked the port. Most scholars place it on land, either near the harbour or in the sanctuary of Helios; its exact site has not been found.

09The Pharos: a lighthouse that named all lighthouses

The youngest wonder rose on the island of Pharos at the entrance to Alexandria's harbour, completed around 280 BCE under the early Ptolemies. Pliny credits its design to Sostratus of Cnidus and says it cost 800 talents. It stood for over 1,500 years, long enough to be measured by Arab travellers. Al-Balawi, visiting in 1166, gave the base as about 30 m a side and described the octagonal and cylindrical stages above it.

Why build it so tall? The Egyptian coast around Alexandria is low, flat and lined with shoals, and a sailor approaching from the open Mediterranean had almost nothing to steer by. A tower visible from far out at sea by day, and marked by a fire at night, turned a dangerous approach into a routine one for the grain ships that fed the Mediterranean world. It was a monument, but also very practical infrastructure.

The tower's three stages, a square base, an octagonal middle and a round top, are a pattern repeated in minarets and later lighthouses. A fire burned at the summit at night, and several medieval accounts speak of a great mirror by day. Roman coins of Alexandria show a statue on top, identified as Zeus or Poseidon. Estimates of the total height cluster around 100 m, with Arab accounts implying about 103 to 118 m.

Earthquakes brought it down in stages: one in 956 toppled the top, a severe one in 1303 wrecked it, and by the mid-14th century the traveller Ibn Battuta found it too ruined to enter. In 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on the site, using its stones. Since 1994, divers led by Jean-Yves Empereur have mapped the seabed beside the fort, finding granite blocks of 49 to 60 tonnes, sphinxes, obelisks and colossal Ptolemaic statues. In 2025, parts of the entrance and foundation paving were lifted for a project to rebuild the tower digitally.

Words that survived

The Pharos outlived its stones in language. The French phare, Italian and Spanish faro and Portuguese farol all mean lighthouse and all come from the name of the island. The Mausoleum did the same for tombs. Two of the seven are ruins, but they are still in our dictionaries.

10What remains uncertain

  • Where the Hanging Gardens were, if they were one real place: Babylon, Nineveh, or partly a literary composite.
  • The exact pose and location of the Colossus of Rhodes.
  • The Pharos's exact height and the true nature of its famous 'mirror'.
  • The fate of Pheidias's Zeus after Olympia.

The mystery rating for the set is 3 out of 5, and almost all of that comes from the Gardens. For the other six, the evidence ranges from very good (the pyramid, the Mausoleum sculptures, the Pharos blocks) to decent (the Colossus, known mainly from texts). Together they show what ancient builders prized: height, costly materials, famous artists, and above all the power to make a visitor stop and stare.

The big debates

Were the Hanging Gardens really at Nineveh?

Yes: the Greek accounts describe Sennacherib's garden at Nineveh.Sennacherib's inscriptions on his garden, canals, Jerwan aqueduct and bronze water-raising devices; a Nineveh relief of an irrigated terraced garden; the silence of Babylonian texts (Dalley 1994, 2013).
No, or not shown: the Gardens were at Babylon, or largely literary.Every classical source names Babylon; Berossus was a Babylonian; no garden structure has been excavated at Nineveh; parts of Babylon remain unexcavated.

The bold claim: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were actually Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

Dalley's case is careful and fits the Assyrian texts and images well, and it explains the Babylonian silence. But it relies on the Greek writers having confused two cities, and there is no excavated garden at Nineveh to confirm it. Leading specialists remain divided.

Did the Colossus straddle the harbour?

Yes: it stood astride the harbour mouth, with ships sailing between its legs.Medieval travellers' stories and Renaissance engravings such as van Heemskerck's.
No: it stood on land.No ancient source describes the pose; bronze legs spread across a harbour mouth could not carry the load; a fall would have blocked the harbour; ancient accounts describe the statue lying on the ground for centuries.

The bold claim: The Colossus of Rhodes stood with one foot on each side of the harbour entrance.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The image appears more than a thousand years after the statue fell. Ancient writers who saw its fallen pieces never mention a harbour pose, and the engineering of a 33 m bronze with its legs spread over open water does not work. Its exact site and pose are unknown, but a straddle is ruled out.

Could the Pharos's mirror burn ships?

Yes: a great mirror focused sunlight to set enemy ships on fire.Medieval Arab and later European legends about the Pharos mirror.
No: at most a polished surface to reflect daylight or firelight as a signal.No ancient source mentions the weapon; focusing enough sunlight to ignite a ship at sea from a tower would need an enormous, precisely curved mirror aimed at a moving target.

The bold claim: The Pharos of Alexandria carried a mirror that burned enemy ships at sea.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The mirror is reported only in medieval accounts written long after the tower had been damaged, and the burning story belongs to the same legendary tradition as Archimedes' death ray. A reflector for signalling is plausible; a ship-burning weapon has no evidence behind it.

Roman Mediterranean

Roman concrete

Harbour piers that have sat in seawater for 2,000 years, and white lumps once dismissed as sloppy mixing that may be tiny repair kits.

Roman builders burned limestone into quicklime, then combined it with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and chunks of rock or broken brick. Instead of pouring a fluid slurry, they laid the mortar and tamped the aggregate in by hand, layer by layer, behind timber formwork or brick facings. Evidence from Privernum and from an unfinished house at Pompeii suggests many crews used 'hot mixing': quicklime blended dry with ash and only then wetted, which releases heat, speeds setting and leaves behind white, calcium-rich lime clasts. For harbours, the lime and ash mortar was lowered into flooded wooden forms and set underwater. Over centuries, seawater percolating through the concrete dissolved some of the volcanic material and grew new interlocking minerals, including aluminous tobermorite and phillipsite.

The myth

Roman concrete is a lost super-material, stronger than anything we can make, whose secret recipe modern science cannot crack.

The reality

The basic recipe was written down by Vitruvius and has been reproduced in the lab and at sea. Roman concrete is weaker in compression than modern structural concrete. Its real advantages are chemical: volcanic ash that keeps reacting, lime clasts that can reseal cracks, and no steel inside to rust. The open questions are about details, such as how widespread hot mixing was and how recipes varied from site to site.

Wow

A breakwater poured around 50 BCE in the Bay of Naples still stands, and inside it crystals that are hard to make even in a modern lab have been growing out of seawater.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive11 min read · 2,411 words · 2 animated drawings

01The lumps everybody ignored

Pick up a fist-sized chunk of Roman concrete and you will see grey volcanic grit, dark nuggets of rock, perhaps a red sliver of broken tile. Look closer and you will also see white specks, some as small as a grain of rice, some the size of a pea. For more than a century, archaeologists and engineers glanced at these lime clasts and shrugged. They looked like the Roman equivalent of lumps in gravy: evidence that someone in a hurry had not stirred the mortar properly.

That shrug turned out to be a mistake. In 2023 a team led by Admir Masic at MIT studied samples from a city wall at Privernum, south-east of Rome, and argued that the white lumps were not sloppiness but a signature. They were the leftovers of a particular way of making mortar, and they may be part of the reason so much Roman concrete is still standing. Two years later the same group walked onto a Roman building site at Pompeii that had been abandoned mid-job in 79 CE, and found the raw materials still sitting in piles.

The white specks that looked like lazy mixing may be a built-in repair kit, waiting centuries for a crack.

This is the story of a material that built harbours, aqueducts, markets and the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth. It is also a story about how much you can learn by taking old claims, and old lumps, seriously. Roman concrete is not magic, and it is not simply 'stronger' than ours. But it does things modern concrete struggles with, and chemists are only now working out how.

02Dust from Puteoli

The Romans did not invent lime mortar; builders around the Mediterranean had burned limestone for centuries. Heat limestone to around 900 °C and it gives off carbon dioxide and turns into quicklime, a caustic white powder. Add water and it becomes slaked lime, which slowly hardens again by soaking up carbon dioxide from the air. That is fine for plaster, but it sets slowly and never under water.

The breakthrough came from the volcanic landscape around the Bay of Naples. Mix lime with the right volcanic ash and the ash's glassy, silica- and alumina-rich particles react with the lime to form a hard binder, even in wet conditions. The Romans called the best of it pulvis Puteolanus, the dust of Puteoli (modern Pozzuoli), and we still call such materials pozzolans. By the 2nd century BCE builders in Campania and Rome were using lime and ash mortars packed with chunks of tuff, the soft volcanic stone the region is made of.

There is also a kind of powder which from natural causes produces astonishing results. ... This substance, when mixed with lime and rubble, not only lends strength to buildings of other kinds, but even when piers of it are constructed in the sea, they set hard under water.

Vitruvius, De architectura 2.6.1, trans. M. H. Morgan (1914)

Vitruvius, writing in the 20s BCE, even gives a recipe for marine work: take the powder from the country between Cumae and the promontory of Minerva and mix it 'in the proportion of two to one', two parts ash to one of lime. A century later Pliny the Elder, who would die in the eruption of 79 CE, sounded almost indignant that such a humble material should be so powerful. Who could marvel enough, he asked, that the dust of the hills of Puteoli, once submerged, 'turns into a single mass of stone that withstands the attacks of the waves and becomes stronger every day' (Natural History 35.166, trans. H. Rackham, 1952).

It is worth noticing how the Romans actually built with it. Modern concrete is poured as a fluid and flows around steel bars. Roman builders usually laid a bed of stiff mortar, then set fist-sized pieces of stone or brick into it, called caementa, and tamped them down, course after course. On land the concrete core was often hidden behind a facing of brick or small stone blocks. The word 'cement' comes from those rubble chunks, not from the binder.

03Pouring stone into the sea

The boldest use of the new material was in harbours. Between 2002 and 2009 the Roman Maritime Concrete Study (ROMACONS), led by Christopher Brandon, Robert Hohlfelder, Marie Jackson and John Peter Oleson, drilled cores out of Roman piers, breakwaters and pilae (free-standing concrete blocks) at sites from Italy to Israel, Egypt, Crete and Turkey. They found blocks of remarkable size. Off Nisida in the Bay of Naples one pila has sides of up to 15.2 m and stands over 9.5 m tall. At Portus Iulius, the naval harbour Agrippa built in the 30s BCE, the outer pila measures about 10 by 10 m and more than 6 m high.

How do you place concrete in the sea? Vitruvius describes driving a cofferdam of oak stakes with ties between them into the water, and the cores and timber impressions show several solutions in practice. In one common approach, the 'flooded form', a box of posts and planks was built on the seabed and the mortar was simply lowered into the seawater inside it, where it set without ever drying out. At Caesarea in Judaea, Herod's engineers went further, building double-walled wooden boxes about 11 by 15 by 4 m on shore, towing them out and sinking them, and casting barge-shaped forms full of concrete. One block from the North Breakwater measures roughly 15 by 11.5 by 2 m.

Caesarea is also a lesson in logistics. The ROMACONS team estimates the harbour needed around 35,000 cubic metres of concrete, and the volcanic ash in it came from the Bay of Naples, shipped across roughly 2,000 km of sea. Timber from a pila at Baia has been radiocarbon dated to about 50 BCE, so some of these structures have been sitting in salt water for two thousand years.

How do we know? Building a pila the Roman way

In 2004 the ROMACONS team built a test pila in the harbour of Brindisi: a wooden form about 2 by 2 by 2 m, in water about 1.7 m deep. They mixed two parts pozzolana from Bacoli with one part lime using seawater, lowered the mortar in wicker baskets with trip lines, laid it in layers about 20 cm thick and threw tuff chunks in by hand, tamping as they went. About 8 m³ of concrete took 273 person-hours. Cores drilled later let them compare their block with the ancient ones.

04Crystals that grow out of seawater

Modern concrete does not love the sea. Salt water attacks the cement paste and, above all, the steel reinforcement inside it. Roman harbour concrete seems to have made peace with its environment instead, and Marie Jackson's team at the University of Utah has spent years working out why.

In 2013 they reported aluminous tobermorite, a rare layered calcium silicate mineral, in the lime-rich parts of a breakwater from the Baianus Sinus in the Bay of Naples. Tobermorite is prized in engineering because its crystals are strong and platy, but making it synthetically usually requires high temperatures. In 2017, working on cores from the Baianus Sinus and Portus Neronis breakwaters and a pier at Portus Cosanus in Tuscany, they reported something stranger: tobermorite and a zeolite mineral called phillipsite had also grown later, at ordinary seawater temperatures, inside pores, in cracks and in the altered edges of volcanic crystals and pumice.

Their interpretation is a slow, continuous reaction. Seawater percolates through the concrete, dissolves some of the volcanic glass and minerals, and the resulting alkaline fluids precipitate new, interlocking crystals. In other words, the sea that should be destroying the structure appears to be feeding it. Jackson's team has pointed out that this is what Pliny described: a mass of stone 'stronger every day'. He meant it as rhetoric, but the chemistry is now consistent with him.

The sea that should be destroying the pier appears to be feeding it, one crystal at a time.

It is important not to overstate this. The new minerals are observed in a handful of sampled structures, and 'growing crystals' is not the same as a measured increase in strength over centuries. The work does suggest, though, that the volcanic ash was not just a filler. It was a reactive ingredient that kept working long after the builders went home.

05Hot mixing and the crack that heals itself

Back on dry land, the Privernum samples posed a different question: what are the white lime clasts? Vitruvius and Pliny both talk about lime that has been slaked (soaked in water) before use, and scholars long assumed Roman builders worked the same way. If you start with well-slaked lime paste, you should not get chunky white lumps.

Linda Seymour, Admir Masic and colleagues mapped the clasts with electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy and found textures that point to high temperatures. Their proposal, published in Science Advances in 2023, is 'hot mixing': quicklime, not only slaked lime, was mixed with the ash and aggregate, and then water was added. Quicklime reacts violently with water, heating the whole batch by roughly 55–60 °C and, locally, to more than 200 °C. That heat speeds up setting, allows chemical reactions that would not happen in a cold mix, and leaves behind brittle, porous nodules of calcium-rich material: the lime clasts.

Here is the clever part. Because the clasts are weak and brittle, a crack running through the concrete tends to pass through them. Water that later enters the crack meets a fresh, high-surface-area reservoir of calcium, dissolves some of it, and carries a calcium-rich solution along the crack. That calcium can then recrystallise as calcium carbonate, or react with the volcanic ash, sealing the gap.

The team tested the idea with modern mixes. They made concrete with and without quicklime, cracked the samples, re-mated the halves with a gap of about 0.5 mm and ran water through them at 10 to 30 litres an hour. Over one to three weeks the flow through the lime-clast samples fell to practically zero; the controls kept leaking throughout the 30-day test. It is a laboratory result on modern analogues, not a measurement on an ancient wall, but it shows the mechanism works.

06A building site frozen in 79 CE

Stand in a half-finished house at Pompeii in the summer of 79 CE. Walls are being rebuilt, perhaps after earthquake damage. Blocks of yellow tuff brought from the Naples area are stacked up, broken roof tiles have been set aside for recycling, and amphorae have been reused to hold lime. Then Vesuvius erupts and everything stops.

That is roughly what archaeologists found at a house in Regio IX, insula 10, excavated in recent years. In a study published in Nature Communications in December 2025, E. Vaserman, James Weaver, Admir Masic and colleagues from MIT and the Pompeii Archaeological Park analysed the site's materials. Among them were piles of dry, premixed lime and volcanic ash, with fragments of quicklime several millimetres across, ready to be wetted and used. The team also recovered tools such as bronze and iron plumb bobs and balance scales, and found the site organised into separate storage areas for tiles, tuff and premixed mortar.

Fresh from the field

The Pompeii study (Vaserman et al. 2025) gives the first direct archaeological snapshot of hot mixing in progress: dry lime and ash blended in advance, with quicklime fragments that match the lime clasts seen in finished Roman walls. It also shows that what a Roman architect wrote and what a Roman crew did were not necessarily the same thing. Vitruvius describes slaked lime; this crew was, it seems, working with quicklime.

One site cannot tell us how every Roman builder worked for six centuries. What it does is turn hot mixing from an inference, based on textures under a microscope, into something you can see sitting on a building site. It also underlines a theme of this whole story: the most useful evidence is often in the mess, not in the manuals.

07Why your concrete cracks and theirs sometimes does not

In 1824 an English bricklayer, Joseph Aspdin, patented Portland cement, named for its resemblance to Portland stone. It is made by firing limestone and clay at around 1,450 °C into clinker, then grinding it with gypsum. Mixed with sand, gravel and water it forms concrete that is strong, fast and cheap, and when steel bars are cast inside to handle tension, you can build bridges and towers the Romans could only dream of.

That same design creates the weak point. Steel rusts, and rust takes up more room than the steel it came from. Once water and salts reach the reinforcement, it expands, cracks the concrete from the inside and lets in more water. Jackson has put it bluntly: in the sea, much of our construction would be 'a mass of corroding steel' long before two thousand years had passed. Roman concrete, with no steel inside, never faced that problem.

  • Strength: modern structural concrete is generally much stronger in compression than Roman mortars. Rome built massive walls because it had to.
  • Durability: Roman mixes keep reacting with water; lime clasts can reseal cracks; there is no steel to corrode.
  • Carbon: Portland clinker needs around 1,450 °C against roughly 900 °C for Roman lime, and cement production is responsible for about 8% of global CO₂ emissions (Lehne and Preston, Chatham House, 2018).
  • Speed: Portland concrete sets and gains strength quickly and predictably, which modern construction schedules depend on.

That is why engineers are interested. Nobody plans to build skyscrapers from tuff and lime, but Roman-inspired additives, such as volcanic ash replacing part of the Portland cement, or lime clasts added to encourage self-healing, could make some modern concretes last longer and emit less carbon. Several research groups are now testing such blends, including for structures that must survive in seawater.

08Busting the super-concrete myth

Every few years a headline announces that scientists have 'finally cracked' the secret of Roman concrete, as if it were a lost formula locked in a vault. The reality is less mysterious and more interesting. The recipe was never lost: Vitruvius wrote it down, and ROMACONS mixed and cast it in the sea in 2004. What researchers have been uncovering is why particular mixes behave the way they do, and how Roman practice varied.

There is also a survivor's bias. We see the Roman concrete that lasted: the Pantheon, harbour piers, aqueduct cores. We do not see the countless Roman structures that cracked, slumped or were quarried away. Some Roman builders cut corners, some local ashes were poor pozzolans, and plenty of Roman buildings needed repairs within decades. The surviving examples are a filtered sample of the best-built and best-placed.

Open questions remain. How common was hot mixing across the empire, and did recipes differ between regions, periods and building types? How much of the durability of harbour concrete comes from the ash, how much from the lime, how much from the placement method? And can the slow, centuries-long reactions that help Roman concrete be sped up enough to be useful to engineers who cannot wait two thousand years for results?

The recipe was never lost. What we are learning is why the best Roman mixes still work.

What is not in doubt is the core lesson. The Romans built with materials that kept reacting with their surroundings, and they sometimes left in 'flaws' that turned out to be features. For a civilisation that produced some of history's great engineers, it is fitting that their humblest ingredient, a pinch of white lime in a grey mortar, is still teaching us something.

The big debates

Is Roman concrete simply better than modern concrete?

Yes: it lasts far longer.Harbour structures have survived about 2,000 years in seawater, where modern reinforced concrete can degrade within decades.
No: it is a different material with different strengths.Roman mortars are weaker in compression and slower to gain strength; their durability comes from reactive ash, lime clasts and the absence of corroding steel, plus survivor bias.

The bold claim: Roman concrete is stronger than modern concrete.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

In raw strength, modern structural concrete generally wins by a wide margin. What the best Roman concretes have is longevity in particular settings, especially the sea, thanks to chemistry that keeps working and the lack of steel reinforcement. 'Better' depends on the job; 'stronger' is simply not what the evidence shows.

Did Roman builders routinely hot-mix with quicklime?

Yes: the clasts and the Pompeii site point that way.Lime clast textures at Privernum indicate high-temperature reactions, and the Pompeii building site had dry premixed lime and ash with quicklime fragments.
Not yet shown to be universal.Vitruvius and Pliny describe slaked lime, and the direct evidence comes from a small number of sites and periods.

The bold claim: Hot mixing with quicklime was a common Roman technique, not a one-off.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

Two independent lines of evidence, microscopic textures and an actual building site, fit hot mixing, and lime clasts are common in Roman mortars. But sampling is still limited, and Roman practice varied across a huge empire and six centuries. The claim is well supported for some sites; its generality is still being tested.

Is Roman concrete a lost secret?

Yes: modern science cannot reproduce it.Popular articles regularly describe the recipe as lost or mysterious.
No: the recipe survives and has been reproduced.Vitruvius records the mix; ROMACONS cast a Vitruvian pila at sea in 2004; labs have made hot-mixed, self-healing analogues.

The bold claim: The Roman recipe is a lost secret that modern science cannot reproduce.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The ingredients and proportions are documented in ancient texts and have been replicated. What is new is an understanding of the mechanisms, such as seawater-grown minerals and self-healing lime clasts. That is ordinary science filling in details, not the recovery of a lost formula.

Rome, Italy

The Pantheon dome

A 43.3 m concrete dome with a hole in the top, standing unreinforced for nineteen centuries: Rome's boldest engineering bet still pays out.

A ring foundation carries a cylindrical drum about 6 m thick, hollowed by niches and threaded with brick relieving arches that channel loads into eight solid piers. On top, the dome was laid in horizontal courses of unreinforced concrete over a huge timber centering. The builders graded the aggregate by height: dense travertine low down, then tuff and brick, and finally light tuff and volcanic scoria or pumice near the top, so the concrete gets lighter as it rises. The shell thins from about 6 m at its base to about 1.2 m at the oculus, whose rim of upright tiles acts as a compression ring. Stepped rings outside add weight to the haunches, and 140 sunken coffers inside remove it where it is least useful.

The myth

The Pantheon stands because of a secret Roman super-concrete that modern engineers cannot explain.

The reality

Its survival is well understood: a thick drum, graded lightweight concrete, a thinning shell, stepped rings and a compression ring at the oculus keep the forces in compression. The dome cracked early along its meridians and now works partly like a ring of arches. Continuous use and maintenance helped too. What remains uncertain are the details of its formwork, its construction sequence and who designed it.

Wow

Its 43.3 m dome has been the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world for about 1,900 years, and it has a hole almost 9 m wide in the top.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,276 words · 2 animated drawings

01A hole in the sky

Walk out of the bright, noisy Piazza della Rotonda, between granite columns as thick as tree trunks, through bronze doors taller than a two-storey house, and the city goes quiet. You are standing inside a sphere. The floor is a disc 43.3 m across; the dome above rises so that its top is exactly 43.3 m over your head. If you could inflate a giant ball in here, it would just touch the floor and kiss the roof.

At the very top there is no roof at all. The oculus, a round opening about 8.3 to 8.9 m across depending on who measures it, is the building's only window. On a sunny day a disc of light, sharp-edged as a spotlight, crawls slowly across the coffers and down the walls. On a rainy day the rain falls straight in, and drains away through small holes in a floor that slopes gently to shed water.

Nineteen centuries on, no one has built a larger unreinforced concrete dome.

This is the Pantheon, rebuilt in the early 2nd century CE and in continuous use ever since, first as a temple and, from 609, as a church. It is probably the best-preserved major building of ancient Rome. How a structure this bold, made of concrete with no steel inside, has survived earthquakes, lightning, looting and nearly two thousand winters is a story of clever geometry, careful material choices and a couple of lucky breaks.

02Agrippa's name, Hadrian's building

Look up at the porch and the inscription seems to settle the question of authorship: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT, 'Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this'. Agrippa, Augustus' right-hand man, did build a Pantheon here around 27 to 25 BCE. But that building burned in 80 CE, was restored under Domitian, and burned again after a lightning strike in 110. What stands today is a complete rebuild.

For a long time it was credited to Hadrian, who became emperor in 117. Then archaeologists looked at the bricks. Roman brickyards often stamped their products with the names of owners, managers or consuls, which makes them datable. Lise Hetland's 2007 study and Mark Wilson Jones' later work showed that nearly all the stamps in the building are late Trajanic or early Hadrianic, pointing to construction starting around 114 CE, under Trajan, and finishing under Hadrian, with dedication around 125 to 128.

At Rome he restored the Pantheon, the Voting-enclosure, the Basilica of Neptune, very many temples, the Forum of Augustus, the Baths of Agrippa, and dedicated all of them in the names of their original builders.

Historia Augusta, Life of Hadrian 19.10, trans. D. Magie (Loeb, 1921)

So the inscription is a courtesy, not a lie: Hadrian, according to his ancient biographer, liked to put the original builders' names on the monuments he restored. It is also a neat reminder to read ancient labels with care. Who actually designed the new Pantheon is unknown. Hadrian was a keen amateur architect; Trajan's great engineer Apollodorus of Damascus has been suggested; the brick stamps make a Trajanic start likely, but no document names the architect.

03A sphere in a cylinder

The plan is disarmingly simple: a rectangular porch, a transitional block, and a round hall, the rotunda. The rotunda is a drum whose interior height to the springing of the dome equals the dome's radius, 21.65 m, so the hemisphere on top completes a perfect sphere. The drum wall is about 6.4 m thick, but it is not solid. It is carved into seven great niches plus the entrance bay, and threaded with hidden chambers and brick arches.

From outside, the dome looks surprisingly low. That is because the drum wall rises well above the springing, to about 30 m, wrapping the heavy lower part of the dome. Above that, a series of stepped rings climbs the outside of the shell before it smooths into the gentle cap around the oculus. You see the sphere only from inside, which is precisely the point.

The numbers are round in Roman terms. The diameter is usually equated with 150 Roman feet and the oculus with 30, and the portico columns were cut as 40-foot shafts. The building is a statement about geometry and the cosmos as much as about engineering. The ancient historian Cassius Dio, writing about Agrippa's earlier building, suggested the name came either from the many gods whose statues it held or because its vaulted roof resembled the heavens. Both readings fit the building we have.

Why a sphere? Roman architects inherited from Greek geometry a deep respect for the circle and the sphere as the most perfect of forms, and Vitruvius opens his discussion of temple design with the proportions of the human body inscribed in a circle and a square. A building whose interior is literally a sphere, lit from a single point at its summit, turns that ideal into something you can walk inside. It is also, conveniently, a form that concrete can achieve and cut stone cannot easily match: a single continuous shell poured course by course, without a forest of internal supports.

04Heavy at the bottom, light at the top

A dome is an arch spun around a vertical axis. Its weight pushes down, and near the base it also pushes outwards, trying to burst the ring it sits on. Unreinforced concrete handles squeezing very well but copes badly with being pulled apart. The Pantheon's designers attacked the problem from several directions at once, and the most elegant is the concrete itself.

They graded the aggregate, the chunks of stone set into the mortar, by weight. In the foundation ring they used dense travertine. In the lower drum, travertine and tuff; higher up, tuff and broken brick; then brick; and in the upper dome, light tuff and volcanic scoria or pumice, some of it apparently brought from the Vesuvius region. Estimates of the concrete's density fall from about 1,600 kg per cubic metre at the dome's base to about 1,350 near the oculus. Modern normal concrete is around 2,400.

It makes a big difference. In their 1986 structural study, Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson found that if the dome had been built with heavy concrete throughout, the stresses in it would have been substantially higher, by their estimate some 80 percent. Instead, their model gives peak tensile stresses of only about 0.13 MPa, small enough for Roman concrete to tolerate in much of the structure.

How do we know what is inside?

Nobody has sliced the Pantheon in half. The aggregate zones come from places where the concrete is exposed: damaged areas, openings in the upper drum, repairs, and observations made during restorations since the 19th century. They have been summarised by Mark and Hutchinson (1986), Lynne Lancaster (2005) and Mark Wilson Jones (2003, 2015). The exact heights of each zone are approximate, which is why diagrams, including ours, show them simplified.

The shell thins as it rises, from about 6 m at its base to about 1.2 m at the oculus. Inside, 140 coffers in five rings of 28 step back into the concrete. They are decorative, originally perhaps with bronze rosettes, but they also cut out dead weight. And the coffers shrink as they rise, a trick of perspective that makes the dome seem even higher than it is.

05Cracks, rings and a keystone made of air

Here is a surprising fact: the Pantheon's dome is cracked, and has been for a very long time. Mark and Hutchinson showed that the lower part of the dome is under hoop tension, a stretching force around its circumference. Unreinforced concrete cannot hold much of that, so the dome cracked along its meridians, like the segments of an orange, probably soon after it was built. Wilson Jones has traced cracks in the rotunda up to about 7 cm wide.

Hoop tension is easy to picture if you think of a wooden barrel. Squeeze the top of a dome and its lower part wants to bulge outwards, just as barrel staves would spring apart without their iron hoops. Later dome builders added literal hoops: Brunelleschi in Florence and the builders of St Peter's in Rome buried chains of stone, timber or iron in their domes to hold them in. The Pantheon has no such chains. Its builders relied instead on sheer mass in the drum and haunches, and, whether by design or luck, on a shape that could crack without losing its balance.

Cracking sounds alarming, but it changed how the dome works rather than destroying it. With the lower part split into wedges, the dome behaves partly like a ring of arches leaning against each other and sharing a common crown. For that to be stable, the line of thrust in each arch has to stay inside the masonry all the way down to the ground. The heavy haunches, loaded by the step rings, and the massive drum make sure it does.

At the top, where you might expect a keystone, there is a hole. The oculus is edged with a ring of tiles set on edge, in several courses, and originally a bronze cornice. Squeezed from all sides by the leaning segments, the ring works in compression, rather like the keystone of every arch at once. Leaving the top open also removes the heaviest, most awkward part of any dome, the crown.

Where every other dome needs a keystone, the Pantheon has a ring of tiles around empty air.

In the drum, relieving arches of brick, visible in places on the exterior wall, span over the niches and steer the loads into eight solid piers. Beneath it all, a ring foundation of heavy concrete spreads the weight into the soft ground of the Campus Martius, which settled unevenly and may explain some of the cracking.

06Building the impossible centering

The concrete had to be laid on something while it set. For a 43 m dome that means timber centering on a colossal scale, and none of it survives. How it was arranged is one of the building's real unknowns.

One influential proposal, by Wilson Jones, imagines a doughnut-shaped timber tower about 11.5 m across rising from the floor to carry the thin upper shell, while the thick lower courses were laid on lighter formwork spanning between the drum and the tower. The lower dome's horizontal courses could partly support themselves as they were built, like a corbelled vault, which would reduce the load on the timber. Concrete was probably carried up in baskets, and the builders may have used the step rings as working platforms.

The porch holds another puzzle. Its sixteen columns have monolithic shafts of Egyptian granite, grey from Mons Claudianus in the Eastern Desert and pink from Aswan, each about 11.9 m tall including base and capital and weighing about 60 tonnes. Oddly, the pediment of the porch does not quite fit the transitional block behind it, and there is a ghostly second pediment higher up. Wilson Jones has argued that the design called for 50-foot shafts, which never arrived, and that the builders had to make do with 40-foot ones, lowering the porch. It is an attractive hypothesis, though not the only explanation offered.

  • Travertine, tuff and brick came from quarries and brickyards around Rome.
  • Light volcanic scoria for the upper dome likely came from the Bay of Naples region.
  • The granite column shafts were quarried in Egypt and shipped across the Mediterranean and up the Tiber.
  • The dome's outer surface was covered in gilded bronze tiles, later replaced with lead.

07Temple, church, tomb, time machine

The Pantheon survived partly because it never stopped being useful. In 609 Pope Boniface IV, with permission from the Byzantine emperor Phocas, consecrated it as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres. A building in use is a building that gets repaired.

It did not escape unharmed. In 663 the Byzantine emperor Constans II stripped the gilded bronze tiles from the roof. In the 1620s Pope Urban VIII, of the Barberini family, removed bronze beams from the porch roof, much of it reportedly for cannon; a Roman wit coined the line 'what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did'. The great bronze doors, about 7.5 m high, are often described as ancient, though they have been repaired many times and their exact date is still debated.

The building became a burial place for artists and kings. Raphael was laid to rest here in 1520, and two kings of united Italy lie here too. Its design echoed down the centuries, in Renaissance churches, in Thomas Jefferson's Rotunda at the University of Virginia and in countless libraries and banks.

Chasing the sun

Robert Hannah and Giulio Magli (2011) tracked the disc of light from the oculus through the year. At noon at the equinoxes it falls on the band where the dome springs from the drum; around 21 April, the traditional birthday of Rome, it lights the entrance. They argue the building worked as a symbolic sundial linking the emperor, the sun and time, while stressing that it was not a precise astronomical instrument.

08What we still do not know

The Pantheon is not a mystery in the sense that we cannot explain why it stands. Structural models, material studies and centuries of observation give a coherent answer: sound geometry, graded concrete, a heavy drum and a design that tolerates cracking. Recent chemistry on Roman mortars, including the self-healing lime clasts found in hot-mixed concrete elsewhere, may add a little to the story, but so far nobody has sampled the dome's concrete in that detail.

The genuine unknowns are human. We do not know the architect's name. We do not know exactly how the centering was built, how long the dome took, or how the building site was organised. We do not know for sure what stood in the niches, or how the interior was originally lit and decorated beyond what survives. And the sun effects, though real and beautiful, leave open how much was planned and how much is a happy consequence of a round hole in a round roof.

The engineering is well understood. The people who built it remain almost entirely nameless.

Stand under the oculus and look up. The light that falls on your face travelled 150 million km from the sun and passed through a hole cut on purpose in a concrete shell poured nineteen centuries ago. The builders could not have known their dome would outlast the empire, the gods it was built for and the language of its inscription. But they built as if they did.

The big debates

Was the Pantheon built to catch the sun on special days?

Yes: the light marks meaningful dates.Hannah and Magli show the noon light marks the dome's springing at the equinoxes and lights the entrance around 21 April, Rome's founding day, fitting imperial sun symbolism.
Not necessarily: any round oculus makes moving light.No ancient text describes such alignments, the building faces roughly north for urban reasons, and dates near 21 April span several days of lit doorway.

The bold claim: The oculus and entrance were deliberately designed so the sun lights the doorway on Rome's birthday.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The light effects are real and measurable, and they fit what we know about Roman solar and imperial symbolism. But intention is hard to demonstrate without a text, and some effects would follow from almost any domed rotunda with an oculus facing this direction. It remains an attractive, arguable interpretation.

Did Hadrian design the Pantheon himself?

Yes: Hadrian was an architect-emperor.Ancient sources describe his passion for architecture, and he designed parts of his villa at Tivoli and the Temple of Venus and Roma.
Unlikely or unknown: the project began under Trajan.Brick stamps indicate a start around 114, three years before Hadrian's accession; Apollodorus of Damascus has been suggested, but no source names the architect.

The bold claim: Hadrian personally designed the Pantheon.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The brick-stamp evidence places the start of construction under Trajan, and there is no ancient statement that Hadrian drew up the design. He finished and dedicated the building, and may have influenced it, but authorship of the design remains unknown.

Was the porch meant to be taller?

Yes: 50-foot columns were planned.The mismatched pediments and the proportions of the transitional block fit a design for 50-foot shafts later reduced to 40-foot ones (Wilson Jones).
Other explanations are possible.The irregularities could reflect design changes for other reasons or a separate building phase, and no document records a shortage of columns.

The bold claim: The Pantheon's porch was built lower than planned because giant 50-foot columns failed to arrive.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The architectural clues are real and the hypothesis explains several awkward details at once. It depends on reconstructing a lost intention, and alternatives exist, so it is best treated as a strong idea rather than an established fact.

Northern China

The Great Wall of China

Not one wall but dozens, built over two thousand years from tamped earth, reeds, stone and brick, and 21,196 km of it survives.
