The Great Wall is a family of walls built, abandoned and rebuilt by many states and dynasties. Most of it is rammed earth: damp local soil tipped between wooden boards and pounded with rammers into dense layers a hand's breadth thick, lift after lift. In the deserts of Gansu, Han dynasty builders layered gravel and sand with reeds and tamarisk branches. The famous walls around Beijing are Ming work of the 15th and 16th centuries: a cut-stone footing, skins of fired brick set in lime mortar, and a core of earth and rubble, topped by a paved walkway, crenellated battlements and brick watchtowers. Some Ming masonry used lime mortar mixed with sticky rice soup, whose starch helps produce a tougher, more water-resistant binder.

The myth

The Great Wall is one continuous wall, and the only human-made object you can see from the Moon.

The reality

It is a network of many walls, trenches, towers and forts of different ages, with gaps where mountains and rivers did the job. From low Earth orbit a wall 5–9 m wide is far below the resolving power of the naked eye and blends into the landscape; China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, reported in 2003 that he could not see it. From the Moon, some 384,000 km away, no individual human structure is visible to the eye.

Wow

Much of the surviving rammed-earth wall is wrapped in a living skin of mosses, lichens and cyanobacteria, and a 2023 study found this biocrust makes the earth several times more resistant to erosion.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,220 words · 2 animated drawings

01A wall that is really a crowd

Climb the steep brick steps at Badaling on a winter morning, when the tour buses have not yet arrived, and the wall does what every photograph promises. It rolls over the ridges like a grey dragon, tower after tower, until it vanishes into the haze. It is easy to believe you are looking at a single, continuous structure running from the sea to the desert.

You are not. The Great Wall is not one wall but dozens, built, abandoned, reused and rebuilt by many states and dynasties over more than two thousand years. In 2012 China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage finished a national survey and put the total length of all walls, trenches and natural barriers from all periods at 21,196 km, recording more than 43,000 individual sites: wall sections, towers, forts and passes. That is a little over half the circumference of the Earth, but it is spread across northern China in overlapping lines, spurs and loops, not one neat line.

The Great Wall is less a single monument than a two-thousand-year argument about where the frontier should be.

Most of it is not the brick-and-stone wall of postcards. It is earth: pounded soil, gravel, reeds and branches. The brick parts near Beijing are the latest and grandest chapter, built by the Ming dynasty in the 15th and 16th centuries. To understand the wall, you have to start much earlier, and much lower down, with a pile of dirt and a wooden board.

Even the name hints at this. In Chinese the wall is Changcheng, simply 'the long wall', or Wanli Changcheng, 'the long wall of ten thousand li'. A li is a traditional unit of distance of roughly half a kilometre, and 'ten thousand' in Chinese often means 'countless' rather than an exact figure. The name was never a survey measurement; it was a way of saying 'endless'. Modern surveyors, armed with GPS and satellite imagery, have now given that poetic phrase a number, and the number turned out to be even bigger than the poets implied.

02From rival states to the First Emperor

Long before China was one country, its rival states walled their borders, against each other as much as against outsiders. The earliest such walls date back to around the 7th century BCE. When the state of Qin conquered its rivals in 221 BCE, its king became the First Emperor, and he sent his general Meng Tian north against the Xiongnu, the powerful nomadic confederation of the steppe.

According to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later in the Shiji (chapter 88), Meng Tian commanded some 300,000 men and built a wall that followed the lie of the land, using mountains and passes, from Lintao in the west to Liaodong in the east, a distance of more than 10,000 li. Much of this 'Qin wall' linked and extended older state walls. Sima Qian's numbers are those of a historian, not an auditor, but archaeology confirms long stretches of Qin earthwork across the north.

The cost in lives is remembered too. Chinese folklore tells of Meng Jiangnü, whose husband was conscripted to build the wall and died there; her weeping, the story goes, brought a section crashing down to reveal his bones. It is a legend, not a record, but it captures how the wall was experienced by the families of the conscripts: as a place people were sent and did not come back from.

The Han dynasty, which followed Qin, pushed walls and beacon towers far to the west, through the Gansu corridor towards Dunhuang and beyond, to protect the trade routes later known as the Silk Road. Some of their walls still stand, in places where no one would expect earth to survive two thousand years.

03Built from dirt: the art of rammed earth

The technique behind most of the Great Wall is called hangtu, rammed earth, and it has been used in China since the Neolithic. It needs no kiln, no quarry and no mortar, only soil, timber and a lot of muscle. Builders set up two parallel lines of boards held by posts and ties, tipped a layer of damp local soil between them, and pounded it with rammers until it was dense and hard. Then they added another layer, and another. When the boards were full, they were lifted and the next 'lift' began.

How thick were the layers? A 2026 study by Chengrui Ge and colleagues used 3D scanning at 15 Ming rammed-earth sites in Gansu, Qinghai and Shaanxi. They measured layers between about 10.4 and 15.6 cm thick, still marked with the small round pits left by rammer heads 5.8 to 9.4 cm across. Those pits are the fingerprints of individual workers' blows, preserved for five hundred years.

Fresh from the field

Ge et al. (2026, Coatings) combined field 3D scanning, soil analysis and compression tests at 15 Ming Great Wall sites across five climate zones in north-west China. They found that both the source of the soil and the ramming technique, such as layer thickness and the density of tamper pits, influenced how strong the finished earth is. Local builders adapted the method to local dirt.

In the Gobi, even soil was scarce. Along the Han frontier near Dunhuang and Yumen Pass, builders stacked layers of gravel and sand between mats of reeds and tamarisk branches, a kind of desert plywood. The plants bound the gravel together and the dry climate preserved them. Walls of this type, more than two thousand years old, still stand several metres high.

04The Ming make it monumental

The wall most visitors walk on is the youngest. The Ming dynasty came to power in 1368 after expelling the Mongol Yuan, and for decades relied more on garrisons and campaigns than on walls. That changed after 1449, when a Ming emperor was captured by the Oirat Mongols at Tumu. Defence became the priority, and walls became policy.

In 1474 the official Yu Zijun built a wall around the Ordos region about 1,100 km long, with roughly 40,000 men. Over the following century the lines around the capital were doubled and tripled. In the 1560s and 1570s the generals Qi Jiguang and Tan Lun began building hollow brick watchtowers on the walls near Beijing, where soldiers could shelter and store weapons; plans for some 3,000 were scaled back to about 1,200. The 2009 survey of the Ming system measured about 8,852 km in total: 6,260 km of built wall, 360 km of trenches and 2,233 km of natural barriers such as steep ridges and rivers.

A Ming wall of the Badaling type, built from 1505 onwards, is a layered machine. Its base is cut stone. Its outer skins are fired brick set in lime mortar. Its core is rammed earth and rubble. On top runs a paved walkway, around 7.5 to 7.8 m above the ground, wide enough, as guides like to say, for five horses abreast. On the northern side a crenellated battlement with loopholes shields defenders; on the southern side a lower parapet stops people falling off; stone spouts throw rainwater clear of the wall's face.

The builders did not pick easy ground. Near Beijing the Ming wall deliberately follows ridgelines, climbing slopes so steep that the walkway turns into staircases, because the crest of a mountain is the hardest place to attack. Bricks were fired in kilns close to the wall and carried up by people, carts and, according to local tradition, goats and donkeys with panniers. Some Ming bricks carry moulded inscriptions naming the military unit that made them and the year, a reminder that the wall was built by soldiers and conscripts organised like an army, stretch by stretch, with each unit answerable for its own section.

05Sticky rice and lime

One ingredient in some Ming masonry sounds like a kitchen joke: rice. For centuries Chinese builders added soup made from glutinous, or sticky, rice to lime mortar for tombs, pagodas and city walls. In 2010 the chemists Yang, Zhang and Ma published an analysis of such mortars in Accounts of Chemical Research and explained why it works.

The key is amylopectin, a branched starch that makes sticky rice sticky. As lime mortar hardens, calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate crystals. Amylopectin acts as an inhibitor, controlling how those crystals grow so that they stay small and pack into a compact microstructure. The result is an organic-inorganic composite: calcium carbonate held in an organic framework. In their tests, sticky rice-lime mortar was stronger, more stable and more compatible with old masonry than plain lime, and it has since been tried in restoration work.

The mortar in some Ming walls is a composite material, part mineral and part rice pudding.

The researchers trace the technique back about 1,500 years, and it is well documented in Ming and Qing construction. Whether a particular stretch of the Great Wall used it depends on local practice and budgets, so it is best described as a Ming technique used in some walls, not a universal ingredient.

06Smoke by day, fire by night

A wall on its own stops very little. What made the Great Wall work was the system around it: garrisons, forts at the passes, and chains of beacon towers within sight of one another. Han dynasty documents on wooden strips, found at frontier posts in Gansu, record signals, patrols and rations in striking detail, showing a bureaucracy that ran along the wall as well as behind it.

Under the Ming, signals combined smoke or fire with cannon shots, so that the size of a raid could be passed along the line. One Ming code, as it is usually summarised, used one fire and one shot for a band of up to about 100 raiders, rising step by step to five fires and five shots for 10,000 or more. Beacon fuel included firewood, hay and sulphur; stories that wolf dung was burned for its dense smoke are popular, though the phrase 'wolf smoke' may be as much literary as literal.

  • Beacon towers stood on high ground, in sight of the next tower along the line.
  • Forts guarded passes such as Jiayuguan in the west and Shanhaiguan by the sea.
  • Watchtowers on the wall itself sheltered soldiers, weapons and supplies.
  • Ditches and natural barriers filled the gaps where building a wall made no sense.

Did it work? Sometimes. The walls slowed raiders, channelled them towards defended passes and bought time for armies to gather. But large, determined forces broke through repeatedly, and in 1644 the Manchu Qing entered China through Shanhaiguan after a Ming general opened the gate. A wall is only as strong as the politics behind it.

07Can you see it from the Moon?

No. It is one of the most persistent myths about any monument, and it was born long before anyone went to space. The English antiquary William Stukeley suggested in 1754 that the wall might be visible from the Moon; the idea was repeated in popular books and in Ripley's Believe It or Not! in the 1930s and has been in school textbooks ever since.

The physics is simple. The Moon is about 384,000 km away; at that distance a wall a few metres wide is hopelessly small. Even from the International Space Station, about 400 km up, a wall 6 m wide subtends roughly 3 arcseconds, while the human eye can resolve details down to about 60 arcseconds (1 arcminute), as the optometrist Norberto López-Gil pointed out in 2008. Worse, the wall is built of local earth and stone and blends into the landscape around it. Highways, airports and city lights, which are wider or brighter, are far easier to spot.

What astronauts say

In 2003 Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut, said he looked for the wall from orbit and could not see it. Photographs taken from the space station with long camera lenses have picked out sections of it under ideal lighting, but that is the camera doing the seeing. The honest summary: invisible from the Moon, and not visible to the naked eye from orbit under normal conditions.

The myth survives because it is a lovely idea: one human creation so vast it registers on a cosmic scale. The truth is more interesting. The wall's greatness is not in its width but in its length, its age and the millions of people who built, guarded and lived along it.

08A living skin and an uncertain future

Rammed earth has one great enemy: water. Rain washes it, wind scours it and frost cracks it. Large stretches of the Great Wall have eroded to shapeless mounds, and people have long carted away bricks and earth for their own buildings. Yet some rammed-earth sections have survived remarkably well. A 2023 study suggested one reason.

Yousong Cao, Bo Xiao and colleagues sampled eight Ming rammed-earth sections along some 600 km of the wall in north-western China. They found that about two-thirds of the surfaces they sampled were covered in biocrusts: thin living skins of cyanobacteria, mosses and lichens that bind soil particles together. Compared with bare rammed earth, crusted samples were less porous and less erodible and, in some tests, around three times as mechanically stable. Moss-dominated crusts in semi-arid areas protected the earth better than crusts in more arid ones.

That challenges a common conservation instinct, which is to scrape plants off ancient walls. For rammed earth, at least, the living skin may be doing more good than harm. A 2025 follow-up in Current Biology catalogued the diverse microbial community in these crusts, and researchers are now debating where the line lies between protective and harmful growth.

The wall's future depends on choices like that, and on tourism, road building, climate and money. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. The best-known stretches are heavily restored; many remote sections are crumbling quietly. The Great Wall has always been a work in progress. It still is.

The big debates

Can you see the Great Wall from space?

Yes: it is so long it must be visible.The claim appears in popular books from the 18th century onwards, and cameras on the space station have photographed it.
No, not with the naked eye.From 400 km a 6 m wall spans about 3 arcseconds, far below the eye's c. 60 arcsecond limit; astronauts including Yang Liwei report not seeing it; from the Moon it is thousands of times smaller still.

The bold claim: The Great Wall is the only human-made structure visible to the naked eye from the Moon.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Simple optics rules it out: the wall is far too narrow and too similar in colour to its surroundings. From the Moon no individual structure is visible to the eye at all. From low orbit, wider and brighter features such as highways, airports and city lights are much easier to see, and the wall appears only in zoomed photographs.

Did the wall keep invaders out?

Yes: it worked as a system.Walls, beacons and forts slowed raids, channelled attackers towards defended passes and gave armies warning.
No: it was repeatedly breached.Nomadic armies broke through many times; the Mongols conquered all of China in the 13th century and the Qing entered through Shanhaiguan in 1644.

The bold claim: The Great Wall was an effective barrier that kept northern invaders out of China.

Receipt MeterMixed record
BustedRock solid

Against small raids the wall system often worked, which is why dynasties kept investing in it. Against large, organised armies, or when defenders changed sides, it did not. Its success depended on garrisons, supplies and politics more than on masonry.

Are workers buried inside the wall?

Yes: it is 'the longest cemetery on Earth'.Huge numbers of conscripts died building it, and legends such as Meng Jiangnü's tell of bones inside the wall.
Deaths yes, bodies in the fill no.Workers who died were most likely buried near camps; human remains built into the rammed-earth or brick fill have not been documented as a practice.

The bold claim: The bodies of dead workers were built into the fabric of the wall.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The deaths were real and the suffering is well recorded, but the specific idea that bodies were used as fill or deliberately entombed in the wall rests on folklore. Human remains would weaken rammed earth, and archaeological documentation of such a practice is lacking.

Wadi Musa, Jordan

Petra's water system

A desert kingdom that caught every winter storm, tamed a killer gorge and built a swimming pool to show it could.

Mystery

43 × 23 m, 2.5 m deep, over 2,000 m³Garden pool

The Nabataeans treated every drop as money. At the mouth of the Siq, the gorge that leads into the city, they built a dam and cut a tunnel about 88 m long so that winter flash floods in Wadi Musa were sent around the mountain instead of down the narrow canyon. Along the Siq itself they carved an open channel into one cliff and laid a pipeline of interlocking clay pipes in a groove on the other, bringing water from the spring of Ain Musa into the city. Small settling basins let silt drop out. Reservoirs such as the Zurraba, and many rock-cut cisterns plastered against leaks, stored the winter's rain for the long dry summer. Hydraulic engineer Charles Ortloff's modelling suggests some pipelines were run partly full, near their best possible flow, which avoids the bursts that pressurised clay pipes suffer.

The myth

Petra was a 'lost city' in a barren desert, rediscovered in 1812, and its survival there needed some forgotten or impossible technology.

The reality

Local Bedouin knew Petra all along; Burckhardt was simply the first European to describe it. Its water engineering is carved in plain sight: dams, a tunnel, channels, clay pipes, settling basins and cisterns, all using known methods. What remains debated is how many people lived there, and which parts of the network are Nabataean and which were added or repaired under Roman rule.

Wow

In the middle of a city that gets less rain than most deserts' edges, King Aretas IV's engineers built an ornamental pool 43 m long with an island pavilion, apparently to show visiting merchants how much water Petra could afford to waste.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,287 words · 2 animated drawings

01The storm that fills a year

Picture a December afternoon above Petra. The sky over the limestone uplands turns the colour of slate, and for an hour or two rain hammers the bare rock. Very little soaks in. Within minutes every gully is running, the gullies feed the dry bed of Wadi Musa, and a brown wall of water, carrying gravel and uprooted shrubs, heads downhill towards a crack in the mountain barely wider than a lorry.

That crack is the Siq, the famous gorge that leads visitors to the Treasury. It is about 1.2 km long and in places only about 3 m wide. Funnel a flash flood into it and you get something close to a fire hose. In 1963, as the Associated Press later recounted, rising water in the Siq killed 22 French tourists and a local guide.

Yet two thousand years ago this same valley held a capital city of perhaps 20,000 people, according to one widely used estimate, with baths, gardens, fountains and an ornamental pool. Petra receives roughly 150 to 200 mm of rain a year, most of it in a handful of winter storms. The story of Petra is really the story of how the Nabataeans turned those few violent days into a year of water, and how they kept the violent part out of their front door.

Petra's engineers did not fight the desert's rain. They caught it, steered it and saved it for July.

02Who were the Nabataeans?

The Nabataeans were Arab traders who grew rich moving incense, spices and other luxury goods across the deserts between Arabia, Egypt and the Mediterranean. By the late 4th century BCE Greek writers already knew them as a people who could vanish into waterless country where armies could not follow. The trick, those writers said, was water that nobody else could find.

They are exceptionally fond of freedom; and, whenever a strong force of enemies comes near, they take refuge in the desert, using this as a fortress; for it lacks water and cannot be crossed by others, but to them alone, since they have prepared subterranean reservoirs lined with stucco, it furnishes safety.

Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 19.94.6, trans. Russel M. Geer, Loeb Classical Library (1954)

Diodorus was writing in the 1st century BCE about events of around 312 BCE, probably drawing on an eyewitness source, so the passage describes a nomadic habit rather than the later city. But it captures the mindset that built Petra: plaster the walls of a cistern so it does not leak, hide its mouth, and let the desert do your defending. Over the next three centuries that habit scaled up into urban engineering. The high point came under King Aretas IV (ruled 9 BCE to 40 CE), when the city's greatest monuments, and much of its plumbing, took their surviving form. Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE, and the city carried on, repaired and adapted, for centuries more.

03Closing the front door: the dam and the tunnel

The Nabataeans solved the Siq problem with a piece of engineering that still works. Just before the gorge entrance, at a spot called Bab as-Siq, they built a dam across Wadi Musa. On its own a dam would only create a lake that eventually overtopped. So they also cut a tunnel, about 88 m long, straight through the sandstone ridge beside the entrance. When the flood arrived, the dam turned it aside and the tunnel carried it into a neighbouring valley, Wadi al-Mudhlim. From there the water ran around the back of the massif, joined Wadi al-Mataha and reached the city centre by a longer, gentler route, well away from the people walking through the Siq.

Walk into the tunnel today and you can see the chisel marks on its walls. The modern dam that stands at the entrance was built in 1964, after the 1963 disaster, on top of the Nabataean one; the Petra Development and Tourism Region Authority notes that the ancient dam was larger. In 2014 Jordan added an electronic flood-warning system that watches rain gauges and water sensors around the site, a modern layer on an ancient idea.

Upstream, the Nabataeans also scattered small check dams across side gullies. Each slowed the runoff, dropped some of its gravel and gave the water time to sink into the ground or be led into cisterns. Surveys with ground-penetrating radar in Petra's northern hinterland have traced more of these barriers. The overall pattern is a landscape tuned to turn a flood into a series of manageable trickles.

04Plumbing a canyon

With the floods gone, the Siq became the city's main water main. According to Ueli Bellwald's team, who excavated the gorge floor for the Petra National Trust, the works date to the last decades of the 1st century BCE, together with the paved road. Two separate lines ran along it. On one side, an open channel was cut into the foot of the cliff and in places covered with stone slabs. On the other, a groove was carved into the rock face about a metre above the road, and into it the builders laid a pipeline of fired clay pipes.

The pipes are the clever part. Each section is roughly 35 cm long with a bore of about 14 cm, and one end is narrower so it slots into the next, like a stack of paper cups. Along the route, small settling basins slowed the flow so sand and lime could settle out before the water reached the city. Visitors can still see pieces of the pipeline, and of the channel, in the walls of the Siq.

Charles Ortloff, a hydraulic engineer who has spent decades modelling ancient water systems, calculated how these pipelines behaved. His conclusion is that several were designed to flow partly full, close to what engineers call critical flow, the condition at which a channel of given size and slope carries the most water for the least depth. A pipe flowing partly full is under little pressure, so its mortared clay joints are far less likely to leak or burst than a pipe running full. For the Siq line, his model gives about 0.017 to 0.023 m³ per second at slopes of 1 to 2 degrees, or very roughly 1,500 to 2,000 m³ a day.

How do we know?

Ortloff's numbers come from measuring surviving pipe sizes, channel dimensions and slopes, then applying standard open-channel hydraulics. That is a reconstruction, not a flow meter reading from antiquity. We cannot know how often the pipes were blocked, repaired or running below capacity. What the modelling does show is that the design choices, such as pipe size, slope and settling basins, are consistent with engineers who understood how to move water steadily without pressure.

05Springs, reservoirs and a city of cisterns

The Siq line began at Ain Musa, the Spring of Moses, which rises in the uplands where the modern town of Wadi Musa now stands. Ortloff estimates its output at around 1,000 to 4,000 m³ a day, depending on season and year. Near the spring, the Zurraba reservoir, with a capacity of about 10,000 m³, acted as a buffer, storing water so that the city's supply did not simply follow the spring's rhythm. Other springs, including Ain Braq and Ain Dibdiba, fed further pipelines that entered Petra by other routes.

Then there was the rain itself. Across the city and the surrounding hills, the Nabataeans cut cisterns into the rock and plastered them to keep them watertight. Roofs, courtyards and even bare rock slopes were shaped so that runoff flowed into channels and on into storage. Many cisterns had settling tanks in front of them, so the first dirty flush of a storm was held back. The sheer number of these features, from tiny basins to large tanks, is what made the system resilient: when one source failed, others remained.

Keeping all this working was a year-round job. Every storm washed sand into channels and cisterns, so settling tanks and basins had to be dug out; plaster cracked and had to be patched; clay pipes broke and were replaced. Nabataean water was as much a matter of daily maintenance as of clever design. When, centuries later, the people and money for that maintenance dwindled, the system did not fail in a single dramatic moment. It silted up, one basin at a time.

  • Catch: shape slopes, roofs and gullies so that rain runs where you want it.
  • Slow: check dams and settling tanks take the energy and the silt out of the water.
  • Store: plastered cisterns and reservoirs hold winter water through a rainless summer.
  • Deliver: gravity-fed channels and low-pressure clay pipelines carry water to fountains, baths and houses.

Ortloff's working figure for the city at its height is about 20,000 people, a number often repeated. It is best read as a plausible order of magnitude rather than a census. Population estimates for Petra depend on assumptions about how many houses were occupied at once, and there is still no complete map of domestic buildings.

06A swimming pool in the desert

For most of the 20th century, a large terrace beside Petra's colonnaded street was labelled the 'Lower Market'. Beginning in 1998, excavations led by Leigh-Ann Bedal showed it was nothing of the sort. Under the rubble lay a great pool, 43 by 23 m and 2.5 m deep, holding over 2,000 m³ of water. In the middle stood an island pavilion about 11.5 by 14.5 m, open to the water on at least three sides. Around it were gardens, walkways and an intricate network of channels, filtering basins and ceramic pipes, fed from a tank on the escarpment above.

Bedal dates the complex to the end of the 1st century BCE, early in Aretas IV's reign, and compares it to the paradeisos, the walled pleasure garden that spread into the Mediterranean world after Alexander's campaigns in the east. She reads the pool as deliberate conspicuous consumption: a traveller arriving from the desert would see, at the heart of the city, an expanse of open water that evaporated freely in the sun. Few statements of wealth and control could have been clearer.

In a place where water meant life, a pool you could row a boat across was the loudest boast in the kingdom.

The complex stayed in use after the Roman annexation and was abandoned sometime in the late 2nd or 3rd century CE. By the time of the great earthquake of 363 it was already out of use, and the quake left it in ruins.

07The Treasury: carved from the top down

At the end of the Siq the gorge opens and the Treasury, al-Khazneh, fills the view: a two-storey facade about 39.5 m high, with columns, pediment and a round pavilion topped by an urn. It is usually attributed to the reign of Aretas IV and is widely interpreted as a royal tomb or memorial, not a treasury at all. The name comes from a local legend that the urn held a pharaoh's gold; the bullet marks on it were left by people who tried to shoot it open. Inside, the rooms are plain, with a main chamber and side chambers adding up to around 2,000 m³ of space.

How do you carve a building out of a cliff? Unfinished facades elsewhere at Petra show the likely answer: the stonecutters started at the top and worked downward, so the finished upper parts never had to be reached from below and no scaffolding tower was needed against the rock face. They probably cut ledges and steps, dressed the stone as they descended, and used the rising floor of rubble as a working platform. It is a method that punishes mistakes, since nothing can be added back, and the Treasury's crisp detailing is a measure of how well the carvers planned.

Fresh from the field

In 2003 and 2005, excavations in front of the Treasury found tombs beneath the forecourt, with the remains of at least 11 people. In August 2024 a Jordanian and American team, including the Department of Antiquities and the American Center of Research led on site by Pearce Paul Creasman, opened another tomb there and found 12 skeletons with bronze, iron and ceramic objects, including a small juglet. The finds are not yet fully published. Radiocarbon, luminescence and DNA samples are being analysed, and remote sensing hints at more features deeper under the courtyard.

08The earthquake of 363 and the long fade

On the night of 19 May 363 CE a powerful earthquake struck the region. A letter attributed to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, lists Petra among the towns damaged, and archaeology backs this up: collapsed buildings across the city date to this event. The quake also broke the water system. Bellwald's team found that afterwards only one of the Siq's two water lines was repaired, which suggests a city with fewer people and fewer resources, choosing the line that mattered most.

Petra did not end in 363. Churches were built there in the 5th and 6th centuries, and some occupation continued into the 7th. But trade routes had shifted, and without constant maintenance a water network like Petra's slowly silts up. Channels clogged, cisterns cracked, pipes were robbed for their clay. By the time Johann Ludwig Burckhardt arrived in 1812, disguised as a traveller seeking to make a sacrifice at the tomb of Aaron, the city was a ruin known well to the local Bedouin but not to Europe.

09Myths, arguments and what is still open

The biggest myth is the 'lost city'. Petra was never lost to the people who lived around it; Burckhardt was the first European to write about it, which is a different thing. The second myth is that its survival in the desert needed some unknown technology. Every component of the system, from the tunnel to the plaster, uses methods known across the ancient Mediterranean and Near East. What is impressive is the combination and the planning.

The real arguments are more interesting. How many people did Petra hold, and when? Estimates of about 20,000 are often quoted, but they rest on water budgets and assumptions rather than a count of houses. Which parts are Nabataean and which were added or rebuilt under Rome is also debated, because pipelines were repaired and rerouted over centuries. And some scholars caution against assuming that the critical-flow design was intended, rather than being the result of rules of thumb that happened to work well.

What nobody disputes is that a small kingdom of traders built one of the ancient world's most carefully managed urban water systems in a place that gets less rain in a year than London does in four months. The chisel marks are still in the tunnel. The next winter storm will still be sent around the mountain.

The big debates

Did Nabataean engineers deliberately design pipes for critical flow?

Yes, by designOrtloff's hydraulic models show several pipelines sized and sloped to run partly full near critical flow, which maximises delivery while keeping pressure, leaks and bursts low.
Rule of thumb, not theoryNo Nabataean engineering text survives. Builders may have reached good designs by trial and error; the modern concept of critical flow did not exist.

The bold claim: Petra's pipelines were engineered to run near maximum efficient flow without pressure.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The measured pipe sizes and slopes are consistent with near-critical, low-pressure flow, and that is a sensible design for mortared clay pipes. But the evidence is a modern reconstruction. Whether the builders understood the principle or simply learned what worked cannot be tested directly, so the result is plausible rather than established.

Was Petra a lost city until 1812?

RediscoveredBurckhardt's 1812 visit introduced Petra to European scholarship and travel writing.
Never lostLocal Bedouin lived in and around the site, grazed flocks there and guided Burckhardt to it. Crusaders also knew the area.

The bold claim: Petra was lost to the world until a European found it.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The city was abandoned as an urban centre, but people living nearby always knew it. Burckhardt was the first European to describe it in print. Calling it 'lost' reflects a European point of view, not the history of the site.

How many people did Petra's water support?

About 20,000 or moreWater-budget estimates based on spring output, reservoirs and cisterns, used by Ortloff and others.
Unknown, possibly fewerNo full survey of housing exists, and different parts of the city were occupied at different times.

The bold claim: Nabataean Petra held around 20,000 people at its height.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The figure is a reasonable estimate of what the water system could supply, but capacity is not the same as population. Until domestic areas are mapped and dated more fully, any headcount remains an informed guess.

Lintong, Xi'an, China

The Terracotta Army

Thousands of life-size soldiers, each with his own face, mass-produced by named workshops to guard an emperor's tomb nobody has yet opened.

Mystery

The warriors were built like modular machines. Workshops shaped solid clay legs on a plinth, built hollow torsos up from coils or slabs of clay, attached separately made arms and hands, and pressed heads in a small number of two-part moulds. Then craftsmen added ears, hair, moustaches and expressions by hand, so that faces vary endlessly. Many pieces carry the stamped or incised names of workshop foremen, a quality-control system that lets archaeologists trace who made what. The finished figures were fired at roughly 950–1,050 °C, coated with two layers of East Asian lacquer, painted with mineral pigments including the synthetic 'Chinese purple', armed with real bronze weapons and lined up in timber-roofed corridors in pits east of the emperor's tomb.

The myth

Qin metalworkers chrome-plated their bronze swords to stop them rusting, a technology the West only invented in the 20th century.

The reality

A 2019 analysis of 464 weapon parts found chromium on only a small fraction, mostly fittings that had touched lacquered wood. The chromium came from the lacquer, not from deliberate plating. The weapons survived well because of the mildly alkaline, fine-grained burial soil and the bronze's tin-rich composition.

Wow

No two excavated faces are known to be identical, yet the army came off something close to an ancient production line, with named supervisors signing their work.

Mystery meterA few loose ends
The deep dive10 min read · 2,307 words · 2 animated drawings

01A head in the well

In March 1974, during a drought, a group of farmers in Lintong, east of Xi'an, were digging a well. A few metres down their spades hit fragments of fired clay, then something stranger: a head, life-size, with a moustache. Among the diggers was Yang Zhifa, who would spend much of the rest of his life signing books in the museum that grew over his field.

What they had found was the edge of pit 1 of the Terracotta Army. Over the following years archaeologists uncovered a subterranean army about 1.5 km east of the burial mound of Ying Zheng, the king of Qin who in 221 BCE conquered his rivals and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. Estimates now run to more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses and 150 cavalry horses in the three main pits, most of them still in the ground.

It is an army built to face east, for eternity, towards the kingdoms its emperor had just destroyed.

The Terracotta Army is often described as one of the wonders of the ancient world, and it deserves it. But its real fascination is not just its size. It is the combination of an industrial production system with astonishing individuality, and the fact that the greatest treasure of all, the emperor's own tomb, remains unopened.

02An emperor who planned for ever

Ying Zheng became king of Qin in 246 BCE, aged about thirteen, and work on his tomb began almost at once, as was usual for rulers of the time. After unification the project grew to match his new status. The historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, says that more than 700,000 people from across the empire were sent to work on it. That figure is probably rounded and may include convict labour on other state projects, but the scale of what survives makes clear this was an enormous undertaking.

The tomb complex covers dozens of square kilometres. At its centre is the mound, a truncated pyramid of rammed earth that still rises some 50 m or more above the plain, depending on where it is measured from, surrounded by the remains of inner and outer walls. Around it archaeologists have found some 200 accompanying pits holding stables with real horses, bronze waterbirds, stone armour, acrobats and officials. The army pits lie outside the walls, to the east.

Why an army? The First Emperor spent his life at war and then trying to escape death, sending expeditions to find elixirs of immortality. A tomb furnished like a palace and guarded like a capital was a way of carrying his power into the afterlife. The soldiers are arranged in battle formation and face east, the direction from which his defeated rivals had come.

Standardisation was a Qin obsession. After unification the First Emperor's government imposed common weights and measures, a single script, a standard coinage and even a fixed width for cart axles, so that wagons could run in the same ruts across the empire. The terracotta army is that mindset turned into sculpture. The same state that insisted every measuring cup hold the same volume also organised its tomb builders into units working to shared templates, with each unit's output labelled and checked. Seen this way, the army is not only a work of art or a religious offering. It is a monument to bureaucracy, and a very effective one.

03Pit 1: an army in corridors

Pit 1 is the biggest: roughly 230 m long and 62 m wide, dug several metres into the loess. Its builders divided it with ten rammed-earth walls into eleven corridors, most of them more than 3 m wide. They floored the corridors with bricks, stood the figures in ranks, and roofed the whole pit with massive timber beams covered with reed mats and layers of earth. Then they buried it.

The formation is a textbook of Qin warfare. At the eastern end a vanguard of archers stands three rows deep. Along the outer corridors, flank guards face outwards. The main body, infantry in columns with war chariots among them, fills the central corridors, and a rear guard faces west. Pit 1 alone is estimated to hold about 6,000 figures and horses. Pit 2, to the north-east, holds a mixed force of cavalry, chariots, archers and infantry; tiny pit 3, with 68 figures and a chariot, looks like a command post.

The army did not rest in peace for long. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, his dynasty collapsed within four years. The pits were broken into, weapons were taken and the timber roofs burned, a destruction traditionally blamed on the rebel general Xiang Yu. The roofs fell in, smashing the figures. Almost every warrior on display today has been pieced together from fragments, like a vast three-dimensional jigsaw.

The ranks are not all the same. Archers kneel or stand in different poses, ready to shoot in turn. Charioteers stretch out their arms to hold long-vanished reins. Cavalrymen stand beside their saddled horses. Officers are taller and wear more elaborate armour and headgear, and a handful of so-called generals, with tasselled caps and bellies that strain against their armour, are the tallest of all. Their postures and hand positions match the weapons they once held, so that even where the wood and bronze have gone, archaeologists can often tell who carried a crossbow and who a spear.

04A production line with faces

How do you make thousands of life-size ceramic soldiers in a few decades? You design them like a kit. Each warrior was assembled from standard parts, and the tomb's workshops seem to have divided the labour much like a modern factory.

The legs are solid clay, strong enough to carry the weight above, and stand on a square plinth. The torsos are hollow, built up from coils or slabs like large storage jars, then smoothed and carved with armour plates, belts and robe folds. Arms were made separately and joined with wet clay; hands, often moulded, slot into the sleeves. Heads were pressed in two-part moulds, and scholars have identified a limited number of basic face types, around ten. Then came the personal touches: ears, hair, topknots, moustaches and expressions added and modelled by hand.

The result is uncanny. Walk along the ranks and you meet young men and old, stern faces and cheerful ones, different hairstyles and beard types. No two excavated faces are known to be identical. A computer-vision study of the warriors' ears in 2014, led by Andrew Bevan, found enough variation to suggest that individual figures were distinct, though whether they portray real individuals is another matter.

How do we know? Reading the workshop marks

Many figures carry short stamped or incised inscriptions, often a personal name, sometimes with a place or workshop. Archaeologists have recorded the names of dozens of foremen. Some came from government workshops that also made roof tiles and drains; others seem to have been local potters. The marks served as quality control: if a piece failed, the state knew exactly who to hold responsible, and Qin law was not gentle.

The figures were fired, probably at roughly 950 to 1,050 °C, which required large kilns and huge quantities of fuel. Some weigh well over 100 kg. Getting thousands of them into the pits without breakage was an achievement in itself.

05Real weapons, and a chrome myth

The terracotta soldiers held real bronze weapons: swords, spears, halberds, crossbows and tens of thousands of arrowheads, more than 40,000 bronze items in all. Some carry dates between 245 and 228 BCE, inscribed with the names of officials responsible for their manufacture. A 2014 study by Marcos Martinón-Torres and colleagues showed that the arrowheads, bundled in groups of 100, were made in many small, parallel workshop cells rather than on one giant production line: an efficient, flexible system that could keep producing if one cell failed.

When archaeologists in the 1970s and 1980s found swords that still gleamed and detected chromium on some bronze surfaces, a story took off. Qin smiths, it was said, had invented chrome plating to prevent rust, two thousand years before it was patented in the West. It became a staple of documentaries and museum tours.

In 2019 a team from UCL and the Emperor Qin Shihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, led by Martinón-Torres, tested the idea properly. They analysed 464 bronze weapon parts. Only 37, about 8 percent, had detectable chromium, and it turned up mostly on fittings such as sword pommels, crossbow triggers and spear ferrules, not on blades or arrowheads. The pattern pointed to a source: the lacquer on the wooden hafts, scabbards and crossbow stocks, which contains chromium and had sat in contact with the metal for two millennia.

The shine was not a lost anti-rust technology; it was good bronze in kind soil.

Why, then, are so many weapons so well preserved? The team pointed to the burial environment. The loess soil is fine-grained and mildly alkaline, with a pH of about 8.1 to 8.5, low in organic matter, and it limits oxygen and moisture. Add tin-rich bronze, and you have metal that corrodes very slowly. It is a good example of how a romantic story can be tested with a portable X-ray fluorescence gun and some patience.

06An army in colour

Today the warriors are the colour of dust, but they were painted. Each figure was first coated with two layers of East Asian lacquer, the sap of the lacquer tree, known in Chinese as qi, which formed a dark, glossy base. Over it painters applied mineral pigments: red from cinnabar and iron oxides, green from malachite, blue from azurite, white from bone and a startling purple.

That purple, often called Chinese or Han purple, is a synthetic pigment, a barium copper silicate made by heating raw materials to high temperature. It is one of the earliest man-made pigments known, and its presence on the warriors shows how much chemistry went into their finishing.

The paint is fragile. When a figure is excavated, the lacquer, which has been damp for two thousand years, dries in Xi'an's air and curls within seconds; it can flake off within minutes, taking the paint with it. Conservators from China and Germany have developed methods to consolidate the lacquer as it is uncovered, but much colour was lost in earlier excavations. This is one reason why archaeologists move slowly and why much of the army is still underground.

What colour were they?

Surviving traces suggest bright, varied uniforms: robes in red, green, blue or purple; dark lacquered armour with coloured laces and rivets; pinkish faces with painted eyes and hair. Colours seem to vary between individuals rather than following a strict uniform code, which some scholars suggest may reflect soldiers supplying their own clothing, as letters from Qin soldiers asking their families for clothes imply. Reconstructions are informed guesses based on these traces.

07Rivers of mercury

And then there is the tomb itself. Sima Qian's description, written about a century after the burial, is one of the most extraordinary passages in ancient history. In his account, workers dug down through three layers of groundwater, sealed the chamber with bronze, and filled it with models of palaces and towers and rare treasures. Craftsmen set crossbows to shoot anyone who broke in. Mercury was made to flow in imitation of the hundred rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, and the great sea; the heavens were depicted above and the earth below. Lamps were fuelled with the fat of 'man-fish', perhaps whales or seals, so they would burn for a long time. According to Sima Qian, the craftsmen who knew the tomb's secrets were sealed inside.

How much of this is true? Nobody knows, because the burial chamber has never been opened. But there are intriguing hints. Geochemical surveys of the soil over the mound, beginning in the early 1980s, reported mercury concentrations well above the surrounding background, and remote-sensing work suggests a large underground chamber roughly where Sima Qian implies. Some researchers caution that later contamination could explain part of the signal, so the mercury rivers remain plausible rather than confirmed.

The most famous tomb in China may also be one of the most toxic places to open.

Chinese authorities have repeatedly decided not to excavate the chamber. The reasons are practical as well as cultural: there is currently no way to protect whatever lies inside, from painted lacquer to silk, once it meets the air, and mercury vapour would be a hazard to the excavators. The terracotta paint problem is a small-scale warning of what could be lost.

08Portraits, propaganda and patience

The Terracotta Army still poses real questions. Were the warriors modelled on actual soldiers, or were their faces an artistic way of showing a vast, varied army? The workshop evidence suggests a system designed to produce variety from standard parts, which is not quite the same as portraiture. Who were the workers, and how many died? Burials of labourers found near the tomb, some with fragments of tiles inscribed with their names and home towns, give a grim glimpse of the human cost.

There are also questions about how the army fits into the wider complex. Each new pit, of acrobats, officials, bronze birds or stone armour, makes it clearer that the soldiers were only one part of an entire imperial world recreated underground. The army guards the approach; the emperor's afterlife court lies deeper.

And there is the matter of patience. Excavation of pit 1 has continued in campaigns since the 1970s, and new figures still emerge, each needing years of conservation. Most of the army, and the emperor himself, remain in the ground. For once, the archaeologists' motto is not 'dig faster' but 'wait until we can do it properly'.

The First Emperor wanted to rule for ever. His dynasty lasted fifteen years. But the potters, painters and bronze-casters who built his army, whose names we can sometimes still read in the clay, have given us something he never intended: a portrait of the people of his empire, standing in their ranks, waiting.

The big debates

Did Qin smiths invent chrome plating?

Yes: chromium was found on shiny weapons.Early analyses in the 1970s–80s detected chromium on some well-preserved bronze surfaces.
No: the chromium came from lacquer.Of 464 parts analysed in 2019, only c. 8% had chromium, concentrated on fittings in contact with lacquered wood; blades and arrowheads, the best-preserved items, had almost none.

The bold claim: Qin metalworkers deliberately chrome-plated bronze weapons to prevent corrosion.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The distribution of chromium matches contact with chromium-rich lacquer, not deliberate treatment, and the best-preserved weapons do not carry it. The preservation is explained by alkaline, fine-grained soil and tin-rich bronze. The old claim was a reasonable guess from limited data that did not survive systematic testing.

Are there really rivers of mercury in the tomb?

Probably yes, in some form.Sima Qian describes mercury rivers, and soil surveys over the mound have reported mercury well above background levels.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

An ancient written source and independent geochemical anomalies point the same way, which is more than most tomb legends can claim. But without excavation or less ambiguous remote sensing, the amount and arrangement of any mercury remain unknown.

Is every warrior a portrait of a real soldier?

Yes: the faces are individual.No two faces are known to be identical, and a 2014 study of ear shapes found strong variation between figures.
Individual, but not necessarily portraits.Heads come from a limited set of moulds with added features, a system designed to create variety efficiently; no text says real soldiers sat for them.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

The individuality is real and deliberate, but individuality is not the same as likeness. The production evidence fits craftsmen varying standard parts to suggest a real, diverse army. Whether some sculptors worked from actual people is possible but cannot currently be demonstrated.

Rapa Nui, south-eastern Pacific

The moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island)

Nearly a thousand stone ancestors, a quarry full of unfinished giants, and an oral tradition that said they walked. It seems they did.

Mystery

Carvers shaped the statues directly out of the volcanic tuff of the Rano Raraku crater, using hand-held basalt picks, and freed them from the bedrock along a keel under the back. Finished statues were lowered down the slope and stood upright. Rapanui oral tradition says the moai 'walked' to their platforms. Archaeologists Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt tested this: with ropes on both sides and one behind, a team rocked an upright replica from side to side so that it shuffled forward. Their 2025 analysis of 962 moai found that statues abandoned along the ancient roads have wide D-shaped bases and a forward lean that make this kind of walking stable, and that the roads, about 4.5 m wide and concave, would keep a rocking statue centred. Red stone topknots (pukao) from a separate quarry were probably rolled to the platforms and up ramps.

The myth

The islanders chopped down every tree to roll statues on logs, their population crashed from over 15,000 into warfare and cannibalism (the 'ecocide' story), and the moai were impossible to move without outside help.

The reality

Ancient genomes published in 2024 show no population crash before European contact, and a 2024 satellite study of rock gardens suggests the island supported roughly 3,000 to 4,000 people, close to what Europeans saw in 1722. The island was deforested, probably with help from introduced rats, and a long drought from the mid-1500s coincided with changes in ritual. The catastrophic losses came after 1860, through slave raids and disease. The walking hypothesis explains transport without logs or outsiders, though scholars still debate details.

Wow

A roughly 4-tonne replica 'walked' 100 m in about 40 minutes pulled by just 18 people, and statues abandoned on the roads have exactly the shapes you would carve if you meant them to walk.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,310 words · 2 animated drawings

01A crater full of giants

Climb the slope of Rano Raraku at dawn and the hillside is watching you. Heads rise out of the grass at every angle, some buried to the chin, some tilted as if listening. Above them, in the rock face itself, lie statues that were never finished: faces half cut, bodies still joined to the mountain along their backs. Around 394 moai remain here, in and around the quarry that supplied about 95 percent of all the statues on the island.

Rapa Nui is one of the most isolated inhabited places on Earth, a triangle of volcanic land about 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island. Polynesian voyagers reached it around 1200 CE, give or take a century by current radiocarbon studies. Over the next few hundred years their descendants carved nearly a thousand moai, most between about 1250 and the 1500s, and set many of them on stone platforms, called ahu, around the coast, with their backs to the sea and their faces towards the land and the people.

The moai are not faces of strangers. They are ancestors, set up to watch over their descendants.

For three centuries, outsiders have asked two questions about them. How did people with no metal tools, no wheels and no large animals move statues weighing many tonnes? And what happened to the society that made them? In the past fifteen years, both answers have changed.

02Carving a moai

Rano Raraku is an extinct volcano made of lapilli tuff, compacted volcanic ash that is soft enough to carve with stone tools yet firm enough to hold fine detail. Thousands of basalt picks, called toki, have been found around the quarry. Carvers outlined a statue on the rock face, cut channels along its sides, and shaped the face and front while the figure lay on its back. The back was left attached to the bedrock by a narrow keel, which was cut through last.

An average moai stands about 4 m tall with a base about 1.6 m wide and weighs around 12.5 t. Proportions are distinctive: a huge head, often around a third or more of the height, with a heavy brow, long nose, thin pressed lips and elongated ears. Arms run down the sides and the long-fingered hands meet over the belly. There are no legs; the figure ends at the hips.

Not all moai were small. Paro, the tallest ever erected, stood almost 10 m tall and weighed about 82 t; the heaviest erected statue, at Ahu Tongariki, is reported at around 86 t. And then there is El Gigante, still lying in the quarry: about 21 m long, with published weight estimates starting around 145 to 165 t and running higher. It was never finished, and it is hard to imagine it could ever have been moved.

03The statues that walked

Ask how the moai reached their platforms and Rapanui tradition has an answer that sounds, at first, like poetry: they walked. One chant tells of an early ancestor who knew how to make statues walk. For much of the 20th century, visiting researchers treated this as a figure of speech and tried other methods: dragging statues on wooden sledges, lying face up or face down, or rolling them over logs. Several of those methods work in experiments. But they need lots of timber and lots of people, and they do not explain a curious fact: many statues abandoned along the old roads are lying in positions that do not fit dragging.

The walking idea was not new in the 2010s. In 1986 the Czech engineer Pavel Pavel, working with Thor Heyerdahl, rocked an upright moai forward with ropes on the island, but it was slow going and chipped the statue's base, and many archaeologists remained sceptical. In 1998 Jo Anne Van Tilburg, who has spent decades documenting every moai on the island, led an experiment for the television series NOVA in which a replica lying on a wooden sledge was hauled over a track of rails. Both approaches worked, after a fashion. The question was which one matched the evidence left on the ground.

In 2012 archaeologists Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt, working with Rapanui archaeologist Sergio Rapu Haoa, built a concrete replica weighing 4.35 t, with the shape of a road moai. They tied three ropes around its head. Four people held each side rope and ten held a rope running back from the head. When the side teams pulled in turn, the statue rocked onto one edge of its base and swung the other side forward. The rear team kept it from toppling forward. Rock, swing, rock, swing: the statue shuffled ahead in a zigzag. In about 40 minutes the team moved it 100 m.

It only works because of the statue's shape. Road moai, the ones left along the ancient routes from the quarry, have wide, D-shaped bases with a curved front edge, and they lean forward, by about 5 to 15 degrees from vertical. The lean puts the centre of mass ahead of the base, so each sideways rock tips the statue into a small step. Statues standing on the ahu look different: their bases were later reshaped so that they stand straight.

04Roads built for walking

In 2025 Lipo and Hunt published a long reply to their critics in the Journal of Archaeological Science. They used 3D models of 962 moai and looked closely at the 62 statues found along the roads. The roads themselves, which run for more than 25 km out from Rano Raraku, are about 4.5 m wide and concave in cross-section, a little like a shallow gutter. A rocking statue walking along a concave road tends to drift back to the middle, which is exactly what you want when moving several tonnes of top-heavy stone.

Fallen road moai also fit. On downhill stretches most lie face down, as if they toppled forward; on uphill stretches most lie on their backs, as if they tipped backwards. Lipo and Hunt estimate speeds of roughly 0.3 km per hour and a journey of about 10 km in five or six working days for a typical statue. They argue that the evidence of shape, roads, fallen statues and experiment, together with the oral tradition, all points the same way.

The walking method also changes the labour question. Moving a statue upright takes no rollers and very little wood beyond rope fibre, and a crew of a few dozen people could do it in days rather than weeks. That fits a population of a few thousand far better than the old image of vast armies dragging statues across a stripped island. It also helps explain why the roads mattered so much: a smooth, gently concave track was the one piece of infrastructure the method really needed.

How do we know?

Four independent lines of evidence support walking: the physical form of road moai (wide D-shaped bases and a forward lean); the shape of the roads; the positions of statues that fell in transit; and full-scale experiments with replicas. Critics, including researchers who have championed sledges or log rails, point out that a successful experiment shows a method was possible, not that it was the only one used, and that the largest statues pose problems for every method.

05Hats of red stone

Many moai on the ahu once wore pukao, massive cylinders of red volcanic scoria from the small crater of Puna Pau, about 12 km from Rano Raraku. They are often called hats, though many scholars read them as topknots of hair, and the colour red was sacred across Polynesia. The biggest reach about 2 m across and weigh up to around 13 t.

Getting a 13 t cylinder onto the head of a statue 10 m tall sounds absurd. In 2018 Sean Hixon, Carl Lipo, Ben McMorran and Terry Hunt studied the surviving pukao and argued that they were rolled from Puna Pau as rough cylinders, finished near the platforms, and rolled up earthen ramps to the top of the standing statues using a rope technique called parbuckling. The middle of a long rope is fixed at the top of the ramp, the two ends are wrapped around the cylinder, and pulling the ends makes the cylinder roll up the slope. By their calculations fewer than 15 people could move even the largest pukao this way.

06Standing up, and opening their eyes

Arriving at the coast was not the end of the journey. A statue had to be raised onto its ahu, a long platform of fitted stones, often with a paved ramp sloping down on the landward side and burial chambers inside. How it was lifted is less debated than how it travelled, because the method has been reproduced. In the mid-1950s, during Thor Heyerdahl's expedition, a group of Rapanui men re-erected a toppled moai at Anakena using wooden poles as levers and stones packed underneath, raising it a few centimetres at a time until it tipped upright. Their method needed no machines, only patience, timber poles and a growing pile of rocks.

Once on the ahu, the statue changed. Its base was trimmed so that it stood straight rather than leaning forward, and, on many platform moai, deep eye sockets were carved into the face. Excavations at Anakena in the late 1970s recovered fragments of eyes made of white coral with pupils of dark stone, suggesting that some statues were given inlaid eyes at the moment they became active ancestors. Road moai, abandoned on the way, never received eye sockets.

This difference matters for the walking argument. It means the island has two kinds of moai with different shapes: the ones in transit, shaped for moving, and the ones in place, reshaped for standing and seeing. The same statue could be both, at different moments of its life.

07The collapse that wasn't

For decades, Rapa Nui was the world's favourite cautionary tale. Made famous by Jared Diamond's book Collapse (2005), the story went like this: islanders chopped down every tree to move statues, their population soared to 15,000 or more, then crashed into famine, war and cannibalism before Europeans arrived in 1722. The moai became symbols of self-destruction.

Recent evidence tells a different story. In June 2024, Dylan Davis and colleagues mapped rock gardens, the stone mulches the islanders used to grow sweet potatoes in poor, windy soils, using shortwave infrared satellite imagery and machine learning checked against ground surveys. They found rock gardens covering less than 0.76 km², under half of one percent of the island, far below earlier estimates of 4.3 to 21.1 km². Their model suggests a maximum population of about 3,900, give or take 800, close to the roughly 3,000 people that early European visitors described. Critics argue the mapping misses some gardens and other ways of farming, so the exact figure is debated.

Three months later came the genomes. J. Víctor Moreno-Mayar and colleagues sequenced 15 Rapanui individuals and found no genetic bottleneck in the 1600s. The population seems to have grown steadily until the 1860s. The same genomes carry around 10 percent Native American ancestry from contact sometime between about 1250 and 1430, centuries before Columbus.

The genomes also help answer a much older question. Rapanui have long had oral histories of voyaging, and Pacific peoples were among the greatest navigators in human history. The Native American ancestry suggests that either Rapanui sailed to South America and returned, or South Americans reached the island. Either way, this remote island was not sealed off from the world. It was the easternmost point of a vast Polynesian ocean of contact.

Fresh from the field

In 2025 Robert Stein and colleagues published a sediment record from the island's crater lakes showing a long, persistent drought beginning in the mid-1500s. It coincides with the decline of moai building and the rise of the Birdman ritual at Orongo, which intensified around 1600 to 1650. The authors conclude that the changes do not require warfare or demographic collapse; people reorganised around a drier island.

08What really broke Rapa Nui

None of this means the island's history was gentle. The palm forests did disappear, cut and burned for farmland, with seeds eaten by the Polynesian rats that arrived with the first canoes. By the time Europeans came, the statue era was winding down and the moai were gradually toppled, until by the late 1860s none stood on its ahu. Why they fell is still discussed: conflict, deliberate ritual decommissioning, earthquakes and neglect have all been proposed.

The real catastrophe came from outside. In 1862 Peruvian slave raiders seized around a third of the population. Smallpox, carried back by the few survivors who were returned, followed. By 1877 only about 111 Rapanui are reported to have remained on the island. The 'ecocide' story, with its blame on the islanders, did much to hide this history of violence done to them.

The mystery was never really how the moai moved. It was why outsiders found it so hard to believe the islanders' own account.

09Myths, verdicts and open questions

The claim that the moai could not have been moved without outside help, whether from lost continents or visitors from elsewhere, has no evidence behind it. Every stage, from quarry to road to platform to pukao, has a documented, tested method using ropes, stone tools, earth ramps and people. The question is not whether the Rapanui could move moai. It is which of several workable techniques they used, and when.

  • Walking statues: strong evidence, still debated in details, especially for the largest moai.
  • Ecocide-driven collapse before 1722: contradicted by genomes and population estimates.
  • Deforestation: real, with rats and farming both playing a part.
  • Why the moai were toppled: still an open question.

Much remains unknown. How did Rapanui society organise the labour and food for statue building? What did individual moai mean to the lineages that raised them? How exactly did the transition to the Birdman ritual unfold? These questions are increasingly studied with Rapanui researchers and communities, who have their own long knowledge of the statues.

Stand again on the slope of Rano Raraku as the Sun comes up. The unfinished giants are still in the rock. Some of their brothers are still on the roads, face down where they fell on the way to their platforms, with the D-shaped bases and forward lean of statues that were meant to walk.

The big debates

Did the moai walk?

Yes, upright and rockingOral tradition; D-shaped bases and forward lean of road moai; concave roads c. 4.5 m wide; positions of fallen road statues; a 4.35 t replica moved 100 m in 40 minutes by 18 people.
Other or mixed methodsSledge and log-rail experiments also work; experiments show what is possible, not what was actually done; the largest statues are problematic for any method.

The bold claim: Most moai were moved upright, rocked from side to side along prepared roads.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

Several independent lines of evidence, from statue shape and road design to fallen statues, experiments and tradition, agree with walking. Critics raise fair points about alternatives and about the giants, but no competing method explains the road moai's shapes and fall positions as well.

Did an 'ecocide' collapse destroy Rapanui society before 1722?

Yes, collapseDeforestation, abandoned statues, and early estimates of a population of 15,000 or more that crashed before contact.
No collapse before contactGenomes of 15 individuals show no 1600s bottleneck; rock gardens support only about 3,900 people at most; a drought record points to reorganisation, not ruin.

The bold claim: The islanders' own environmental destruction caused a population crash before Europeans arrived.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Deforestation happened, but the claimed pre-contact population crash is contradicted by genetic evidence and by revised population estimates that match what Europeans saw in 1722. The demographic disaster came after 1862 with slave raids and disease. Details such as the exact population are still debated.

Were the pukao rolled up ramps onto standing statues?

Yes, parbuckled up rampsWear patterns and shapes of surviving pukao, remains of ramps, and physics showing 15 or fewer people could roll the largest ones.
Placed with the statue lying downAn older idea is that the pukao was fixed before the statue was raised, lifting both together.

The bold claim: Pukao were rolled up earthen ramps and placed on already-standing moai.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The 2018 study fits the physical evidence and requires modest labour, but it is a reconstruction from the stones themselves. No direct record of the operation survives, and other methods cannot be fully excluded.

Nazca and Palpa, Peru

The Nazca Lines

A hummingbird the length of a football pitch, drawn by moving stones, and 303 more figures found in one AI-assisted season.
