Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa, 1994UNESCO

The Nazca pampa is covered with reddish-brown stones darkened by a coating of iron and manganese oxides, lying on paler, finer ground. To draw, people moved the dark stones aside and piled them along the edges, exposing a light line. Figures could be laid out from a small sketch with wooden stakes and cords, measuring out from a baseline or grid; a 1982 experiment by Joe Nickell and five relatives reproduced a 134 m condor in a Kentucky field this way. Line-type figures such as the hummingbird are drawn as a single continuous path. Smaller relief-type figures on slopes were made by clearing and heaping stones. The extremely dry, stable desert surface has preserved them for some two thousand years.

The myth

The lines can only be seen from the air, so they must be runways or signals made for, or by, visitors from space.

The reality

Many figures can be seen from nearby hills and foothills, and the small relief figures sit beside ancient footpaths where walkers would pass them. The lines are shallow scrapes in loose gravel, useless as runways. Excavated pottery, cairns and footpath networks tie them to the Paracas and Nasca cultures, and the leading interpretations involve water, fertility and ritual walking. Exactly what each figure meant remains debated.

Wow

An AI system trained on a few hundred known figures helped archaeologists find 303 new figurative geoglyphs in about six months of fieldwork, nearly doubling a total that had taken almost a century to build.

Mystery meterA few loose ends
The deep dive10 min read · 2,281 words · 2 animated drawings

01Drawings you can walk

On the high desert plain between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, about 400 km south of Lima, the ground is a flat sheet of dark stones stretching to the foothills of the Andes. It barely rains. There is almost nothing to hear except wind. Scratched into this surface, over some 450 km², are straight lines running for kilometres, great triangles and trapezoids, spirals, and animals: a monkey with a curled tail, a spider, a condor, a whale, and a hummingbird about 93 m from beak to tail.

They were made by the Paracas and Nasca peoples, roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE, long before the Inca. They are called geoglyphs, drawings on the ground. Together, the lines add up to more than 1,300 km. UNESCO listed the Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa as a World Heritage Site in 1994, and they remain one of the most famous, and most misunderstood, archaeological sites on Earth.

Seen from the ground at midday, many lines almost vanish. Early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the Sun is low, the slight dip of a cleared line and its stone borders catch shadows and the drawings spring out. That is one reason travellers crossed the pampa for centuries without describing the figures, and one reason the first systematic maps were made only in the 20th century.

Nobody needed an aircraft to make them. They needed a sketch, some stakes and cord, and a lot of walking.

02How to draw on a desert

The trick is contrast. The pampa is covered with a layer of small, angular stones. Over thousands of years, a thin skin of iron and manganese oxides, the so-called desert varnish, has darkened their exposed faces to a reddish brown. Beneath them lies paler, finer sediment. Pick up the dark stones along a strip, drop them at the edge, and a pale line appears. Do the same along a curve and you have drawn a figure.

The lines are shallow, generally described as only 10 to 15 cm deep, and widths vary from about 30 cm to more than a metre for figure outlines, with much wider cleared areas for the trapezoids. The removed stones often form low borders. Why have such fragile marks lasted two thousand years? Because the Nazca pampa is one of the driest places in the world, receiving only a few millimetres of rain in a typical year, and the stony surface is stable. The same stones that make the drawings possible also protect the ground from wind.

There are two broad kinds of figure. Line-type geoglyphs, like the hummingbird and the monkey, are big outlines drawn with a single continuous line on flat ground. Relief-type geoglyphs are smaller, usually on slopes, and were made by clearing and piling stones so the figure stands out as an area rather than an outline. Many of the relief-type figures, especially around Palpa, are thought to be older, from the Paracas period.

03The people of the pampa

The first geoglyph makers belonged to the Paracas culture, famous for the richly embroidered textiles wrapped around mummy bundles on the Paracas peninsula to the north. Many of the hillside relief figures around Palpa, with their round-eyed human and animal forms, echo Paracas art. From roughly 100 BCE the Nasca culture took over the region. Nasca potters painted vessels in many colours with hummingbirds, monkeys, killer whales, spiders and mythical beings, many of the same subjects that appear on the pampa, and this shared imagery is one of the strongest links between the lines and their makers.

Nasca people farmed narrow river valleys in one of the driest regions on Earth. Water was everything. Near Nazca, underground aqueducts called puquios, with spiral access shafts, still bring groundwater to fields; many researchers attribute at least some of them to the Nasca, although their dating is debated. The same concern with water runs through Nasca art, ritual and, it seems, the lines themselves.

04Stakes, cords and a Kentucky condor

How do you draw a 93 m bird accurately when you cannot see it whole from the ground? In 1982 the investigator Joe Nickell decided to find out. With five relatives, working in a field in Kentucky, he reproduced the Nazca condor at full size, about 134 m long. They used only tools that would have been available to the Nasca: a small drawing, wooden stakes and string. They plotted points by measuring from a baseline, joined them with cord, and marked the line. Photographs taken from the air showed a figure remarkably close to the original.

Nickell's point was not that he knew the exact Nasca method, but that no exotic method was needed. Other researchers have suggested different techniques, such as sighting along stakes for straight lines and drawing arcs from a fixed stake with a cord, the way a gardener marks a round flowerbed. Traces of stakes have been reported at the ends of some lines. Several methods may have been used, and small teams working for days, not armies working for years, would have been enough for a single figure.

How do we know?

Replications show what is possible, not what happened. The real evidence for the Nasca makers comes from pottery in Nasca styles found on and beside the lines, from the similarity of the figures to images on Nasca ceramics and textiles, from stone cairns and small structures at line ends, and from radiocarbon dates on associated material. Together they place most of the figures in the Paracas and Nasca periods.

05Maria Reiche, guardian of the lines

The lines were noted in the 1920s by the Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe, who described them as ceremonial paths. In June 1941 the American historian Paul Kosok, studying ancient irrigation, stood on the pampa at sunset on the southern winter solstice and watched the Sun go down near the end of one of the lines. He called the pampa the largest astronomy book in the world.

Kosok's assistant, the German-born mathematician Maria Reiche (1903–1998), made the lines her life's work. From the 1940s until her death she measured, mapped and swept them, living near the pampa, and argued that many lines pointed to astronomical events. She also fought to protect them from road building and agriculture. Much of the protection the lines enjoy today is due to her.

Her astronomical theory has fared less well. In the late 1960s the astronomer Gerald Hawkins tested line directions against the rising and setting points of the Sun, Moon and bright stars and found no more matches than chance would predict. Later work by Anthony Aveni and colleagues found that some lines relate to the Sun, especially around the time of year when water arrives in the rivers, but that astronomy cannot explain the whole system.

06What were they for?

After decades of fieldwork, the leading interpretations share one theme: water. The Nazca region depends on rivers fed by rain in the Andes, and on underground water. Aveni's teams found that many straight lines radiate from 'line centres', natural hills or mounds, often near water sources, and that lines tend to run towards the rivers. The anthropologist Johan Reinhard linked the lines to Andean traditions of mountain and water worship. David Johnson proposed that some lines mark underground water flowing along geological faults, an idea that remains debated.

A second theme is movement. The figures are drawn as single paths that can be walked from one end to the other. Broken pottery, often fine vessels deliberately smashed, lies along lines and at their ends, suggesting offerings. Clive Ruggles and Nicholas Saunders studied a huge labyrinth-like figure on the pampa, a single path several kilometres long that leads walkers in and back out, and argued that walking it was the point: the drawings were made to be experienced from the ground, by people moving through them in procession.

Some lines lead towards Cahuachi, a large Nasca ceremonial centre of adobe mounds by the Nazca river. Many researchers see the pampa as a ritual landscape tied to Cahuachi and to seasonal ceremonies for water and fertility. No single explanation covers every line, and there is no reason to expect one: the geoglyphs were made over nearly a thousand years.

Then there are the trapezoids and triangles, huge cleared areas that can stretch for hundreds of metres. They may have been gathering places, or spaces for ceremonies, or simply bigger versions of the paths. Aveni and others noted that many sit near line centres and that their narrow ends often point in the same direction as nearby watercourses. Excavations at their edges have found pottery and small stone structures, reinforcing the picture of places used, not just drawn.

07Runways for visitors?

In 1968 Erich von Däniken's bestseller Chariots of the Gods? suggested that the long straight lines and trapezoids looked like an airfield, and that the figures were meant to be seen from the sky. The idea has been repeated on television ever since. It is easy to test.

Could anything land here? The lines are shallow scrapes in loose gravel over soft sediment; any heavy vehicle, as the 2018 truck incident showed, leaves deep ruts. Must they be seen from the air? No. Many figures can be seen from the surrounding hills, and the new relief figures sit right next to ancient footpaths. Could people make them without aerial guidance? Yes: replications with stakes and cords show it. And who made them? The pottery, the styles, the dates and the parallels with Nasca art all point to the people who lived there.

The hillside figure nicknamed 'the astronaut' is a good example. It is a relief-type figure on a slope with a round head and big eyes, one hand raised. Similar round-eyed figures appear in Paracas and Nasca art. The nickname is modern; the figure is Andean.

08Fresh from the field: 303 new figures

Finding new geoglyphs had been slow. By 2022, after almost a century of research, 430 figurative geoglyphs were known, and the historical discovery rate was only a handful per year. Yamagata University in Japan, which has run fieldwork at Nazca since 2004, teamed up with IBM Research to try a different approach: train an AI model on high-resolution aerial images of known figures, then let it flag candidates across the whole pampa.

The results, published by Masato Sakai and colleagues in PNAS in 2024, were dramatic. Checking the AI's candidates on foot during about six months of field survey between September 2022 and February 2023, the team confirmed 303 new figurative geoglyphs, nearly doubling the total. The AI was especially good at spotting small relief-type figures that humans had overlooked on photographs. People still did the decisive work: every candidate had to be checked on the ground before it counted.

  • Relief-type figures mostly show humans or things modified by humans: domesticated camelids, decapitated heads and people (81.6 per cent).
  • They lie on average 43 m from ancient footpaths that cross the pampa, well within viewing distance for walkers.
  • Large line-type figures mostly show wild animals (64 per cent), such as birds, monkeys and other wild creatures.
  • Line-type figures lie on average 34 m from the network of straight lines and trapezoids, suggesting community-level rituals.

The authors conclude that the small relief figures were probably made and viewed by individuals or small groups travelling along the trails, perhaps as messages or markers, while the giant line figures were built and used by whole communities for ritual activities. That is a big step from guessing about purposes to testing them with distributions.

How does such an AI work? In simple terms, it is shown hundreds of image tiles containing known geoglyphs and many more without them, and learns the visual patterns of cleared lines and heaped stones. Run across the whole pampa, it ranks tiles by how likely they are to contain a figure. The archaeologists then study the top candidates and walk out to check them. In 2019 an earlier phase of the Yamagata and IBM collaboration had already announced 143 new figures, including one found with AI help, so the 2024 result is the product of years of refinement.

09Fragile giants

The same simplicity that makes the lines easy to make makes them easy to damage. A footprint on the pampa can last for decades. In December 2014, activists placing a protest banner near the hummingbird left footprints across the fragile surface. In January 2018 a truck driver drove off the Pan-American Highway and across part of the site, scarring three straight lines. Informal settlements, mining and farming press against the edges of the protected zone.

Peru's Ministry of Culture patrols the area and restricts access, and viewing towers beside the highway let visitors see some figures without walking on them. Overflights from the Nazca airfield show the big figures to tourists. The irony is gentle: the lines were probably made to be walked, and today the best way to protect them is not to walk on them at all.

10What we still don't know

We know how the lines were made and roughly when and by whom. We have good evidence that they were walked, that they were linked to water and ceremony, and that different kinds of figures served different audiences. What remains uncertain is the specific meaning of individual figures, how the choice of animals relates to Nasca beliefs, how labour was organised over centuries, and how many geoglyphs are still undiscovered. With AI surveys continuing, the count is likely to keep rising.

The next steps are already visible. Drone photography and high-resolution satellite images make it possible to monitor damage almost in real time. Excavations along the newly mapped trails could date the small relief figures more precisely and show who used the paths. Comparing the positions of figures with ancient settlements, cemeteries and water sources, now possible with far larger datasets, may finally show how the pampa worked as a whole: which figures belonged to which communities, and how the ritual landscape changed as the Nasca world changed. The questions that once invited fantasy are turning into questions that data can answer.

The Nazca Lines do not need visitors from elsewhere to be astonishing. They show a desert people turning an entire landscape into a place for ceremony, one line at a time, with a precision that still delights anyone who walks, or flies, above them.

The big debates

Were the lines runways or signals for visitors from space?

Yes: they look like airfields and are best seen from the air.Von Däniken (1968) pointed to long straight lines and trapezoids resembling runways and figures seemingly designed to be viewed from above.
No: they are shallow ritual paths made by local people.The surface is loose gravel on soft ground; many figures are visible from hills and trails; replication shows they can be made from the ground; Nasca pottery and styles tie them to local cultures (Aveni 2000; Sakai et al. 2024).

The bold claim: The Nazca Lines were made as runways or signals for extraterrestrial visitors.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Every testable element fails: the ground cannot bear landings, aerial viewing is not needed, simple methods suffice, and the archaeology identifies the makers. The idea survives on television, not in the evidence.

Were the lines an astronomical calendar?

Yes: many lines point to celestial events.Kosok saw a solstice sunset along a line in 1941; Reiche spent decades arguing for solar, lunar and stellar alignments.
Mostly no.Hawkins's tests found no more alignments than chance; Aveni's work found some solar links, but most lines relate better to water, walking and line centres.

The bold claim: The main purpose of the Nazca Lines was to record astronomical alignments.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

With hundreds of lines in every direction, some will point at something in the sky by chance. Statistical tests do not show a strong astronomical design, although a few lines may well have had solar meanings.

Were the lines made for walking rituals linked to water?

Yes: paths for ceremony.Figures are single walkable lines; smashed pottery offerings lie along them; lines radiate from line centres towards water; figures relate to trails (Ruggles & Saunders 2012; Sakai et al. 2024).
Only partly.Some lines may have marked water sources, boundaries or routes; meanings likely changed over nearly a thousand years.

The bold claim: Nazca geoglyphs were made mainly for ritual walking connected to water and fertility.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

Several independent kinds of evidence point the same way, and the 2024 distribution study adds real data. But purposes surely varied between lines, periods and communities, so a single explanation should be held loosely.

South India, Sri Lanka and Damascus

Damascus (wootz) steel

A steel cake from a sealed clay pot, hammered at dull red heat, became a blade that looks like flowing water.

Mystery

Smiths in South India and Sri Lanka packed iron and carbon-rich plant matter into clay crucibles, sealed them and fired them for many hours until the charge melted into a small cake of steel with about 1.5% carbon. The cakes were traded west, to Persia, Syria and Central Asia, where swordsmiths forged them slowly at a dull red heat, reheating and hammering again and again. Tiny traces of vanadium and similar elements, left in the steel from the original ore, made sheets of hard iron carbide particles line up during these cycles. Etching the finished blade in acid revealed those sheets as a shimmering 'watered' pattern.

The myth

Damascus steel was a lost magical recipe: blades sliced floating silk, cut through gun barrels, contained deliberate nanotechnology and still cannot be copied today.

The reality

The blades were excellent for their time, not supernatural. The pattern comes from carbide banding caused by trace impurities, a mechanism Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch described in 1998 and used to forge convincing replicas. What faded after about 1750 was probably a supply of suitable ore and the craft knowledge around it. Carbon nanotubes reported in one 17th-century sabre in 2006 are interesting chemistry, but there is no evidence that they explain the pattern or the blade's performance.

Wow

The pattern on a genuine wootz blade is not a surface decoration at all: it is the steel's own microstructure, sheets of carbide particles spaced about 0.05 mm apart, made visible by a light etch.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,249 words · 2 animated drawings

01A blade that looks like running water

Tilt a genuine Damascus sabre under a lamp and the steel seems to move. Pale threads curl across a darker ground, gathering into ripples, whorls and ladders, as if someone had frozen the surface of a stream. Medieval writers called it watered steel. Collectors in Europe called it damask, after the patterned silk. The swordsmiths of Persia and Syria who made it prized the pattern as a guarantee: you could not fake it by painting or engraving, because it was the metal itself.

That last point is what makes these blades a scientific story as well as a romantic one. The pattern is a map of the steel's internal structure, sheets of hard iron carbide particles spaced roughly 30–70 micrometres apart, made visible by a light acid etch. To get those sheets you need an unusual steel, an unusual forging routine and, as it turned out, a pinch of an element nobody at the time knew existed.

The pattern was not painted on. It was the steel showing its own skeleton.

The raw material did not come from Damascus at all. It came, as small round cakes, from crucible workshops in South India and Sri Lanka, and it was known in the West by an English mangling of the South Indian word ukku, steel: wootz.

02Steel from a sealed clay pot

Most iron in the ancient and medieval world was never melted. Smelters reduced ore in a furnace to a spongy bloom and hammered out the slag. Crucible steel was different and far harder to make. A smith packed pieces of iron into a small clay crucible together with carbon-rich plant matter, such as wood and leaves, sealed the mouth with clay and set a batch of crucibles in a furnace. Firings could last up to about 24 hours at temperatures that probably exceeded 1,300 °C, hot enough for the iron to soak up carbon and melt into liquid steel.

When the furnace cooled, the crucibles were broken open to release a cake of steel with about 1.5% carbon, roughly twice the carbon of a good modern kitchen knife. Nineteenth-century observers in Mysore described crucibles holding around 400 g of iron. Verhoeven and his colleagues put typical traded cakes at about 2.3 kg. Sri Lankan crucibles from Hattota Amune, dated to about 680–990 CE, are smaller still: narrow-necked flasks with a body only about 45 mm wide that could have produced little more than a button of steel.

Sri Lanka had another trick. On exposed ridges near Samanalawewa, Gill Juleff excavated rows of iron-smelting furnaces from the second half of the first millennium CE, built along the western edges of hills to catch the strong monsoon wind. Her experimental furnace, driven by nothing but the wind, produced high-carbon steel directly. Picture, perhaps, a line of glowing clay walls on a hillside during the monsoon, roaring without a single bellows. It is not wootz itself, but it shows how inventive South Asian iron-making was long before European industry.

Slow cooling mattered. As the melt solidified it grew tree-like crystals called dendrites, and the last liquid to freeze, between the dendrite arms, was enriched in trace elements. That invisible chemical striping, set in the crucible, was the seed of the pattern that would appear hundreds of kilometres away and months later on a finished blade.

How do we know?

Three kinds of evidence meet here. Archaeologists have excavated crucible fragments and slag at sites such as the Knuckles range and Yodhawewa in Sri Lanka, Merv in Turkmenistan and Akhsiket in Uzbekistan. European travellers of the late 18th and 19th centuries watched the last Indian workshops operate. And metallurgists have sectioned surviving blades and ingots under the microscope to read the process backwards.

03The long road to Damascus

By the 9th century crucible steel was a Eurasian industry. At Merv, in today's Turkmenistan, a 9th to early 10th-century workshop made steel by co-fusion, melting cast iron with wrought iron. In the Ferghana Valley, excavators at Akhsiket and Pap have found hundreds of thousands of crucible fragments from the 9th–12th centuries. At Chahak in southern Iran, Rahil Alipour, Thilo Rehren and Marcos Martinón-Torres found crucible steel containing about 1% chromium, apparently added on purpose, and linked it to a mysterious ingredient named in a recipe by the scholar al-Biruni.

Indian cakes kept moving west throughout. By the late 1600s, according to trade records summarised by Sharada Srinivasan and Srinivasa Ranganathan, tens of thousands of wootz ingots were being shipped from the Coromandel coast to Persia. Blades forged from them were sold in the markets of Damascus, and whether the city lent its name to the steel, or the name comes from an Arabic word for water, or from a smith called Damasqui whom al-Biruni mentions, is still debated.

The Arab philosopher al-Kindi, writing in the 9th century, already sorted swords by the steel they were made from, where they were forged and the look of their surface. The watered pattern was a trademark and a quality mark, and buyers learned to read it the way a modern wine buyer reads a label.

A wootz cake was not easy to work. Steel with 1.5% carbon behaves very differently from the softer iron most smiths knew. Heated as hot as an ordinary bar, it could crack or crumble under the hammer, and 19th-century European smiths who tried it reported exactly that frustration. The Persian and Syrian masters succeeded because they worked it cooler and more patiently, drawing the cake out into a bar over many heats. That patience, it turns out, was not just a workaround. It was the very thing that made the pattern.

04Why the pattern appears

For two centuries European scientists tried and failed to copy wootz. Michael Faraday analysed it in 1819 and concluded that aluminium was the secret, which turned out to be slag contamination. The breakthrough came from an unlikely partnership in the 1980s and 1990s: John Verhoeven, a materials scientist at Iowa State University, and Alfred Pendray, a Florida bladesmith who had spent years trying to forge patterned blades from small crucible ingots.

A quick primer helps. Steel is iron with a little carbon. Up to about 0.8% carbon, the carbon can be absorbed into a fine layered mixture called pearlite. Beyond that, the surplus forms cementite, an iron carbide that is extremely hard and rather brittle. In an ordinary high-carbon steel, cementite tends to form continuous networks around the grains, and the steel snaps. In a good wootz blade the cementite is broken up into separate particles, lined up in sheets and held in a tougher pearlite matrix: hard grit in a resilient binder, a little like gravel set in concrete.

Pendray could sometimes get a pattern and sometimes not, from ingots that looked identical. Chemical analysis of genuine old blades supplied the clue. Four swords first studied by the Swiss metallurgist Zschokke in 1924 contained between 50 and 270 parts per million of vanadium, with smaller contributions from elements such as molybdenum and manganese. When Pendray and Verhoeven added about 40 ppm or more of vanadium to their melts, the bands appeared reliably. Without it, they did not.

The mechanism, set out by Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch in 1998, runs roughly like this. Vanadium segregates to the spaces between dendrite arms as the ingot freezes. During forging, the steel is heated to a dull red, about 50–100 °C below the temperature at which its carbides would fully dissolve, then hammered and allowed to cool. Each cycle, some carbide dissolves and then re-forms preferentially where the vanadium-rich regions are. After six to eight cycles, the particles have gathered into distinct sheets, and continued forging flattens the sheets parallel to the blade's surface.

Grinding the finished blade cuts across those gently undulating sheets at shallow angles, which is why the surface shows curls and ripples rather than straight lines. Smiths could steer the look: filing grooves or drilling shallow holes before the final forging produced the 'ladder' and 'rose' patterns collectors love.

A few dozen parts per million of vanadium, carried from the ore, decided whether a smith got a masterpiece or a plain grey blade.

05Nanotubes in a sabre

In November 2006 the journal Nature published a one-page report that went around the world. Marianne Reibold, Peter Paufler and colleagues at the Technical University of Dresden had dissolved a small sample from a 17th-century sabre, attributed to the smith Assad Ullah and supplied by the Bern Historical Museum, in hydrochloric acid and examined the residue with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy. They reported multiwalled carbon nanotubes, and elongated nanowires of cementite that the tubes may have encapsulated.

Headlines announced that medieval smiths had used nanotechnology. That is where a fair hearing becomes important. The finding is genuinely interesting: it shows that complex carbon nanostructures can form in an ordinary historical forging process, perhaps with trace metals acting as catalysts, as the authors suggested. But it was one sample from one blade, the method involved dissolving the steel before looking, and the paper did not test whether the nanostructures affect the pattern or the performance.

I doubt that they play any role in the unique banded microstructure that gives Damascus steels their beautiful surface patterns.

John Verhoeven, quoted in Chemical & Engineering News (November 2006)

Verhoeven also pointed out that similar nanostructures might be expected in pearlite, a constituent of countless ordinary steels. The honest verdict: nanotubes are a real observation awaiting replication and context, not the secret of the sword. The pattern is fully explained, at the scale you can see, by micrometre-sized carbide particles.

Keep the scales in mind. The carbide particles that draw the pattern are about 5–15 micrometres across, visible in an ordinary optical microscope. The reported nanotubes are roughly a thousand times smaller, measured in nanometres, and could only be seen after the steel around them had been dissolved away. They sit inside the story, not at the centre of it.

06Legends of the edge

Some of the most famous stories about Damascus blades come from fiction. In Walter Scott's 1825 novel The Talisman, Saladin slices a silk cushion and a floating veil with his scimitar, while Richard the Lionheart smashes an iron bar with his broadsword. The scene is memorable, but it is a novelist's invention, and later retellings added gun barrels and rocks.

Real blades were superb for their time because they combined a very hard steel with enough toughness to survive combat. Carbide particles in a softer matrix can give an edge a fine, slightly serrated bite. Yet modern tests do not show magic. Metallurgist Larrin Thomas has summarised sharpening experiments in which crucible Damascus did not take a keener edge than good modern carbon steels, and cutting tests in which it did not clearly outlast them at comparable hardness.

  • Plausible: wootz blades were harder and held an edge better than most contemporary iron and steel swords.
  • Legend: cutting through rifle barrels or stone without damage.
  • Fiction: Saladin's floating silk, from Walter Scott's novel.
  • Confusion: most modern 'Damascus' knives are pattern-welded, made by forge-welding layers of different steels, a different and much older technique.

The name itself added to the muddle. In the 19th century, gunmakers sold shotgun barrels as 'Damascus' because they were twisted and forge-welded from strips of iron and steel, giving a patterned surface. Those barrels had nothing to do with crucible steel, and several failed under the pressure of modern smokeless powder, which is one reason the word 'Damascus' drifted so far from its original meaning.

07A lost art, found again

The finest watered blades seem to end around 1750, and quality declined into the early 19th century. The last eyewitness account of traditional crucible steelmaking in Sri Lanka dates from 1903. Why did the art fade? Verhoeven and Pendray's answer is careful and quite convincing: the Indian ore deposits that happened to carry the right trace elements were exhausted or became inaccessible, and when new sources arrived, the knowledge needed to exploit them had gone.

Other pressures probably helped. Cheap European steel and firearms changed what buyers wanted, and colonial disruption hit the small village industries that made crucible steel. None of this required a secret formula to vanish, only a chain of ore, crucible makers, traders and smiths to break.

Rediscovery came in stages. In Russia, Pavel Anosov produced patterned 'bulat' steel in the 1830s and 1840s. In the 20th century, metallurgists recognised that the pattern came from carbide banding in hypereutectoid steel. And in the 1990s Pendray forged blades whose structure and pattern match museum originals closely enough to convince specialists.

Fresh from the field

Recent work continues to widen the picture. The 2021 Chahak study showed that Persian crucible steelmakers used chromium centuries before modern alloy steels. A 2026 review by Chakravarty, Mondal and Mishra in the Indian Journal of History of Science surveys wootz production in India and argues for more systematic study of excavated crucibles and ingots.

08What we still do not know

The physics of the pattern is well understood, which is why the mystery level here is low. The open questions are historical. When exactly did crucible steelmaking begin? Kodumanal in Tamil Nadu, occupied from about the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd century CE, offers promising but still preliminary evidence. Were Indian, Sri Lankan and Central Asian crucible traditions invented separately or connected by trade? Which ore bodies supplied the vanadium, and did smiths recognise good sources by experience?

There is also the question of how much smiths understood. They certainly knew which cakes worked and which forging rhythm brought the pattern out, and some added ingredients on purpose, as the Chahak chromium shows. But they worked without any concept of carbides, dendrites or parts per million. Their knowledge lived in hands, eyes and apprenticeship, and that is exactly the kind of knowledge that can disappear within a generation.

The secret was never one ingredient. It was an entire supply chain, from ore to crucible to hammer, and it broke.

Stand in front of a watered blade in a museum case and you are looking at the fingerprints of that chain: a South Indian ore, a sealed clay pot, a long voyage west and hundreds of patient hammer blows at a dull red heat.

The big debates

Do carbon nanotubes explain the blades' pattern or strength?

Yes, they are part of the answerReibold et al. (2006) reported multiwalled carbon nanotubes and cementite nanowires in a 17th-century sabre and suggested they may help explain the banding and the steel's properties.
No, not on present evidenceThe pattern is fully accounted for by micrometre-scale carbide bands reproduced in modern experiments; the nanotube result comes from one sample, and Verhoeven doubted any role in the banding.

The bold claim: Medieval smiths used nanotechnology, and nanotubes are the secret of Damascus steel.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The nanotube observation is real and worth replicating, but no study has linked it to the pattern, hardness or toughness of wootz blades. The banding mechanism is explained and reproduced without it, and the smiths had no way to know nanostructures existed, so calling it deliberate nanotechnology goes beyond the evidence.

Why did the art of watered steel fade after about 1750?

Ore ran outVerhoeven and Pendray argue the Indian ores carrying the right trace elements were exhausted or became inaccessible, and later ores lacked them.
Markets and craft collapsedCheap imported steel, firearms and colonial-era disruption undermined village crucible industries and apprenticeship chains.

The bold claim: The loss of watered steel was caused by exhaustion of trace-element-rich ores combined with the loss of craft knowledge.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The impurity mechanism makes ore chemistry a genuine bottleneck, and the timing fits the decline of Indian crucible industries. But nobody has yet traced specific ore bodies to specific blades, and economic and political changes almost certainly played a part, so this remains a well-grounded explanation rather than a settled one.

Constantinople and the Byzantine fleets

Greek fire

A burning liquid sprayed from bronze tubes on warships saved Constantinople, then vanished so completely that its recipe is still unknown.

No recipe survives, so everything here is inference from texts and experiments. Byzantine writers describe a liquid kept in the ships, heated, and projected through a bronze tube called a siphon, which could set enemy ships alight and kept burning on the water. John Haldon and Maurice Byrne proposed in 1977 that crude oil was heated in a sealed bronze tank, pressurised by a force pump, released through a valve and lit at the nozzle by a flame. In 2002 Haldon, with Andrew Lacey and Colin Hewes, built a working version with a double-cylinder bronze pump and light crude oil, and it threw a burning jet about 15 m.

The myth

Greek fire was a miracle chemical that water could not put out, perhaps an early napalm or gunpowder, and modern science has no idea what it was.

The reality

Most historians think it was a petroleum-based liquid, perhaps thickened with resins, projected by a heated, pressurised siphon. That explains fire on water, a jet of flame and the thick smoke the sources describe. Sources say sand, strong vinegar or old urine could put it out. Gunpowder and saltpetre were unknown in the Mediterranean at the time. The exact recipe and apparatus remain genuinely unknown, and every reconstruction is an informed hypothesis.

Wow

The secret was guarded so tightly, as an imperial monopoly on both the recipe and the trained crews, that the Byzantines themselves seem to have lost it before the empire fell.

01Fire that walked on water

Imagine rowing towards Constantinople in the 670s. The city's sea walls are ahead, and a line of long, low warships slides out to meet you. At the bow of each, under a raised platform, a crew member aims a bronze tube. There is a roar, a gout of thick black smoke, and a jet of liquid fire arcs across the water, sticks to your hull and keeps burning on the sea around you. Throwing water on it only seems to spread it.

That is roughly what Byzantine and Arab sources describe, and it is why this weapon became a legend. Western crusaders later called it Greek fire. The Byzantines, who thought of themselves as Romans, had plainer names: sea fire, liquid fire, prepared fire, Roman fire.

For five centuries, the most feared weapon at sea was a liquid, a pump and a crew trained to keep a secret.

The mystery is not whether it existed. Dozens of passages across five centuries show that it did. The mystery is what exactly was in the tank, how it was pushed through the tube, and how a state could guard the answer so well that the answer died with it.

02The refugee with a recipe

The story begins with a single line in the Chronographia of Theophanes the Confessor, written in the early 9th century from older sources. Under the year corresponding to about 672 CE, he records the arrival of a refugee from the eastern provinces then under Arab rule.

At that time Kallinikos, an artificer from Heliopolis, fled to the Romans. He had devised a sea fire which ignited the Arab ships and burned them with all hands.

Theophanes, Chronographia (entry for c. 672 CE), trans. Harry Turtledove (1982)

Context explains why a single engineer mattered so much. In the 630s and 640s the eastern Roman Empire had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt, its richest provinces, to the new Arab state. By the 650s Arab fleets built in Syrian and Egyptian shipyards were raiding Cyprus, Rhodes and the Aegean coasts, and in 655 they defeated the imperial navy off the coast of Lycia. For the first time in centuries, Constantinople faced a serious enemy at sea. A weapon that could burn ships before they came alongside was worth a fortune.

Heliopolis here is the Syrian city now called Baalbek, not the one in Egypt. Theophanes calls Kallinikos an architect or artificer, a technical man, and the timing was perfect. The Umayyad Caliphate had been pushing into the Aegean and was preparing to attack the imperial capital itself.

It is worth being cautious about the inventor story. Incendiary weapons were old news: Assyrians, Greeks and Romans had all thrown burning pitch, sulphur and oil. Petroleum seeps were known around the Black Sea and in Mesopotamia. What seems to have been new was the combination of a particular fuel with a way of projecting it as a pressurised jet from a ship. Kallinikos may have brought the key idea, or later tradition may have pinned a gradual development on one memorable name.

03Saving Constantinople, twice

According to Theophanes, the emperor Constantine IV had large 'cauldron-bearing' warships equipped with siphons, and fire played a decisive part in repelling Arab fleets that blockaded the city from a base at Cyzicus in the 670s. The traditional account describes a siege lasting from 674 to 678. Some historians, notably Marek Jankowiak, now argue that the 'first siege' is a later reshaping of a shorter blockade in the late 660s. Either way, the fire entered the record as a city-saving weapon.

The second great test came in 717–718, when a huge Arab army and fleet besieged Constantinople by land and sea. Theophanes describes Byzantine ships attacking the enemy fleet with fire siphons and burning many vessels. Combined with a harsh winter, disease, supply failures and Bulgar attacks on the besiegers, the defence held, a turning point in the history of the eastern Mediterranean.

Later uses are scattered through the chronicles: against the rebel Thomas the Slav in the early 820s, against a Rus' fleet led by Prince Igor that attacked the Bosporus in 941, and against a Pisan fleet around 1099, described by the princess and historian Anna Komnene. By then the weapon had acquired theatre as well as power.

And the fire which was to be directed against the enemy through tubes he made to pass through the mouths of the beasts, so that it seemed as if the lions and the other similar monsters were vomiting the fire.

Anna Komnene, Alexiad XI.10, trans. Elizabeth A. S. Dawes (1928)

04How the siphon may have worked

The Byzantine word siphōn simply means a tube, and the sources never draw the machine. What they do give are clues. Emperor Leo VI's military handbook, the Taktika, written around 900, instructs that a dromon should carry a siphon in its prow, sheathed in bronze, to shoot the prepared fire at the enemy, and it mentions a newer hand-held version. Other passages mention cauldrons, heat and the roar and smoke of discharge.

The ship mattered as much as the pump. The standard 10th-century warship was the dromon, a long, narrow galley that John Pryor and Elizabeth Jeffreys reconstruct at about 31–32 m, with two banks of oars, 25 oars per bank on each side. A heavy dromon carried around 230 rowers and 70 marines. The main siphon sat in the bow under a raised fighting platform, and large ships may have carried extra siphons amidships. Low, fast and packed with men, the dromon could close to within range, fire, and back off before the enemy could grapple.

From these clues, John Haldon and Maurice Byrne argued in 1977 for a clever but physically simple system. Put crude oil in a sealed bronze tank. Warm it over a small fire so it thins and its vapour pressure rises. Add pressure with a force pump, the same kind of bronze pump Romans used for fire-fighting and water supply. Open a valve, and the liquid rushes along a pipe to a swivelling nozzle, where a small flame lights it as it leaves.

Every part of that system was within Byzantine reach. Double-cylinder force pumps are described by Hero of Alexandria and survive archaeologically from Roman sites. Bronze casting, valves and soldered pipes were ordinary technology. The genius, if the hypothesis is right, lay in combining them, and in training crews who could handle a pressurised tank of hot oil in the bow of a pitching wooden ship without incinerating themselves.

How do we know?

We do not know for certain. The mechanism is reconstructed from a small set of texts, especially Leo VI's Taktika, Theophanes, Anna Komnene and scattered references to cauldrons and bronze tubes, plus knowledge of Roman pumps. No siphon has ever been excavated. That is why the drawings here are marked as reconstructions, with dashed outlines where the design is guessed.

05Testing the idea with real fire

In 2002, for a television documentary, Haldon worked with engineers Andrew Lacey and Colin Hewes to build a full working model. It had a cast bronze double-cylinder force pump worked by two people, an oil reservoir, bronze piping, simple one-way flap valves and a swivelling nozzle. Wooden pistons were wrapped in hemp and flax and sealed with tallow. For fuel they used light crude oil from Azerbaijan, geologically similar to sources the Byzantines could have reached around the Black Sea and Caucasus.

It worked. The apparatus threw a jet of burning oil about 15 m, with flame temperatures reported above 1,000 °C, far enough to reach a neighbouring ship without the two hulls touching. Smoke billowed and the burning liquid spread across water, just as the sources describe. The team also learned what could go wrong: the connecting pipes had to be protected, for instance by packing them in sand, so that flames could not creep back towards the tank.

A successful reconstruction is not the same as recovering the original, and Haldon is careful to say so. It shows that the texts can be satisfied by technology the Byzantines had. It does not tell us their exact recipe, pressures or nozzle design. Other arrangements, such as a pump system with no heating at all, cannot be ruled out.

The experiment answers 'could it work?' with a loud yes. It cannot answer 'was it exactly like this?'

06What was in the tank?

Over the centuries, writers have proposed almost every flammable substance known to the medieval world. The main hypotheses fall into a few families.

  • Petroleum-based: light crude oil or naphtha, possibly distilled or 'prepared', often with pine resin added to make it sticky and longer-burning. This is the majority view today.
  • Quicklime: calcium oxide heats up violently when wet, which once seemed a neat explanation for fire that water could not quench. Most scholars now reject it as the main ingredient, because quicklime alone cannot produce a projected jet of flame.
  • Saltpetre and gunpowder: popular in older books, but saltpetre-based mixtures are not documented in the Mediterranean until the 13th century, centuries after Greek fire appeared.
  • Sulphur and other additives: possible minor ingredients, mentioned in later medieval incendiary recipes, but no Byzantine text confirms them.

The petroleum case rests on several converging clues. Constantine VII's handbook on foreign peoples, the De administrando imperio, names oil-bearing places around the Black Sea and Caucasus, such as Tamatarcha and Zichia. Descriptions of fire floating and spreading on water fit a light oil. Thick smoke fits incomplete combustion of crude petroleum. And the sources' list of extinguishers, sand, strong vinegar and old urine, fits a burning oil that water scatters but a smothering or wetting agent might suppress.

Resin is the best candidate for the 'prepared' part. Adding pine resin to oil raises its viscosity, helping it cling to a hull and burn longer. It is chemistry any Byzantine workshop could manage. But no text states it outright, and we should say so plainly.

There is one more practical clue. Greek fire needed a steady, reliable supply. Crude oil seeps around the Black Sea and Caucasus were far from Constantinople, reached through trade and diplomacy with peoples such as the Khazars. If the fuel was a particular light crude from a few specific places, then the weapon was only as secure as those routes, a point that becomes important at the end of the story.

07A secret too well kept

The Byzantines treated the fire as a state secret, perhaps the most successful one in medieval history. In the mid-10th century Emperor Constantine VII told his son that the preparation of the liquid fire must never be handed to any foreign people, whatever they asked. He wrapped the rule in a sacred origin story: the recipe, he wrote, had been revealed from heaven to Constantine the Great, the empire's founder, and anyone who betrayed it would be struck down. He even told of an official who had been bribed into giving some away and was consumed by fire from the sky as he entered a church.

Historians such as Alex Roland have argued that the Byzantines protected the secret by splitting it. One group of specialists knew how to prepare the fuel, another built and serviced the siphons, and ships' crews learned only to operate them. Nobody outside the inner circle held the whole system.

The secrecy seems to have been strategic as well as practical. Enemies did capture Byzantine equipment from time to time. According to Theophanes, the Bulgar khan Krum seized a stock of the fire and its siphons in 812 but could not use them. If true, it suggests that the hardware alone was useless without the prepared fuel and the knowledge of how to handle it.

That strategy worked for centuries, and then it failed from the inside. After the late 11th century, references to ship-mounted siphons become rare. When crusaders stormed Constantinople in 1204, the defenders used improvised fire ships, but no chronicle describes the famous siphons. Haldon suggests that loss of access to Caucasus oil, as Byzantine influence around the Black Sea shrank, may have undermined the whole supply chain. Other explanations include the collapse of the navy itself and the death of the few specialists who knew the process.

Fresh from the field

Popular interest keeps renewing the debate: in July 2026 historians Michael Charles and Eva Anagnostou-Laoutides reviewed the evidence for a general audience, again favouring a crude-oil and resin mixture delivered by a pressurised siphon. No new physical evidence, such as an excavated siphon or chemically analysed residue, has yet been found.

08What is still unknown

Greek fire earns a high mystery rating because the core questions remain open. We do not have the recipe. We do not know whether the oil was distilled, whether resin, sulphur or other substances were added, or in what proportions. We do not know the siphon's exact layout, the operating pressure, or how often it was actually decisive rather than simply terrifying. And some of its most famous victories, like the first siege, are themselves under historical review.

Other powers eventually built their own incendiary weapons. Arab armies fielded specialist naphtha troops, and fire pots and burning arrows became common across the medieval Mediterranean. But none of them seems to have matched the Byzantine combination of a pumped liquid jet mounted on a fast warship.

Archaeology might still help. Small ceramic containers, often called 'grenades', are found across the medieval Mediterranean and Near East, and some may have carried incendiary liquids. Chemical analysis of residues inside such vessels, and of any bronze fittings from Byzantine wrecks such as those excavated at Yenikapı in Istanbul, is the kind of evidence that could one day move the debate from texts to tangible remains.

It was less a miracle substance than a system: oil, bronze, a pump, a ship and a guarded body of know-how.

The strongest evidence points to a petroleum-based liquid projected by a heated, pressurised siphon, a hypothesis that has now been built and fired. The rest remains uncertain, and perhaps it always will, unless a wreck on the floor of the Sea of Marmara one day gives up a corroded bronze tube.

The big debates

Was Greek fire based on petroleum?

Yes, crude oil with additivesFire floating on water, heavy smoke, named oil sources around the Black Sea in De administrando imperio, and a successful 2002 reconstruction using light crude oil.
Other key ingredientsEarlier writers proposed quicklime or saltpetre; later medieval recipes add sulphur and resins, and no Byzantine recipe confirms petroleum explicitly.

The bold claim: Greek fire was a petroleum-based liquid, probably light crude oil perhaps thickened with resins.

Receipt MeterStrong
BustedRock solid

Several independent lines of evidence point the same way: descriptions of the fire's behaviour, Byzantine interest in specific oil-bearing regions, the known chemistry of alternatives, and an experiment that reproduces the described effects. The exact recipe is still missing, so this is strong support for the base fuel, not a full solution.

Did the siphon heat and pressurise the liquid?

Heated pressure siphonReferences to cauldrons, braziers and bronze tubes; Roman force-pump technology; the working 2002 model.
Other designs possibleNo siphon has been excavated; the texts are brief and could fit a simpler pump without heating, or different arrangements of tank and nozzle.

The bold claim: Byzantine ships used a heated, pump-pressurised bronze siphon with a lit nozzle.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The design fits the texts and has been shown to work with technology the Byzantines possessed. But it is reconstructed from a handful of short passages, and other layouts could also satisfy them. Until a siphon or a detailed technical text is found, it remains a well-tested hypothesis.

Was Greek fire an early form of gunpowder?

YesSome 19th and 20th-century writers linked 'fire that roars' to saltpetre mixtures.
NoSaltpetre-based mixtures are not documented in the Mediterranean before the 13th century, and the sources describe a projected burning liquid, not explosions.

The bold claim: Greek fire contained saltpetre and was a precursor of gunpowder.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The chronology does not work: Greek fire appears in the 670s, centuries before saltpetre mixtures are attested in the region, and its described behaviour is that of a burning liquid jet. Partington's classic study and later work by Haldon both reject the gunpowder identification.

The 'Baghdad battery'

A palm-sized clay jar with a copper tube and an iron rod inside: ancient battery, or something far stranger and more human?

The object is a small unglazed clay jar. Inside stood a sheet of copper rolled into a tube about 9 cm long, closed at the bottom with a copper disc and held in place with bitumen. An iron rod hung inside the tube, fixed by a bitumen stopper, with its top poking out. Filled with an acid such as vinegar, the same arrangement makes a weak galvanic cell, which is why Wilhelm König suggested in 1938 that it was a battery, perhaps for gilding. Very similar jars from nearby Seleucia and Ctesiphon contained bronze tubes with remains of rolled organic material, such as papyrus, which points many archaeologists towards a container for written scrolls or a ritual deposit.

The myth

The ancient Mesopotamians had electricity: they used batteries like this to electroplate jewellery, light temples or even run lost machines inherited from an advanced civilisation.

The reality

Any two different metals in an acid make a small voltage, so replicas do work as feeble cells. But no wires, conductors, electrodes, plated objects or texts about electricity have been found anywhere in the ancient Near East, and gilding of the period was done with mercury and heat, not current. Close parallels contained rolled organic material, which fits a container for scrolls or a sealed ritual object. The function remains uncertain; the battery reading lacks supporting evidence.

Wow

The world's most famous 'ancient battery' has been missing since the Iraq Museum was looted in 2003, so every modern experiment rests on old photographs, reports and König's drawing.

01A jar that launched a thousand theories

It would fit in your hand. A pale, unglazed clay jar about 14 cm tall, a little bulbous, with a narrow neck. Inside it, a sheet of copper rolled into a tube. Inside the tube, a corroded iron rod, held in place by a plug of black asphalt. That is all. And yet since 1938 this modest object has been called the 'Baghdad battery', and it has turned up in school textbooks, museum exhibitions, science television and countless books about lost ancient technologies.

The reason is simple and genuinely intriguing. Copper and iron in an acid really do make electricity. Pour vinegar into a replica and a voltmeter twitches. So the question is not whether this arrangement can make a current. It can. The question is whether anyone, two thousand years ago, ever used it to do so.

Part of the jar's fame comes from timing. König described it in the late 1930s, when electrification was still transforming daily life and radio was new. The idea that ancient people might have beaten Volta, who built the first battery in 1800, by some two thousand years was irresistible. Over the following decades the jar became a staple of books arguing that ancient people possessed lost high technology, and replicas became a favourite science fair project. It is easy to see why: it is simple, cheap and it really does make a spark of current.

This article gives the battery idea a fair hearing. It tests the idea against what archaeologists found in the ground, what the object is made of, what ancient craftspeople already knew, and what the jar's closest relatives contained.

Any two metals in an acid make a battery. The real question is whether anyone ever plugged anything into this one.

02From a hill near Baghdad to the Iraq Museum

The jar came from Khujut Rabu, a low mound near Baghdad not far from Ctesiphon, the great capital of the Parthian and then the Sasanian empires. It was found in 1936 during work at the site and entered the Iraq Museum. There it caught the eye of Wilhelm König, an Austrian working at the museum in the 1930s (sources describe him variously as an assistant and as head of its laboratory), who had a painter's training and a keen interest in ancient crafts.

Picture the setting. Ctesiphon and its twin city Seleucia, on opposite banks of the Tigris, were among the largest cities of the ancient world, crowded with merchants, officials, artisans and scholars speaking Aramaic, Greek and Persian. Workshops produced glazed pottery, glass, textiles and silver vessels. Several religious communities lived side by side, and many households used written charms and inscribed objects for protection. A small sealed jar with a metal tube inside would not have been out of place in that world, whatever it was for.

In 1938 König published a short article in the German journal Forschungen und Fortschritte with a cautious question for a title: Ein galvanisches Element aus der Partherzeit?, 'A galvanic cell from the Parthian period?'. He described the jar, the copper cylinder and the rod, and noticed that the iron was badly corroded, as if by an acid. He had seen silver objects from ancient Iraq with extremely thin gold layers, and he wondered whether jars like this, filled with an acidic liquid, had supplied current to gild them.

The dating is itself uncertain. König placed the jar in the Parthian period, roughly 250 BCE to 224 CE. Many later specialists think a Sasanian date, between 224 and 651 CE, is more likely, based on comparisons with similar finds. Without the original excavation records being fully published, a firm date is hard to pin down.

03Cousins from Seleucia and Ctesiphon

The Khujut Rabu jar is not alone, and its relatives matter more than it does. In 1930, excavators from the University of Michigan working under Leroy Waterman at Seleucia on the Tigris found several clay vessels sealed with bitumen that contained bronze or copper cylinders. Inside some of those cylinders were traces of rolled organic material, described as papyrus.

At Ctesiphon, a German expedition in 1931–1932 found further vessels. According to reports of these finds, one contained a number of bronze tubes, each holding decayed rolled material, and others held iron nails, bronze pieces and lead sheets. The excavator Ernst Kühnel interpreted similar objects as containers for written charms or blessings.

This is a crucial clue. If jars built the same way sometimes contained rolled scrolls, the simplest reading is that the Khujut Rabu jar belonged to the same family: a small sealed container for something written, whose contents rotted away, leaving acids and corrosion that look, to a modern eye, like the residue of an electrolyte.

Rolling a text and sealing it in a metal tube was a widespread habit in the ancient world. Across the Roman Empire and the Near East, people wore thin sheets of gold, silver or lead inscribed with protective words, rolled tight and slipped into small metal capsules. Archaeologists find these amulet cases in graves and houses from Britain to Syria. Seen against that background, a copper tube holding a rolled text inside a sealed jar looks far less mysterious.

How do we know?

Mostly from old excavation reports, a few photographs and König's description and drawing. The original jar cannot currently be examined, the Seleucia and Ctesiphon parallels are scattered across collections, and no modern chemical analysis of residues inside the Khujut Rabu cylinder has been published. That limits how confident anyone can be about its use.

04Turning it on: the experiments

The battery idea is testable, and people tested it. Around 1940, Willard Gray, an engineer at General Electric in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, built a replica from König's description, filled it with a copper sulphate solution and reported that it worked, briefly, as a cell. Later the German Egyptologist Arne Eggebrecht reported using several replicas with grape juice to deposit a thin layer of gold onto a small silver figure, though no written documentation of that experiment was published.

In 2005 the television programme MythBusters built ten replica jars, filled them with lemon juice and wired them in series. Together they produced a little over 4 V, around half a volt per jar. Most recently, in January 2026, independent researcher Alexander Bazes published a reconstruction in the journal Sino-Platonic Papers arguing that the jar may have worked as two cells at once, reaching about 1.4 V, comparable to an AA battery.

How does such a cell work? Iron gives up electrons more readily than copper. In an acid, iron atoms at the rod's surface dissolve as ions, leaving electrons behind in the metal. If a wire links the iron to the copper, those electrons flow through the wire to the copper, where they are consumed by reactions in the liquid, typically producing hydrogen. The flow is an electric current. Without a wire outside the jar, the same reactions still happen, but they simply corrode the iron, with no useful current anywhere.

So the physics is not in doubt. A copper–iron couple in an acid produces, in theory, about 0.78 V, and real replicas give roughly 0.5–2 V depending on the liquid. The currents are tiny, measured in milliamperes, and fade as the iron corrodes. That is enough to tingle a tongue, move a meter or slowly deposit a film of metal. It is not enough to light anything but a modern low-power LED, which did not exist in antiquity.

The experiments settle what the jar could do. They say nothing about what it did do.

05The problem of the missing wires

Here the battery case runs into trouble. A battery is only useful if you connect it to something. The Khujut Rabu jar has no terminal on the copper cylinder, which was sealed inside the jar with bitumen, an excellent electrical insulator. To draw current you would have to attach a wire to the copper, and nothing on the object shows how that was done.

  • No wires or conductors have been found with any of these jars.
  • No electroplated objects from ancient Mesopotamia have been identified; thin gold layers of the period match known non-electrical methods.
  • No text in Aramaic, Middle Persian, Greek or any other language of the region describes electricity, currents or plating by current.
  • Related jars held multiple bronze tubes or organic scrolls, which do not fit a single working cell.
  • The iron rod's top sits inside a bitumen plug, again awkward for making a connection.

It is worth being fair here. Ancient smiths could certainly draw copper wire, so the absence of wires is not because they were impossible to make. The point is that none has been found with these jars, in any report, and nothing about the jar's construction provides a place to attach one. For a device whose whole purpose would be to deliver current somewhere else, that silence is significant.

William Hafford, an archaeologist at the Penn Museum, points out that modern replicas tend to follow König's drawing, which reconstructed the object as a battery in the first place, so it is no surprise that they behave like batteries. Elizabeth Stone, a specialist in Mesopotamian archaeology, put the field's view bluntly to a History.com reporter in 2026: she knew of nobody working in the area who thought it was a real battery.

06Gold without electricity

König's gilding hypothesis was a sensible idea in 1938, because he had seen very thin gold layers on silver objects. But ancient craftspeople had excellent ways to gild without current. The most important was fire-gilding, also called mercury gilding. Gold is dissolved in mercury to make a paste, the paste is brushed onto a metal surface, and the object is heated so that the mercury evaporates, leaving a thin, firmly bonded layer of gold.

According to conservation scientist Katharina Anheuser, fire-gilding was used in China from about 300 BCE and in Europe from about 200 CE, and it remained the main gilding method until electroplating arrived in the 19th century. Sasanian silversmiths were masters of it: many of their famous silver plates carry scenes picked out with mercury gilding. Thin gold leaf, applied with adhesives or by burnishing, was even older. None of this needs a battery, and the physical traces left by fire-gilding, such as residual mercury, are recognisable in laboratory analysis.

Other techniques were available too. Craftspeople in several regions practised depletion gilding, treating a gold alloy so that the base metals at the surface were removed, leaving a gold-rich skin. Gold leaf could be beaten thinner than a micrometre and burnished onto a surface. Laboratory study of ancient gilded objects routinely identifies which method was used, and electroplating is not among the methods found on objects from antiquity.

In other words, the problem König was trying to solve already had a well-documented solution. That does not make his question foolish. It makes the battery answer unnecessary.

07Other explanations: medicine, scrolls and ritual

If not for gilding, could a small current have had some other use? In 1993 the classicist Paul Keyser suggested, in the Journal of Near Eastern Studies, that such cells might have been used for mild electrical pain relief, much as Greek and Roman doctors applied electric fish to patients with headaches or gout. It is a creative idea, and the electric-fish practice is well documented in ancient medical writers, but there is no evidence that anyone used jars this way.

The explanation favoured by many archaeologists is more modest. The jar was a small container, perhaps for a written scroll, sealed with bitumen, whose organic contents decayed into acids that corroded the iron. Hafford goes further, reading jars of this type as ritual deposits: the iron rod as a nail, the copper tube as a sealed case for a protective text, the whole object buried for its symbolic power rather than any practical function. Protective inscriptions were common in the region in this period, most famously on clay incantation bowls buried under houses.

Bazes, interestingly, bridges the two camps. His 2026 paper takes the electrochemistry seriously but proposes that any current was a side effect with a ritual meaning, visibly corroding the metal and perhaps the written prayer sealed inside, rather than a power supply for a device.

Each explanation makes predictions that could be checked. If the jar held an electrolyte, residues of acetic acid or wine and a particular pattern of copper and iron corrosion products should survive. If it held a scroll, fibres, ink traces or impressions of a rolled sheet might remain inside the cylinder. If it was a ritual deposit, its findspot should resemble those of other buried protective objects, such as under a floor or at a threshold. Frustratingly, the published record of the 1936 find is too thin to say which of these fits, and the object itself is not available to test.

The most human explanation may also be the most likely: a sealed prayer in a jar, not a power pack.

08Lost again, and what remains unknown

In April 2003, during the invasion of Iraq, the Iraq Museum in Baghdad was looted and thousands of objects were taken. The Khujut Rabu jar is reported to have disappeared at that time, and its current whereabouts are unknown. Many objects have since been recovered and returned, but we could find no verified report that this one has been among them.

That loss is painful for science as well as for Iraq's heritage. Modern techniques could analyse residues in the copper cylinder, identify whether the corrosion products came from vinegar, wine, organic decay or something else, and look for traces of written material. Until the jar is found, or a parallel from Seleucia or Ctesiphon is analysed with the same care, key questions stay open.

  • When exactly was it made, Parthian or Sasanian?
  • What liquid, if any, did it hold?
  • Were the parallel jars' tubes all scroll holders, or did they vary?
  • Is the iron rod a structural pin, a ritual nail or an electrode?

The honest verdict is that the jar's function is uncertain, the scroll or ritual container reading fits the evidence best, and the battery hypothesis, however fun, has no supporting archaeological evidence. It remains a wonderful classroom demonstration and a reminder to ask not only whether something could work, but whether anyone ever used it that way.

The big debates

Was the jar a working battery?

YesReplicas produce roughly 0.5–2 V; the iron shows acid corrosion; Bazes (2026) argues for an efficient two-cell design.
No evidence it was used as oneNo wires, terminals, electrical devices or texts; the copper is sealed in insulating bitumen; similar jars held scrolls and multiple tubes.

The bold claim: The Khujut Rabu jar was built and used as an electric battery.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

That the arrangement can make a voltage is not in dispute. But there is no archaeological evidence that anyone drew current from it: no conductors, no powered devices, no electroplated objects and no texts. The closest parallels point to containers. Unless the jar or a parallel yields new evidence, the battery reading has no receipts.

Was it used for electroplating gold or silver?

YesKönig saw very thin gold layers on ancient silver; Eggebrecht reported plating a figure with replicas.
NoFire-gilding with mercury was well established and explains thin gold layers; no electroplated ancient object has been identified; Eggebrecht's experiment was not documented in print.

The bold claim: Ancient Mesopotamian smiths used jars like this to electroplate metal objects.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

The gilding König observed has a documented non-electrical explanation, mercury fire-gilding, whose traces are detectable in analysis, and no object from the region has been shown to be electroplated. The one experiment claiming success was never properly published. The claim rests only on possibility.

Was it a container for a scroll or a ritual deposit?

YesSimilar jars from Seleucia and Ctesiphon held bronze tubes with rolled organic material; protective texts were common in the period.
Not yet shown for this jarNo scroll remains have been reported from the Khujut Rabu cylinder itself, and the original cannot now be analysed.

The bold claim: The jar was a sealed container for a written scroll, probably with a protective or ritual purpose.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

This reading fits the construction, the bitumen seals and the contents of close parallels without requiring any unknown technology. But direct evidence from the Khujut Rabu jar is missing, its context is poorly published and the object is lost, so the case rests on analogy.

Late Roman glass

The Lycurgus Cup

A Roman glass cup that glows jade green by day and blood red when lit from within, thanks to specks of gold and silver.
