The cup is a cage cup, or diatretum. A glassworker first made a thick-walled blank of a special glass that contained tiny amounts of silver and gold. Cutters then spent a very long time grinding most of that wall away with rotating wheels and abrasives, leaving the figures of the myth standing proud of the inner cup and linked to it by small hidden bridges of glass. The colour comes from the metal: during heating, the dissolved silver and gold came together as alloy particles about 50–100 nanometres across. Those particles scatter green light back towards the viewer and let red light pass through, so the glass changes colour depending on where the light comes from.

The myth

The Romans understood nanotechnology and deliberately engineered nanoparticles with modern precision, or the cup was made with a lost chemical secret no one can reproduce.

The reality

Roman glassmakers clearly knew that adding tiny amounts of precious metal and controlling the heat produced this remarkable glass, and their control of trace amounts was impressive. But they had no concept of particles, electrons or plasmonics; the effect was reached by experiment, recipe and skill. Very few dichroic glasses survive, so how reliably they could repeat it is uncertain. Modern scientists explain the colour with plasmon physics and have borrowed it for sensors and reproductions.

Wow

The particles that turn the cup red are about a thousand times thinner than a human hair, and there are so few of them that the whole cup contains only a tiny fraction of a gram of gold.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,105 words · 2 animated drawings

01A cup that changes its mind

In a gallery of the British Museum stands a glass cup about the size of a large coffee mug. Lit from the front, as most museum objects are, it looks like polished jade: an opaque, slightly milky green, carved with writhing figures. Then someone places a light inside it, and the whole cup turns a deep, glowing red, like wine held up to a candle. Same glass, same cup, two completely different colours.

This is the Lycurgus Cup, made in the Late Roman Empire in the 4th century CE. It is famous for two separate reasons. The first is craftsmanship: it is one of the finest surviving cage cups, vessels whose decoration was cut free from the body so that it stands away from the surface like a net. The second is physics. Its colour change comes from metal particles only tens of nanometres across, which is why materials scientists sometimes call it the oldest known piece of nanotechnology.

Picture it, perhaps, on the table of a wealthy household in the 4th century, in a dining room lit by oil lamps. By daylight the cup would have looked like carved green stone. As evening fell and a lamp was set behind it, or wine was poured and the vessel lifted towards the flame, the green would have warmed to amber and then to red. We do not know how its owners used it, or even whether it was meant for drinking at all, since the delicate cage makes it awkward to hold. But it is easy to imagine the gasp around the table.

Two colours from one glass: green where light bounces back, red where light passes through.

Both claims deserve a careful look, because the story of how the cup was made is at least as remarkable as the story of what it does.

02A king trapped by a vine

The figures on the cup tell a savage myth. Lycurgus, a king of the Edonians in Thrace, attacked the god Dionysus and his followers. The earliest version appears in Homer's Iliad, where the hero Diomedes cites Lycurgus as a warning about fighting gods.

He it was that drove the nursing women who were in charge of frenzied Bacchus through the land of Nysa, and they flung their thyrsi on the ground as murderous Lycurgus beat them with his oxgoad.

Homer, Iliad 6.132–135, trans. Samuel Butler (1898)

Later versions of the story add the episode shown on the cup. One of Dionysus's followers, the nymph Ambrosia, is attacked by Lycurgus and calls for help. She is transformed into a vine, which wraps around the king and holds him fast. On the cup, Lycurgus is caught mid-struggle, almost naked, tangled in the vine's branches. Around him the god's companions close in: Dionysus himself with his thyrsus, the staff tipped with a pine cone, and his panther; Pan; and a satyr preparing to hurl a rock.

Why this scene? Wine and Dionysus suit a drinking cup, and the colour change, from green to wine red, may have seemed a delightful echo of the vine and its grapes. Some scholars have also suggested a political meaning, linking the punished king to a defeated ruler of the early 4th century, perhaps the emperor Licinius, defeated by Constantine in 324 CE. That reading is possible but cannot be confirmed.

03How to carve a cage from glass

Cage cups, known in Latin as diatreta, are among the most difficult objects ancient craftspeople ever made. Only a few dozen are known, most of them fragmentary, and they date mainly to the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. Nearly all have an openwork net of glass rings standing away from an inner bowl. The Lycurgus Cup is unusual because, instead of a net, its 'cage' is a crowd of figures.

The method that most specialists accept is subtractive. A glassworker first blew or cast a thick-walled blank, a plain cup with walls far thicker than the finished object. Cutters then removed glass with rotating wheels fed with abrasives, and with drills and files, working from the outside in. They cut the figures in high relief, then carefully undercut behind them, leaving the figures linked to the inner wall only by small bridges of glass hidden behind limbs and drapery. One slip could crack the blank and waste weeks of work.

The tools were simple, and that is what makes the result so astonishing. Roman glass cutters used wheels of stone or metal, turned by a bow or a treadle-driven lathe, fed with a slurry of abrasive sand or emery in water. Drills and small files did the finer work. Every curve of the vine, every finger of the satyr, had to be ground out a fraction of a millimetre at a time, with constant checks to avoid cutting through a bridge or cracking the thin inner wall.

In the 1990s the German glass researcher R. Lierke proposed that cage cups were partly shaped in moulds while the glass was hot, which would reduce the amount of cutting. Her idea sparked useful debate, but most experts have not accepted it for the Lycurgus Cup, whose surfaces show the marks of cutting and polishing, as Ian Freestone and colleagues note.

How do we know?

By looking very closely. Tool marks, polished surfaces, the shapes of the hidden bridges and the way the figures join the wall all record how the glass was worked. The gilt-silver mounts on the rim and foot are later additions, and they were temporarily removed during research in 1958, allowing the glass to be studied more fully.

04Green by day, red by lamplight

What causes the colour change? For centuries nobody could say. Harden and Toynbee's classic 1959 study described the glass in detail but could not see what was inside it. The answer came in 1990, when David Barber and Ian Freestone examined tiny fragments of the cup under an analytical transmission electron microscope, an instrument that can image and analyse particles far too small for any optical microscope.

They found scattered particles of a silver-gold alloy, typically about 70 nm across and ranging from roughly 50 to 100 nm, with a little copper. Chemical analysis showed the glass contains only about 300 parts per million of silver and about 40 parts per million of gold. The rest is ordinary Roman soda-lime-silica glass, about 73.5% silica, 13% soda and 6% lime.

Metal particles this small behave very differently from a lump of metal. Their free electrons can be set sloshing back and forth together by light of particular wavelengths, an effect physicists call a localised surface plasmon resonance. At resonance, the particles absorb and scatter light strongly. In the Lycurgus glass, the particles absorb much of the green and blue part of the spectrum and scatter greenish light, while letting red light pass. Freestone and colleagues sum it up this way: the gold is mainly responsible for the reddish transmission and the silver for the greenish reflection.

So the two colours are two views of the same process. Lit from outside, you see mostly light scattered back towards you by the particles: green. Lit from inside, you see mostly light that made it through the glass: red. Real viewing mixes both, which is why the cup can look olive, amber or purple-red in between.

Composition and size matter a great deal. Gold particles on their own tend to make glass ruby red, which is the basis of the gold ruby glass that European glassmakers such as Johann Kunckel made famous in the 17th century. Silver on its own tends towards yellow, the colour of the silver stain used in medieval stained glass. The Lycurgus glass sits between the two, with alloy particles whose mixed composition and fairly large size give both a strong green scatter and a red transmission. Change the recipe or the heating, and the balance tips.

The cup is not dyed green or red. It is a filter and a mirror at the same time, and the lamp decides which one you see.

05Did the Romans do nanotechnology?

It is tempting to say yes, and headlines often do. The honest answer is more interesting. The Romans did make nanoparticles, and they did it on purpose in the sense that someone deliberately added silver and gold to the glass batch and controlled the heating to get this effect. Such low concentrations suggest that the precious metal was added in a finely divided form, perhaps as dust, filings or a dilute solution, and thoroughly mixed.

But they had no idea that particles were involved, let alone how light interacts with electrons. Their knowledge was practical: a recipe, a sequence of heating and a skilled eye that could judge when the glass had 'struck' its colour. We might call it nanotechnology by craft rather than by design.

How do such particles form? In a hot glass melt, small amounts of gold and silver can dissolve as individual atoms or ions, and the glass then looks nearly colourless. When the glass is held at a suitable temperature, or reheated after cooling, the metal atoms drift together and cluster into particles, which grow until they are large enough to colour the glass. Glassmakers call this 'striking' the colour. It is highly sensitive to temperature and time, which may be one reason why so few ancient dichroic glasses survive.

The effect was also hard to control. Only a handful of dichroic glasses of this kind survive, and they vary: a fragment of a cage cup in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, showing a satyr, shifts from olive green to reddish amber rather than jade to ruby. A letter attributed to the emperor Hadrian, preserved in the unreliable Historia Augusta, mentions 'cups of changing colours' among precious gifts, which hints that such glass was known and prized, though the passage cannot be tied to this cup.

  • Deliberate: adding precious metals to glass to colour it.
  • Probably deliberate: the heat treatment that brings out the colour.
  • Not understood: that the colour came from particles 50–100 nm across.
  • Uncertain: how often workshops could reproduce the effect.

06A 1,600-year-old idea in modern labs

The physics behind the Lycurgus Cup is now central to a branch of modern science called plasmonics. Gold and silver nanoparticles are used in pregnancy tests, where they give the familiar red line, and in sensors that detect tiny changes in their surroundings, because the colour a particle scatters shifts when the material around it changes.

In 2013 a team at the University of Illinois led by engineer Gang Logan Liu took direct inspiration from the cup. They imprinted billions of tiny cup-shaped wells onto a plastic plate and coated them with metal nanoparticles, creating what they called nano Lycurgus cup arrays. When liquids were placed on the plate, its colour changed: light green for water, red for oil. The researchers reported that the prototype was about 100 times more sensitive to changes in salt levels than comparable commercial sensors.

The same principle turns up in everyday medicine. The coloured line in many rapid diagnostic tests is made by gold nanoparticles a few tens of nanometres across, which appear red for exactly the kind of reason the Lycurgus Cup glows red: their electrons resonate with green light and remove it from what reaches your eye.

The Romans knew how to make and use nanoparticles for beautiful art. We wanted to see if this could have scientific applications.

Gang Logan Liu, quoted in Smithsonian Magazine (2013)

Other groups have used silver and gold nanoparticles in polymers, including 3D-printable materials, to recreate the cup's green-to-red switch. The old glassmakers would have recognised the effect at once, even if the explanation would have baffled them.

07From a dealer's shop to Room 41

Where the cup was found is unknown. It first appears in print in 1845, in the possession of a collector recorded as M. Dubois. By 1857 it belonged to the banker Lionel de Rothschild, and it was lent to a major exhibition in London in 1862. Not every viewer was impressed: the German art historian Gustav Waagen dismissed it as barbaric and debased, a reminder that taste changes as much as science does.

In 1958 Victor, Lord Rothschild sold the cup to the British Museum for £20,000, with £2,000 contributed by the Art Fund. Its metal mounts were removed for study that year and later reunited with the glass. Today it is on display in Room 41, among objects of the Late Roman and early Byzantine world.

Where was it made? The quality of the cutting points to one of the great glass centres of the Late Roman world. Rome and Alexandria have both been proposed, but there is no inscription or workshop evidence to settle it.

08What remains uncertain

Compared with many ancient wonders, the Lycurgus Cup holds few deep mysteries. We know what it is made of, why it changes colour and, broadly, how it was cut. Its mystery level is low. The open questions are about people and places.

  • Which workshop made it, and where?
  • In what form was the silver and gold added, and how did the glassmakers control the heat?
  • Was the glass made for this cup, or was a dichroic blank bought from a specialist glassmaker and then cut elsewhere?
  • Does the myth carry a political message about Constantine and Licinius, or is it simply a good wine story?
  • How many cutting hours did it take? Estimates range widely, and no ancient source records it.

Perhaps the best way to think of it is as a meeting point. A myth about wine and the punishment of pride, a feat of cold-working that pushed glass to its limits, and a trace of precious metal that happened to put physics on display. Roman craftspeople did not need to understand plasmons to make something that still stops visitors in their tracks. They needed patience, experience and an eye for light.

The science is modern. The wonder was always there, waiting for someone to put a lamp inside.

The ingredients and probably the heating were deliberate, so the Romans did intentionally make a material whose properties depend on nanoparticles. But they did not know that particles existed or controlled their size by design. Calling it nanotechnology is fair as a description of the material, misleading as a description of Roman knowledge.

Was the cage cut from a solid blank, or partly moulded?

Basin of Mexico

Teotihuacan

A planned metropolis of perhaps 100,000 people, laid out 15.5 degrees off north, whose own name for itself is still lost.

Teotihuacan grew from scattered villages after about 100 BCE into a city planned on one tilted grid, about 15°28′ east of true north. Its great pyramids are mostly fill: earth, rubble and adobe held in place by stone retaining walls, then faced with stone and thick lime plaster that was often painted. The Pyramid of the Sun rose in a few big episodes, with radiocarbon dates from inside it clustering in about 170–310 CE; the Pyramid of the Moon was enlarged at least six times over its first earlier structure. Builders quarried local volcanic stone, including red tezontle and basalt, and carried fill in baskets, with no draft animals and no wheeled carts. Around 150–200 CE the Feathered Serpent Pyramid went up over more than 200 sacrificial burials, and beneath it a 103 m tunnel was cut, filled with offerings and sealed around 250 CE.

The myth

The Aztecs built Teotihuacan, or giants did; or its pyramids are a scale model of the solar system, laid out with a lost unit of measurement or knowledge from somewhere far away.

The reality

The city was already centuries in ruins when Nahuatl speakers named it Teotihuacan, 'the place where the gods were made'. Excavation shows a home-grown, multi-ethnic city with neighbourhoods of migrants from Oaxaca and elsewhere, built on a calendar-linked grid. Solar-system readings do not survive careful survey. Real open questions remain: the city's own name and language, who ruled it, and why its centre burned around 550 CE.

Wow

Around 250 CE people sealed a 103 m tunnel under the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, its walls dusted with glittering mineral powder and liquid mercury left near its far end. Nobody saw it again until a sinkhole opened in 2003.

Mystery meterReal open questions
The deep dive10 min read · 2,186 words · 2 animated drawings

01The place where the gods were made

Stand at the foot of the Pyramid of the Moon just after sunrise and look south. A dead-straight avenue, about 40 m wide, runs away from you for more than two kilometres, lined with the stumps of temples. On your left the Pyramid of the Sun sits like a man-made mountain. Behind you rises Cerro Gordo, a real one. It is hard to shake the feeling that the whole view was composed, and it was.

By the time the Aztecs came here in the 1400s, the city had been a ruin for roughly nine centuries. They did not know who had built it, so they gave it a name that fitted its grandeur: Teotihuacan, usually translated as 'the place where the gods were made' or 'where the gods were born'. They also gave its main street the name we still use, the Avenue of the Dead, because they took the rubble mounds along it for tombs. They were wrong about that, but their awe was well placed.

It is told that when yet [all] was in darkness, when yet no sun had shone and no dawn had broken, it is said, the gods gathered themselves together and took counsel among themselves there at Teotihuacan.

Florentine Codex, Book 7, trans. A. J. O. Anderson and C. E. Dibble (1953)

In that Aztec story, two gods throw themselves into a bonfire at Teotihuacan to become the Sun and the Moon. It is a myth about the city, not from it. The people who actually lived here left no readable history of their own, and we still do not know what they called their home, which language they spoke, or who governed them. What they did leave is an astonishing amount of physical evidence, and some of the best of it has turned up in the last twenty years.

02A city drawn with one ruler

Teotihuacan began as a cluster of farming villages in a side valley of the Basin of Mexico around 100 BCE. Within three centuries it had become a city of roughly 20 km² and, by the most common estimates, somewhere between 75,000 and 125,000 people. René Millon's Teotihuacan Mapping Project, which began in 1962 and walked and recorded the whole urban area, showed something unusual: almost everything was built on one grid.

That grid is not aligned to true north. Streets, walls and buildings run about 15°28′ east of north, and the cross-streets at right angles to them. When the archaeoastronomer Ivan Šprajc measured the major buildings, he found the east–west axis of the Pyramid of the Sun points to where the Sun sets on about 29–30 April and 12–13 August. The interval between those two sunsets, counted through the winter, is 260 days, exactly the length of the sacred calendar used across Mesoamerica. The north–south axis, meanwhile, lines up with the summit of Cerro Gordo.

The builders bent a river to fit their plan. That tells you how seriously they took the grid.

The commitment was total. The Río San Juan, which crosses the city, was straightened into a channel that follows the grid where it passes the ceremonial core. The same orientation, give or take a degree, appears in modest homes on the edge of town. Planning on this scale needs surveyors, a shared unit of length and an authority that everybody obeys. Saburo Sugiyama has argued that many buildings were set out in multiples of a unit of about 83 cm, a proposal that fits a surprising number of measurements, though not every scholar accepts it.

How do we know the angle?

The 15.5 degree figure is not a guess from a satellite photo. Šprajc (2000) took azimuths with a theodolite along the preserved walls and base lines of the Pyramid of the Sun and the Ciudadela, corrected for the local horizon, and calculated the dates on which the Sun would set along those lines around the city's heyday. The results cluster tightly, which is why the calendar reading is taken seriously.

03Mountains made by hand

The Pyramid of the Sun is about 222–225 m a side, almost as broad as Khufu's pyramid at Giza, though at roughly 63–65 m it is less than half as tall. It is not a solid stone mountain. Inside, tunnels dug by archaeologists show layers of earth, rubble and adobe held in by stone retaining walls, with an outer skin of stone and lime plaster that was once painted. How tall it originally stood is uncertain, partly because Leopoldo Batres, who rebuilt it between 1905 and 1910 for Mexico's independence centenary, stripped away some of the outer fabric, a decision archaeologists still lament.

In 1971 a cave was found under the pyramid, reached by a stairway near its front. It had been dug or reshaped by people and was sealed long ago. When exactly the pyramid itself rose is a lively argument. Excavations from 2008 to 2011 produced radiocarbon and pottery dates that place its main construction at about 170–310 CE. Rebecca Sload re-analysed the dates in 2015 and argued that the cave's use began in the first century CE, with the later dates marking a ritual closing rather than the first building. The debate below sets out both sides.

At the north end of the avenue the Pyramid of the Moon, about 43 m high, grew in at least seven stages between roughly 100 and 400 CE, each one wrapping the last. Saburo Sugiyama and Rubén Cabrera's tunnels through it, begun in 1998, found five dedicatory burial complexes inside the layers. They held sacrificed people, some of them apparently foreigners, along with pumas, wolves, eagles and serpents, animals linked with warfare. Sacred mountains, in other words, were also stages for political theatre.

04The serpent's secret tunnel

The third great monument sits inside the Ciudadela, a walled enclosure about 400 m square at the southern end of the avenue. The Feathered Serpent Pyramid, built around 150–200 CE, is famous for its facade of stone serpent heads. Excavations in the 1980s found that it had also been dedicated with more than 200 sacrificial burials, many of them young men buried with weapons and ornaments, laid out in patterns that suggest careful planning.

On 2 October 2003, after a heavy rainstorm, a hole about a metre wide opened in the plaza at the pyramid's foot. The archaeologist Sergio Gómez Chávez of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) looked down it and saw a shaft. It took years of radar survey, fundraising and permits before digging started in earnest. The team sank a shaft 14 m deep and about 5 m wide, found a deliberately sealed entrance, and began to clear a passage that runs 103 m east to a point under the centre of the pyramid, about 18 m below the surface.

The builders had packed the tunnel with nearly 1,000 tonnes of earth and stone, sealed behind a series of walls, so every metre had to be emptied by hand. Two small remote-controlled robots, named Tlaloque and Tláloc II, were sent ahead to film the unexplored stretches. By 2014 the team had recovered more than 50,000 objects: shells, jade and greenstone, carved figures, obsidian blades, wooden objects, seeds and animal bones. The walls and ceiling had been rubbed with powdered minerals, including magnetite, pyrite and hematite, which would have glittered in torchlight like a starry sky.

Hundreds of clay balls, 40–130 mm across, lay in the chambers near the end. Their golden-yellow crust is jarosite, a mineral that forms when pyrite weathers, so they were probably once coated in shining 'fool's gold'. And in 2015 Gómez announced traces of liquid mercury near the tunnel's end. Liquid mercury has turned up at only a handful of Mesoamerican sites; it may have been made by heating the red mineral cinnabar, and the team interprets it as a symbol of an underworld lake or river.

Fresh from the field

In March 2026 INAH published the full study of the tunnel, Proyecto Tlalocan: 'Camino bajo la tierra', en Teotihuacan, coordinated by Sergio Gómez Chávez and Julie Gazzola, with 14 chapters by 15 specialists. Among its findings is turquoise, which the team reports identifying at Teotihuacan for the first time. It points to exchange with northern Mexico and the American Southwest, alongside the known links to the Maya region and the Gulf Coast. The tunnel was in use from around the start of the Common Era and sealed around 250 CE.

The hope that the tunnel would end in a royal tomb has not been fulfilled, at least not yet. That matters, because Teotihuacan is strangely quiet about its rulers. Unlike Maya cities, it has no portraits of named kings and no obvious royal burials. Either power was shared among several groups, or it was displayed in ways we have not learned to read.

05Life in the apartment blocks

Most Teotihuacanos did not live in temples. They lived in walled apartment compounds, of which the mapping project recorded about 2,000. A typical compound was a single-storey block of rooms, patios and small shrines, housing perhaps 60–100 people, often several related families sharing a trade. Some compounds made obsidian tools, others pottery, figurines or lapidary work. The better-off ones had painted murals of gods, priests, jaguars and flowering trees.

  • Tetitla, Atetelco and Zacuala: compounds known for their fine murals.
  • Teopancazco: a neighbourhood centre with evidence of foreign cooks, tailors and craftworkers.
  • La Ventilla: a district with a large plaza and a rare set of painted glyphs on its floor.

Life expectancy was not high, and skeletons show hard work and seasonal hunger. But the compounds were solid, drained and plastered, and for centuries they kept a very large population housed in one place, something few ancient cities managed so well.

06A city of migrants

On Teotihuacan's western edge lies a neighbourhood archaeologists call the Oaxaca Barrio, Tlailotlacan. Its houses used pottery in the style of the Zapotec valley of Oaxaca, roughly 400 km to the southeast, and at least one tomb was built in the Oaxacan way. People there appear to have kept their homeland's customs for centuries.

Chemistry backs this up. Oxygen isotopes in teeth and bones record the water a person drank while those tissues formed, and water differs from place to place. Christine White, Michael Spence and colleagues found that the enclave's residents kept moving between Teotihuacan, the Oaxaca homeland and other diaspora communities, with some children apparently spending years away before returning. It looks strikingly like a modern migrant community, with ties that stretch across hundreds of kilometres.

Other districts held people with Gulf Coast and Maya-lowland connections. Teotihuacan was not a monoculture but a magnet, and its planners found room for all of them inside the same tilted grid.

07Strangers at Tikal, 378 CE

Some 1,000 km away, in the Maya city of Tikal in Guatemala, carved inscriptions record that on a day in January 378 CE a man called Siyaj K'ahk' 'arrived'. According to the epigrapher David Stuart's reading, Tikal's king Chak Tok Ich'aak 'entered the water', a phrase for dying, on that same day. Soon a new king, Yax Nuun Ahiin, took the throne; he was the son of a figure the texts call Spearthrower Owl, and on a later Tikal monument, Stela 31, he is shown dressed as a Teotihuacan-style warrior.

Whether this was conquest, a coup backed by Teotihuacan, or a political alliance dressed up in foreign prestige is still argued. In 2021 a team led by Stephen Houston reported, using lidar and excavation, a compound at Tikal that copies the layout of Teotihuacan's Ciudadela at a smaller scale, with Teotihuacan-style incense burners and green obsidian points from central Mexico. Whatever happened in 378, Teotihuacan's influence reached deep into the Maya world.

08Fire in the centre

Around 550 CE, the temples and elite buildings along the Avenue of the Dead were burned. Sculptures were broken and some buildings were dismantled. A Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates from the neighbourhood of Teopancazco, published in 2009, places the end of the city's main Classic phase at about 550 CE, roughly a century earlier than once thought.

The fire picked its targets. Temples and palaces burned; many ordinary homes did not.

That selectivity is why many archaeologists favour an internal revolt, perhaps against an elite that had grown rich while the rest of the city struggled. Others keep outside attackers in the frame. Either way, people did not vanish. The population fell sharply but some lived on among the ruins for centuries, and later groups farmed and built in the valley.

09Legends, measurements and what is still unknown

Teotihuacan attracts big theories. In the 1970s an engineer, Hugh Harleston Jr., proposed that the city's monuments were laid out as a scale model of the solar system, using a unit of about 1.059 m. The idea still circulates online. It does not hold up: the matches depend on choosing convenient points, and they include planets nobody could see before telescopes. The alignments that do show up clearly are to sunsets, a sacred calendar and a mountain, which is what we would expect from what we know about Mesoamerican religion.

The genuinely unsolved questions are more interesting. Who ruled? Why no royal portraits? What did the Teotihuacanos call themselves? In 2025 the linguists Magnus Pharao Hansen and Christophe Helmke argued in Current Anthropology that some signs in Teotihuacan writing can be read as an early Uto-Aztecan language, ancestral to Nahuatl, Cora and Huichol. If they are right, the Aztecs who named the ruins may have been distant linguistic relatives of the builders. The proposal is bold and is being debated; the corpus of signs is small, and many readings remain uncertain.

So the city keeps its secrets, but it no longer keeps them silently. A sinkhole, a radar scan and a lot of patient digging have given us a glittering underworld, sealed for 1,750 years. The next surprise may already be waiting under a patch of grass.

The big debates

When was the Pyramid of the Sun built?

Later: mostly in the late second to early fourth century CE.Tunnelling into the pyramid in 2008–2011 produced radiocarbon and ceramic evidence placing its main construction at about 170–310 CE (Sugiyama, Sugiyama and Sarabia 2013).
Earlier: begun in the first century CE, with the late dates marking a remodelling.Sload (2015) modelled new dates from the cave below with Bayesian statistics and argued its use began in the mid first century, reading the third-century dates as a ritual closing of the cave and a redefinition of the pyramid.

The bold claim: The Sun Pyramid we see was essentially built in the third century CE, not the first.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

Both camps use real radiocarbon dates; they disagree about which events those dates record. Samples from fill can be older than the construction they end up in, and ritual activity can add later dates, so the choice of model drives the answer. More dated samples from sealed contexts inside the pyramid are needed before either reading can be called settled.

Is the city a scale model of the solar system?

Yes: distances between monuments encode planetary orbits in a special unit.In the 1970s Hugh Harleston Jr. proposed a unit of about 1.059 m and argued that spacings along the Avenue matched the orbits of the planets.
No: the layout follows the calendar, the landscape and ordinary units.Surveys show the grid follows sunset dates and the peak of Cerro Gordo (Šprajc 2000). Sugiyama (1993) found a unit of about 83 cm that fits many buildings without any astronomy of orbits.

The bold claim: Teotihuacan's builders laid out the planets' orbits to scale.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

The planetary matches depend on choosing which points to measure and on including planets unknown before telescopes, which the builders could not have seen. The same measurements are better explained by a calendar-linked grid and a human-scale unit of length. Nothing in the city's art or writing refers to such a model.

Who set fire to the city's centre around 550 CE?

Insiders: a revolt against the ruling elite.Burning concentrates on temples and elite buildings along the Avenue of the Dead, and statues were smashed, which looks targeted rather than random (Millon 1988).
Outsiders: raiders or rival groups from beyond the valley.The city was already declining, and new groups with different pottery traditions appear in the valley in the following century.

The bold claim: The fire of about 550 CE was an internal uprising, not an invasion.

Receipt MeterMixed record
BustedRock solid

The selective pattern of destruction fits an internal upheaval well, and the revised radiocarbon chronology places it around 550 CE (Beramendi-Orosco et al. 2009). But archaeology rarely records who held the torch, and the two explanations are not exclusive: a weakened city could suffer both.

Near Masvingo, Zimbabwe

Great Zimbabwe

A royal city of granite built without a drop of mortar, and a century-long lie about who built it.

Mystery

The builders used the local granite, which naturally peels off its domed outcrops in flat sheets. By heating a rock surface with fire and letting it cool quickly, perhaps helped by water, they could make sheets split away on purpose. The slabs broke at right angles into brick-like blocks, which were trimmed with hammerstones and laid in level courses without any mortar. The best walls have two carefully fitted faces and a core of rubble, and both faces lean inward as they rise, a slope called batter that makes a tall dry-stone wall stable. Near the top of the Great Enclosure, blocks set on edge form a decorative chevron band. A Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates (Chirikure et al. 2013) suggests walling began in the late 12th or early 13th century and peaked in the 14th and 15th.

The myth

Great Zimbabwe was built by Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba, because, colonial writers claimed, Africans could not have built it.

The reality

Excavations by David Randall-MacIver (1905) and Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929), and all later research, show that it was built by the ancestors of the Shona-speaking people of the region. Pottery, house remains, architecture and radiocarbon dates all fit local development. The foreign-builder claims served colonial politics, and Rhodesian authorities pressured archaeologists into keeping them alive into the 1970s.

Wow

The Great Enclosure is the largest single ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa: nearly a million granite blocks stacked into a wall up to about 11 m high, held together only by weight, gravity and good fitting.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,248 words · 2 animated drawings

01Into the passage

Step through the north entrance of the Great Enclosure and the world narrows. On your left and right, two walls of grey granite rise far above your head, their faces made of thousands of neat, flat blocks, each about the size of a large book. The corridor between them, the Parallel Passage, is so tight in places that two people can barely pass. It curves, and curves, and then opens onto a small court where a solid cone of stone, taller than a three-storey house, stands in silence.

This is Great Zimbabwe, in the south-east of the modern country that took its name from it. Between about 1200 and 1450 CE it was the capital of a wealthy state on the Zimbabwe plateau, whose rulers controlled cattle, farmland and gold, and traded, through coastal towns, with the Indian Ocean world. Its builders used no mortar at all. The name itself is usually explained as coming from Shona words meaning 'houses of stone'.

For more than half a century, the most remarkable thing about Great Zimbabwe was not how it was built, but how hard outsiders tried to deny who built it.

Today the answer is settled. What remains open is more interesting: how many people lived here, how its society was organised, and why its rulers eventually moved on.

02A city in three parts

Great Zimbabwe covers roughly 7.2 km² of hills and valleys. Archaeologists usually describe three main areas. The Hill Complex crowns a steep granite ridge above the valley, its walls woven between huge natural boulders; it was the earliest area to be occupied, from around 1000 CE, and is often interpreted as a royal and ritual centre. Below it lies the Great Enclosure, the largest and most famous structure. Around and between them sprawl the valley ruins, smaller walled compounds and the remains of many houses.

The houses themselves were not stone. People lived in round buildings of daga, a hard mix of clay and gravel, many of them finely finished with moulded steps and platforms. The stone walls did not hold up roofs. They defined space: who could go where, what could be seen, and by whom. In that sense the walls are architecture of power, a language of entrances, screens and passages.

When was it all built? The site was dug over so carelessly in the colonial period that the chronology was muddled for decades. In 2013 Shadreck Chirikure and colleagues combined radiocarbon dates with dated imported objects in a Bayesian model. Their result: stone walling probably began in the late 12th or early 13th century and peaked in the 14th and 15th, overlapping with the older centre of Mapungubwe to the south rather than simply following it.

03Walls without mortar

Great Zimbabwe's builders had an unusual gift from geology. The region's granite forms great bare domes, sometimes called whalebacks, and as the rock is heated by day and cooled by night over thousands of years, it peels off in curved sheets, a process called exfoliation. Those sheets split naturally into slabs of fairly even thickness. Accounts of the builders' method describe them speeding this up by lighting fires on the rock surface for hours and then cooling it quickly, perhaps with water, so that sheets cracked away where they wanted them.

Because the granite also tends to break at right angles to those layers, the slabs could be split with hammerstones into brick-like blocks. The masons laid them in courses, each row resting on the one below. In the best walls, such as the outer wall of the Great Enclosure, the courses are remarkably level and the blocks carefully chosen for thickness. The wall is really three walls in one: an outer face and an inner face of fitted blocks, with a rubble core packed between them.

The secret of height without mortar is batter. Both faces lean inward as the wall rises, so the wall is thick at the base, up to about 5 m on the Great Enclosure, and much thinner near the top. The weight of every course presses down and slightly inward, locking the stones together. The archaeologist Roger Summers listed the builders' refinements: levelled foundation trenches, a carefully laid first course, strict selection of facing blocks, level coursing, a consistent batter that suggests the use of a plumb line, and decorative patterns.

Great Zimbabwe was not alone. Across the plateau and beyond, many smaller stone-walled centres were built in the same tradition, which archaeologists call the Zimbabwe Culture. Later sites pushed the decoration further. At Naletale, built centuries later, the walls carry bands of check, dentelle, cord, herringbone and chevron patterns, made by alternating pale granite with reddish-brown banded ironstone. Seen together, these sites show a building tradition that evolved over generations, with its own rules, its own aesthetics and its own experts.

How do we know?

Much of the method can be read from the walls themselves: tool marks, the sizes and shapes of blocks, the rubble cores exposed where walls have collapsed, and unfinished sections. The heating technique is supported by the way local granite behaves and by later traditions, but no direct archaeological 'fire site' links a particular quarry to a particular wall. Architectural historians have also classified walls into styles, from rougher early work to the finely coursed walls of the peak.

04The Great Enclosure and its tower

The Great Enclosure is a vast, roughly elliptical ring. Its outer wall is about 250 m long and rises to about 11 m at its highest (some surveys give about 9.6 m for the tallest surviving stretch), with an average nearer 7 m. It contains around 5,000 m³ of stone, by one estimate nearly a million blocks. Along the top of part of the wall runs a band of chevrons nearly 80 m long, made by setting blocks at angles, about 9 m above the ground.

Inside, walls divide the space into smaller enclosures, including an older circular one about 21 m across, and platforms where daga houses stood. The Parallel Passage runs between the outer wall and an inner wall along the eastern side and leads to the Conical Tower: about 9 to 10 m tall and about 5.5 m across at the base, solid all the way through. Colonial treasure hunters dug under and into it looking for a hidden chamber. There is none.

Look closely at the base of the outer wall and you find another sign of careful engineering: drains. Six original outlets pass through the wall on its north-eastern side, five of them roofed with stone and one originally spanned with wooden beams. A dry-stone wall that traps rainwater behind it builds up pressure and can burst outwards. Letting the water through was as important as stacking the stones well, and it is one reason so much of the wall still stands after more than 600 years of summer storms.

What the tower meant is still debated. Some scholars have compared it to a grain bin, a symbol of a ruler's role in distributing food; others have read it in terms of Shona symbolism of male authority or ancestral power. The Enclosure as a whole has been interpreted as a royal residence, the home of a ruler's senior wife, or a place for initiation. None of these readings can be tested directly, and they may not exclude one another.

05Gold, cattle and the Indian Ocean

Great Zimbabwe's wealth rested first on cattle and farming, and then on a long-distance trade that tied the interior to the coast. Gold from the Zimbabwe plateau travelled to ports such as Sofala on the Mozambique coast, and from there along the Swahili trading network to Kilwa and across the Indian Ocean. In return came luxury goods, some of which ended up buried at Great Zimbabwe.

  • Chinese celadon and other porcelain, among the most prestigious ceramics of the age.
  • Persian glazed pottery.
  • Thousands of glass beads from the Indian Ocean trade.
  • Copper ingots from centres to the north, and locally worked gold, iron and copper.
  • Coins of Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman of Kilwa (reigned c. 1310–1333), whose currency is reported to have circulated as far as Great Zimbabwe.

These objects matter in two ways. They show a city plugged into a trade network that reached China, and they helped archaeologists date the site, because many imports can be dated from where they were made. Yet they also fed a myth: for colonial writers, fine imports were proof of foreign presence. In reality they are what you would expect to find in the capital of an African state that exported gold.

06Birds of soapstone

Among the most striking finds are eight carved soapstone birds, each about 40 cm tall, mounted on columns more than 90 cm high. They are unique to Great Zimbabwe. They combine bird and human features, with lips in place of beaks, and scholars generally read them as emblems of royal or ancestral authority, perhaps linked to birds as messengers.

Their modern history mirrors the site's. In 1889 the hunter Willi Posselt removed one and sold it to Cecil Rhodes, who displayed it at Groote Schuur, his house in Cape Town. Others were taken to South Africa and Germany. South Africa returned four in 1981, a year after Zimbabwe's independence, and Germany returned a pedestal fragment in 2003. Today the bird appears on Zimbabwe's flag, coat of arms and currency.

Fresh from the field

In April 2026 South Africa returned the last soapstone bird held there, the one that had stood in Cecil Rhodes's former bedroom at Groote Schuur, together with ancestral human remains, in a handover ceremony led by the South African Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture, Gayton McKenzie, just before Zimbabwe's 46th independence anniversary.

07A century of denial

When the German explorer Karl Mauch reached the ruins in 1871, he decided they were a copy of the Queen of Sheba's palace, partly because he thought a wooden beam was cedar from Lebanon. It was local sandalwood. In 1891 Theodore Bent, backed by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company, excavated finds that were clearly local, including pottery and iron tools, yet still concluded that a 'northern race' from Arabia had built the city. His successor Richard Hall went further, stripping away between about 1 and 3.7 m of layered deposits in the name of clearing out later 'native' occupation, and destroying much of the evidence that could have answered the question.

The idea that Africans could not have built Great Zimbabwe was useful to colonial settlers: it made the land's past someone else's and its present occupation look like a restoration. Science, when it arrived, disagreed. In 1905 the British Association sent the Egyptologist David Randall-MacIver, who found the houses 'unquestionably African in every detail' and medieval in date. In 1929 the association sent Gertrude Caton-Thompson, who dug carefully where earlier diggers had not reached. Her conclusion, published in 1931, used the language of her time.

Examination of all the existing evidence, gathered from every quarter, still can produce not one single item that is not in accordance with the claim of Bantu origin and medieval date.

Gertrude Caton-Thompson, The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1931)

Every later study, using radiocarbon dating, ceramic sequences, house forms and oral history, has confirmed that the builders were the ancestors of the Shona-speaking peoples of the region.

08Censorship in Rhodesia

You might expect that to have ended the argument. It did not. After white-minority Rhodesia declared independence in 1965, the government was uncomfortable with a great African city at the heart of the country's heritage. Official guidebooks and displays were pressured to present the builders' identity as an open question or to promote foreign origins. Archaeologists working in the country later described being told to be very careful with the press and experiencing censorship as a routine part of their work.

Peter Garlake, the Inspector of Monuments from 1964, whose research showed clearly that Great Zimbabwe was an African achievement, was forced out of the country in 1970; his book Great Zimbabwe appeared in 1973. The veteran archaeologist Roger Summers also left. For the liberation movements, the site became a powerful symbol, and when the country won majority rule in 1980 it took the name Zimbabwe and put the soapstone bird on its flag.

Few archaeological sites have been fought over so openly, or have lent their name to a nation.

09What we still don't know

How many people lived here? Older estimates of up to about 18,000 at the peak are still widely quoted. In 2017 Chirikure and colleagues rebuilt the calculation from house counts and Shona household sizes. If every settled area was occupied at the same time, they estimate only about 2,800 to 4,800 people, and they argue that the total over the site's whole occupation is unlikely to have exceeded about 10,000. Others think these figures are too low. Either way, the monumental scale reflects organisation and prestige more than a vast population.

How was the city organised? One influential model reads the site as a single royal capital, with the king on the hill and royal wives in the valley. Chirikure and Innocent Pikirayi have argued instead that successive rulers each built their own centre, so that the Hill, the Great Enclosure and the valley compounds represent different reigns more than different functions.

And why did it decline in the 15th century? Suggestions include shifts in the gold trade routes northward, exhaustion of grazing, firewood and soils, political fragmentation, and, in recent work by Pikirayi, climate change and falling groundwater. Power moved on to other states, such as Mutapa in the north and Torwa, centred at Khami, in the south-west. The granite walls, needing no mortar and no repairs, simply stayed standing, and they are still standing now.

There is also the everyday work of keeping the site alive. Dry-stone walls bulge and fall when roots, water or shifting foundations disturb them, and early diggers weakened some sections by tunnelling under them. Conservators today monitor and rebuild collapsing stretches using the original techniques, and archaeologists increasingly work with local communities, for whom Great Zimbabwe is not only a monument but a sacred place connected to ancestors. The questions researchers ask are changing too: less about who built the walls, which is settled, and more about the lives of the people who lived around them.

The big debates

Who built Great Zimbabwe?

Foreign builders19th-century claims of Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba, based on imported goods, a misidentified timber and assumptions about African ability.
Local African buildersPottery, daga houses, architecture, radiocarbon dates and oral history all fit ancestral Shona communities; Randall-MacIver (1905), Caton-Thompson (1929) and all later research agree.

The bold claim: Great Zimbabwe was built by foreigners rather than by local Africans.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Every line of archaeological evidence points to local builders, and the foreign-origin idea was sustained by colonial politics, not data. Imported goods show trade, not foreign architects. This question has been closed by evidence since at least 1929.

How many people lived at Great Zimbabwe?

A large cityOlder estimates of up to c. 18,000 people at the peak, based on the site's size and the density of house remains.
Far fewerChirikure et al. (2017) estimate c. 2,800–4,800 if all areas were occupied at once, and under c. 10,000 across the whole occupation.

The bold claim: Great Zimbabwe held about 18,000 people at its height.

BustedRock solid

Population estimates depend on how many houses were occupied at the same time and on household sizes, and much of the evidence was destroyed by early digging. The recent lower figures are carefully argued but disputed. The peak population is genuinely uncertain.

Why did Great Zimbabwe decline?

Trade and politicsGold trade routes shifted north towards the Zambezi, and new states such as Mutapa and Torwa rose.
EnvironmentPressure on grazing, soils and firewood, and proposed climate change with falling groundwater (Pikirayi).

The bold claim: A single cause, such as environmental exhaustion, explains the decline.

Receipt MeterNo receipts yet
BustedRock solid

Several factors are plausible and may have worked together, but no single cause has decisive evidence behind it. Dating of the decline itself is also imprecise, which makes it hard to tie to particular droughts or trade shifts.

Iranian plateau

Qanats and yakhchal ice houses

Hand-dug rivers that run uphill of nothing, and mud domes that kept winter's ice through a 40 °C desert summer.

A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel dug by hand into an alluvial fan until it reaches groundwater, which then flows out by gravity to a village and its fields. Specialist diggers first sank a 'mother well' to find the water table, surveyed a line down to the chosen outlet, and then dug the tunnel from the outlet uphill, sinking a vertical access shaft every 20 to 35 m or so to remove spoil and let in air. A yakhchal used the same desert physics in reverse. In winter, water was let into a long, shallow pond shaded from the sun by a high east–west wall. On clear, dry nights the water lost heat to the cold sky by radiation and by evaporation, and a thin layer froze. Workers broke it up and packed it, insulated with straw, into a deep pit beneath a thick domed roof, where it could last into summer.

The myth

Persian yakhchals made ice in the blazing desert summer using a lost ancient refrigeration technology, with a secret mortar of egg whites and goat hair.

The reality

Ice was made in winter and stored for summer. Clear desert nights, radiative cooling, evaporation and a shade wall made freezing possible; a massive dome, a deep pit, straw and a meltwater drain slowed the melt. The mortar, sarooj, is a lime-based plaster; colourful recipes circulate, but the physics does not depend on them. Qanats are equally well understood. What remains uncertain is when and where they were first invented.

Wow

Iran's qanats have been estimated to add up to more than 270,000 km of hand-dug tunnel, enough to wrap around the equator more than six times.

Mystery meterMostly solved
The deep dive10 min read · 2,304 words · 2 animated drawings

01Ice on a desert afternoon

Imagine a July afternoon in Yazd, in the heart of the Iranian plateau. The air shimmers above mud-brick roofs, summer temperatures here occasionally pass 40 °C, and the nearest permanent river is far away. Yet a few centuries ago you could have bought a cold drink cooled with ice. The ice was not shipped from mountains. It had been made locally, months earlier, on winter nights, and kept in a building that looks like a giant beehive.

That building is a yakhchal, literally an 'ice pit'. And the water that filled its freezing pond usually came from something even more remarkable: a qanat, a tunnel dug by hand for kilometres through gravel and silt, tapping groundwater under the foot of the mountains and leading it out, by gravity alone, to a village that would otherwise be dust.

Two technologies, one idea: in a desert, patience and physics can do the work of pumps and refrigerators.

Neither is mysterious. Both are superb. This is the story of how they work, how we know, and which of the tales told about them hold up.

02A river you cannot see

Much of the Iranian plateau is ringed by mountains that catch rain and snow. Meltwater and runoff pour down into the basins below, and where they leave the mountains they drop enormous fans of gravel, sand and silt, called alluvial fans. Some water sinks into these fans and moves slowly downhill underground. Near the mountains, the water table can be reached by digging; further out onto the plain it sits deep below the surface.

Here is the trick. The ground surface of the fan slopes steeply, but the water table slopes much more gently. So if you dig a tunnel that is almost level, starting out on the plain and heading uphill into the fan, it gets deeper and deeper below the surface until, eventually, it pierces the water table. Water seeps into the upper section of the tunnel and flows down its gentle slope and out into the daylight, where the ground surface has come down to meet it. No pump, no power, no moving parts. As long as the aquifer is recharged, the qanat flows day and night.

The gentle slope

Get the slope wrong and a qanat fails. Too steep and the fast water scours the tunnel floor and collapses the walls; too flat and it silts up. In shorter qanats the gradient typically falls between about 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 1,500, according to standard summaries; the longest are almost level. For a tunnel 1 km long, that is a drop of well under a metre, achieved by eye, cord and water level, underground.

03The diggers and the dig

Qanats were dug by specialists, the muqannis, whose skills passed down through families. The work began with the most important gamble: the mother well. At the head of the fan, the diggers sank a trial shaft to find the water table and test whether it held enough water. If the mother well hit a good flow, the qanat was worth building.

Next came the survey. Working back down the fan to the place where the water should emerge, near the fields, the team marked out a line and worked out the depth each point along it must reach so that the tunnel would descend gently all the way. Along this line they sank vertical shafts, commonly every 20 to 35 m or so. The shafts let the diggers go down and come up, brought in air, and gave a way to haul out the spoil, which was dumped around each shaft mouth. That is why a qanat seen from the air looks like a line of craters marching across the desert.

Then the tunnel itself was dug, and here the order matters. The muqannis started at the outlet and worked uphill, towards the mother well. Any water that seeped in during digging drained out behind them rather than flooding the face they were working on. Each short stretch linked one shaft to the next. Spoil went up the shafts in buckets hauled by a windlass. The tunnels were usually just big enough for a person to crouch and dig; where the ground was soft, they could be lined with hoops of fired clay.

Keeping direction underground, with no compass readings to rely on, was a matter of sightlines. Each new shaft was sunk on the surveyed line, so every short stretch of tunnel had a fixed target: the bottom of the next shaft. Traditional accounts describe diggers using lamps to keep a straight line between shafts, and many tunnels show small kinks where two headings met slightly off. The result is not a perfectly straight pipe but a string of carefully joined segments, each one checked against the gentle fall that the whole system depends on.

It was dangerous work in darkness, bad air and loose gravel, and it never really ended. Qanats need regular cleaning and repair, and a family of muqannis might maintain the same channels for generations.

04The giant of Gonabad

In 2016 UNESCO inscribed eleven Iranian qanats together on the World Heritage List as 'The Persian Qanat'. The most famous is the Qasabeh qanat at Gonabad, in Khorasan in the north-east. Figures published with the nomination put it at 33,113 m long with 427 wells. Its mother well is widely reported as around 300 m deep. A few sources give larger figures, and its discharge is quoted at around 160 litres per second in one recent geotourism study, so treat the exact numbers as reported values, not measurements you can check on a single page.

Its age is also a matter of claim rather than measurement. Local tradition and many published accounts place its origin in the Achaemenid period, around 2,500 years ago. That is plausible for the region, but dating a tunnel that has been cleaned out and repaired for centuries is hard. What is certain is that it still delivers water to Gonabad.

Sharing that water was an institution in itself. Across Iran, a qanat's flow was divided among shareholders by time. One traditional method used a water clock: a bowl with a small hole, floated in a larger vessel, that sank at a steady rate. Each sinking marked a unit of time, and each farmer received a set number of units. Disputes over water were settled by counting bowls.

05How old is the idea?

The Greek historian Polybius, writing in the 2nd century BCE, preserved a memory of Persian water policy while describing a campaign in the Iranian plateau. He explains that the local wells and underground channels had been dug at great cost because the Persians had offered a generous reward.

They say that at the time when the Persians were the rulers of Asia they gave to those who conveyed a supply of water to places previously unirrigated the right of cultivating the land for five generations

Polybius, Histories 10.28.3, trans. W. R. Paton, Loeb Classical Library (1925)

That points to the Achaemenid Persian empire (c. 550 to 330 BCE) as a great age of qanat building, and Achaemenid-period qanats are known well beyond Iran, including in the oases of Egypt's Western Desert during the reign of Darius I. But the invention itself may be older. In 2015 Morteza Fattahi published optically stimulated luminescence dates for spoil heaps of the Miam qanat in north-east Iran that suggest construction around 3,600 to 4,300 years ago. It is a single study of a single system, and luminescence dates on reworked spoil can be tricky to interpret, so the claim is intriguing rather than settled.

Other scholars argue that qanat-like systems arose independently in several places, including south-eastern Arabia, where the similar aflaj of Oman have their own long history. Most agree that the technique spread along with Persian and later Islamic-era states, reaching North Africa, Spain, Central Asia and western China, where the karez of Turpan still flow.

06Freezing water with the night sky

Now to the ice. The Iranian plateau has a gift for anyone who wants to make it: winter nights that are clear, still and very dry. Everything warm glows in infrared light, and a pond is no exception. On a cloudy or humid night, the sky sends a lot of that energy back. On a clear, dry night it sends back much less, because there is little water vapour overhead, and the pond's surface can cool below the air temperature around it. Add evaporation, which carries heat away as water turns to vapour in dry air, and a shallow sheet of water can freeze even when the air above it is a little above 0 °C.

Iran's ice makers maximised that effect. A yakhchal complex typically had a long, shallow pond or set of channels running east–west, and along its south side a tall wall, often around 10 m high and sometimes up to about 15 m. In winter the Sun at noon stands low in the southern sky, around 35 degrees above the horizon at Yazd's latitude, so the wall kept the pond in shadow for most or all of the day. By night the pond saw the whole sky.

Harvesting was brisk, cold work. Before dawn, before the low Sun could creep over the wall, workers cracked the new ice, lifted out the slabs and carried them across to the ice house, often only a short walk away. Then the pond was flooded again for the next night. A good cold spell could fill a store; a mild winter could leave a town short of ice all summer. Ice was a seasonal harvest, as dependent on the weather as wheat.

In 2017 building engineers Pochee, Gunstone and Wilton modelled the pond at Meybod, near Yazd, using real weather data. In the coldest week their model has the pond losing about 60 watts per square metre to the sky by radiation and about 20 by evaporation, against small gains from the ground and the air. Letting in about 10 cm of water each evening and harvesting whatever froze, the model gives at best about 12 mm of ice in a night, and roughly 49 m³ over a season from a pond of about 416 m². Workers on real ice ponds probably flooded thin layers repeatedly and built up thicker sheets over several nights, then broke them up and carried the slabs to the store.

How do we know?

Pochee and colleagues built a physical model of heat flow in and out of the pond and fed it hourly weather records for Yazd. Their model only allows freezing at or below 0 °C at the surface, so it is conservative. Separate physics explains why the surface itself can drop below the air temperature. The numbers are estimates for one site, not records kept by ice makers, which is why we quote ranges.

07A dome built to keep the cold in

Making ice is half the problem; keeping it for six months is the other. The store was a deep pit, at Meybod about 5 m deep, covered by a tall conical dome of mud brick, about 15 m high there and around 18 m at one ice house in Kerman. The walls are enormously thick at the bottom, about 2 m, thinning to around half a metre near the top. Their outside was finished with sarooj, a traditional lime-based plaster valued for being water-resistant. Popular articles list egg whites and goat hair among its ingredients; recipes varied, and the documented core is lime mixed with materials such as clay and ash.

  • Thermal mass: thick earthen walls take a long time to warm up, damping the summer heat.
  • Depth: the pit sits in the ground, which stays much cooler than the summer air.
  • Cold air stays low: dense cold air pools in the pit instead of escaping.
  • Insulation: layers of straw or chaff between and over the ice slow melting.
  • Drainage: meltwater is led away, because standing water melts ice fast.

Many domes have a small opening at the top. It is often described as a vent that lets warm air out, and some yakhchals were paired with windcatchers, the tall towers that funnel breezes into buildings across the region. Pochee's team suggested that at Meybod the opening may mainly have been a rooflight, to let workers see inside. Both functions are plausible, and different ice houses may have worked differently.

A yakhchal is a battery for cold: charged on winter nights, slowly spent through the summer.

08Myths that melt on contact

The most common myth, repeated in countless social-media posts, is that yakhchals made ice in summer. They did not. They stored winter ice. That is still an impressive feat, and it needs no lost technology.

The second myth is about age. You will often read that yakhchals date back to 400 BCE. That figure travels widely but is poorly sourced, and the ice houses that survive are mostly a few centuries old; Meybod's is reported to be about 400 years old, and some were still in use in the 1960s. Ice storage in pits is ancient and widespread, so older Iranian versions are likely, but the famous domes you can visit today are not Achaemenid.

A third misunderstanding is that qanats somehow make water. They do not create it; they collect groundwater that the mountains supply. That matters, because it means qanats can run dry when the aquifer is drained, which is exactly what is happening now.

09Running dry, and what we still don't know

Qanats balanced supply and demand almost automatically: they can only deliver what the aquifer gives. Modern pumped wells are different, and since the mid-20th century they have drawn down water tables across Iran. Around 50,000 qanats are thought to have been in use in the middle of the 20th century; estimates for recent years range from about 22,000 to about 37,000 working systems. When the water table falls below a qanat's tunnel, the qanat simply stops. Researchers such as Mark Manuel, Dale Lightfoot and Morteza Fattahi argue that the old systems offer lessons in sustainable groundwater use that modern pumping has forgotten.

Open questions remain. Where and when was the first qanat dug, and was it invented once or several times? How far do the new luminescence dates push back the technique? How much ice did real yakhchals produce in a typical winter, and how long did it last? Answering them needs more dating, more surveys and more of the knowledge still held by the last generation of muqannis.

Meanwhile, in Gonabad, water that fell as snow on the mountains years ago still comes out of the ground at the end of a tunnel dug by hand. It is one of the oldest working machines in the world, and it has no moving parts at all.

The big debates

Were qanats invented once, in Iran?

Yes, Iranian originThe densest and longest systems are on the Iranian plateau; Polybius links them to Persian policy; luminescence dates from the Miam qanat suggest great age.
Several inventionsSimilar systems in south-eastern Arabia (aflaj) have their own early history; the principle is simple enough to be discovered more than once.

The bold claim: The qanat was invented on the Iranian plateau and spread from there.

Receipt MeterHot debate
BustedRock solid

Iran is clearly the heartland of the technology and the Achaemenid state spread it widely. But early dates rest on few studies, qanats are hard to date, and parallel development in Arabia is a serious possibility. The origin question is open.

Did yakhchals make ice in summer?

YesPopular posts describe 'ancient desert refrigerators' producing ice in the heat.
No, they stored winter iceDescriptions of the ice ponds, shade walls and storage pits, and thermal models of Meybod, all show ice made on winter nights and kept for summer.

The bold claim: Persian yakhchals produced ice during the summer.

Receipt MeterBusted
BustedRock solid

Everything about the design points to winter freezing and seasonal storage. The shade walls and ponds only work on cold, clear nights, and the dome and pit are built to slow melting. Storing ice for months in a hot desert is the real achievement.

Could the ponds freeze on nights above 0 °C?

Yes, sometimesRadiative cooling to a clear, dry sky and evaporation can pull a water surface below the air temperature.
Mostly on frosty nightsThe Meybod model conservatively assumes freezing at 0 °C and still finds useful ice only in the coldest weeks; Yazd winters do drop below freezing.

The bold claim: Yakhchal ponds could make ice even when the night air was slightly above freezing.

Receipt MeterPlausible
BustedRock solid

The physics is well established and explains why desert ice ponds worked so well. How often this happened at real sites is not documented, and most production probably came on nights that were cold anyway. The mechanism is sound; its practical share is uncertain.
